(2018) reported that VDOT-predicted threshold pace was statistically indistinguishable from laboratory lactate-threshold pace in RECREATIONAL runners, differing only in collegiate athletes. And the internal cross-check is clean: Garmin's auto-detected lactate-threshold HR of 177 is 88.1% of his true HRmax of 201, sitting precisely on Daniels' 88% threshold anchor. Two independent systems agreeing on the same physiological point is about as much validation as is available outside a lab.

WHAT VDOT IS BAD FOR HERE, AND THIS IS THE CENTRAL PROBLEM. Its marathon prediction is systematically wrong for this athlete in a knowable, quantifiable direction. VDOT's cross-distance equivalence assumes a population fatigue curve. Vickers & Vertosick (2016), on 2,303 recreational runners, showed that family of model is well calibrated to the half marathon and then dramatically underestimates the marathon — at least 10 minutes too fast for half of runners — and that weekly mileage is a separate predictor the model does not contain. This athlete is a severe case. His VDOT computed from three of his own performances: 51.3 from the 25 April 5 km, 42.0 from the 19 July half, 39.2 from the 10 May marathon. A twelve-point collapse from 5 km to marathon. His personal Riegel exponent is 1.164 (from the April 5 km to the May marathon, three weeks apart, the cleanest pairing) against a population value of 1.06. He is precisely the profile the task description named: 3:54/km over 5 km, 5:31/km over the marathon.

The consequence in numbers. A 1:44 half gives VDOT 43.1, whose marathon prediction is 3:35:49 at 5:07/km. Garmin independently predicts 3:36:12. They agree because they share the same population-curve assumption, and they are wrong in the same direction for the same reason — which is exactly why their agreement is not corroboration. Applying his own exponent of 1.164 to that same 1:44 half gives 3:53:01 at 5:31/km, which is the pace he actually ran in May. Under that model, six weeks of training buys him nothing unless durability itself moves. That is the sobering and correct framing.

THE VOLUME QUESTION. Daniels' own progression rule is roughly +1 mile per run per week, no more often than every third week. Going 24.4 km/week average to 60 km in one step, then to 100 km by week three, is on the order of four times that rate. Nielsen et al. (2014), on 874 novice runners, found >30% progression over a 2-week window associated with more distance-related injuries than <10%; the first step here is +150%. The evidence tier is observational and the population is novices rather than marathoners, so it is directional rather than dispositive — but it points one way and there is nothing pointing the other. The ramp is ratified in writing and is not mine to reverse. What follows from it is that VDOT's role must shrink: the intensity design must consume as little of the recovery budget as possible so that the volume, which is the ratified experiment, gets all of it.

THE SIX-WEEK QUESTION. Daniels' 2Q marathon programme is 18 weeks. What survives compression to six is its SHAPE — two quality days, 2-3 easy days between them, Q1 threshold, Q2 long-with-marathon-pace, everything else easy, hard per-workout caps. What does not survive is the phase progression: there is no time for a repetition phase, an interval phase and then a threshold/marathon phase, so the block starts and stays in the final phase. That is the right compression for a marathon and would be the wrong one for a 5 km.

NET. Use VDOT for E, T and R. Use it as one input, not the answer, for M — the marathon pace target should be the durability-corrected figure, revised by the Lincoln Half. Do not use it for I, because there should be no I work. The tradition's largest contribution to this particular block is negative: it tells you, with arithmetic rather than opinion, which paces NOT to run, and it identifies the athlete's limiter as durability rather than speed, which turns the whole design into a volume block with a small threshold garnish. A planner that emitted a bare "quality" label was not wrong about the shape of the week so much as silent about the one number that could hurt him.
research.howToValidate:
Six checks, all computable from data rocket already holds or from FIT files it will receive. Each names what result would falsify the design.

1. THRESHOLD-PACE HR CHECK — first T session, week 1, ~17 September. Prescribed pace and prescribed HR band must agree. Run the reps at the VDOT T pace (4:48/km on the 1:44 column) and record average HR of the work intervals. Expect 177-185 bpm. If HR sits at 190+, the half was over-raced or fluky and the VDOT is too high — drop it by 1-2 points and re-derive every pace. If HR sits below 170, the VDOT is too low — but do NOT raise it before week 3, because early-block freshness (his TSB is +24.7) flatters the first session. This is the cheapest possible falsification test and it happens on day four.

2. AEROBIC DECOUPLING ON THE LINCOLN HALF — 4 October, the block's designated instrument. Split the 21.1 km at marathon pace into halves and compute the ratio of pace to heart rate in each half; report the percentage drift. The widely used practitioner threshold is 5%. If decoupling over 21 km at 5:28-5:31/km is under 5%, his durability has genuinely improved and the marathon target may move toward the VDOT figure (5:07-5:15/km). If it exceeds 5%, the target stays at 5:31/km and the last three weeks stay conservative. Rocket has the full FIT stream and can compute this without any new measurement. Honesty note: the 5% figure is coaching convention, not a validated cut-point — treat it as a threshold for a conversation, not a hard gate.

3. PERSONAL RIEGEL EXPONENT, TRACKED — rocket has 57 activities. Compute k = ln(T2/T1) / ln(D2/D1) for every pair of best efforts, and plot it over time. Current baseline: k = 1.164 from the April 5 km to the May marathon, 1.178 from the 5 km to the July half. The block's entire thesis is that volume lowers k. A 1:44 half on 12 September followed by a Lincoln Half on 4 October at an equivalent-or-better effort with lower decoupling is direct evidence k is falling. If k has not moved by 4 October, six weeks did not change durability, the marathon target should be set from k = 1.164, and rocket should say so rather than let optimism into the number.

4. TANDA BACK-TEST, THEN FORWARD-RUN — this is the best available independent check because it uses training data instead of race data, so it does not share VDOT's failure mode. Tanda (2011): Pm (s/km) = 17.1 + 140 exp(-0.0053 K) + 0.55 P, with K = mean weekly km and P = mean training pace in s/km. STEP ONE, back-test: rocket holds his training for the 8 weeks before the 10 May marathon. Compute Tanda's prediction and compare it to his actual 3:55:54. The residual is his personal Tanda offset. STEP TWO, forward-run: with the block delivered, K over the 8 weeks to 24 October is about 57 km/week; at a mean training pace of 5:45/km the raw prediction is 3:38:15, at 6:00/km it is 3:44:03. Apply the offset from step one. If the offset-corrected Tanda and the durability-corrected Riegel figure land within a few minutes of each other, that is genuine convergence from two unrelated models and the target is trustworthy. If they diverge by more than about 8 minutes, take the slower and say why. Caveat to encode: Tanda's sample finished 2:47-3:36, faster than this athlete, so he sits outside the fitted range — the back-test is not optional.

5. GARMIN CALIBRATION AS A STANDING FILTER — the 1.118 median over-prediction factor across three realised efforts is already computed and should become a persistent, versioned athlete parameter rather than a one-off observation. Any device-supplied prediction, threshold pace or race estimate gets multiplied by it before display, and the raw value is kept alongside so the factor can be re-fitted after 24 October (n will then be four). Immediate application: Garmin's 4:20.9/km lactate-threshold pace becomes 4:51.6/km, which lands within 4 s/km of the VDOT-derived T pace of 4:48. Two systems that disagreed by 27 s/km agree once the known bias is removed. That is a real validation of the T pace and a template for how rocket should treat every device number.

6. VOLUME-RAMP SAFETY GATE, THE REVERSAL INSTRUMENT — the block already carries a reversal condition judged at the end of week 2 (27 September), but nothing currently measures it. Encode Nielsen's variable directly: rolling 2-week progression ratio of weekly distance. Baseline 24.4 km/week; week 1 at 60 km is +150%, and the 2-week window through 80 km is far past the >30% category associated with distance-related injury. That number will be red for the whole block by construction, so it is not a useful gate on its own. Pair it with two things that are: (a) morning resting HR against his 57-smoothed / 50-raw baseline — a sustained rise of 5+ bpm over 5 days is a genuine signal; and (b) HR at fixed easy pace, i.e. average HR on E runs held at 6:00-6:15/km, which should drift DOWN across the block. If easy-pace HR rises for two consecutive weeks while training load is held, that is the reversal condition firing, and it is measurable entirely from data rocket receives automatically.

WHAT WOULD FALSIFY THE WHOLE DESIGN. If, on 4 October, he covers 21.1 km at 5:30/km with an average HR at or above 178 and decoupling above 8%, then the block has not built durability, the volume ramp has cost more than it bought, and the correct response is to abandon the 3:36-3:45 ambition entirely and target 4:00-4:05 with a longer taper. Rocket should be able to reach that conclusion from the FIT file without anyone having to argue for it.
contraindications: Do NOT derive VDOT from his 5 km performances. His 25 April 5 km (3:54/km) gives VDOT 51.3, which yields a threshold pace of about 4:15/km. Running cruise intervals at 4:15/km on a fourfold volume ramp is the fastest available route to injury. The marathon-relevant VDOT is 39-43, not 51. Rocket must select the VDOT input by RACE DISTANCE PROXIMITY to the goal event, always preferring the longest recent quality race.

Do NOT use Garmin's lactate-threshold PACE of 4:20.9/km as the threshold pace. It is 27 s/km faster than the VDOT-derived value and roughly his 10 km race pace. Use Garmin's threshold HEART RATE of 177 (which is 88.1% of his true HRmax and agrees with Daniels' anchor) and discard the pace. This is a specific, encodable rule: trust device HR anchors, distrust device pace anchors, for this athlete.

Do NOT use 196 or 195 as HRmax. His profile value and his belief are both wrong; every HR zone in this design is computed from the measured 201 recorded on 14 June. Using 196 shifts the threshold band down by about 4 bpm and the easy ceiling by 3 bpm, which is enough to make easy runs read as compliant when they are not.

Do NOT prescribe any I-pace (95-100% VO2max) or R-pace interval sessions in this block. His 5 km-derived VDOT of 51.3 against his marathon-derived 39.2 says top-end speed is his strongest quality, not his limiter. VO2max adaptations to interval training are generally reported over 6-8 week interventions, so a 6-week block would pay the full mechanical cost for a partial return in the wrong currency. The 10 km race on 11 October is the only supra-threshold dose the block needs. Strides of 6 x 20 s are the sole exception and total 1 km per week.

Do NOT use VDOT's marathon prediction as the goal pace. For a 1:44 half it predicts 3:35:49 at 5:07/km; Garmin independently predicts 3:36:12. Their agreement is not corroboration — both rest on the same population fatigue curve, and Vickers & Vertosick (2016) showed that curve dramatically underestimates marathon time in recreational runners. This athlete's own exponent (1.164 vs population 1.06) puts the same half at 3:53:01. Prescribe M-pace work at the durability-corrected figure and let the 4 October Lincoln Half move it.

Do NOT race the Lincoln Half on 4 October. It is prescribed at marathon pace inside a 33 km session with a hard HR ceiling of 172 bpm. Racing it three weeks out, at the end of the 100 km peak week, would compromise both the peak week and the taper for information rocket can obtain more cheaply from the 11 October 10 km.

Do NOT raise VDOT mid-block on the strength of a good session or the 11 October 10 km. Daniels permits +1 VDOT after 4-6 weeks of CONSISTENT training with no race; this block is 6 weeks on a volume he has never carried, with two races in it, which is not consistent training. Hold the 12 September VDOT flat for E/T/R purposes and use the 10 km only as a downside check.

Do NOT apply Daniels' published 2Q marathon plan verbatim. It is an 18-week programme written for a stable weekly mileage, and this is a 6-week block on a ramp of 60/80/100/80/60. What transfers is the shape — two quality days, 2-3 easy days between, T on one, long-plus-M on the other, hard per-workout caps — not the week-by-week content.

Record two knowing deviations from Daniels rather than hiding them. The Lincoln Half session is 33 km, which is 33% of the peak week against his 25-30% long-run cap and about 3 hours against his 2.5-hour ceiling; and its 21.1 km at marathon pace exceeds the M cap on both the 20%-of-week and 110-minute tests. These follow from the athlete's ratified plan and should be surfaced as accepted deviations in rocket's output, not silently absorbed.

Flag the run-FREQUENCY ramp as a separate, unratified risk. His maximum is 4 runs in any week; a 100 km week with two quality days requires 6-7. The volume increase was ratified in writing; the frequency increase was not discussed and carries its own tissue-loading cost. It should be surfaced to him explicitly before week 3, not assumed as an implementation detail.

Handle a bad 12 September half explicitly rather than by guessing. If he does not race it flat out, aborts, or runs slower than about 1:52, do not extrapolate a VDOT from it. Fall back to the 19 July half (1:46:35 over 21.14 km, VDOT 42.0), which is his best genuine continuous half. Never derive paces from the 26 July run — 17:27 of stopped time across 22 laps makes its timer pace meaningless as a performance.

Every number in this design belongs in config/training.ts with its source, not scattered through the planner. The constants requiring provenance comments: HRmax 201 (measured 2026-06-14, overriding profile 196); LTHR 177 (Garmin auto-detect 2026-08-08, = 88.1% HRmax, agrees with Daniels' T anchor); Daniels-Gilbert regression coefficients -4.60 / 0.182258 / 0.000104 and 0.8 / 0.1894393 / -0.012778 / 0.2989558 / -0.1932605 (Daniels & Gilbert 1979); VDOT percentage anchors E 0.59-0.74, T 0.88, I 1.00, R ~1.10 (Daniels' Running Formula 3rd ed.); per-workout caps T 10%, I 8%/10 km, R 5%, M 20%/110 min, long run 25-30%/2.5 h (same source); personal Riegel exponent k = 1.164 (computed from his 2026-04-25 5 km and 2026-05-10 marathon, vs Riegel population 1.06); Garmin over-prediction factor 1.118 (median of three realised efforts); Tanda coefficients 17.1 / 140.0 / -0.0053 / 0.55 (Tanda 2011, requires a personal offset from back-testing his May marathon before forward use).

verification.tradition: Jack Daniels / VDOT — pace prescription from a single race performance

checks.claim: VDOT values derived from his races: 5 km 25 Apr = 51.3; half 19 Jul = 42.0; marathon 10 May = 39.2; hypothetical halves 1:44/1:40/1:48 = 43.1/45.1/41.3
checks.note: Independently recomputed from the stated Daniels-Gilbert equations: 51.33, 42.00, 39.26, 43.11, 45.12, 41.26. Every figure reproduces to two decimals. The equations as quoted also reproduce Daniels' published table (VDOT 43 marathon pace 5:07/km), so the coefficients are transcribed correctly.

checks.claim: Derived training paces on the 1:44 column: T 4:48/km, E 5:31-6:36/km, R 4:00/km, M 5:06.9/km (3:35:49 marathon)
checks.note: Recomputed by inverting the oxygen-cost curve: T(0.88)=4:47.7, E(0.59-0.74)=6:35.6-5:30.6, R(1.10)=4:00.2, and solving VDOT(42195,t)=43.11 gives 3:35:50 at 5:06.9/km. The 1:40 and 1:48 columns also check out (T 4:37.3 and 4:58.0). Arithmetic is clean.

checks.claim: 'A 1:44 half (VDOT 43.1) predicts about 47:45' for the 10 km
checks.note: Solving VDOT(10000,t)=43.11 gives 46:55, not 47:45 — 50 s out, and it is the number used to set expectations for the 11 Oct race and to judge whether the block is over-reaching. The same 50 s error propagates into check 5 of the validation plan ('materially below the half-derived VDOT').

checks.claim: Strides total 'a fifth of Daniels' 5% weekly R cap even in the 60 km weeks'
checks.note: 5% of 60 km is 3.0 km; 1.0 km/week is a third of that, not a fifth. A fifth is only true in the 100 km week. Trivial in consequence but it is a stated safety margin that is 67% smaller than advertised in the weeks it is quoted for.

checks.claim: His personal Riegel exponent k = 1.164, and applying it to a 1:44 half gives 3:53:01 at 5:31/km — 'IDENTICAL to the pace he actually ran in May', presented as validation of the durability correction
checks.note: This is a tautology, not a validation. k=1.164 was fitted from the 25 Apr 5 km and the 10 May marathon. Under that same k, his 5 km predicts a half of 1:44:03 — i.e. the '1:44 column' IS his April 5 km re-expressed. Feeding it back through the same exponent necessarily returns the May marathon pace. Confirmed numerically: k(5k->mar)=1.1634, and 1179.4 s x (21097.5/5040)^1.1634 = 1:44:03. Zero independent information; the design's headline evidence for the durability correction is circular.

checks.claim: k = 1.164 is the right exponent to project a half to a marathon
checks.note: k is not constant across his own data: 1.163 (5k->marathon), 1.179 (5k->half), 1.131 (half->marathon). The half->marathon pair is the one that matches the extrapolation actually being made, and it gives 3:47:48 (5:24/km) rather than 3:53:02 (5:31/km) — a 5-minute, 7 s/km difference in the prescribed M pace. Using the wider-span exponent is the conservative choice, which is defensible, but the design presents 1.164 as 'his exponent' rather than as one of three, and never states that the directly relevant pair disagrees. Also: two races two-to-three months apart, n=2, no error bars, and a single marathon in which fuelling, weather or pacing failure is indistinguishable from poor durability.

checks.claim: Garmin over-predicts by a median factor of 1.118, so Garmin's threshold pace 4:20.9/km becomes 4:51.6/km, 'landing within 4 s/km of the VDOT-derived 4:48' — two independent systems agreeing
checks.note: Three problems. (1) The factor does not reproduce: from the three realised efforts and the 2026-09-07 predictions given, actual/predicted = 0.974 (5 km), 1.083 (half), 1.091 (marathon); median 1.083, not 1.118. The marathon miss is 19:42, not 27 min. (2) The bias is not a scalar — it is below 1.0 at 5 km and above at half/marathon, which is exactly the distance-dependent decay the rest of the document argues for. Applying a marathon-fitted factor to a ~60-minute threshold pace is a category error. (3) With the verifiable 1.083 the 'agreement' evaporates: 4:20.9 x 1.083 = 4:42.6/km, 5 s/km faster than VDOT's 4:48, not 4 s/km slower. The convergence is an artefact of an unverified multiplier, and is presented as 'a real validation of the T pace'.

checks.claim: Scudamore et al. 2018 shows VDOT-predicted threshold pace is indistinguishable from lab lactate-threshold pace in recreational runners — 'the only direct empirical evaluation' and the design's empirical support for its T pace
checks.note: The paper exists exactly as cited (J Strength Cond Res 2018;32(4):1137-1143, doi 10.1519/JSC.0000000000001942) and the quoted statistics are verbatim correct (pTH vs LTpace: ATH t(8)=-4.17 p=.003 d=1.49; REC t(8)=1.64 p=.139 d=0.57). Two things are overstated. First, a non-significant result at n=9 with d=0.57 is absence of evidence, not equivalence — that is an underpowered null, and the paper is cross-sectional. Second and more damaging: the VDOT inputs in that study were indoor 5 km time trials. This design's own first contraindication forbids deriving VDOT from his 5 km. So the single empirical support cited transfers to a derivation method the design explicitly rejects, and says nothing about half-marathon-derived T pace.

checks.claim: Rosenblat et al. network meta-analysis: 13 studies, 348 athletes, no POL-vs-PYR difference (VO2max SMD 0.06 p=0.68; TT SMD 0.05 p=0.34), significant performance-level interaction (SMD 0.63, p<0.05) with recreational athletes favouring pyramidal
checks.note: Paper verified and the counts are right, but three defects. (1) Miscited: it is Sports Med 2025;55(3):655-673, not '2024;54' (DOI correct). (2) All three SMDs are negative in the source (-0.06, -0.05, -0.63); signs were dropped, which is what determines which arm the interaction favours. (3) Decisive for the design: the performance-level interaction was found for VO2max only — the time-trial comparison showed no such interaction. The design uses it to justify the intensity architecture of a marathon block, where the outcome that matters is performance, not VO2max. Also the trial population had VO2max 46.6-68.3 in supervised interventions; 'recreational' there is not a 24.4 km/week runner. The claim that 'the method used to draw zone boundaries did not add heterogeneity' is not in the abstract and I could not verify it.

checks.claim: Rosenblat et al. 2019 is listed for completeness with no effect estimates quoted; the 2024/2025 analysis is the successor and current position
checks.note: Verified: JSCR 2019;33(12):3491-3500, PROSPERO CRD42016050942, doi 10.1519/JSC.0000000000002618. The omission is material. That meta-analysis is the only one that compares polarised against THRESHOLD training specifically — which is what this block is, a threshold-weighted pyramid — and it reports a moderate effect FAVOURING polarised for time-trial performance (ES = -0.66, 95% CI -1.17 to -0.15). The 2025 network analysis compared POL vs PYR, not POL vs THR, so it does not supersede that result on this question. The document cites the paper, declines to quote the number, and the number it declines to quote points against its own design. Its inclusion criteria (VO2max >50, >2 years training) would include this athlete.

checks.claim: Nielsen et al. 2014 provides the empirical basis for the volume-ramp reversal condition: >30% two-week progression raises distance-related injury rate
checks.note: Paper verified (JOSPT 2014;44(10):739-747, doi 10.2519/jospt.2014.5164, 874 novice runners). But the headline result is null: 'no statistically significant differences in injury rates were found across the 3 exposure groups'. The distance-related subgroup is HR 1.59, 95% CI 0.96-2.66, P = .07 — a confidence interval crossing 1, in a study the authors label explicitly exploratory and for which they call for RCTs. The design describes it as 'a higher rate', which is stronger than the source supports. It is also, per the document's own note, novices rather than marathoners. Directionally right, evidentially thin, and it is carrying the entire safety rationale.

checks.claim: Vickers & Vertosick 2016: Riegel well calibrated to the half then dramatically underestimates the marathon, at least 10 min too fast for half of runners; weekly mileage independently associated with velocity; tempo more strongly associated at shorter distances
checks.note: Verified verbatim against the abstract (BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil 2016;8:26, doi 10.1186/s13102-016-0052-y, N=2303, 2:1 split). This is the strongest and most population-appropriate citation in the document and it is used correctly. Worth adding that the paper's own alternative models roughly halved mean squared error versus Riegel (228/208 vs 381) — a better-calibrated tool exists in the very source being cited, and the design does not use it.

checks.claim: Joyner & Coyle 2008 as the three-determinants framework justifying VDOT
checks.note: Verified: J Physiol 2008;586(1):35-44. Narrative review of elite athletes, correctly labelled as such in the document. The inference drawn from it (a performance index contains all three, so cannot identify the limiter) is a fair reading.

checks.claim: Q1 threshold volume scales with the ramp: 6.0 / 8.0 / 10.0 / ~5 / 6.0 / 3.0 km of T work, capped at Daniels' 10% of weekly distance
checks.note: The cap is applied to a mileage he does not have, which makes it not a cap. Daniels' percentage limits are indexed to weekly mileage precisely because habitual mileage proxies training age and tissue tolerance. This athlete's 24-week average is 24.4 km and his all-time peak week is 57.1 km; 10% of his ACTUAL base is 2.4 km of threshold, and 10% of his best-ever week is 5.7 km. Prescribing 5 x 2 km (10 km, ~16 km with warm-up) at 4:48/km in week 3 is roughly four times the dose his real training history licenses, in the same week as a 33 km session, at a pace 14 s/km faster than his best-ever half-marathon race pace. Every T cap in the block is computed off a fictional base; the document applies them 'at their limit' by explicit design.

checks.claim: Threshold pace 4:48/km is appropriate and the HR band 177-185 confirms it
checks.note: The pace itself is defensible on his own numbers — under population Riegel his 60-min race pace from the July half is 4:53/km, under his own steep exponent 4:39/km, so 4:48 brackets correctly, and 177 = 88.1% of 201 does land on Daniels' anchor. Two caveats. The whole column is anchored to a 1:44 half he has never run (his best is 1:46:35, VDOT 42.0, T = 4:54/km); the 1:44 figure is presented as the default throughout, which is optimistic anchoring on an unrun race three days away. And the veto band's ceiling of 185 bpm (92% HRmax) is too permissive for a 10 km threshold session — his July half at 5:02/km averaged 174, so 2 km reps at 4:48 will sit near 180-185, i.e. the veto only fires once he is already above threshold. Set the veto at 181.

checks.claim: Easy running: HR 131-159 bpm, 'run the bulk at 6:00-6:20/km with HR under 155'
checks.note: Band arithmetic is right (0.65-0.79 x 201 = 130.7-158.8) but the top of it fails the brief's own easy test: 75% of 201 is 151 bpm, and both the 159 ceiling and the 155 practical guidance sit above it. On a ramp from 24 to 100 km/week the easy ceiling is the single most load-bearing number in the plan; it should be set at 150, not 155-159. Separately, the document notices but does not resolve that the fast end of E (5:31/km) equals the prescribed M pace — which means the Q2 'marathon-pace blocks' are, by its own numbers, easy running with a label on it, and the Lincoln Half's 172 bpm ceiling would never bind at that pace until late drift.

checks.claim: Race-week structure: 3 x 1 km T on Tuesday, plus 12 km with 3 km at M on Wednesday
checks.note: Violates the one Daniels rule the design says it is preserving under compression — 2-3 easy days between quality sessions. Two quality sessions on consecutive days, three and four days before a marathon, on an athlete who has just completed the largest volume block of his life. Also inconsistent with the document's own stated Q1 placement (Wednesday) elsewhere.

checks.claim: The 11 Oct 10 km is 'just below threshold rather than at VO2max' but is 'the only exposure to 95-100% VO2max in the whole block'
checks.note: Self-contradictory within one sentence, and the first half is wrong physiologically: threshold is conventionally the ~60-minute race pace, so a 47-48 minute 10 km is run at or above threshold throughout (~90% VO2max, 92-95% HRmax), not below it. Consequence for the plan: the design justifies zero I-work partly on the grounds that this race supplies the top-end dose, while simultaneously describing it as sub-threshold. One of the two is load-bearing and it cannot be both.

checks.claim: Frequency ramp flagged as a separate unratified risk (max 4 runs/week historically vs 6-7 required)
checks.note: Correct, well-identified, and arguably the most important safety observation in the document. Two runs a week are new stimulus for tissue that has never seen them, independent of total distance. Credit where due: this is surfaced rather than buried, and correctly labelled unratified.

checks.claim: Tanda 2011 back-test/forward-run as the independent cross-check: K=57, P=345 s/km gives 3:38:15; P=360 gives 3:44:03
checks.note: The arithmetic of the stated formula reproduces exactly (310.3 and 318.6 s/km). I could not verify the paper, its coefficients, its sample or the '~4 min error' claim — J Hum Sport Exerc is not indexed in PubMed and this session's web-search budget was exhausted. The document's own caveat is the right one and understated: his 3:56 sits outside the fitted 2:47-3:36 band, and a two-parameter fit on 22 runners extrapolated beyond its range is a weak oracle. Note also that with his actual K (24.4) and P=5:45 the same formula returns 3:52, close to his realised marathon — which is mildly encouraging but is a single point and not a back-test.

checks.claim: Zero I-pace and zero R-pace intervals is the correct omission for this athlete
checks.note: The reasoning holds independently: his 5 km VDOT (51.3) versus marathon VDOT (39.2) genuinely does say speed is not the limiter, six weeks is short for a VO2max intervention, and high-mechanical-load running on an unprecedented volume ramp is the wrong risk to add. This is the strongest judgement in the document and it survives scrutiny. Caveat only that Rosenblat 2019 (see above) is the one piece of evidence pointing the other way and was not weighed.

checks.claim: 'Six weeks of training buys him nothing unless durability itself moves' — the durability-corrected 5:31/km target
checks.note: Conservative and correct in direction, and the correct framing to give the athlete. It is arrived at circularly (see the k=1.164 finding) but it lands in the right place: any target derived from population equivalence curves will flatter him, and Vickers & Vertosick is real evidence for exactly that. Recommend re-deriving it from the half->marathon exponent (1.131 -> 3:47:48) as a second column rather than resting on the tautological one.

fabricatedCitations: None of the ten citations is fabricated. Six were retrieved and confirmed to exist with the claimed authors and journals (Scudamore 2018, Vickers & Vertosick 2016, Rosenblat network MA, Rosenblat 2019, Nielsen 2014, Joyner & Coyle 2008).

MISATTRIBUTED — Rosenblat et al. network meta-analysis: cited as 'Sports Med. 2024;54'. The paper is Sports Med. 2025;55(3):655-673 (DOI 10.1007/s40279-024-02149-3 is correct; the DOI stem is 2024 because it was accepted then, which is likely how the error arose). Anyone chasing volume 54 will not find it.

MISREPORTED EFFECT SIGNS — same paper: the three SMDs are -0.06, -0.05 and -0.63 in the source, reported as +0.06, +0.05 and +0.63. The sign determines which arm the recreational-athlete interaction favours.

MISREPORTED SIGNIFICANCE — Nielsen 2014: reported as showing a higher distance-related injury rate above 30% progression. The source reports HR 1.59, 95% CI 0.96-2.66, P = .07, on top of a null primary result ('no statistically significant differences in injury rates were found across the 3 exposure groups'). Non-significant, exploratory, and it is the design's only safety citation.

MATERIAL OMISSION — Rosenblat 2019: the document cites it and explicitly declines to quote its effect estimate. The estimate is ES = -0.66 (95% CI -1.17 to -0.15) favouring POLARISED over THRESHOLD distribution for time-trial performance — the only meta-analysis directly testing the comparison this block actually makes, and it points against the design. Not fabrication, but the citation is present while the finding is absent.

UNVERIFIED IN THIS SESSION (web-search budget exhausted; not indexed in PubMed): Daniels & Gilbert, Oxygen Power (1979) — self-published monograph, but its two equations as quoted reproduce Daniels' published VDOT tables to within a second per km when I ran them, so the coefficients are almost certainly transcribed correctly. Daniels' Running Formula 3rd ed. (Human Kinetics, 2014). Riegel, American Scientist 1981;69(3):285-290 — the document already flags this as not re-retrieved. Tanda, J Hum Sport Exerc 2011;6(3):511-520 — the coefficients could not be checked against any source; every Tanda number in the validation plan rests on an unverified formula.

One further provenance gap: the per-workout caps (T 10%, I 8%/10 km, R 5%, M 20%/110 min, long run 25-30%/2.5 h) are attributed to Daniels' Running Formula and are consistent with how that book is commonly summarised, but they are one coach's judgement with no dose-response data behind them — which the document does say, and which matters more than it lets on, because the design then treats them as config-level gates.
verification.riskForThisAthlete:
Moderate-to-high, and the risk is concentrated in one week and one arithmetic habit rather than spread evenly.

The paces themselves are not the danger. T 4:48/km, E 5:31-6:36/km and R 4:00/km all recompute correctly and all sit within what his own races and heart rate support; the refusal to prescribe interval or repetition sessions is the right call and is the best judgement in the document. Two specific pace-side corrections are still needed: the easy ceiling of 155-159 bpm exceeds 75% of his measured 201 (=151) and should come down to 150, because on a ramp from 24 to 100 km/week the easy ceiling is the only thing standing between him and running every kilometre at moderate intensity; and the threshold HR veto should be 181, not 185, or it fires only after he is already above threshold.

The danger is the volume-cap logic. Daniels' 10%/20%/8% caps are percentages of weekly mileage because weekly mileage is a proxy for accumulated tissue tolerance. Applying them to 100 km — a volume he has never run, against a 24.4 km average and a 57.1 km lifetime peak — makes the caps arithmetic rather than protective. Week 3 (28 Sep - 4 Oct) is the worst of it: 10 km of threshold at 4:48/km on the Wednesday (roughly four times what his real base licenses), a 33 km Sunday session containing 21.1 km at marathon pace, six to seven runs in a week where his career maximum is four, all inside a 100 km week he has never approached. The document flags the frequency ramp as unratified, which is right, but then schedules it anyway.

Two smaller structural hazards: race week places quality on consecutive days (Tuesday and Wednesday), breaking the 2-3-easy-days rule the design says it is preserving; and racing the 10 km flat out 13 days out is defensible only because the athlete had already committed to it.

The reversal instrument is weaker than presented. Nielsen's >30% finding is P = .07 with a CI crossing 1, on novices, inside a study with a null primary result. The morning-resting-HR and HR-at-fixed-easy-pace checks the document adds are the real gate, and they are good ones — measurable from data rocket already receives, with a clear falsification condition. Those should be given primacy and Nielsen demoted to a footnote, because if the plan's safety case rests visibly on a non-significant hazard ratio, a sceptical athlete is entitled to discount it.

Finally, a decision-quality risk rather than an injury one: the entire pace column is anchored to a 1:44 half he has not yet run (best actual 1:46:35), and the durability correction that produces the 5:31/km marathon target is arithmetically circular — the 1:44 half IS his April 5 km re-expressed through the same exponent, so 'it lands exactly on what he ran in May' is an identity, not a confirmation. The target is probably right; the evidence offered for it is not evidence. Re-derive it from the half-to-marathon exponent (1.131, giving 3:47:48) alongside the 1.164 figure, present both, and let the 4 October session choose. And do not ship the Garmin 1.118 multiplier: from the three efforts in the brief the median ratio is 1.083, the 5 km ratio is 0.974 (Garmin under-predicts him at 5 km), so a single scalar is invalid across distances and the 'two systems agree once bias is removed' convergence disappears when the verifiable factor is used.
arithmeticErrors: 10 km prediction from VDOT 43.11 is 46:55, not 'about 47:45' — 50 s error, and it is the number used to judge whether the block has over-reached at the 11 October race.
Strides: 1.0 km/week is a third of Daniels' 5% cap in a 60 km week (3.0 km), not 'a fifth ... even in the 60 km weeks'. A fifth is true only in the 100 km week.

Garmin over-prediction factor: from the three realised efforts and the 2026-09-07 predictions in the brief, actual/predicted = 0.974 (5 km), 1.083 (half), 1.091 (marathon). Median 1.083, not 1.118. The document propagated the brief's headline number without checking it against the brief's own components — and the 5 km ratio below 1.0 shows a single scalar cannot be right.

Consequential knock-on: 4:20.9/km x 1.083 = 4:42.6/km, which is 5 s/km FASTER than the VDOT T pace of 4:48, not 4 s/km slower. The claimed convergence of Garmin and Daniels reverses direction under the verifiable factor.
Garmin's marathon prediction of 3:36:12 versus his realised 3:55:54 is a 19:42 miss, not the '27 minutes' repeated from the brief.

Riegel exponent used for a half-to-marathon projection is the 5 km-to-marathon value (1.1634). The directly relevant pair, half-to-marathon, gives 1.1312 and a 3:47:48 marathon (5:24/km) rather than 3:53:02 (5:31/km) — a 5-minute, 7 s/km difference in the prescribed marathon-pace work. The 5 km-to-half pair gives a third value, 1.1791.

Circularity, not strictly an arithmetic slip but produced by one: under k=1.164 his 25 April 5 km predicts a half of 1:44:03. The '1:44 column' is therefore his 5 km restated, so recovering his May marathon pace from it is an algebraic identity. Verified: 1179.4 s x (21097.5/5040)^1.1634 = 1:44:03.

Easy-pace ceiling: 0.79 x 201 = 158.8 bpm and the practical guidance of 'under 155' both exceed the 75%-of-HRmax easy test (150.75 bpm). Not a miscalculation of the band, but the band's top is used as though it were an easy ceiling when it is not.
Rosenblat network meta-analysis effect sizes are reported with signs dropped: source values are SMD -0.06 (VO2max), -0.05 (time trial) and -0.63 (performance-level interaction).

domains.title: Seiler and the polarised / pyramidal intensity-distribution debate

research.tradition: Seiler's three-zone training-intensity-distribution model (polarised vs pyramidal vs threshold), and its applicability to a low-volume runner attempting a 6-week volume ramp to 100 km/week
research.corePrinciple:
The model says nothing about what a session looks like. It answers one question: of the total endurance work in a week, how much sits below the first metabolic threshold, how much between the two thresholds, and how much above the second.

The three zones are anchored to two physiological breakpoints, NOT to percentages of maximum heart rate. Zone 1 is below the first ventilatory/lactate threshold (VT1/LT1) — the intensity at which ventilation first rises disproportionately and blood lactate first drifts above resting (~2 mM). Below VT1 you are in true metabolic steady state: lactate clearance matches production, fat oxidation is high, sympathetic activation and autonomic disturbance are modest, and the session's cost in recovery is roughly linear with its duration. Zone 2 is between VT1 and VT2 — lactate is elevated but still clearable, a state you can hold for tens of minutes but which carries a disproportionate autonomic and glycogen cost per kilometre. Zone 3 is above VT2/the maximal lactate steady state — lactate accumulates without bound, duration is limited to minutes, and the stimulus is largely central/cardiac and VO2-kinetic.

The mechanism the model proposes: Zone 1 volume and Zone 3 intensity drive adaptation through different, largely non-overlapping pathways — Zone 1 via mitochondrial biogenesis, capillarisation, plasma volume and stroke volume, accumulated over hours; Zone 3 via near-maximal cardiac output and high recruitment, accumulated over minutes. Zone 2 sits in between and delivers a blunted version of both while carrying most of the fatigue cost of Zone 3. Seiler's argument is that Zone 2 is therefore the least efficient place to spend a limited recovery budget: it costs like hard training and adapts like easy training. Hence the recommendation to push work to the two ends of the distribution and largely vacate the middle.

The critical and near-universally misread detail: Seiler's "80/20" is a count of SESSIONS classified by their primary goal, not a share of kilometres or minutes. In Seiler & Kjerland (2006) the same athletes' training was pyramidal when quantified by time-in-zone and polarised when quantified by session goal — the identical training, two different labels, depending purely on the accounting method. Almost every practical misapplication of this model traces to that one confusion.

sources.citation: Seiler, S., & Kjerland, G.Ø. (2006). Quantifying training intensity distribution in elite endurance athletes: is there evidence for an "optimal" distribution? Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, 16(1), 49–56.
sources.claim: Establishes the three-zone model anchored to VT1 and VT2 measured by treadmill gas exchange, and — critically — shows that the SAME training data yields different distribution labels depending on the quantification method (time-in-zone vs session-goal). This is the single most important methodological caveat in the whole literature and the origin of most misapplication.
sources.population: 11 male junior elite cross-country skiers. Not runners, not recreational, training volumes far above this athlete's.

sources.citation: Seiler, S. (2010). What is best practice for training intensity and duration distribution in endurance athletes? International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 5(3), 276–291.
sources.claim: The foundational synthesis. Descriptive studies of nationally/internationally competitive endurance athletes converge on ~80% of training SESSIONS at low intensity (<2 mM lactate) and ~20% dominated by high-intensity work at ~90% VO2max. Also states that intensification studies in already well-trained athletes provide no convincing evidence that more high-intensity work yields long-term gains.
sources.population: Elite endurance athletes training 10–13 times per week (roughly 15–30 h/week). This is a narrative synthesis of descriptive data, not a trial. The population is about as far from this athlete as it is possible to get while still being endurance runners.

sources.citation: Stöggl, T., & Sperlich, B. (2014). Polarized training has greater impact on key endurance variables than threshold, high intensity, or high volume training. Frontiers in Physiology, 5, 33. DOI 10.3389/fphys.2014.00033
sources.claim: The strongest single interventional result for polarised training. 48 well-trained athletes randomised to high-volume, threshold, HIIT, or polarised for 9 weeks. Polarised produced the largest gains: VO2peak +11.7%, time to exhaustion +17.4%, peak velocity/power +5.1%.
sources.population: 48 well-trained cyclists, runners, triathletes and XC skiers. Mixed-sport, well-trained. Note the effect sizes are implausibly large for a 9-week block in trained athletes, which has drawn criticism; the high-volume group's stimulus was arguably under-dosed.

sources.citation: Stöggl, T.L., & Sperlich, B. (2015). The training intensity distribution among well-trained and elite endurance athletes. Frontiers in Physiology, 6, 295.
sources.claim: Compiles observed time-in-zone distributions: 84–95% Z1 / 2–11% Z2 / 2–9% Z3 in preparation phases across elite rowers, cyclists and skiers. Note that these are PYRAMIDAL-to-very-low-intensity numbers by time — nothing like '20% hard' by volume. Also documents that percentage-of-VO2max anchoring produces inhomogeneous metabolic strain between individuals.
sources.population: Elite and well-trained endurance athletes across multiple sports. High volume.

sources.citation: Esteve-Lanao, J., Foster, C., Seiler, S., & Lucia, A. (2007). Impact of training intensity distribution on performance in endurance athletes. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 21(3), 943–949.
sources.claim: With Zone 3 held equal (~8%) in both groups, an 81/12/8 distribution produced greater 10.4 km improvement than 67/25/8. The comparison is specifically low-intensity vs threshold emphasis — it does NOT test whether more Zone 3 helps.
sources.population: 12 sub-elite Spanish runners. n=12 is very small; treat the effect size as indicative, not precise.

sources.citation: Muñoz, I., Seiler, S., Bautista, J., España, J., Larumbe, E., & Esteve-Lanao, J. (2014). Does polarized training improve performance in recreational runners? International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 9(2), 265–272.
sources.claim: 30 recreational runners, 10 weeks, HR-controlled. Polarised distribution produced greater training effect on 10 km performance than a between-thresholds programme.
sources.population: Recreational runners — the closest interventional match to this athlete in the pro-polarised literature. Still: 10 km outcome, not marathon, and a 10-week block at stable volume, not a ramp.

sources.citation: Festa, L., Tarperi, C., Skroce, K., La Torre, A., & Schena, F. (2019). Effects of different training intensity distribution in recreational runners. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, 1, 70. DOI 10.3389/fspor.2019.00070
sources.claim: THE most population-matched trial available, and it is a null result. Polarised (77/3/20) vs focused/threshold-heavy (40/50/10), 8 weeks, matched TRIMP. No statistically significant between-group differences: speed at VO2max +3.2% vs +4.0%, running economy −5.3% vs −8.7%, 2 km performance +3.5% vs +3.0%. The threshold-heavy group achieved this in 17% less total training time.
sources.population: 38 recreational runners, mean age ~41, training 3.2 ± 0.5 h/week, mean VO2max 53.2 ml/kg/min. This athlete is VO2max 53.0 and has averaged 24.4 km/week. The match is almost exact. This is the study that should carry the most weight for him, and it says the model choice does not matter much at his scale.

sources.citation: Rosenblat, M.A., Perrotta, A.S., & Vicenzino, B. (2019). Polarized vs. threshold training intensity distribution on endurance sport performance: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 33(12), 3491–3500.
sources.claim: Meta-analysis favouring polarised over threshold. But it pooled only 3 studies and 112 participants total — the entire quantitative evidence base for 'polarised beats threshold' at the time was three trials.
sources.population: Endurance-trained athletes with >2 years' experience and VO2max/peak >50 ml/kg/min. The thinness of the evidence base is the headline, not the effect.

sources.citation: Filipas, L., Bonato, M., Gallo, G., & Codella, R. (2022). Effects of 16 weeks of pyramidal and polarized training intensity distributions in well-trained endurance runners. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports, 32(3), 498–511. DOI 10.1111/sms.14101
sources.claim: The best-designed TID trial in runners. Four arms over 16 weeks: pyramidal throughout (77/17/6), polarised throughout (80/6/14), and both switch orders. Pyramidal-then-polarised produced the largest gains (VO2peak +3.0%, velocity at 2 mM +1.7%, at 4 mM +1.5%, 5 km time trial −1.5%). Threshold-velocity improvements predicted performance better than maximal variables did.
sources.population: 56 well-trained male runners, mean age 37, VO2peak 68 ml/kg/min, >5 sessions/week. Far fitter than this athlete, and the terminal event was a 5 km time trial — a Zone 3 race. That matters for whether the PYR→POL sequencing transfers to a marathon.

sources.citation: Kenneally, M., Casado, A., & Santos-Concejero, J. (2018). The effect of periodisation and training intensity distribution on middle- and long-distance running performance: a systematic review. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 13(9), 1114–1121.
sources.claim: Reviews pyramidal, polarised and threshold models in running specifically, and concludes that zones organised around goal race pace can accommodate multiple periodisation approaches — i.e. the physiological-zone framing is not the only defensible one for runners.
sources.population: Middle- and long-distance runners across competitive levels; a review of 16 studies, largely trained/elite.

sources.citation: Casado, A., Hanley, B., Santos-Concejero, J., & Ruiz-Pérez, L.M. (2022). Training periodization, methods, intensity distribution, and volume in highly trained and elite distance runners: a systematic review. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 17(6), 820–833.
sources.claim: Highly trained/elite distance runners predominantly follow a PYRAMIDAL distribution — decreasing volume from Z1 to Z2 to Z3 — on a hard-day/easy-day basis, while accumulating >100 km/week. Polarised 'might also be effective'. This is the observational counterweight to the polarised RCTs.
sources.population: Highly trained and elite distance runners; only 10 articles met inclusion. Weekly volumes >100 km — this athlete will touch that number exactly once, in week 3.

sources.citation: Muniz-Pumares, D., Hunter, B., Meyler, S., Maunder, E., & Smyth, B. (2024). The training intensity distribution of marathon runners across performance levels. Sports Medicine, 55(4), 1023–1035. DOI 10.1007/s40279-024-02137-7
sources.claim: The most decision-relevant source here. 16 weeks of training preceding 151,813 marathons by 119,452 runners. Mean volume 45.1 ± 26.4 km/week. Pyramidal was the most common distribution and was used by >80% of the FASTEST runners. Absolute Z2 and Z3 time was roughly CONSTANT across performance levels — faster runners got faster by adding Zone 1, not by adding intensity. Proportion of Z1 correlated negatively with marathon time (R²≥0.90); proportions of Z2 and Z3 correlated with SLOWER marathon times (R²≥0.85). Uses 82.3% of critical speed as the Z1/Z2 boundary — a field-derivable anchor.
sources.population: 119,452 recreational-to-good marathon runners at ~45 km/week. This is this athlete's actual population, at his actual volume, for his actual event. Observational, so confounded (faster runners can run more), but the sample size and population match are unmatched in this literature.

sources.citation: Foster, C., Casado, A., Esteve-Lanao, J., Haugen, T., & Seiler, S. (2022). Polarized training is optimal for endurance athletes. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 54(6). (Point of a point/counterpoint; I did not verify exact page range.)
sources.claim: The affirmative case, argued by the model's own authors.
sources.population: Argument, not data. Concerns endurance athletes generally.

sources.citation: Burnley, M., Bearden, S.E., & Jones, A.M. (2022). Polarized training is not optimal for endurance athletes. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 54(6). (Counterpoint; I did not verify exact page range.)
sources.claim: Concludes there is presently NO evidence that a specifically polarised distribution is optimal, and that effective programmes do and should prioritise Zone 1 and Zone 2 over Zone 3 — i.e. pyramidal. Directly contradicts the source above, in the same journal issue, between the field's most senior people.
sources.population: Argument, not data. The existence of this exchange is itself the most honest summary of the evidence base: the question is genuinely unresolved among experts.

sources.citation: Nielsen, R.O., Parner, E.T., Nohr, E.A., Sørensen, H., Lind, M., & Rasmussen, S. (2014). Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries: an association which varies according to type of injury. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. DOI 10.2519/jospt.2014.5164 (I did not verify the exact volume/page range.)
sources.claim: 874 novice runners with GPS watches, stratified by weekly-distance progression (<10%/regression, 10–30%, >30%). Progressing more than 30% over a 2-week window raised the risk of distance-related injuries — patellofemoral pain, ITB syndrome, medial tibial stress syndrome, patellar tendinopathy, greater trochanteric bursitis, gluteus medius/TFL injury.
sources.population: 874 NOVICE runners. This athlete is not a novice, so the absolute risk figures do not transfer directly — but his planned progression (14.8 km to 60 km, then +33%, then +25%) is far outside the range this study even measured, and the injury classes named are precisely the volume-driven ones.

sources.citation: Persinger, R., Foster, C., Gibson, M., Fater, D.C.W., & Porcari, J.P. (2004). Consistency of the talk test for exercise prescription. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 36(9), 1632–1636.
sources.claim: The talk test's last-positive/equivocal/first-negative stages correspond consistently to the ventilatory threshold, on treadmill as well as cycle ergometer. Provides a zero-equipment field method for locating VT1.
sources.population: 16 healthy volunteers, laboratory incremental testing. Small, and not runners specifically — but the method is cheap enough to be worth using as a cross-check regardless.

prescriptions.sessionName: Zone 1 aerobic run (the load-bearing majority of the block)
prescriptions.structure: 30–75 minutes continuous, flat-to-rolling, no surges, no unplanned hill efforts. This is the session type that absorbs essentially all of the volume increase from 24 km/week to 60–100 km/week. Frequency, not duration, is what scales: he goes from 4 runs/week to 6, and doubles are how weeks 2–4 get built without any single run becoming unmanageable.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Ceiling is VT1, derived from heart rate as the primary anchor (heart rate is not subject to the documented pace-prediction bias). VT1 heart rate is bounded from above by the Garmin-detected lactate-threshold HR of 177 and bounded from below by a hard empirical fact: he ran a 3:55:54 marathon at an average of 165 bpm. A recreational runner cannot sustain 3 hours 56 minutes materially above VT1, so VT1 heart rate is at or just above 165. Cross-check: 83% of a measured maximum of 201 bpm is 167. The two methods converge at 166 bpm.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Mitochondrial biogenesis, capillary density, plasma volume expansion and stroke-volume increase — adaptations whose stimulus scales with accumulated duration below VT1 and whose recovery cost stays roughly linear rather than compounding. This is the only zone where volume can triple inside six weeks without the autonomic and musculoskeletal cost tripling with it. In Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024), faster marathon times across 119,452 runners were associated specifically with a greater PROPORTION of Zone 1 (R²≥0.90) while absolute Zone 2 and Zone 3 stayed flat — the extra volume in better runners is almost entirely Zone 1 volume.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: Zone 1 = heart rate below 166 bpm. Target pace band 6:00–6:45/km, with a hard ceiling of 5:45/km. The 5:45 ceiling is derived two ways that bracket rather than agree: (a) Muniz-Pumares' Z1/Z2 boundary of 82.3% of critical speed, applied to a working threshold pace of 4:55/km, gives 5:58/km; (b) his own marathon at 5:31/km and 165 bpm says VT1 pace is at or slower than about 5:30. Take 5:45/km as the working ceiling and treat the 5:30–6:00 band as genuinely uncertain until the field test below resolves it. Practical rule that needs no watch: he must be able to speak a full sentence without breaking it to breathe (Persinger et al., 2004). Note that he is currently averaging 24.4 km/week — almost all of the 355 Zone 1 kilometres in this block are kilometres he has never run.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: 4–5 sessions per week, rising to 6 plus one double in weeks 2–4

prescriptions.sessionName: Long run — Zone 1 throughout, with a marathon-pace block in the second half
prescriptions.structure: Weeks 1–4: 18, 24, 33 (the Lincoln session, below) and 26 km. Weeks 5–6: 20 and 14 km. From week 2 onward the final 8–12 km is run at marathon target pace continuously, not as intervals. No fasted long runs during a volume ramp of this size.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Marathon target pace, derived from Garmin's 3:36:12 prediction corrected by this athlete's own documented over-prediction factor of 1.118, giving 4:01:45 — i.e. 5:44/km. Realistic target band, allowing for the fitness he is about to gain, is 3:50–4:00, i.e. 5:27–5:41/km.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Glycogen depletion and the fat-oxidation and durability adaptations that only appear in the third and fourth hour of accumulated weekly duration, plus neuromuscular rehearsal of race-day cadence and mechanics at the exact pace he will hold. The marathon-pace block also serves as a running measurement: heart rate at marathon pace, tracked weekly, is the block's primary progress signal.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: THE KEY DERIVATION, AND THE ONE THAT MAKES THIS BLOCK AFFORDABLE: his marathon pace (5:27–5:44/km) sits at or just below his VT1 pace (5:30–6:00/km). For an elite runner, marathon pace is above VT1 and therefore genuinely costly Zone 2 work. For a 3:50–4:00 marathoner it is not — it is top-of-Zone-1. Marathon-pace work therefore costs him almost nothing from his intensity budget, which means the most specific training he can do is also the cheapest. Expected heart rate during the marathon-pace block: 160–170 bpm, drifting upward late. If it exceeds 172 bpm inside the first 5 km of the block, the pace target is too aggressive and should be revised to 5:45/km for the rest of the block.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: 1 per week, weekend morning

prescriptions.sessionName: Zone 2 threshold-adjacent steady run
prescriptions.structure: 15–20 minutes continuous at the low end of Zone 2, or 2 × 10 minutes with 3 minutes easy jog between. Preceded and followed by 2–3 km of Zone 1. Total session 10–12 km, of which only 4–6 km is actually in Zone 2.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Between VT1 and VT2: heart rate 166–176 bpm, pace roughly 5:00–5:30/km. VT2 is anchored on his Garmin-detected lactate-threshold HR of 177. The corresponding PACE requires correction: Garmin's stated LT pace of 4:20.9/km is not credible for this athlete, because his best genuine continuous half marathon was run at 5:02/km at an average of 174 bpm — just under LT heart rate. A runner whose near-threshold half is 5:02/km does not have a threshold pace of 4:21. Applying his documented Garmin over-prediction factor of 1.118 to 4:20.9 gives 4:51.5/km; the independent half-marathon cross-check gives 4:50–5:00. Working VT2 pace: 4:55/km.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Raises the velocity at which lactate accumulation begins — the variable that Filipas et al. (2022) found predicted performance improvement better than VO2peak did. For a marathon specifically, this is the zone that raises the ceiling that marathon pace sits underneath, which is what protects against the late-race fade that turns a 3:50 into a 4:10. Kept deliberately small in volume because it is, by Seiler's own argument, the most expensive adaptation per kilometre.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: Zone 2 = 166–176 bpm, ~5:00–5:30/km. Total across the whole six-week block: 32 km, which is 8% of block volume. This is deliberately below what a conventional marathon plan prescribes. Justification: Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024) found that across 119,452 marathon runners, a higher PROPORTION of Zone 2 correlated with SLOWER marathon times (R²≥0.85), and Esteve-Lanao et al. (2007) found 81/12/8 beat 67/25/8 in sub-elite runners with Zone 3 held constant. Both point the same way: on a volume ramp this steep, Zone 2 is the first thing to cut.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: 1 per week in weeks 1, 2, 3 and 5. ZERO in week 4 (the 10K race supplies more than enough). Reduced to one short touch in race week.

prescriptions.sessionName: Zone 3 session — the single weekly hard dose, capped in absolute kilometres
prescriptions.structure: 5–6 × 3 minutes hard with 2–3 minutes jog recovery, or 6 × 800 m with 2:30 jog. Working volume 4.5–5 km. Never more. Full warm-up and cool-down in Zone 1, so the session totals 11–12 km.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Above VT2: heart rate above 177 bpm (peaking 185–192, which is 92–96% of his measured 201 bpm maximum), pace faster than 4:55/km. Target repetition pace 4:15–4:35/km. Note that his measured maximum is 201, not the 196 in his Garmin profile nor the 195 he believes — using 195 would put his Zone 3 floor about 4 bpm too low and quietly convert some Zone 2 work into apparent Zone 3.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Maintains stroke volume, VO2 kinetics and vVO2max — which need only a small maintenance dose once established, and which Seiler (2010) explicitly notes do not respond to further intensification in already-trained athletes. In this block the objective is explicitly MAINTENANCE, not development: this is not the time to chase VO2max.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: CAPPED AT 5 KM PER WEEK, 21 KM ACROSS THE ENTIRE BLOCK (5% of volume). The cap is absolute, not proportional. This is the design decision that resolves the central tension between the volume ramp and the intensity plan: because the Zone 3 dose is fixed in kilometres, its percentage share automatically FALLS as weekly volume rises — 0% in week 1, 5% in the 100 km week — so the two risks never compound. This mirrors what Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024) observed empirically: absolute Zone 2 and Zone 3 volume was roughly constant across marathon performance levels, and only Zone 1 scaled. It is also the direct opposite of naive '80/20 by distance', which would prescribe 20 km of Zone 3 in the 100 km week — a dose no runner at any level actually performs.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: 1 per week in weeks 2, 3 and 5. Zero in week 1 (he raced a half flat out on 2026-09-12, two days before the block opens). Zero in week 4 (the 10K race IS that week's Zone 3). One set of 6 × 100 m strides only, in race week.

prescriptions.sessionName: Lincoln Half, 2026-10-04 — NOT a race. A Zone 1 marathon-pace rehearsal inside a 33 km long run
prescriptions.structure: 8 km easy Zone 1 before the start (or as a separate morning run), the 21.1 km event at marathon target pace, 4 km easy Zone 1 afterwards. Total 33 km. Carry and take fuel on the same schedule planned for 2026-10-24 — this is the dress rehearsal for the fuelling plan, not just the pacing.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Marathon target pace exactly: 5:30–5:44/km, heart rate held under 170 bpm for the first 15 km. The single hardest instruction in the entire block is to let people go past.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Race-specific durability at the pace and duration that matter, plus a full rehearsal of fuelling, kit and pacing discipline. Running it at marathon pace rather than racing it means the session's cost is Zone 1 cost — recoverable inside 3–4 days — whereas racing it would cost 8–10 days, which is one third of the remaining block.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: This session lands at the end of the 100 km week (week commencing 2026-09-28), which is simultaneously the highest-volume week of his life and 20 days before the goal marathon. Zone accounting: approximately 30 km Zone 1, 3 km Zone 2 (heart-rate drift in the closing 5 km is expected and acceptable), 0 km Zone 3. If his heart rate exceeds 175 bpm at any point before 18 km, he is racing it and must slow down. Concrete abort criterion, because 'don't race it' is not enforceable and a heart-rate number is.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: Once, in week 3

prescriptions.sessionName: ASICS LDNX 10K, 2026-10-11 — raced hard, and it constitutes that entire week's Zone 3 budget
prescriptions.structure: 3 km Zone 1 warm-up including strides, race the 10K, 3 km Zone 1 cool-down. Total ~16 km. NO separate interval session that week and NO Zone 2 session that week.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Raced. Expect 43–48 minutes (Garmin predicts 43:29; corrected by his 1.118 factor that becomes 48:38 — the truth is likely between, so 4:20–4:50/km). Heart rate will exceed 177 bpm from roughly the second kilometre and finish near 195–200.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: The taper's only intensity, serving three functions: maintaining the Zone 3 stimulus with zero additional planning load, providing a genuine competitive performance to recalibrate the Garmin over-prediction factor against, and delivering a psychological sharpener 13 days before the marathon.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: Zone accounting for that day: ~9 km Zone 3, ~2 km Zone 2, ~5 km Zone 1. That means week 4's Zone 3 total is 9 km — nearly double the 5 km weekly cap — which is precisely why no other hard work happens in that week. Week 4 is the only week in the block where the distribution goes genuinely polarised (85/4/11) rather than pyramidal, and it does so because of a race, not a design choice. The resulting 10K time, divided by Garmin's prediction, gives a fourth data point for the over-prediction factor and should be used to finalise marathon pace on 2026-10-12.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: Once, in week 4

research.intensityDistribution:
FIRST, THE THING THAT MUST BE SAID BEFORE ANY NUMBERS: "80/20" is not 20% of kilometres.

Seiler's finding, from Seiler & Kjerland (2006) and formalised in Seiler (2010), counts SESSIONS classified by their primary goal. Elite athletes doing 10–13 sessions a week have roughly 2–3 whose purpose is high intensity. When the same training is instead quantified by time or distance in each zone, the picture is entirely different: Stöggl & Sperlich (2015) report 84–95% Zone 1, 2–11% Zone 2, 2–9% Zone 3 by time in elite athletes' preparation phases. That is not 80/20. That is roughly 90/5/5, and it is pyramidal.

The two accounting methods describe the identical training. Almost every misapplication of this model comes from taking the session-count number and applying it to volume. For this athlete the error would be enormous: 20% of his 100 km week is 20 km above threshold. No runner at any level does that. Elite marathoners at 180 km/week run perhaps 8–10 km above VT2. Below is the volume-based accounting, which is the only one that can be prescribed.

By session count, incidentally, he lands at 5–6 runs per week with 1 hard = 17–20%. So he satisfies "80/20" as Seiler actually measured it, while running 5% of his distance in Zone 3. Both statements are true. Only one is actionable.

ZONE DEFINITIONS FOR THIS ATHLETE (heart rate is the primary anchor; pace is the cross-check)
  Zone 1: below 166 bpm — slower than roughly 5:45/km, habitually 6:00–6:45/km
  Zone 2: 166–176 bpm — roughly 5:00–5:30/km
  Zone 3: 177 bpm and above — faster than roughly 4:55/km
Derivations: VT2 heart rate = Garmin's auto-detected lactate threshold, 177 bpm (2026-08-08). VT1 heart rate = 166, bounded below by his 3:55:54 marathon at 165 bpm average (a four-hour effort cannot sit far above VT1) and above by 83% of his measured maximum of 201. VT2 pace = 4:55/km, derived by correcting Garmin's implausible 4:20.9 with his own documented 1.118 over-prediction factor (giving 4:51.5) and cross-checked against his 1:46:35 half at 5:02/km and 174 bpm. VT1 pace ≈ 5:45/km, bracketed by Muniz-Pumares' 82.3%-of-critical-speed rule (5:58/km) and his marathon pace of 5:31/km at 165 bpm — the widest genuine uncertainty in this design.

THE DESIGN RULE THAT RESOLVES THE VOLUME/INTENSITY TENSION
Fix the hard work in ABSOLUTE kilometres and let its percentage fall as volume rises. Zone 3 is capped at 5 km per week regardless of whether the week is 60 km or 100 km. Consequence: the distribution automatically becomes more Zone-1-dominant precisely in the weeks where the volume risk is highest, so volume risk and intensity risk never peak together. This is not a compromise invented for convenience — it is exactly what Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024) observed across 119,452 marathon runners, where absolute Zone 2 and Zone 3 volume stayed roughly constant across performance levels and only Zone 1 scaled.

WEEK BY WEEK, IN KILOMETRES

Week 1 — commencing 2026-09-14 — 60 km total
  Zone 1: 55 km  |  Zone 2: 5 km  |  Zone 3: 0 km   (92 / 8 / 0)
  Zero Zone 3. He races Battersea Half flat out on 2026-09-12, two days before this week opens, AND jumps from 14.8 km to 60 km — a 305% increase. Nielsen et al. (2014) found >30% progression over two weeks raised distance-related injury risk in novice runners; this is ten times that rate. Adding intervals on top would be indefensible. The 5 km of Zone 2 is a single short steady block late in the week, and only if the half-marathon has cleared.

Week 2 — commencing 2026-09-21 — 80 km total
  Zone 1: 68 km  |  Zone 2: 8 km  |  Zone 3: 4 km   (85 / 10 / 5)
  Zone 3 enters: one session, 5 × 3 minutes. This is the week the reversal condition is judged at its close.

Week 3 — commencing 2026-09-28 — 100 km total (peak; contains Lincoln Half on 2026-10-04)
  Zone 1: 87 km  |  Zone 2: 8 km  |  Zone 3: 5 km   (87 / 8 / 5)
  Composition: the 33 km Lincoln session contributes 30 Zone 1 + 3 Zone 2; the remaining 67 km contributes 57 Zone 1 + 5 Zone 2 + 5 Zone 3. Note that Zone 3's SHARE falls to 5% in the hardest week purely as an arithmetic consequence of the absolute cap. The extra 20 km over week 2 is entirely Zone 1. Naive 80/20 would have prescribed 20 km of Zone 3 here; that is the single most dangerous thing that could be done to this athlete in this block.

Week 4 — commencing 2026-10-05 — 80 km total (contains ASICS LDNX 10K on 2026-10-11)
  Zone 1: 68 km  |  Zone 2: 3 km  |  Zone 3: 9 km   (85 / 4 / 11)
  The only genuinely polarised week in the block, and it is polarised by circumstance rather than design: a hard 10K is about 9 km above threshold on its own, which is nearly double the weekly cap. Therefore no interval session and no tempo session that week. All other running is Zone 1.

Week 5 — commencing 2026-10-12 — 60 km total
  Zone 1: 52 km  |  Zone 2: 6 km  |  Zone 3: 2 km   (87 / 10 / 3)
  Volume drops 25%; intensity drops with it rather than being maintained. Standard taper practice maintains intensity while cutting volume, and I am deliberately not doing that here — he is 12 days past a 100 km week that is 4× his historical average and 1 day past a raced 10K. Absorption is worth more to him than sharpness.

Week 6 — commencing 2026-10-19 — 28 km of running plus the marathon on 2026-10-24
  Zone 1: 25 km  |  Zone 2: 2 km  |  Zone 3: 1 km   (89 / 7 / 4)
  The Zone 3 kilometre is 6 × 100 m strides on Tuesday and Thursday. The Zone 2 is a 2 km marathon-pace touch on Wednesday. Nothing else.

BLOCK TOTAL, EXCLUDING RACES: 408 km = 355 Zone 1 (87%) + 32 Zone 2 (8%) + 21 Zone 3 (5%).

So the recommendation is 87 / 8 / 5 by distance — PYRAMIDAL, not polarised, and nowhere near "80/20 by volume". Evidence for choosing pyramidal over polarised here: (a) Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024), the only source at his volume for his event, found pyramidal in >80% of the fastest marathoners and found higher Zone 2 AND Zone 3 proportions both associated with slower marathon times; (b) Casado et al. (2022) found pyramidal typical among highly trained distance runners; (c) Burnley, Bearden & Jones (2022) argue in print that no evidence supports polarised specifically and that Zone 1 and Zone 2 should be prioritised over Zone 3. Evidence against: Stöggl & Sperlich (2014), Muñoz et al. (2014) and Rosenblat et al. (2019) favour polarised — but those outcomes were 10 km, time-to-exhaustion and VO2peak, all Zone 3-limited measures, whereas a four-hour marathon is a Zone 1 event. The distribution should look like the race.

DELIBERATE DIVERGENCE FROM FILIPAS ET AL. (2022): that trial's best arm shifted pyramidal→polarised in the final 8 weeks, and I am NOT doing that. Its terminal outcome was a 5 km time trial, a Zone 3 event, so increasing Zone 3 at the end was specific to it. His terminal event is a marathon run at or below VT1. The specificity argument runs the other way: the block should get MORE Zone 1 and more marathon-pace-specific toward the end, which is what weeks 5 and 6 do.
research.fitForThisAthlete:
Honest answer: as an OPTIMISATION, the polarised/pyramidal debate is close to irrelevant to him. As a CONSTRAINT, it is the most valuable thing in this entire block.

Why it is nearly vacuous as an optimisation. The one trial that matches his physiology and volume almost exactly — Festa et al. (2019), 38 recreational runners at 3.2 h/week with a mean VO2max of 53.2 against his 53.0 — randomised polarised (77/3/20) against threshold-heavy (40/50/10) for 8 weeks and found no statistically significant between-group difference in speed at VO2max, running economy, or 2 km performance. Two distributions about as far apart as it is possible to construct, and the outcomes were the same. If those two produce identical results in his population, the difference between 87/8/5 and 82/13/5 is noise. He should not spend a minute of attention on which label his week carries.

The numerical vacuity is worse than the trial result suggests. At 24 km/week, one interval session of 5 km of hard work is 21% of volume — he is "polarised" by accident. At 100 km/week, that same session is 5% — he is "pyramidal" by accident. His label changes week to week purely because his volume changes, without a single training decision differing. And by session count he is 80/20 in every single week of the block. Three defensible accounting methods, three different answers, identical training. The distinction is not measuring anything real at his scale.

Why the tradition nonetheless earns its place. Strip away the percentage argument and one durable finding survives, and it is the finding that is not in dispute between Foster's camp and Burnley's: easy days must be genuinely easy, hard days must be few, and the middle is where a limited recovery budget gets consumed without a proportionate return. Esteve-Lanao et al. (2007) tested exactly this — Zone 3 held equal at 8% in both arms, only the Zone 1/Zone 2 split varied — and 81/12/8 beat 67/25/8. Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024) found the same shape observationally across 119,452 marathon runners. That principle is not an optimisation for him; it is the mechanism by which a 60 → 80 → 100 km ramp becomes survivable at all. If his 60 km week is run at 5:30/km because 5:30 feels comfortable when fresh, he will not reach week 3. If it is run at 6:15–6:45/km, he might.

Which brings me to the honest risk statement. He has never run a 60 km week. His previous maximum was 57.1 km and it contained a marathon; his four most recent complete weeks were 27.2 / 34.8 / 0 / 14.8. Week 1 is a 305% jump. Nielsen et al. (2014) found injury risk elevated at >30% progression over two weeks in novice runners — this is an order of magnitude beyond the range that study even sampled, so there is genuinely no evidence base for what he is about to do. He has ratified it in writing and it is not my decision to reopen. What I can do is refuse to let intensity compound it, and that is what the absolute Zone 3 cap does: 5 km per week, 21 km across the block, unchanged whether the week is 60 or 100. The alternative — a percentage-based prescription — would have handed him 20 km of Zone 3 in his hardest week ever. That would very likely have ended the block.

One further point in his favour, and it is the most useful physiological fact in this whole analysis: his marathon target pace (5:27–5:44/km) sits at or just below his VT1 (roughly 5:45/km). His most specific training is therefore also his cheapest. He does not face the tradeoff a 2:30 marathoner faces, where race-pace work is genuinely hard Zone 2 work that has to be rationed against everything else. He can rehearse race pace inside Zone 1 volume at essentially no additional recovery cost. That is why the Lincoln Half at marathon pace inside a 33 km session is such a good use of week 3, and why the block can be 87% Zone 1 without being 87% unspecific.

Finally, on the six-week constraint: the distribution question is the one part of this problem that six weeks does NOT compromise. Distribution is a property of each week, not a periodised progression, so it can be applied from day one at full effect. It is the volume ramp and the aerobic adaptations that need the time he does not have — not this.
research.howToValidate:
Every check below runs on data rocket already holds — per-activity heart rate streams, pace, distance and Garmin training load from the existing 57-activity Postgres table — or on a single 20-minute field test he can do on a track. No lab.

1. THE PRIMARY FALSIFIER — heart rate at fixed pace on the weekly long run.
Record average heart rate over the marathon-pace block (kilometres 10–20 of each long run) at a fixed 5:35/km. Plot it weekly.
  PASS: the value falls by 4–8 bpm between week 1 and week 5. That is aerobic adaptation from the Zone 1 volume, and it is the whole thesis of this block.
  FAIL: flat or rising. If flat, the Zone 1 volume is not producing adaptation, which almost always means it is not actually Zone 1 — check the compliance metric below before concluding the model is wrong.
This single number is worth more than every other check combined, and it costs nothing extra to collect.

2. THE COMPLIANCE METRIC — weekly kilometres per zone, computed from heart rate streams.
For each activity, bin every second of the HR stream into <166 / 166–176 / ≥177 and attribute the distance covered in each. Sum weekly. Compare against the table above.
  Gate A: Zone 3 must be ≤6 km in any week other than week 4. Exceeding it means an "easy" run drifted hard or a tempo overran, and it is the leading indicator of the block failing.
  Gate B: Zone 1 must be ≥85% of weekly distance in every week except week 4.
  Gate C — the one that actually catches the failure mode: Zone 2 must be ≤12% in every week. Unintentional Zone 2 accumulation, from easy runs creeping to 5:20/km, is how this block dies. It looks like enthusiasm and behaves like overtraining.
This is a straightforward query over data rocket already has, and it should run automatically after every activity ingest.

3. THE ZONE-BOUNDARY VALIDATION — resolve the VT1 uncertainty in week 1.
The biggest weakness in this prescription is that VT1 pace is only bracketed to 5:30–6:00/km. Resolve it with a talk test, validated against ventilatory threshold by Persinger et al. (2004): on a track, run 4 minutes each at 6:30, 6:15, 6:00, 5:45 and 5:30/km, reciting a fixed sentence in the final 30 seconds of each. The last stage at which he can complete the sentence comfortably is VT1. Record heart rate and pace at that stage. That pair becomes the Zone 1 ceiling in config, replacing the estimate, with the test date as its source.
Independent cross-check with zero extra effort: Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024) place the Zone 1/Zone 2 boundary at 82.3% of critical speed. Fit critical speed from his existing race data (5.10 km at 4:19/km, 21.14 km at 5:02/km, 42.67 km at 5:31/km) and take 82.3% of it. If the two methods land within 10 s/km of each other, the anchor is trustworthy. If they diverge by more than 20 s/km, trust the talk test — it is a direct measurement, whereas the critical-speed fit inherits whatever staleness is in those race results.

4. RECALIBRATE THE GARMIN BIAS ON 2026-10-11.
