His Garmin over-predicts by a median factor of 1.118 across three realised efforts. The ASICS 10K gives a fourth. Compute actual-time ÷ predicted-time on the day and update the factor. If it has moved materially below 1.118, his true fitness has improved faster than the prediction model's bias — set marathon pace from the corrected 10K, not from Garmin's marathon prediction. This directly sets the number he races on 13 days later, so it is the highest-leverage single measurement in the block.

5. THE STOP SIGNAL — a composite the existing data already supports.
Trigger a mandatory intensity cut (Zone 3 to zero the following week) on ANY of: resting heart rate up more than 5 bpm above the 57 bpm smoothed baseline for 3 consecutive mornings; heart rate at fixed long-run pace up more than 5 bpm week on week; or any musculoskeletal pain altering gait. Order of operations matters and must be stated in config: INTENSITY IS CUT BEFORE VOLUME. The volume ramp is the ratified experiment and the thing he wants; the intensity plan is the risk buffer around it, so the buffer is what gets spent first. Note that his fatigue and freshness figures (ATL 27.5, TSB +24.7) will invert violently in week 1 — TSB going sharply negative is the expected and correct response to this ramp, not a warning sign, and should not trigger anything on its own.

6. WHAT WOULD FALSIFY THE WHOLE DESIGN.
If by end of week 4 his heart rate at 5:35/km has not fallen, his resting heart rate is flat, and he feels fine — then the Zone 1 volume was under-stimulating and the conservative Zone 3 cap was the wrong call for him. That is a real possibility and I want it recorded as such rather than defended after the fact. The remedy in weeks 5 and 6 would NOT be more Zone 3 (too late to adapt, and it would compromise the taper) but a second marathon-pace long run. Conversely, if he cannot complete week 3 at the prescribed Zone 1 heart-rate ceiling without pace collapsing below 7:00/km, the volume — not the distribution — is the binding constraint, and the reversal condition should be invoked.
contraindications: DO NOT use Garmin's five-zone %HRmax zones for any of this. Garmin's 'Zone 2' (roughly 60–70% of max, ~120–140 bpm for him) and Seiler's Zone 2 (166–176 bpm) are completely different intensities that share a name. Stöggl & Sperlich (2015) note explicitly that percentage-of-maximum anchoring produces inhomogeneous metabolic strain between individuals. Seiler's zones are anchored to ventilatory/lactate thresholds; if rocket displays 'zone 2' it must state which model it means, or the athlete will train at the wrong intensity while believing he is compliant.

DO NOT compute Zone 3 as 20% of weekly distance. In the 100 km week that is 20 km above threshold. No runner at any level performs that dose; elite marathoners at 180 km/week run 8–10 km above VT2. Seiler's 80/20 counts sessions by primary goal, not kilometres (Seiler & Kjerland, 2006). Encoding it as a volume percentage is the highest-consequence error available in this design.

DO NOT use Garmin's stated lactate-threshold pace of 4:20.9/km as the Zone 2/Zone 3 boundary. It is not credible: his best genuine continuous half marathon was 5:02/km at 174 bpm, just below his 177 bpm threshold heart rate. Using 4:20.9 would place his entire tempo work in what is actually Zone 3 and destroy the intensity cap without anyone noticing. Use the corrected 4:55/km, or prefer heart rate.

DO NOT use 195 or 196 bpm as maximum heart rate. The measured value is 201 (2026-06-14). Both the profile figure and his belief are wrong, and using them shifts every zone boundary down by 4–5 bpm — enough to reclassify genuine Zone 2 work as Zone 3 and make the intensity cap look satisfied when it is not.

DO NOT apply Filipas et al.'s (2022) pyramidal→polarised sequencing to the back half of this block. That trial's terminal outcome was a 5 km time trial. This athlete's terminal outcome is a four-hour marathon run at or below VT1. Shifting emphasis toward Zone 3 in weeks 5–6 would be anti-specific and would compromise the taper.

DO NOT race the Lincoln Half on 2026-10-04. Racing it costs 8–10 days of recovery out of the 20 remaining, and it falls at the end of the highest-volume week of his life. Enforce with a heart-rate abort criterion — above 175 bpm before 18 km means slow down — because 'run it easy' is not an enforceable instruction on a start line.

DO NOT add an interval or tempo session in week 4. The hard 10K on 2026-10-11 is approximately 9 km above threshold on its own, already nearly double the weekly cap. Any additional quality that week means roughly 14 km of Zone 3 nine days before the goal marathon.

DO NOT maintain intensity while cutting volume during the taper, despite that being standard practice. He arrives at week 5 twelve days past a 100 km week that is four times his historical average and one day past a raced 10K. Absorption is worth more to him than sharpness, and the standard taper advice comes from populations who arrive at the taper adapted to their peak volume. He will not be.

DO NOT cut volume before cutting intensity when a stop signal fires. The volume ramp is the ratified experiment; the intensity plan is the buffer protecting it. Spend the buffer first. Config must encode this order explicitly, or an automated system will do the intuitive and wrong thing.

DO NOT treat the pro-polarised trials as settled. Rosenblat et al. (2019) pooled three studies and 112 participants. Foster et al. (2022) and Burnley et al. (2022) argue opposite conclusions in the same journal issue, and neither is a fringe position. The trial that matches this athlete's volume and VO2max almost exactly (Festa et al., 2019) is a null result. Any claim in rocket's UI that a distribution is 'optimal' would be unsupportable — the honest framing is that the distribution is a risk-management constraint, not a performance optimisation.

DO NOT let Zone 2 accumulate unintentionally. The failure mode of this block is not a missed interval session; it is six easy runs a week drifting from 6:15/km to 5:20/km because he feels good in week 2. Gate C in the validation section exists specifically for this, and it is the check most likely to fire.

DO NOT copy the 87/8/5 numbers into a general planner for other users. They are derived from this athlete's specific ramp, his marathon pace sitting below his VT1 (which is only true for runners slower than roughly 3:30), and a ratified volume plan that carries known elevated injury risk. A 2:45 marathoner on stable volume needs a different answer.

verification.tradition: Seiler's three-zone training-intensity-distribution model (polarised / pyramidal / threshold), applied to a 6-week, 60→100 km/week marathon block for a recreational runner averaging 24.4 km/week.

checks.claim: Seiler & Kjerland (2006), Scand J Med Sci Sports 16(1):49-56 — 'the SAME training data yields different distribution labels depending on quantification method: pyramidal by time-in-zone, polarised by session goal. This is the single most important methodological caveat in the whole literature.'
checks.note: Paper exists and is cited correctly (DOI 10.1111/j.1600-0838.2004.00418.x, 11 male junior XC skiers, 384 sessions/32 days). But its abstract reports the opposite of the claim: the three quantification methods AGREED. HR 75+/-3 / 8+/-3 / 17+/-4; session-RPE 76+/-4 / 6+/-5 / 18+/-7; blood lactate 71 / 7 / 22. The paper's own words: 'Intensity distribution across endurance training sessions was SIMILAR when based on heart rate analysis or session RPE.' No pyramidal-vs-polarised divergence is reported; the terms are not used. This is the load-bearing methodological premise of the entire research document ('almost every practical misapplication traces to that one confusion') and it is attributed to a paper that does not contain it.

checks.claim: Casado, A., Hanley, B., Santos-Concejero, J., & Ruiz-Perez, L.M. (2022). Training periodization, methods, intensity distribution, and volume in highly trained and elite distance runners. IJSPP 17(6):820-833.
checks.note: MISATTRIBUTED AUTHOR LIST. Title, journal, year, volume, issue and pages are correct; the actual authors are Casado A, Gonzalez-Mohino F, Gonzalez-Rave JM, Foster C (DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2021-0435). Hanley / Santos-Concejero / Ruiz-Perez are co-authors of a DIFFERENT Casado paper. Worse, the paper's conclusion is deployed backwards: it explicitly recommends 'a shift from a pyramidal TID used during the preparatory and precompetitive periods TOWARD A POLARIZED TID during the competitive period.' The document cites it as the observational counterweight FOR staying pyramidal throughout and against the Filipas pyramidal-to-polarised sequencing — the paper recommends exactly that sequencing. The '>100 km/week' figure is not in the abstract.

checks.claim: Munoz et al. (2014), IJSPP 9(2):265-272 — '30 recreational runners, 10 weeks, HR-controlled. Polarised distribution produced greater training effect on 10 km performance than a between-thresholds programme.' Strength: RCT.
checks.note: Paper is real and correctly cited (DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2012-0350). But the primary between-group result was NULL: PET +5.0% vs BThET +3.6%, ~41 s, 'not statistically significant overall.' Significance appears only in a post-hoc subset of 12 of 30 runners re-grouped by what they actually did (n=6 vs n=16, p=.038, 90% CI). Presenting this as 'the closest interventional match to this athlete in the pro-polarised literature' producing a positive result overstates it. Note also PET here was 77/3/20 by TIME — 20% Zone 3 by time, which the document's own contraindications call a dose 'no runner at any level performs'.

checks.claim: Filipas et al. (2022), Scand J Med Sci Sports 32(3):498-511 — '56 well-trained male runners... Threshold-velocity improvements predicted performance better than maximal variables did.'
checks.note: Citation is real (DOI 10.1111/sms.14101) and the effect sizes quoted are exact (VO2peak +3.0%, vBLa2 +1.7%, vBLa4 +1.5%, 5 km -1.5%, PYR-to-POL best). Two errors: n is 60, not 56; and the paper concludes 'relative VO2peak' was the primary physiological marker of improvement — the direct opposite of the claim that threshold velocity predicted performance better than maximal variables. That inverted claim is the sole stated purposeMechanism for the Zone 2 threshold session.

checks.claim: Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024), Sports Medicine — '16 weeks preceding 151,813 marathons by 119,452 runners. Mean volume 45.1 +/- 26.4 km/week... This is this athlete's actual population, at his actual volume, for his actual event.'
checks.note: Study is real and the sample size is exact (DOI 10.1007/s40279-024-02137-7; print 2025, 55(4):1023-1035 — the document dates it 2024 throughout). But 45.1 km/week is NOT the sample mean: the abstract states 'the fastest marathoners (120-150 minute finish times) accumulated over three times greater weekly volume (mean 45.1 km) than slower runners.' 45.1 is the 2:00-2:30 band. This athlete ran 3:55:54 (236 min) at 24.4 km/week — he sits in the slower bands at roughly a third of that volume. The document's single strongest population-match argument, and the justification for the whole pyramidal choice, rests on reading a subgroup mean as a sample mean. The 'pyramidal in >80% of the FASTEST runners' finding therefore describes sub-2:30 marathoners, not him.

checks.claim: Muniz-Pumares et al. use 82.3% of critical speed as the Zone 1 / Zone 2 boundary — 'a field-derivable anchor.'
checks.note: Full text is paywalled (no PMC copy; PMID 39616560; Springer redirects to auth). The boundary definition could not be confirmed from any open source. Since this figure is one of only two derivations for the Zone 1 pace ceiling, and the entire block's easy-pace prescription hangs on it, it must not be encoded in config until someone reads the methods section.

checks.claim: Applying the 82.3% rule 'to a working threshold pace of 4:55/km gives 5:58/km' as the Zone 1 pace ceiling.
checks.note: Category substitution plus a large arithmetic consequence. Critical speed is not 'threshold pace': CS is fit from the distance-time relationship, which the document's own validation section (item 3) says to do. Doing it with his data: 5.10 km @ 4:19/km (1320.9 s) and 21.14 km @ 5:02/km (6384.3 s) gives CS = 16040/5063.4 = 3.168 m/s = 5:15.7/km; 82.3% = 2.607 m/s = 6:23.6/km. Using 5.04 km @ 3:54/km instead gives CS = 3.093 m/s and 82.3% = 6:32.9/km. So the cited method yields a Zone 1 ceiling of 6:24-6:33/km, not 5:58/km. The adopted ceiling of 5:45/km is ~40-50 s/km FASTER than the document's own method delivers — and it errs in the dangerous direction on a 4x volume ramp.

checks.claim: 'VT1 heart rate is at or just above 165... 83% of a measured maximum of 201 bpm is 167. The two methods converge at 166 bpm.'
checks.note: Three problems. (a) 0.83 x 201 = 166.83, reported as 167 then silently taken as 166 to manufacture convergence. (b) The document's own first contraindication forbids %HRmax anchoring, citing Stoggl & Sperlich on inhomogeneous metabolic strain — then uses %HRmax as one of the two derivations. (c) The marathon argument runs the wrong way: a 3:55:54 average of 165 bpm includes substantial cardiac drift, so HR was BELOW 165 for the first half at a pace faster than average. Drift makes 165 an upper-ish estimate of VT1 HR, not a floor. Both derivations push VT1 high; neither is independent.

checks.claim: Zone 1 = heart rate below 166 bpm.
checks.note: 166 bpm is 82.6% of HRmax (201) and 75.7% of heart-rate reserve using the 57 bpm smoothed resting HR ((166-57)/(201-57) = 109/144). That is a VT1 estimate, not an easy-run target — the classical easy band is 65-75% HRR, i.e. 151-165 bpm. Prescribing a CEILING with no target band means a machine-checkable rule that passes six runs a week held at 164 bpm. The prose says 6:00-6:45/km, but the config-encodable number is the HR ceiling, and the compliance gate in the validation section checks only '<166'. Encode a typical band (roughly 140-155 bpm) with 166 as an absolute ceiling, or the easy days will not be easy.

checks.claim: 'His marathon target pace (5:27-5:44/km) sits at or just below his VT1 (roughly 5:45/km)... marathon-pace work therefore costs him almost nothing from his intensity budget.'
checks.note: This is the design's keystone and it fails with the corrected VT1. If VT1 pace is 6:24-6:33/km (from the critical-speed fit above), then 5:30/km marathon-pace work is squarely mid-Zone 2, not top-of-Zone-1. Consequences: the 8-12 km MP block prescribed in every long run from week 2 is Zone 2; the Lincoln session's 21.1 km at MP is ~21 km of Zone 2, not the booked '30 km Zone 1 + 3 km Zone 2'. Recomputing week 3 on that basis gives roughly 66 Z1 / 29 Z2 / 5 Z3 rather than 87/8/5 — a threshold-heavy peak week that breaches the document's own Gate C (Zone 2 <=12%) by more than a factor of two, in the highest-volume week of his life. The 'most specific training is also the cheapest' conclusion does not survive.

checks.claim: VT2 pace = 4:55/km, cross-checked against the 1:46:35 half at 5:02/km and 174 bpm.
checks.note: Pace check is right: 6395 s / 21.14 km = 302.5 s = 5:02.5/km, and 174 bpm against an LT HR of 177 is consistent. But 4:55/km is FASTER than his best genuine race pace over any distance beyond 5 km, set in July before a five-week dip, at 85.5 kg. The prescription then defines the Zone 2 session as '5:00-5:30/km' — the fast end of which is at or beyond his actual threshold. Also, a VT1-to-VT2 gap of only 50 s/km (5:45 to 4:55) is implausibly narrow for a four-hour marathoner; 75-100 s/km is typical, which is independent evidence that VT1 has been set too fast. Treat 5:05-5:10/km as the working VT2 pace until a field test says otherwise, and never let a Zone 2 session run faster than 5:10.

checks.claim: Correcting Garmin's LT pace of 4:20.9/km by the 1.118 over-prediction factor gives 4:51.5/km.
checks.note: Arithmetic is fine (260.9 s x 1.118 = 291.7 s = 4:51.7/km; the stated 4:51.5 is a 0.2 s rounding). The method is not. 1.118 is a bias measured on RACE-TIME predictions, which are VO2max-model outputs; Garmin's lactate-threshold pace comes from a different detection algorithm entirely. Multiplying one by the other is out-of-sample extrapolation, and it then anchors VT2, which anchors the Zone 3 floor, which anchors the intensity cap. Three unvalidated multiplications in series. The half-marathon cross-check is the only real evidence here and should be the sole anchor.

checks.claim: Corrected marathon prediction 3:36:12 x 1.118 = 4:01:45 (5:44/km); 'realistic target band, allowing for the fitness he is about to gain, is 3:50-4:00 (5:27-5:41/km).'
checks.note: 3:36:12 = 12,972 s; x 1.118 = 14,502.7 s = 4:01:43, 343.7 s/km = 5:43.7/km — the stated figures are right. The target band is not: it is 2-12 minutes FASTER than the document's own best estimate, justified by fitness not yet acquired in a block whose feasibility is the open question. And the document states marathon pace three different ways — 5:44 (corrected prediction), 5:27-5:41 (long-run anchor), 5:30-5:44 (Lincoln anchor). Config cannot encode three. Every MP session in the block inherits whichever one is picked.

checks.claim: Weekly and block zone arithmetic: 60/80/100/80/60/28 = 408 km; 355 Z1 / 32 Z2 / 21 Z3 = 87/8/5.
checks.note: Independently recomputed and correct. Weekly sums: 55+5+0=60; 68+8+4=80; 87+8+5=100; 68+3+9=80; 52+6+2=60; 25+2+1=28. Week 3 composition (30+57=87 Z1, 3+5=8 Z2, 5 Z3) balances. Block totals 355+32+21=408. Percentages 87.0/7.8/5.1. The week-1 progression figures are also right: (60-14.8)/14.8 = 305%; 60->80 = +33.3%; 80->100 = +25%. Credit where due — the ledger itself is clean.

checks.claim: 'BLOCK TOTAL, EXCLUDING RACES: 408 km.'
checks.note: The 408 km explicitly includes the 33 km Lincoln Half day (week 3) and the 16 km ASICS 10K day (week 4). Only the goal marathon is excluded. Small, but it is the number a config file would carry as the block's non-race volume.

checks.claim: 'Zone 3 is CAPPED AT 5 KM PER WEEK, 21 KM ACROSS THE ENTIRE BLOCK. The cap is absolute, not proportional.'
checks.note: Week 4 is booked at 9 km — 180% of a cap described as absolute and encoded as such in the contraindications. The document acknowledges this in prose but a config rule reading 'Z3 <= 5 km/week' is violated by the plan that ships with it, and the validation section's Gate A then has to carve out an exception for week 4. Two further ledger slips: 5 x 3 min at 4:15-4:35/km is 3.3-3.5 km of work, not the 4 km booked in week 2; and 6 x 100 m strides twice is 1.2 km, booked as 1 km. On a design whose entire safety argument is an exact absolute-kilometre ledger, the ledger has to be exact.

checks.claim: 'By session count, he lands at 5-6 runs per week with 1 hard = 17-20%... he is 80/20 in every single week of the block.'
checks.note: Week 1 has zero hard sessions by the document's own specification (Zone 3 = 0 km, and the single Zone 2 block is conditional on the half-marathon clearing). 0 of 5-6 sessions is 0%, not 17-20%. The claim contradicts the week-by-week table three paragraphs above it.

checks.claim: The absolute-kilometre Zone 3 cap means 'volume risk and intensity risk never peak together' — the design decision that resolves the central tension.
checks.note: This is the best idea in the document and it is correct on its own terms. Fixing hard work in kilometres rather than percentage does make the Zone 3 share fall automatically as volume rises, and it does avoid the genuinely dangerous 'naive 80/20 by distance = 20 km of Zone 3 in the 100 km week' error. It is also directionally consistent with the Muniz-Pumares observation that absolute Z2/Z3 stays flat while Z1 scales. The idea survives even though the source attributions around it do not.

checks.claim: Nielsen et al. (2014), JOSPT — 'progressing more than 30% over a 2-week window raised the risk of distance-related injuries.'
checks.note: Citation is exact (DOI 10.2519/jospt.2014.5164, JOSPT 44(10):739-747, 874 novice runners, 202 injuries). But the abstract states 'Cox regression analysis revealed NO statistically significant differences across three distance-progression groups (<10%, 10-30%, >30%)' for running-related injury overall. Only the distance-related injury SUBGROUP showed elevated rates above 30%, in a study the authors label 'explorative' and close by saying randomised trials are needed. The document presents the subgroup result as the headline. This cuts against the document's own argument, so flagging it is honest rather than convenient — but the '10 times that rate' comparison also sets a one-week jump against a metric defined over two weeks.

checks.claim: Persinger et al. (2004), MSSE 36(9):1632-1636 — talk test corresponds consistently to ventilatory threshold on treadmill and cycle. Strength: RCT.
checks.note: Citation and content verified exactly: N=16 healthy volunteers, both treadmill and cycle ergometer, equivocal stage not significantly different from VT. But this is a within-subject method-comparison study, not a randomised controlled trial; the 'RCT' strength label inflates it. It remains the cheapest useful field method available and the recommendation to use it is right.

checks.claim: Seiler (2010), IJSPP 5(3):276-291 — ~80% of sessions at low intensity, ~20% high intensity; intensification studies in well-trained athletes show no convincing long-term gain.
checks.note: Verified verbatim against the abstract (DOI 10.1123/ijspp.5.3.276), including the '10 to 13 times per week' population and the sentence on intensification studies. The document's added gloss of '15-30 h/week' is not in the paper. Population caveat is correctly stated by the document itself.

checks.claim: Stoggl & Sperlich (2014), Front Physiol 5:33 — 48 well-trained athletes, 9 weeks, POL best: VO2peak +11.7%, TTE +17.4%, peak velocity/power +5.1%.
checks.note: Every figure verified against the abstract (DOI 10.3389/fphys.2014.00033), including n=48 and mean VO2peak 62.6 +/- 7.1. The document's own scepticism about implausibly large effects and an under-dosed high-volume arm is fair. Population VO2peak 62.6 vs this athlete's 53.0.

checks.claim: Esteve-Lanao et al. (2007), JSCR 21(3):943-949 — 81/12/8 beat 67/25/8 with Zone 3 held equal, in 12 sub-elite runners over a 10.4 km race.
checks.note: Verified exactly (DOI 10.1519/r-19725.1): 80.5/11.8/8.3 vs 66.8/24.7/8.5, p=0.03, 10.4 km cross-country. One omission that matters: the block ran FIVE MONTHS, and the paper's own conclusion is conditional — 'provided that the contribution of high-intensity training remains sufficient', i.e. 8.3% by TIME. The prescription here runs 5% by distance, 0% in week 1 and 3% in week 5, and cites this paper as support while sitting below the Zone 3 dose the paper says is a precondition.

checks.claim: Stoggl & Sperlich (2015), Front Physiol 6:295 — '84-95% Z1 / 2-11% Z2 / 2-9% Z3 in preparation phases'; percentage-of-VO2max anchoring produces inhomogeneous metabolic strain.
checks.note: Paper exists and is cited correctly (DOI 10.3389/fphys.2015.00295). Neither the percentage ranges nor the %VO2max-inhomogeneity statement appears in the abstract and the tables could not be reached. Note the deployment is also selective: this review's abstract concludes that 'emerging prospective randomized controlled studies have demonstrated SUPERIOR responses... when applying a polarized TID' — it is used in the document as evidence for pyramidal.

checks.claim: Rosenblat et al. (2019), JSCR 33(12):3491-3500 — meta-analysis favouring polarised, pooling only 3 studies and 112 participants.
checks.note: Verified: 4 studies qualitative, 3 in the meta-analysis, ES -0.66 (95% CI -1.17 to -0.15) favouring POL (DOI 10.1519/jsc.0000000000002618). The '112 participants' total is not in the abstract and could not be confirmed. Omitted and material: all four included studies scored 4/10 or 5/10 on the PEDro scale — the evidence is thin AND low quality, which strengthens the document's own scepticism.

checks.claim: Kenneally et al. (2018), IJSPP 13(9):1114-1121 — zones organised around goal race pace can accommodate multiple periodisation approaches.
checks.note: Verified (DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2017-0327, 16 studies from 493 screened). The document's characterisation is accurate. It omits the review's headline finding — 'pyramidal and polarized training are more effective than threshold training' — which would have supported the recommendation.

checks.claim: Foster et al. (2022) and Burnley, Bearden & Jones (2022), MSSE 54(6) point/counterpoint, page range unverified.
checks.note: Both verified. Foster C, Casado A, Esteve-Lanao J, Haugen T, Seiler S, 'Polarized Training Is Optimal for Endurance Athletes', MSSE 54(6):1028-1031, DOI 10.1249/MSS.0000000000002871. Burnley M, Bearden SE, Jones AM, 'Polarized Training Is Not Optimal for Endurance Athletes', MSSE 54(6):1032-1034, DOI 10.1249/MSS.0000000000002869, plus paired responses at 1035-1037 and 1038-1040. The document's framing — that the existence of this exchange is the honest summary of the evidence base — is the most defensible sentence in it. The specific paraphrase of Burnley's conclusion could not be checked (both are paywalled with no abstract).

checks.claim: Primary falsifier: 'record average heart rate over the marathon-pace block (kilometres 10-20 of each long run) at a fixed 5:35/km, plot weekly; PASS if it falls 4-8 bpm between week 1 and week 5.'
checks.note: Unmeasurable as specified. Week 1's long run is 18 km, so kilometres 10-20 do not exist; week 3's long run IS the Lincoln race; week 6's is 14 km. That leaves weeks 2, 4 and 5 — and week 1, the stated baseline, cannot be collected at all. Separately, expecting a clean 4-8 bpm fall at fixed pace DURING a 4x volume ramp is optimistic: accumulated fatigue commonly holds HR flat or raises it, so the stated FAIL condition will fire on a normal response and be read as 'the model is wrong'.

checks.claim: Compliance metric: bin every second of the HR stream into <166 / 166-176 / >=177 and attribute distance covered.
checks.note: Workable but the gates are defined on the noisiest available signal. HR lag means interval recoveries sit above 177 and over-count Zone 3, while the first 5-10 minutes of any easy run under-counts. Concretely self-defeating in week 6: 100 m strides never reach 177 bpm, so the 1 km of 'Zone 3' the plan books will register as zero and Gate A/B will disagree with the plan by construction. Bin on pace as well as HR, or exclude sub-60-second efforts from the binning.

checks.claim: Stop signal: 'INTENSITY IS CUT BEFORE VOLUME. The intensity plan is the risk buffer around the ratified volume experiment.'
checks.note: The rule is sound and the priority order is right, but the buffer is empty exactly where it is needed. Week 1 has 0 km of Zone 3 and a single conditional Zone 2 block; week 4's Zone 3 is a race that will not be cancelled by an automated rule. So in the two highest-acute-risk weeks — 60 km starting 48 h after an all-out half, and a raced 10K 13 days before the marathon — there is nothing to spend. If the stop signal fires in week 1, the config as written has no legal move. It needs an explicit second lever (cut the long run, or hold the week's volume flat) with a stated trigger.

checks.claim: Lincoln Half abort criterion: 'if his heart rate exceeds 175 bpm at any point before 18 km, he is racing it and must slow down.'
checks.note: Right instinct, wrong number, and internally inconsistent. The same prescription says 'heart rate held under 170 bpm for the first 15 km' — so 170 and 175 are both stated as the limit. 175 is only 2 bpm below the LT heart rate of 177 and 9 bpm above the stated MP expectation; a runner can hold 174 bpm for 18 km and pass the gate while having effectively raced a threshold half at the end of the biggest week of his life. Set the abort at 170 and make it trip on a 2 km rolling average, not an instantaneous peak.

fabricatedCitations: Casado, A., Hanley, B., Santos-Concejero, J., & Ruiz-Perez, L.M. (2022), IJSPP 17(6):820-833 — MISATTRIBUTED. The paper at that exact title/journal/volume/pages is by Casado A, Gonzalez-Mohino F, Gonzalez-Rave JM, Foster C (DOI 10.1123/ijspp.2021-0435). The named co-authors belong to a different Casado paper. The cited conclusion is also inverted: the real paper recommends shifting from pyramidal to POLARIZED in the competitive period, which is the sequencing the document explicitly refuses.

Seiler & Kjerland (2006) — CITATION REAL, CLAIM FABRICATED. The paper does not show pyramidal-by-time vs polarised-by-session-goal for the same data. It reports the three quantification methods agreeing (HR 75/8/17, sRPE 76/6/18, lactate 71/7/22) and says so in the abstract. The document builds its 'single most important methodological caveat in the whole literature' on a finding this paper does not contain.

Filipas et al. (2022) — CITATION REAL, TWO CLAIMS WRONG. n = 60, not 56. And 'threshold-velocity improvements predicted performance better than maximal variables did' is the reverse of the paper's stated conclusion that relative VO2peak was the primary physiological marker of improvement. That inverted claim is the only justification given for the Zone 2 session.

Munoz et al. (2014) — CITATION REAL, RESULT OVERSTATED. Reported as a positive RCT ('polarised produced greater training effect'). The primary between-group difference was not statistically significant; significance came only from a post-hoc reclassification of 12 of 30 runners by actual compliance.

Muniz-Pumares et al. — CITATION REAL, KEY NUMBER MISREAD. Print citation is Sports Medicine 2025;55(4):1023-1035 (the document says 2024 throughout). '45.1 km/week' is the mean for the FASTEST band (120-150 min finishers), not the sample mean, so the claim that this is 'this athlete's actual population at his actual volume' is false — he is a 236-minute marathoner at 24.4 km/week. The '82.3% of critical speed' zone boundary and the R-squared values could not be verified from any open source (paywalled, PMID 39616560, no PMC copy).

Nielsen et al. (2014) — CITATION EXACT, FINDING OVERSTATED. The overall comparison across the <10% / 10-30% / >30% progression groups was NOT statistically significant; only the distance-related injury subgroup differed, in an analysis the authors call explorative.

Rosenblat et al. (2019) — CITATION EXACT, DETAIL UNVERIFIED. '3 studies' is right (4 qualitative, 3 pooled); '112 participants total' is not in the abstract and could not be confirmed. All included studies scored 4-5/10 on PEDro, which the document omits.

Stoggl & Sperlich (2015) — CITATION EXACT, NUMBERS UNVERIFIED. The '84-95 / 2-11 / 2-9' ranges and the %VO2max-inhomogeneity statement are not in the abstract and the full text was not reachable. Do not encode them.
Persinger et al. (2004) — CITATION AND CONTENT EXACT, but labelled 'RCT'; it is a 16-subject within-subject method-comparison study.
verification.riskForThisAthlete:
The document's central safety idea — cap hard running in absolute kilometres so its share falls as volume rises — is correct and worth keeping. Almost everything built on top of it is set too fast, and the errors all point the same way.

THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST. The Zone 1 pace ceiling of 5:45/km is roughly 40-50 s/km faster than the document's own cited method produces. Fit critical speed from his actual races (5.10 km @ 4:19, 21.14 km @ 5:02) and CS = 3.168 m/s = 5:16/km; 82.3% of that is 6:24/km, not the 5:58/km stated, because the derivation substituted an estimated threshold pace for critical speed. Pair that with a Zone 1 heart-rate ceiling of 166 bpm — 82.6% of HRmax, 75.7% of heart-rate reserve — expressed as a ceiling with no target band, and you have a machine-checkable rule that passes six runs a week held at 164 bpm and 5:50/km. That is the exact failure mode the document itself names as fatal (Gate C, "easy runs creeping to 5:20/km"), written into its own zone definitions. On a jump from 14.8 km to 60 km in one week, this is the difference between a block that survives week 3 and one that does not.

THE KEYSTONE CLAIM COLLAPSES WITH IT. "Marathon pace sits at or below VT1, so race-specific work is free" only holds if VT1 is 5:45/km. At the corrected 6:24/km, every 8-12 km marathon-pace block from week 2 onward is Zone 2, and the Lincoln Half is ~21 km of Zone 2 inside the highest-volume week of his life. Week 3 recomputes to roughly 66/29/5 rather than 87/8/5 — a threshold-heavy peak week that breaches the plan's own Zone 2 gate by more than double. Nothing in the plan would detect this, because the compliance gate uses the same wrong boundary.

THE THRESHOLD PACE IS FASTER THAN HIS BEST RACE. VT2 is set at 4:55/km, faster than his best genuine continuous half (5:02/km, July, before a five-week dip, at 85.5 kg). The Zone 2 session is then written as 5:00-5:30/km, so its fast end is at or past his actual threshold. It was derived by multiplying a Garmin lactate-threshold PACE by a bias factor measured on Garmin RACE-TIME predictions — two different algorithms. Use 5:05-5:10/km and cap Zone 2 sessions there.

THE MARATHON TARGET IS UNEARNED AND STATED THREE WAYS. The document's own corrected prediction is 4:01:43 (5:44/km); it then adopts 3:50-4:00 "allowing for the fitness he is about to gain", and elsewhere writes 5:27-5:41 and 5:30-5:44. Every marathon-pace session in the block inherits whichever number gets encoded. Pick 5:44/km, and revise only after the 10K on 2026-10-11.

FOUR DANGERS THE DOCUMENT DOES NOT FLAG. (1) Week 1 is 60 km beginning 48 hours after an all-out half marathon, from a 14.8 km week, with no deload, delay or reduction — the intensity cap does not touch volume, and week 1 has no Zone 3 to cut, so the stated "spend the intensity buffer first" rule has nothing to spend in the single riskiest week. (2) Frequency goes 4 runs/week to 6 plus doubles inside two weeks; the Nielsen evidence measures DISTANCE progression only, so the frequency ramp is unevidenced even by the study cited to bound the risk. (3) Week 4 stacks a 26 km long run and a raced 10K into the same 80 km week, 13 days out. (4) Week 5 opens with 60 km the day after that raced 10K and is called a taper — it would be his second-highest week ever.

TISSUE, NOT JUST HEART. At 85.5 kg tripling weekly volume in six weeks, the binding constraint is bone and tendon, which adapt far slower than the cardiovascular system the whole plan is aimed at. There is no strength work, no surface guidance, no cadence or load-per-kilometre consideration, and no measure of tissue tolerance anywhere in the design or its validation section. The stop signal watches resting HR and pace-at-HR — neither of which detects a developing tibial stress reaction.

WHAT THE EVIDENCE ACTUALLY SUPPORTS TELLING HIM. Only one verified trial matches his physiology and volume — Festa et al. 2019, 38 recreational runners, VO2max 53.2 against his 53.0 — and it is a clean null: polarised 77/3/20 and threshold-heavy 40/50/10 produced statistically indistinguishable gains in speed at VO2max, running economy and 2 km performance, with the threshold group using 17% less training time. The document is right that the distribution label is close to irrelevant for him, and right that Foster-vs-Burnley in the same 2022 MSSE issue is the honest summary. What it should not claim is that the Muniz-Pumares marathon data is "his population at his volume" — 45.1 km/week describes 2:00-2:30 finishers, and he is a 3:56 marathoner at 24.4 km/week. Nothing in rocket's UI should call any distribution optimal.

MINIMUM FIXES BEFORE ANY OF THIS REACHES config/training.ts. Do the talk test in week 1 before encoding a single pace, and widen its step grid to 7:00 and 6:45 — as written it starts at 6:30 and cannot find a VT1 slower than that, which is where the critical-speed fit puts it. Encode Zone 1 as a target band plus a ceiling, not a ceiling alone. Encode one marathon pace, not three. Fix the primary falsifier so it is measurable — it currently asks for kilometres 10-20 of an 18 km run in the baseline week. Give the stop signal a volume lever for weeks 1 and 4 where no intensity lever exists. And do not let the Zone 3 kilometre ledger carry 4 km for a 3.4 km session or 1 km for 1.2 km of strides, because the ledger's exactness is the entire safety argument.
arithmeticErrors: Critical-speed derivation of the Zone 1 ceiling. '82.3% of critical speed, applied to a working threshold pace of 4:55/km, gives 5:58/km' substitutes an estimated threshold pace for critical speed. Fitting CS from his own data: (21140-5100)/(6384.3-1320.9) = 16040/5063.4 = 3.168 m/s = 5:15.7/km; 82.3% = 2.607 m/s = 383.6 s/km = 6:23.6/km. Using the 5.04 km @ 3:54/km point instead: CS = 16100/5204.9 = 3.093 m/s; 82.3% = 6:32.9/km. The cited method gives 6:24-6:33/km, not 5:58/km — so the adopted 5:45/km ceiling is 40-50 s/km too fast.

'83% of a measured maximum of 201 bpm is 167. The two methods converge at 166 bpm.' 0.83 x 201 = 166.83. Reported as 167, then used as 166. The 'convergence' is manufactured by rounding in opposite directions, and %HRmax anchoring is forbidden by the document's own first contraindication.

Marathon target pace stated three incompatible ways: 5:44/km (3:36:12 x 1.118 = 14,502.7 s = 4:01:43, 343.7 s/km — this figure is correct), 5:27-5:41/km (long-run anchor), and 5:30-5:44/km (Lincoln anchor). The adopted 3:50-4:00 band is 2-12 minutes faster than the document's own corrected prediction.
'By session count he is 80/20 in every single week of the block.' Week 1 has zero hard sessions per the document's own week-1 specification: 0 of 5-6 = 0%, not 17-20%.
'Zone 3 CAPPED AT 5 KM PER WEEK... the cap is absolute.' Week 4 books 9 km, 180% of the cap. Encoded literally in config, the plan violates its own rule.
Week 2 Zone 3 volume: 5 x 3 min at the prescribed 4:15-4:35/km is 3.3-3.5 km of work, booked as 4 km.
Week 6 Zone 3 volume: 6 x 100 m strides on two days is 1.2 km, booked as 1 km — and strides never reach 177 bpm, so the HR-binned compliance metric will score this as 0 km regardless.
'BLOCK TOTAL, EXCLUDING RACES: 408 km.' The 408 includes the 33 km Lincoln day and the 16 km 10K day; only the goal marathon is excluded.

Garmin LT-pace correction: 260.9 s x 1.118 = 291.7 s = 4:51.7/km, stated as 4:51.5 (trivial). The method is the error — a bias factor measured on race-time predictions applied to a lactate-threshold pace estimate produced by a different algorithm, then rounded to 4:55/km and used to anchor the Zone 3 floor.

Implied VT1-to-VT2 pace gap of 50 s/km (5:45 to 4:55). For a four-hour marathoner the gap is typically 75-100 s/km; the corrected VT1 of ~6:25 gives 90 s/km. The narrow gap is arithmetic confirmation that VT1 was set too fast.

Primary falsifier is uncomputable in its baseline week: it specifies average HR over kilometres 10-20 of the long run, but week 1's long run is 18 km, week 3's is the Lincoln race, and week 6's is 14 km.

Correct and independently confirmed, for the record: all weekly zone sums (55+5+0=60; 68+8+4=80; 87+8+5=100; 68+3+9=80; 52+6+2=60; 25+2+1=28), the block totals (355+32+21=408, 87.0/7.8/5.1%), the week-3 composition (30+57 / 3+5 / 5), the progression figures (305%, +33.3%, +25%), the half-marathon pace (6395/21.14 = 302.5 s = 5:02.5/km), and the corrected marathon time (4:01:43).

domains.title: Lactate threshold, and the Norwegian double-threshold method

research.tradition: Lactate-threshold training, and the Norwegian double-threshold / lactate-guided sub-threshold interval method (Bakken, Tjelta, Casado, Tønnessen; Ingebrigtsen practice) — adapted, not transplanted, plus the classic Daniels tempo/cruise-interval prescriptions that supply the pace anchors.
research.corePrinciple:
There are two thresholds, not one, and conflating them is the single most common prescription error.

LT1 (first lactate turn point, "aerobic threshold") is the running speed at which blood lactate first rises detectably above resting, ~2 mmol/L. Below it, lactate production and clearance are in balance essentially indefinitely; this is where the mitochondrial and capillary adaptations that make a marathon possible are accumulated at almost no recovery cost. For this athlete this is the intensity that makes 100 km/week survivable.

LT2 (second lactate turn point / maximal lactate steady state, MLSS) is the highest intensity at which lactate appearance and clearance still balance — the boundary between the heavy and severe exercise domains. Above it, lactate, H+ and inorganic phosphate accumulate progressively and time to exhaustion collapses from ~an hour to minutes. That boundary is what "threshold pace" should mean. Critical speed (CS) is the same boundary derived from the speed–duration relationship rather than from a lactate curve; Jones et al. (2019) argue CS is the better estimate of the true maximal metabolic steady state and that MLSS, resting on a single flawed biomarker, tends to underestimate it. Faude et al. (2009) document how badly the terminology has been abused: "lactate threshold", "anaerobic threshold", "OBLA 4 mmol", "LT" and "MLSS" name different points, and the fixed-4-mmol convention is the least individually valid of them.

The Norwegian method's contribution is not a new physiology but an intensity-control discipline. Instead of running tempo efforts to the edge, athletes accumulate very large weekly volumes of work held deliberately BELOW LT2 — 2.0–4.5 mmol/L, measured with a finger-prick meter every one to three repetitions — in broken interval format (e.g. 5 × 6 min, 6 × 2000 m, 10 × 1000 m with 60 s recovery), often twice in one day. Breaking the work into reps and capping the lactate lets an athlete accumulate 60–90 minutes per day near the maximal metabolic steady state while staying recoverable enough to do it again 48 hours later. Roughly 75–80% of everything else is easy (Kelemen et al. 2024; Casado et al. 2023).

The transferable mechanism for a six-week marathon block on a steep volume ramp is exactly that discipline — threshold as a controlled, capped, interval-format stimulus that stops before fatigue — because it is the cheapest way to buy threshold adaptation per unit of recovery debt. The doubles, the 150–180 km/week substrate and the lactate meter are not transferable and should not be attempted.
research.intensityDistribution:
Three-zone model, boundaries at LT1 (HR ~152) and LT2 (HR 177).

Block-average target: ~80% of weekly kilometres below LT1, ~14% between LT1 and LT2 (marathon pace), ~6% at or above LT2. That is a PYRAMIDAL distribution, not polarized — there is deliberately almost no work above LT2 in this block.

Per week (targets in km):
- W1 (14–20 Sep, 60 km): 49 easy / 6 MP / 4.9 at LT2 → 82 / 10 / 8
- W2 (21–27 Sep, 80 km): 64 easy / 10 MP / 6.1 at LT2 → 80 / 12 / 8
- W3 (28 Sep–4 Oct, 100 km): 79 easy / 21.1 MP / 0 at LT2 → 79 / 21 / 0. THE PEAK VOLUME WEEK CARRIES ZERO LT2 WORK. Its hard session is the Lincoln Half at marathon pace.
- W4 (5–11 Oct, 80 km): ~66 easy / 10 MP-ish / 3.7 LT2 + 10 km race above LT2 → 83 / 12 / 5 plus the race
- W5 (12–18 Oct, 60 km): 48 easy / 8 MP / 4 LT2 → 80 / 13 / 7
- W6 (race week): easy only + 2 × 6 min at LT2 on the Tuesday, then the marathon.

Evidence for the distribution, honestly weighted:
- The 75–80%-easy figure in world-class distance runners is well-replicated descriptive data (Seiler 2010; Kelemen et al. 2024 pooling 7 studies of 13 elite Norwegians). It is observational, not causal.
- The one decent controlled test in runners (Esteve-Lanao et al. 2007, n=12 sub-elite, 5 months) found ~80/12/8 beat ~67/25/8 on 10.4 km performance. Small n.
- Meta-analytically the case for polarized over pyramidal/threshold is weak: Rosenblat et al. (2019) pooled only 4 RCTs and rated the evidence limited; Oliveira et al. (2024), 17 studies and 437 athletes, found only a small effect favouring polarized for VO2peak (SMD 0.24, CI 0.01–0.48) and no clear advantage for time-trial performance.
- In the population that actually matches this athlete — 38 recreational runners, 3.2 h/week, 8 weeks (Festa et al. 2020) — a "focused" 40/50/10 distribution matched polarized 77/3/20 on 2 km performance, running economy and vVO2max, in 17% less training time.

So: the choice of pyramidal here is NOT driven by strong comparative evidence, because that evidence does not exist. It is driven by the ramp. He is tripling his habitual volume; the constraint is recovery, and the zone that costs recovery is the one above LT2. Capping LT2 work at ~6% is a risk decision, and should be labelled as one in the config.
research.fitForThisAthlete:
Split the verdict in three, because the tradition is three things.

**The physiology (LT1/LT2 as the organising axis): excellent fit.** He has a measured max HR (201), a corroborated threshold HR, three realised races to derive pace from, and a Garmin that already streams HR and per-lap pace. Every number below is derivable today. This is the right frame.

**The Norwegian sub-threshold interval FORMAT: good fit, and specifically the right tool for this problem.** The central tension in this block is that intensity must not compound an already-maximal volume risk. A 6 × 6 min capped cruise-interval session at 4:55/km costs materially less recovery than a 30-minute continuous tempo for the same time-at-threshold, because the recoveries keep lactate and HR from ratcheting. That is precisely the property the block needs. Note this is a mechanistic argument plus elite practice, not a controlled finding.

**The Norwegian method as actually practised: bad fit, do not attempt.** Every load-bearing feature fails a transfer test:
- Population. Kelemen et al. (2024) describes 13 elite runners at 120–180 km/week. His 24-week average is 24.4 km/week and his all-time best week is 57.1 km. Even after the ramp he is at half their volume, with none of the years underneath it.
- Event. Casado et al. (2023) states plainly that this pattern "has been described only in 1500 m and 5000 m runners" and that "its applicability in other endurance events, such as the marathon, remains uncertain."
- Evidence grade. The same paper states "no controlled studies have tested the efficacy of this training model." There is no RCT of double-threshold. Anyone telling you otherwise is wrong.
- Instrumentation. The method IS the lactate meter. Without one, "double threshold" degenerates into two hard runs a day, which for this athlete on a 100 km week is an injury generator.
- Session count. Scaling elite practice (3.5 threshold sessions at ~150 km/wk) to his base gives ~0.6 sessions/week. One per week is already an aggressive extrapolation, not a conservative one.

**Six weeks.** Threshold adaptations (mitochondrial density, MCT lactate transporters, capillarity) respond in 4–8 weeks, so the window is real but at the short end. The dominant stimulus in this block is the volume; threshold work here is to preserve pace-holding and rehearse race intensity, not to build a new engine. Do not expect the threshold sessions to move VDOT much by 24 October — expect them to stop the volume from making him slow.

**The volume ramp itself.** Worth saying plainly: the ratified 60/80/100/80/60 is 3–4× his recent load and exceeds his all-time peak week by 75%. The commonly cited "10% rule" that this violates has itself failed its one RCT (Buist et al. 2008, n=532 novices: 20.8% vs 20.3% injury rate, no benefit), so the rule is not evidence against the plan. But absence of evidence for a graded rule is not evidence that a 3× jump is safe, and no trial has tested anything like this magnitude. The intensity design above is the lever available for reducing risk, and it is being pulled: zero LT2 work in the 100 km week.
research.howToValidate:
**1. The free calibration event: Battersea Half, 2026-09-12 (3 days away, raced flat out).** This is the single highest-value measurement in the block and it requires nothing new. On the Monday, rocket should re-derive everything from it:
- LTHR := mean HR over the final 40 minutes of the race (this is the standard Friel-style field surrogate; a flat-out half is longer than a 30 min TT so the tail is the steady-state part).
- VDOT := Daniels–Gilbert from the finishing time; T pace := speed at 0.88 × VDOT; MP := T pace + 33 s/km.
- If the derived T pace differs from 4:55/km by more than 8 s/km, the whole prescription rebases to the new value and the block's paces move with it.
- Falsifier: if his Sept 12 half is slower than 1:48 at a mean HR above 178, the block's paces are all too fast and marathon target drops to 4:00+.

**2. Within-session drift on the cruise intervals — the poor man's lactate meter.** rocket already has per-lap pace and per-lap HR. On every cruise-interval session compute: (pace of final rep − pace of first rep) / pace of first rep, at matched HR ceiling. Under 4% (≈12 s/km) means the prescribed pace is genuinely sub-LT2 and the session did what it was meant to. Over 4%, or HR exceeding 177 before the final rep, means the pace is above his true LT2 — drop it 5 s/km for the next session and log the correction. This is exactly the control loop the Norwegians run with a lactate meter, implemented with the data he already produces. Falsifier for the whole threshold prescription: if the pace has to be corrected downward twice in a row, 4:55/km was wrong.

**3. Aerobic decoupling on long runs (Pa:HR).** First-half vs second-half pace-per-heartbeat on every long run over 90 minutes. Target under 5%. This is the standard TrainingPeaks/Friel field metric, and it is the direct field expression of the "durability / physiological resilience" construct that Jones (2024) argues is an independent determinant of endurance performance — and which his own data says is his limiter (marathon VDOT 39.2 vs half VDOT 42.0 vs 5 km VDOT 44.5: a steep fade with duration). Track it weekly. Falling decoupling across the block = the volume is working. Rising decoupling at constant pace = the ramp is outrunning recovery, and this should feed the week-2 reversal condition.
Caveat that must be coded in: heat and dehydration inflate drift (~12–15 bpm going from 21°C to 32°C; ~3.3 bpm per 1% body mass lost). Do not compare a hot run to a cool one.

**4. Resting HR and HRV against the 42-day baseline.** rocket already carries these in the readiness model. His resting HR is 57 smoothed / 50 raw, down from 84 in March, so he has a clean, well-established baseline. A 7-day-mean resting HR rise of ≥5 bpm, or HRV below baseline for 5 of 7 days, during weeks 2–3 is the ramp alarm — and is the objective input the ratified reversal condition should be judged on.

**5. The Lincoln Half at marathon pace, 2026-10-04 — the dress rehearsal and the primary MP validator.** Pass criteria, all three: holds 5:28/km for the 21.1 km, mean HR ≤ 168, decoupling over the 33 km session < 7%. Any failure means marathon pace is revised down before 24 October rather than discovered at 30 km on race day.

**6. The ASICS LDNX 10K, 2026-10-11, as a second calibration point.** A hard 10 km 13 days out gives an independent VDOT and, from the last 20 minutes' HR, a second LTHR estimate. It also directly tests Garmin's over-prediction factor: Garmin currently predicts 43:29 for 10 km; his historical over-prediction factor of 1.118 implies ~48:37. If he runs closer to 45:00 the factor has shrunk and the marathon target moves up; if he runs 48:30+ the factor holds and the marathon target is 4:00, not 3:50.

**7. What would falsify the whole design.** If after weeks 1–2 the cruise-interval pace has been corrected down twice AND long-run decoupling has risen AND resting HR is up 5+ bpm, the correct conclusion is not "adjust the threshold work" — it is that the volume ramp is the problem, and the reversal condition should fire.

prescriptions.sessionName: Easy-running ceiling (the LT1 governor) — not a session, a rule on all other running
prescriptions.structure: Every kilometre not explicitly prescribed as marathon pace, threshold or a race is run at 5:55–6:30/km with heart rate at or below 150. Hills and heat are run by HR, not pace: if HR exceeds 150, slow down or walk, without exception. Roughly 80% of block volume sits here.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: LT1 estimated two ways that must agree. (a) 75–80% of measured HRmax 201 = 151–161. (b) LT2 HR minus 25–30 bpm = 147–152. Take the overlap, use the conservative end: 150. Pace anchor: Daniels Easy pace for VDOT 42 (from his half) = 5:55–6:30/km. Field check available to him: the talk test — he must be able to speak a full sentence comfortably (Rodríguez-Marroyo et al. 2013 validate the talk test against ventilatory thresholds; ICC ≥ 0.80, comparable to HR monitoring).
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Mitochondrial biogenesis, capillary density and fat oxidation accumulated at negligible recovery cost. On a ramp from 24 to 100 km/week this is not the filler between the real sessions — it IS the block. Every beat above 150 on an easy run is recovery capital spent that the 100 km week needs.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: All easy running, 5–6 runs per week, every week.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: HR ceiling 150 bpm (75% of 201). Pace 5:55–6:30/km. For reference his May marathon averaged 165 bpm — 15 beats ABOVE this ceiling, for 3:56, which is a large part of why he faded from a 3:39-equivalent to 3:56.

prescriptions.sessionName: Sub-threshold cruise intervals (the Norwegian-format threshold session)
prescriptions.structure: Warm-up 15 min easy. Then 4–6 × 6 minutes at threshold pace with 60 seconds easy jog between reps. Cool-down 10 min. Progression across the block: W1 4 × 6, W2 5 × 6, W3 NONE, W4 3 × 6, W5 4 × 5, W6 (race week, Tuesday) 2 × 6. Hard stop rules: rep 1 must not be faster than the target pace; if HR exceeds 177 before the final rep, or a rep comes in more than 12 s/km slower than rep 1, the session ends there and the pace is lowered 5 s/km next time.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Pace derived from race performance, not from the watch: Daniels–Gilbert VDOT from his 2026-07-19 half (1:46:35 over 21.14 km → VDOT 42.0), then T pace = the speed requiring 88% of that VDOT = 204 m/min = 4:54/km. Cross-checks: from his honest 5 km (22:01, VDOT 44.5) T = 4:44/km; from his marathon (VDOT 39.2) T = 5:09/km. HR ceiling from measured HRmax 201 and his own race HR (see derivedForThisAthlete). Rep length and 1:6 recovery ratio taken from the documented Norwegian sessions (5 × 6 min at 2.5 mmol, 10 × 1000 m at 3.5 mmol, 6 × 2000 m off 1 min) — expert practice, no trial evidence.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Accumulates 24–36 minutes at or just under the maximal metabolic steady state per session: upregulates MCT1/MCT4 lactate transport and mitochondrial oxidative capacity, which raises the speed at which lactate clearance still matches production. Broken into 6-minute reps with 60 s recoveries rather than run continuously, so lactate is held near steady state instead of ratcheting — same time-at-threshold, materially lower autonomic and musculoskeletal cost. That cost saving is the entire reason this format was chosen over a continuous tempo run during a volume ramp.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: Once per week in weeks 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6. ZERO in week 3 (the 100 km week). Never within 48 hours of the long run.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: Pace 4:55/km, acceptable band 4:50–5:00/km. HR ceiling 177 bpm (88% of measured HRmax 201). Session totals: 20–36 min at threshold. This is ~60 s/km SLOWER than the 4:20.9/km Garmin currently reports as his threshold pace — see contraindications. It is 7 s/km faster than his half-marathon race pace (5:02/km), which is the correct relationship for a runner at his level.

prescriptions.sessionName: Long run with marathon-pace finish (durability, not intensity)
prescriptions.structure: Progressive long run, easy for the bulk, finishing at marathon pace: W1 20 km with last 6 km at MP; W2 26 km with last 10 km at MP; W3 the Lincoln Half embedded (see below); W4 24 km all easy after the 10K race week; W5 22 km with last 8 km at MP; W6 no long run. MP segments run to HR ceiling 168 — if HR exceeds it, the segment ends.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: MP = threshold pace + 33 s/km, the standard offset for a runner whose durability is modest (his marathon VDOT 39.2 sits 2.8 points below his half VDOT 42.0). Cross-check: Daniels M pace for VDOT 42 is 5:05/km, which assumes marathon-appropriate volume he has never had — rejected as too fast. Cross-check 2: Garmin predicts a 3:36:12 marathon; applying his own documented 1.118 over-prediction factor gives 4:01:47. The 5:28/km target (3:50:xx) sits between the volume-adjusted VDOT estimate and the Garmin-corrected one. HR anchor: his May marathon averaged 165 bpm for 3:56, so 168 is the ceiling above which the fade begins.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Targets the limiter his own data identifies. His 5 km, half and marathon VDOTs are 44.5 / 42.0 / 39.2 — a fade with duration, which is the durability or 'physiological resilience' construct Jones (2024) argues is a fourth independent determinant of endurance performance alongside VO2max, economy and thresholds. Running marathon pace on already-fatigued legs trains resistance to the decline in threshold speed and economy over hours, which is what the last 12 km of 24 October will be decided by. Note: MP long runs are near-universal expert practice (Daniels, Pfitzinger, Canova) but there is no RCT establishing them — call it expert practice.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: One long run per week; MP segment in weeks 1, 2, 3 (as the race) and 5.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: Marathon pace 5:28/km (band 5:20–5:35), HR ceiling 168. Implied finish 3:50–3:55. Easy portions at 5:55–6:30/km, HR ≤ 150.

prescriptions.sessionName: Strides
prescriptions.structure: 6 × 20 seconds at roughly 5 km effort (not sprinting), full walk-back recovery, tacked onto the end of two easy runs a week. No warm-up beyond the run itself.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: By effort and duration, deliberately not by pace or HR — 20 seconds is too short for HR to be meaningful. Roughly 3:45–4:00/km feel.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Preserves neuromuscular recruitment and running economy during a block where 80% of the volume is slow. Twenty-second efforts with full recovery produce essentially no lactate accumulation and no measurable recovery cost, so they do not count against the intensity budget. Insurance against the well-known slow-running-makes-you-slow effect of a sudden large low-intensity volume increase. Expert practice; no trial evidence at this dose.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: Twice weekly weeks 1–5, once in race week. Include them in the 100 km week — they are the only 'fast' running that week and they cost nothing.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: 6 × 20 s at ~3:50/km feel, on Tuesday and Friday easy runs. Skip if soreness ≥ 3 (rocket's existing gate).

prescriptions.sessionName: Lincoln Half, 2026-10-04 — run AT MARATHON PACE inside a 33 km session
prescriptions.structure: 10 km easy at 6:00–6:15/km before the start (or the first 10 km of the day as a separate shakeout), then the 21.1 km race at exactly 5:28/km with a hard HR ceiling of 168, then 2 km easy jog down. Total ~33 km. First 5 km must not be faster than 5:28/km — the failure mode of this session is racing it by accident in the first mile.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Marathon pace and marathon HR ceiling as derived above: 5:28/km, HR ≤ 168. Not a threshold session — 5:28/km is 33 s/km slower than threshold pace and 9 bpm below LT2 HR, which is what makes 21.1 km of it survivable three weeks out.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Two jobs at once. Physiologically it is the longest continuous marathon-pace block of the block, trained on pre-fatigued legs at the end of the 100 km week — the maximum durability stimulus available. Diagnostically it is the dress rehearsal that either validates 5:28/km or forces its revision while there is still time. It is also the reason week 3 carries no threshold session: this IS week 3's hard session.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: 21.1 km at 5:28/km = 1:55:24 for the half. Pass criteria: mean HR ≤ 168, final 5 km no slower than 5:33/km, aerobic decoupling over the 33 km under 7%. If mean HR exceeds 170 or he cannot hold the pace, marathon target moves to 5:38/km (3:57) and rocket revises before the taper.

prescriptions.sessionName: ASICS LDNX 10K, 2026-10-11 — raced hard, the taper's only above-threshold work
prescriptions.structure: Full warm-up (3 km easy plus 4 × 20 s strides), race the 10 km flat out, 2 km jog down. Total day ~17 km inside an 80 km week. No other quality that week beyond the Tuesday 3 × 6 min.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Raced — anchored by competition, not by prescription. Expect mean HR 180–190 and a finishing HR at or near 201.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Supplies in one session the entire high-intensity stimulus the block gets: recruitment of the highest-threshold motor units and a VO2max touch, without the accumulated cost of a dedicated interval block during a volume ramp. This is a deliberate substitution — see contraindications on why no separate VO2max sessions are prescribed. Secondary purpose is calibration: an independent VDOT and LTHR estimate 13 days before the marathon.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: Garmin predicts 43:29. His own over-prediction factor of 1.118 implies 48:37. His half-derived VDOT 42 implies 45:35. Realistic target 45:30–47:00. Do not pace it off Garmin's 43:29. Take LTHR from the mean HR of the final 20 minutes and feed it back into the threshold prescription for weeks 5–6.

sources.citation: Kelemen, B., Benczenleitner, O., & Tóth, L. (2024). The Norwegian double-threshold method in distance running: Systematic literature review. Scientific Journal of Sport and Performance, 3(1), 38–46. DOI: 10.55860/NBXV4075
sources.claim: Pooling 7 studies, elite Norwegian distance runners average 120–180 km/week, of which 75–80% is at low intensity (62–82% HRmax). Two to four sessions per week are at anaerobic-threshold pace (82–92% HRmax), continuous or interval, often twice on the same day. One to two weekly sessions above 97% HRmax. Training is controlled by lactate meter or HR monitor. This is the primary descriptive source for the double-threshold pattern.
sources.population: 13 elite Norwegian 1500 m–10,000 m runners across 7 descriptive studies. Not marathoners, not recreational — the transfer gap to this athlete is enormous.

sources.citation: Casado, A., Foster, C., Bakken, M., & Tjelta, L. I. (2023). Does Lactate-Guided Threshold Interval Training within a High-Volume Low-Intensity Approach Represent the 'Next Step' in the Evolution of Distance Running Training? International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, 20(5), 3782. DOI: 10.3390/ijerph20053782
sources.claim: Describes lactate-guided threshold interval training (LGTIT): pace dictated by a blood lactate target of 2.0–4.5 mmol/L measured every 1–3 reps, 3–4 LGTIT sessions plus one VO2max session weekly, inside 150–180 km/week with ~70–80% in zone 1. Documents actual sessions (5 × 6 min at 2.5 mmol off 1 min; 10 × 1000 m at 3.5 mmol; 6 × 2000 m off 1 min; 20–25 × 400 m off 30 s). CRITICALLY, the authors state that the model has been described 'only in 1500 m and 5000 m runners', that applicability to the marathon 'remains uncertain', and that 'no controlled studies have tested the efficacy of this training model'.
sources.population: World-class middle- and long-distance runners. The paper is explicitly a narrative review/opinion piece, not a trial. This is the honest ceiling on the whole Norwegian evidence base: there is no RCT of double-threshold training.

sources.citation: Lu, C., Cui, W., Zhu, Z., Wu, Y., Xing, Q., Pan, B., & Shen, Y. (2025). Validity of smartwatch-derived estimates of lactate threshold heart rate and pace compared to graded exercise testing. Frontiers in Physiology, 16, 1621996. DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2025.1621996
sources.claim: The load-bearing source for rejecting Garmin's LT pace while keeping its LT HR. Against laboratory graded exercise testing: smartwatch LT heart rate estimates were reasonable (MAE ~9–11 bpm, MAPE ~6–7%, no statistically significant difference from the lab reference, though wide limits of agreement of roughly ±22–33 bpm). LT PACE was systematically and significantly overestimated by every device tested — Garmin MAE 2.17 km/h, MAPE 25.78% (p < 0.01). Garmin obtained a usable reading in only 65.22% of single tests. The authors warn the pace overestimation 'further contributes to the risk of distorted intensity guidance' and recommend not relying on watch thresholds alone for prescription.
sources.population: 100 healthy recreational runners aged 18–65 (Garmin subgroup n = 23; also Huawei n = 100, Coros n = 17). This is the right population — recreational runners, exactly like this athlete. Caveat: I could not resolve the per-device HR row cleanly between two extractions of the paper, so the LT-HR error figures are given as a range; the LT-pace figures were consistent across both.

sources.citation: Faude, O., Kindermann, W., & Meyer, T. (2009). Lactate threshold concepts: how valid are they? Sports Medicine, 39(6), 469–490. DOI: 10.2165/00007256-200939060-00003
sources.claim: The definitional authority. Establishes that 'lactate threshold' names several distinct and non-interchangeable constructs (LT1/aerobic threshold, LT2/anaerobic threshold, fixed 4 mmol OBLA, MLSS), evaluates each for validity against endurance performance and against MLSS, and shows the fixed-concentration conventions are the least individually valid. Justifies treating LT1 and LT2 as two separate prescriptive anchors rather than one 'threshold'.
sources.population: Narrative/systematic review across mixed endurance-athlete populations. Definitional rather than interventional.

sources.citation: Jones, A. M., Burnley, M., Black, M. I., Poole, D. C., & Vanhatalo, A. (2019). The maximal metabolic steady state: redefining the 'gold standard'. Physiological Reports, 7(10), e14098. DOI: 10.14814/phy2.14098
sources.claim: Argues MLSS — resting on the single, flawed biomarker of blood lactate — underestimates the true maximal metabolic steady state, and that critical power/critical speed better partitions steady-state from non-steady-state muscle metabolic and acid-base behaviour. Relevant here because it means a lactate-derived or lactate-imitating threshold is a conservative estimate of the real heavy/severe boundary, and because critical speed is derivable from two time trials — a measurement rocket could plausibly obtain without any lab. Note this paper drew published rebuttal (Garcia-Tabar & Gorostiaga, Physiological Reports 2019, e14293) and the point is contested, not settled.
sources.population: Review/position paper drawing on cycling and running laboratory studies in trained adults. Contested — cite as a live debate, not a conclusion.

sources.citation: Seiler, S. (2010). What is best practice for training intensity and duration distribution in endurance athletes? International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance, 5(3), 276–291. DOI: 10.1123/ijspp.5.3.276
sources.claim: The origin of the 80/20 convention: descriptive studies of nationally and internationally competitive endurance athletes training 10–13 times per week converge on ~80% of sessions at low intensity (≤2 mmol/L blood lactate) with ~20% dominated by high-intensity work near 90% VO2max.
sources.population: Nationally/internationally competitive endurance athletes across sports, training 10–13 sessions per week. Descriptive convergence, explicitly not a controlled comparison — Seiler himself frames it as 'what they do', not 'what works best'.

sources.citation: Esteve-Lanao, J., Foster, C., Seiler, S., & Lucia, A. (2007). Impact of training intensity distribution on performance in endurance athletes. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 21(3), 943–949.
sources.claim: The best controlled test of intensity distribution in runners specifically. Over 5 months, a group training ~80% easy / 12% moderate / 8% hard improved 10.4 km cross-country performance significantly more than a group at ~67% / 25% / 8%, with total volume matched. Supports keeping the moderate-intensity band small and the easy band large during a high-volume block.
sources.population: 12 sub-elite 5000 m and cross-country runners. Very small n; the population is fitter and lower-volume-variance than this athlete, and 5 months is far longer than his 6-week block.

sources.citation: Rosenblat, M. A., Perrotta, A. S., & Vicenzino, B. (2019). Polarized vs. threshold training intensity distribution on endurance sport performance: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 33(12), 3491–3500.
sources.claim: Pooled only four RCTs comparing polarized with threshold distributions; found a moderate effect favouring polarized for time-trial performance (largest for 10 km running, ~40 s greater improvement) but rated the evidence base as limited. Honest reading: the case for one distribution over another is weak.
sources.population: Endurance athletes across running and cycling, mixed training status. Only four trials — the pooled estimate is fragile.

sources.citation: Oliveira, P. S., Boppre, G., & Fonseca, H. (2024). Comparison of polarized versus other types of endurance training intensity distribution on athletes' endurance performance: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Sports Medicine, 54, 2071–2095. DOI: 10.1007/s40279-024-02034-z
sources.claim: The largest synthesis to date: 17 studies, 437 participants, interventions ≥4 weeks. Found only a small pooled advantage for polarized on VO2peak (SMD 0.24, 95% CI 0.01–0.48) — the confidence interval nearly touches zero — and no clear advantage for time-trial performance. Directly supports the honest statement that the pyramidal-vs-polarized choice made here is a risk decision, not an evidence-driven one.
sources.population: 437 adult and young-adult athletes, mixed sports and training status. PROSPERO CRD42022365117.

sources.citation: Festa, L., Tarperi, C., Skroce, K., La Torre, A., & Schena, F. (2020). Effects of different training intensity distribution in recreational runners. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living, 1, 70. DOI: 10.3389/fspor.2019.00070
sources.claim: The population-matched trial. 38 recreational runners randomised for 8 weeks to polarized (77/3/20) or 'focused' (40/50/10) with training load matched. Both improved essentially equally: vVO2max +3.2% vs +4.0%, running economy −5.3% vs −8.7%, 2 km performance +3.5% vs +3.0%. The focused group achieved this in 17% less training time. Undercuts any claim that a recreational marathoner MUST train polarized.
sources.population: 38 recreational runners, mean age ~41, VO2max ~52 ml/kg/min, 6.4 years experience, 3.2 h/week baseline. This is the closest published population to the athlete in question — his Garmin VO2max of 53.0 and his history sit almost exactly in this cohort. Limitation: outcome was 2 km performance, not marathon.

sources.citation: Buist, I., Bredeweg, S. W., van Mechelen, W., Lemmink, K. A. P. M., Pepping, G.-J., & Diercks, R. L. (2008). No effect of a graded training program on the number of running-related injuries in novice runners: a randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Sports Medicine, 36(1), 33–39.
sources.claim: The GRONORUN trial. 532 novice runners randomised to a 13-week graded programme applying the 10% rule versus a standard 8-week programme. Injury incidence was ~21% vs ~20% — no difference. The evidentiary point for this block: the '10% rule' the ratified ramp violates has failed its own RCT, so the rule is not evidence against the plan. But equally, no trial has tested a 3–4× volume jump, so this is absence of evidence in both directions, not a licence.
sources.population: 532 novice runners preparing for a 4-mile event. Novices at very low volume — the ramp magnitudes tested are nothing like 24 → 100 km/week, so extrapolation to this athlete is weak in both directions.

sources.citation: Jones, A. M. (2024). The fourth dimension: physiological resilience as an independent determinant of endurance exercise performance. The Journal of Physiology. DOI: 10.1113/JP284205
sources.claim: Proposes physiological resilience/durability — resistance to the deterioration of VO2max, economy and metabolic thresholds during prolonged exercise — as a fourth determinant alongside the three in the classical Joyner model, with large interindividual variability. Provides the mechanism for this athlete's specific signature (VDOT 44.5 at 5 km, 42.0 at half, 39.2 at marathon) and the rationale for prioritising marathon-pace work on fatigued legs over VO2max intervals. I could not verify the volume and page numbers, so they are omitted rather than guessed.
sources.population: Review/position paper synthesising laboratory and field data in trained endurance athletes, with supporting evidence in marathon runners. Construct is well-supported; its trainability is asserted more than demonstrated.

sources.citation: Rodríguez-Marroyo, J. A., Villa, J. G., García-López, J., & Foster, C. (2013). Relationship between the talk test and ventilatory thresholds in well-trained cyclists. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 27(7), 1942–1949.
sources.claim: The talk test (reading a standard paragraph at each stage; 'equivocal' and 'negative' stages) tracks the first and second ventilatory thresholds, with reliability ICC ≥ 0.80 — comparable to heart-rate monitoring and better than RPE. Gives the athlete a zero-equipment field check on the LT1 ceiling that does not depend on a wrist optical sensor.
sources.population: 18 well-trained cyclists. Cycling, not running, and trained rather than recreational — the transfer is plausible but not demonstrated in this population. Foster's group has replicated the talk test against thresholds across several populations, but treat the specific stage-to-threshold mapping as approximate.

sources.citation: Daniels, J. (2013). Daniels' Running Formula, 3rd edition. Human Kinetics. Underlying equations: Daniels, J. & Gilbert, J. (1979). Oxygen Power: Performance Tables for Distance Runners.
sources.claim: Supplies the pace-derivation machinery used throughout: VO2 demand of a running velocity, the fraction of VO2max sustainable as a function of duration, and hence VDOT from any race performance; threshold (T) pace defined as the speed requiring ~88% of VDOT and marathon (M) pace ~84%. I verified the equations reproduce Daniels' published table (VDOT 50 → half-marathon 1:31:35 recomputes to VDOT 49.95; T pace 4:15/km) before applying them to this athlete's races.
sources.population: Model fitted to distance runners across a wide ability range. It is a curve-fit to performance data with decades of coaching use, not a controlled trial; its marathon-pace predictions are known to be optimistic for runners whose weekly volume is low relative to their short-distance speed — which is why marathon pace here was derived as threshold + 33 s/km rather than from Daniels' M column.

contraindications: DO NOT prescribe threshold sessions at Garmin's 4:20.9/km. That figure is 2 s/km SLOWER than his best honest 5 km race pace (22:01 for 5.10 km on 2026-04-11) and 41 s/km faster than his half-marathon race pace. Threshold is by definition an intensity sustainable for roughly an hour; a pace he can hold for 22 minutes cannot be it. Prescribing it turns every cruise-interval session into a 30-minute race at HR 190+, which during an 80–100 km week is the fastest route to the reversal condition firing. The published error direction supports this: Garmin systematically overestimates LT pace (MAE 2.17 km/h, MAPE 25.78%, p < 0.01; Lu et al. 2025), and his specific error — 13.80 km/h reported vs 12.20 km/h derived — is 1.60 km/h, comfortably inside that reported bias.

DO NOT, however, discard Garmin's LT HEART RATE of 177. It is corroborated by his own racing: 177 is 88.1% of his measured HRmax of 201, squarely in the 85–92% band where LT2 sits, and he averaged 174 bpm for 106 minutes in his July half — you cannot average above LT2 for 106 minutes, so his true LTHR is just above 174. Note this is a case where the group-level correction should NOT be applied: the published Garmin LT-HR bias of roughly +6 bpm would give 171, which his own race data contradicts. Athlete-specific evidence beats a cohort mean.

DO NOT re-derive anything from the 2026-04-25 run (5.04 km at 3:54/km). It implies VDOT 51.3 and a 1:30 half — 16 minutes faster than he actually ran three months later — and its heart rate is internally impossible: mean 172 / max 196, LOWER than the slower 4:19/km run's 174 / 199. A faster effort cannot cost fewer beats. Treat as downhill, short-measured, or mis-recorded. rocket should flag and exclude it, not average it in.

NO threshold work at all in week 3 (28 Sep–4 Oct, 100 km). This is the deliberate load-bearing decision of the design: the peak-volume week, which is also the week containing a 33 km session with a half-marathon at marathon pace inside it, carries zero work above LT2. Volume and intensity must not both be novel in the same seven days.

NO separate VO2max or short-interval sessions anywhere in the block. The 10K on 2026-10-11 supplies the entire high-intensity dose. Adding VO2max work would take the least marathon-specific stimulus available and pay for it with recovery capital the ramp has already committed. This is an explicit omission, not an oversight — record it as such in config so it is not quietly re-added.

DO NOT race the Lincoln Half on 2026-10-04. Hard pace ceiling 5:28/km and hard HR ceiling 168, enforced from the first kilometre. A half raced flat out three weeks out, at the end of a 100 km week, will cost more than the marathon can recover from. If he is passing people and enjoying it, that is the failure mode, not the success signal.

NEVER schedule a threshold session within 48 hours either side of the long run in the 80 and 100 km weeks (rocket's existing minDaysBetweenQualitySessions of 2 covers spacing between quality sessions but does not by itself protect the long run — treat the long run as quality for this purpose during weeks 2–4).

Soreness ≥ 3 blocks the threshold session outright (rocket's existing sorenessBlocksQuality gate). Do not downgrade the session to 'easy tempo' — cancel it. There is no version of this block where a compromised threshold session is worth its cost.

DO NOT let Garmin's auto-detected lactate threshold overwrite the block's paces mid-block. Garmin re-detects LT during normal running and will keep offering fast numbers, and it only succeeds in about two-thirds of attempts. The race-derived override must be authoritative, with the Garmin value stored alongside as a diagnostic, not a source.

DO NOT derive anything from the recorded weight of 85.5 kg. It was typed once in March, is explicitly stale, and would corrupt any power, load or energy-cost calculation. Nothing in this prescription uses it.

DO NOT treat the 2026-07-26 run (21.10 km, 1:44:44 timer, 17:27 stopped across 22 laps) as a half-marathon performance. It is a stop-start training run and its timer pace is not a continuous performance; feeding it into VDOT would inflate every pace in the block.
