If the Battersea Half on 2026-09-12 comes in slower than 1:48 at a mean heart rate above 178, treat every pace in this document as provisional and rebase before week 1 starts. Three days is enough time to recompute and not enough time to have committed to a wrong number.

verification.tradition: Lactate-threshold training and the Norwegian double-threshold / lactate-guided sub-threshold interval method (Bakken, Tjelta, Casado, Tønnessen; Ingebrigtsen practice), combined with Daniels–Gilbert VDOT pace derivation as the pace anchor.

checks.claim: Casado, Foster, Bakken & Tjelta (2023), IJERPH 20(5):3782 — describes lactate-guided threshold interval training, 2.0–4.5 mmol/L measured every 1–3 reps, 3–4 such sessions plus one VO2max session weekly inside 150–180 km/week; and states verbatim that the pattern is 'described only in 1500 m and 5000 m runners', that applicability to 'the marathon, remains uncertain', and that 'no controlled studies have tested the efficacy of this training model'.
checks.note: Fully verified. DOI resolves; PubMed record matches (PMID 36900796, 2023 Feb 21). I pulled the PubMed Central full text (PMC10000870) and found all three sentences verbatim, plus the 150–180 km/week, 2–4.5 mmol and 3–4 sessions figures. This is the best-handled source in the set: the research quotes its own strongest counter-evidence accurately rather than hiding it.

checks.claim: Kelemen, Benczenleitner & Tóth (2024), Scientific Journal of Sport and Performance 3(1):38–46 — 7 studies, 13 elite Norwegian runners, 120–180 km/week, 75–80% at 62–82% HRmax, 2–4 threshold sessions at 82–92% HRmax, 1–2 sessions >97% HRmax.
checks.note: Article and every number verified against the journal page. One correction: Crossref gives the issue date as 2023-12-12, so the citation year should be 2023, not 2024. Substance is accurate.

checks.claim: Lu et al. (2025), Frontiers in Physiology 16:1621996 — Garmin lactate-threshold PACE overestimated (MAE 2.17 km/h, MAPE 25.78%), reading obtained in only 65.22% of single tests, LT heart rate acceptable.
checks.note: Verified against the published article. Garmin n=23, Huawei n=100, Coros n=17 all correct; LT-pace figures exact; 65.22% success rate exact. The one slip: the research reports Garmin LT-HR error as 'MAE ~9–11 bpm, MAPE ~6–7%'; the paper's Garmin row is MAE 11.44 bpm, MAPE 7.15% — both outside the stated range, and the error is in the flattering direction.

checks.claim: The Garmin lactate-threshold heart rate of 177 should be kept, because 'the published Garmin LT-HR bias of roughly +6 bpm would give 171'.
checks.note: No such +6 bpm bias exists in the cited paper. Lu et al. report mean ABSOLUTE error (11.44 bpm for Garmin) and explicitly find no statistically significant difference from the lab reference — i.e. no measurable signed bias at all, in either direction. The '+6 bpm' figure is attributed to published literature but is not in the source. The conclusion (keep 177) may still be right on his own race data; the supporting citation is manufactured.

checks.claim: Rodríguez-Marroyo et al. (2013), JSCR 27(7):1942–9 — the talk test tracks the ventilatory thresholds with reliability 'ICC ≥ 0.80 — comparable to heart-rate monitoring and better than RPE'.
checks.note: The paper is real and correctly located (PMID 23007491, 18 highly trained cyclists). But it reports Pearson correlations (r = 0.86/0.94 for workload, 0.79/0.92 for heart rate, 0.79/0.88 for rating of perceived exertion), not intraclass correlation coefficients, and makes no reliability comparison against heart-rate monitoring. Worse, its own numbers refute the 'better than RPE' claim — RPE (0.79/0.88) tracked the thresholds essentially as well as heart rate (0.79/0.92). A statistic of the wrong type has been attached to a real paper and its direction reversed.

checks.claim: Rosenblat et al. (2019), JSCR 33(12):3491–3500 — 'pooled only four RCTs', moderate effect favouring polarized for time trial, 'largest for 10 km running, ~40 s greater improvement', evidence rated limited.
checks.note: Paper verified (PMID 29863593). Four studies met inclusion for the qualitative review but only THREE entered the meta-analysis — 'pooled only four' is wrong. Pooled ES −0.66 (95% CI −1.17 to −0.15) favouring polarized is correct. The '~40 s greater improvement for 10 km running' is not in the abstract or record I could reach: unverified. And the paper's own stated conclusion is that polarized 'may lead to a greater improvement' — the research's gloss ('the case for one distribution over another is weak') is the research's opinion, presented as the paper's finding.

checks.claim: Oliveira et al. (2024), Sports Medicine 54:2071–2095 — 17 studies, 437 participants, small pooled advantage for polarized on VO2peak (SMD 0.24, CI 0.01–0.48), no clear advantage for time trial; supports calling the pyramidal choice a risk decision rather than an evidence-driven one.
checks.note: Every quoted number is exact (PMID 38717713; PROSPERO CRD42022365117 correct; TT SMD −0.01, CI −0.28 to 0.25). But the reporting is selective in one material way. The paper grades the VO2peak result as HIGH certainty of evidence and concludes 'POL is superior to other TIDs for improving VO2peak' — and specifies that superiority occurred in interventions SHORTER THAN 12 WEEKS (SMD 0.40, CI 0.08–0.71). That subgroup is precisely this athlete's six-week case, and it argues against the pyramidal choice. The research quotes the subgroup that suits it (highly trained athletes) and omits the one that does not.

checks.claim: Esteve-Lanao et al. (2007), JSCR 21(3):943–9 — an RCT in which ~80/12/8 beat ~67/25/8 on 10.4 km performance 'with total volume matched'.
checks.note: Paper verified (PMID 17685689); the zone splits are exact (80.5/11.8/8.3 vs 66.8/24.7/8.5) and the performance result is real (−157 s vs −121.5 s, p = 0.03). Two problems. (1) 'Total volume matched' is not supported — the abstract says the proportional contribution of zones 1 and 2 was controlled, not that absolute volume was equalised. (2) The paper's own conclusion carries a caveat the research's design violates: the benefit held 'provided that the contribution of high-intensity training remains sufficient' — 8.3% above the respiratory compensation threshold in BOTH arms. This block has essentially zero work above LT2 in weeks 1–3 and 5–6; its single hardest citation does not endorse that.

checks.claim: Festa et al. (2020) — 38 recreational runners, 8 weeks, polarized 77/3/20 vs focused 40/50/10, matched load; both improved equally (vVO2max +3.2/+4.0%, economy −5.3/−8.7%, 2 km +3.5/+3.0%), focused in 17% less time.
checks.note: Every figure verified verbatim against the abstract (PMID 33344993, Front Sports Act Living 1:70, printed Jan 2020 / eCollection 2019 — the 2020 date is defensible). This is the population-matched trial and it is reported accurately. One caution the research does not make: it compares the cohort's laboratory-measured VO2max (~52) to this athlete's Garmin-ESTIMATED 53.0. A wrist estimate and a lab measurement are not the same quantity, so the 'sits almost exactly in this cohort' claim is softer than stated.

checks.claim: Buist et al. (2008), AJSM 36(1):33–9 — GRONORUN, 532 novices, 10%-rule graded programme vs standard: injury 20.8% vs 20.3%, no benefit.
checks.note: Verified verbatim (PMID 17940147). Numbers exact. One confound the research does not name: the arms differed in DURATION (13-week graded vs 8-week standard), so the trial is not a clean test of ramp rate alone. The research's own honest caveat — that no trial has tested anything like a 4x volume jump — stands and is the more important point.

checks.claim: Faude, Kindermann & Meyer (2009), Sports Med 39(6):469–490; Jones et al. (2019), Physiol Rep 7(10):e14098 with the Garcia-Tabar & Gorostiaga rebuttal (Physiol Rep 2019, e14293); Seiler (2010), IJSPP 5(3):276–291; Jones (2024), J Physiol, DOI 10.1113/JP284205.
checks.note: All four exist exactly as cited, DOIs and page ranges correct. The rebuttal is real (PMID 31758638, Physiol Rep 7(22):e14293) and correctly flagged as a live dispute. Jones (2024) is J Physiol 602(17):4113–4128 — the research said it could not verify volume and pages; they are trivially available, so that hedge reflects incomplete checking rather than a real gap.

checks.claim: Daniels–Gilbert VDOT machinery reproduces the published tables; VDOT from his 2026-07-19 half (1:46:35 / 21.14 km) is 42.0; threshold pace = speed at 88% VDOT = 204 m/min = 4:54/km.
checks.note: I independently implemented the Daniels–Gilbert equations and confirmed the research's own stated self-check (VDOT 50 → half 1:31:35 recomputes to 49.96; T pace 4:15/km). Applied to his half I get VDOT 42.00 and T velocity 204.2 m/min = 4:53.8/km. Marathon VDOT recomputes to 39.25 as claimed. This part of the arithmetic is genuinely correct and genuinely verified.

checks.claim: 'This is ~60 s/km SLOWER than the 4:20.9/km Garmin currently reports as his threshold pace.'
checks.note: 4:55/km is 295 s/km; 4:20.9/km is 260.9 s/km. The gap is 34.1 s/km, not ~60. The same paragraph gets the neighbouring subtractions right (7 s/km vs his half pace, 41 s/km for Garmin vs his half pace), so this is a straight slip — but it nearly doubles the apparent size of the correction being argued for, in the sentence whose whole job is to justify overriding the watch.

checks.claim: 'His half-derived VDOT 42 implies 45:35' for the 10 km, supporting a race target of 45:30–47:00 at the ASICS LDNX 10K on 2026-10-11.
checks.note: VDOT 42 gives a 10 km of roughly 47:45–48:00, not 45:35 (I solved the Daniels–Gilbert pair: a 48:00 10 km returns VDOT 41.97). A 45:35 corresponds to VDOT ~44.6. The error is over two minutes and it is load-bearing: the whole 'realistic target 45:30–47:00' band is anchored on it. Taking his own numbers, the defensible band is ~47:45 (half-derived) to ~48:37 (the Garmin-corrected figure the research itself computes) — the two independent estimates actually agree closely, and the plan discards that agreement in favour of a miscalculation. Practical consequence: he is told to run the first kilometres of a hard race roughly 10–15 s/km too fast, 13 days before the marathon.

checks.claim: 'From his honest 5 km (22:01, VDOT 44.5) T = 4:44/km' — the fast-end cross-check on threshold pace.
checks.note: Two compounding errors. (1) That 22:01 was run over 5.10 km, not 5.00 km; using the actual distance the VDOT is 45.6, not 44.5. (2) Even accepting VDOT 44.5, threshold velocity at 88% is 213.98 m/min = 4:40/km, not 4:44. Both errors happen to narrow the apparent spread between his three race-derived threshold estimates, making the chosen 4:55/km look better bracketed than it is. Correctly computed the spread is 4:37 (5 km) to 5:10 (marathon) — a 33 s/km fan, which is itself the story: his threshold estimate depends enormously on which race you believe.

checks.claim: Threshold pace 4:55/km with a hard heart-rate ceiling of 177, session aborted if 177 is exceeded before the final repetition.
checks.note: These two numbers are mutually inconsistent on his own data and the session will abort itself. He averaged 174 bpm for 106 minutes at 5:02/km in the July half. Running 7 s/km FASTER than that, in six-minute repetitions separated by only 60 seconds of jogging (which is nowhere near enough to clear heart rate), he reaches 177 within two or three reps essentially every time. The plan then says: end the session and drop the pace 5 s/km. Its own validation rule ('if the pace has to be corrected downward twice in a row, 4:55/km was wrong') will therefore fire in weeks 1 and 2 by construction. Either the pace is too fast or the ceiling is decorative, and the plan does not say which governs.

checks.claim: The session is 'the Norwegian-format threshold session' / 'sub-threshold cruise intervals', with the 5 × 6 min structure taken from documented Norwegian practice.
checks.note: The format is copied and the intensity — the entire point of the method — is inverted. I read Casado et al.'s Table 2 in the full text: the '5 × 6 min ... recovering 1 min' session is prescribed at 2.5 mmol/L, in the paper's zone 2, which its Table 1 defines as 82–87% of maximum heart rate and labels 'marathon pace'. The research borrows that rep structure but sets the intensity at Daniels threshold pace with a ceiling of 88% of maximum heart rate — the paper's zone 3 (3.5–4.5 mmol, '10,000 m pace') and above. Calling that 'sub-threshold' contradicts the source it cites. Mapped onto his measured maximum of 201, a genuine Norwegian 2.5 mmol session for him sits at 165–175 bpm, roughly 5:10–5:25/km. The prescribed session is a conventional threshold session wearing a Norwegian label — and it is the one session the whole design is built around.

checks.claim: 'Zero LT2 work in the 100 km week' makes week 3 the de-risked week; volume and intensity are never both novel in the same seven days.
checks.note: Week 3 contains the single hardest session in the entire block: 33 km, of which 21.1 km is continuous at marathon pace at up to 168 bpm (83.6% of maximum), run at the end of the highest-volume week he has ever attempted. Labelling that week low-intensity because no repetition is run at LT2 is a definitional trick, not a risk reduction. Under any load metric — duration at elevated heart rate, musculoskeletal impact, glycogen depletion, days to recover — this is the peak stress week AND the peak volume week simultaneously, which is exactly what the stated principle forbids. The 'lever available for reducing risk' the research says it is pulling has not been pulled.

checks.claim: 'Never within 48 hours of the long run' and the general spacing discipline protect the ramp.
checks.note: The spacing rules are sensible but the plan violates its own framing at the block boundary. He races the Battersea Half flat out on 2026-09-12 and week 1 (60 km — his third-biggest week ever, containing a threshold session AND a 20 km long run with 6 km at marathon pace) begins 2026-09-14, two days later. No post-race recovery allowance appears anywhere. A hard half-marathon needs roughly 7–10 days before quality resumes; here it gets one rest day before the largest training week of his life to date.

checks.claim: Lincoln Half on 2026-10-04: hard heart-rate ceiling of 168 'enforced from the first kilometre', pass criterion 'mean HR ≤ 168'.
checks.note: These are two incompatible rules on the same session. Cardiac drift means heart rate climbs through a long effort at constant pace — his May marathon averaged 165 bpm and would have finished well above that. Over 1:55 at marathon effort he will cross 168 somewhere in the second half at exactly the prescribed pace. A hard ceiling 'enforced from the first kilometre' therefore aborts the session mid-race; a mean of 168 requires a substantial portion of the run to be above 168. As written the athlete cannot satisfy both, and the plan gives him no rule for which to obey when they conflict. The ceiling needs to be a drift-aware band (e.g. ≤165 for the first half, ≤172 thereafter), not a single number.

checks.claim: Post-Battersea recalibration: 'LTHR := mean HR over the final 40 minutes of the race (this is the standard Friel-style field surrogate)'.
checks.note: That is not Friel's protocol and it is biased in the dangerous direction. Friel's field test is a 30-minute all-out time trial with lactate-threshold heart rate taken as the mean of the FINAL 20 MINUTES; for a race he suggests the average heart rate of a roughly one-hour effort. Taking the last 40 minutes of a 1:45 race captures the most drift-inflated and finish-kick-inflated portion of it. On his July half (mean 174 over the whole race) the last-40-minute mean would plausibly read 178–181. That number then becomes the ceiling on every threshold session in the block, raising rather than lowering the intensity — precisely the wrong direction of error during a 4x volume ramp.

checks.claim: Easy-running governor: 5:55–6:30/km with heart rate at or below 150 (75% of maximum 201).
checks.note: The heart-rate number is well-reasoned; the pace band contradicts it. Interpolating his own two data points (5:31/km at 165 bpm in the May marathon, 5:02/km at 174 bpm in the July half) gives roughly 0.31 bpm per second-per-km, which puts 150 bpm at about 6:19/km. So the entire faster half of the prescribed band — 5:55 through 6:15 — sits ABOVE the stated LT1 ceiling, at about 155–160 bpm. Since roughly 80% of 380 km is run to this rule, a runner following the pace band rather than the heart-rate cap spends 300 km above his aerobic threshold. The band should read approximately 6:15–6:50/km. (The 'take the overlap' derivation is also loose: the stated ranges 151–161 and 147–152 overlap at 151–152, and the chosen 150 falls outside it.)

checks.claim: His May marathon fade from a '3:39-equivalent to 3:56' is largely explained by racing at 165 bpm, '15 beats ABOVE this ceiling'.
checks.note: Category error, and it contradicts the research's own later reasoning. The 150 bpm figure is an EASY-RUN ceiling derived from LT1; it has no bearing on race intensity. Averaging 165 bpm (82% of maximum) for a marathon is normal and appropriate — arguably conservative. Meanwhile the research elsewhere states, correctly, that VDOT marathon predictions are systematically optimistic for runners whose weekly volume is low relative to their short-distance speed. That — a 24 km/week average going into a marathon — is the parsimonious explanation for the gap, and the research supplies it itself before discarding it in favour of a heart-rate story its own framework does not support.

checks.claim: Marathon pace = threshold pace + 33 s/km, 'the standard offset for a runner whose durability is modest'.
checks.note: There is no such standard offset. Daniels' own gap between threshold and marathon pace at VDOT 42 is about 11 s/km (4:54 to 5:05); 33 s/km is three times that and is an invention presented as a convention. The resulting 5:28/km target is defensible — it lands between the volume-adjusted VDOT estimate and the Garmin-corrected estimate, as claimed, and is only 3 s/km faster than his actual May marathon pace — but the config note must record it as a judgement call with a stated rationale, not as a named coaching standard, or nobody will ever revisit it.

checks.claim: Excluding the 2026-04-25 run (5.04 km at 3:54/km) because 'a faster effort cannot cost fewer beats' — mean 172 / max 196 versus the slower run's 174 / 199.
checks.note: The exclusion is right; the stated reason is not. That run is 19:40 long and the 4:19/km run is 22:01 — over two extra minutes of cardiac drift comfortably explains a 2 bpm higher mean in the slower effort, so nothing physiologically impossible has occurred. My recomputation confirms VDOT 51.3 and a ~1:30 half-marathon equivalent, which is the real reason to exclude it: it is a 9-point VDOT outlier against three consistent efforts. Keep the exclusion, fix the justification — the wrong rule ('faster always means more beats') will generate false exclusions if rocket ever codes it.

checks.claim: 'Six evenings a week plus weekends' availability supports the prescribed 5–6 runs per week.
checks.note: The plan understates the frequency change it requires and never flags it. His most runs in ANY week on record is 4. Week 3 needs 100 km with a 33 km day, leaving 67 km across the rest of the week — that is 6 further runs of about 11 km, so 7 running days. Even week 2 (80 km) needs 6. That is a 50–75% increase in running FREQUENCY on top of a 3–4x increase in volume, and the research's risk discussion addresses only volume. Session frequency and consecutive-day loading are independent drivers of bone stress injury; running six or seven days a week for the first time is a novel stressor in its own right and belongs in the reversal-condition monitoring.

checks.claim: 'Strides: 6 × 20 seconds at roughly 5 km effort (not sprinting) ... roughly 3:45–4:00/km feel.'
checks.note: Internally inconsistent by about 30 s/km. His 5 km race pace is 4:19/km; 3:50/km is nearer his mile pace. As a 20-second effort with full walk-back recovery this is not dangerous, but the config must not carry both descriptors — if rocket ever converts 'feel' to a target pace, the stride prescription becomes near-maximal sprinting twice a week during a 100 km block, which is a hamstring and calf risk on fatigued legs.

checks.claim: Weekly intensity distribution table: W4 = 80 km as ~66 easy / 10 marathon-pace / 3.7 at LT2 plus a 10 km race; block average ~80/14/6.
checks.note: Week 4's components sum to 89.7 km inside a week specified as 80 km, and across weeks 1–5 the table sums to 389.8 km against the ratified 380 km. Separately, the table assigns 10 km of marathon pace to week 4 while the long-run prescription says week 4 is '24 km all easy' and lists marathon-pace segments only in weeks 1, 2, 3 and 5 — no session in the plan delivers week 4's marathon-pace kilometres. Recomputing the block average from the plan's own rows gives 78.5 / 14.1 / 7.4 (or 4.8% at LT2 if the race is excluded), not 80 / 14 / 6. None of these is individually large, but a config file built from this table will not balance, and the week-4 contradiction means somebody has to guess what week 4's session actually is.

checks.claim: Population transfer is handled honestly — the Norwegian method 'as actually practised' is explicitly rejected for this athlete.
checks.note: Credit where due, and this is the strongest part of the work. The five transfer failures listed (population, event, evidence grade, instrumentation, session-count scaling) are each real and each verified: Kelemen's cohort genuinely is 13 elite Norwegians at 120–180 km/week; Casado genuinely does say the marathon application is uncertain and that no controlled study exists; the 3.5-sessions-scaled-to-0.6 arithmetic checks out on his 24.4 km/week base. The failure is not in the diagnosis, it is that the prescription then quietly reintroduces what the diagnosis rejected — the format is retained at an intensity the source never used, and the volume the source pairs it with is separately being tripled.

fabricatedCitations: NONE FABRICATED — all 15 references exist. I resolved every DOI and confirmed every one against Crossref, PubMed, or the publisher. That is the good news, and it is the thing the athlete specifically asked about. The problems below are misattribution and misreporting, not invention.

MISATTRIBUTED STATISTIC — Rodríguez-Marroyo et al. (2013), JSCR 27(7):1942–9. The paper is real and correctly cited, but it reports Pearson correlations (r = 0.79–0.94), not 'ICC ≥ 0.80'. It makes no reliability comparison against heart-rate monitoring, and its own data contradict the claim that the talk test is 'better than RPE' — RPE correlated with the thresholds at r = 0.79/0.88, essentially the same as heart rate at 0.79/0.92.

MISATTRIBUTED STATISTIC — the 'published Garmin LT-HR bias of roughly +6 bpm' in the contraindications. Lu et al. (2025) report mean ABSOLUTE error of 11.44 bpm for Garmin and explicitly find no statistically significant difference from the laboratory reference. There is no signed +6 bpm bias in that paper or, as far as I can find, anywhere else.

MISREPORTED — Lu et al. (2025) Garmin lactate-threshold HEART RATE error given as 'MAE ~9–11 bpm, MAPE ~6–7%'. The paper's Garmin row is MAE 11.44 bpm, MAPE 7.15%. The research flags its own uncertainty here, which is honest, but the stated range is wrong in the direction that strengthens its argument for trusting Garmin's heart rate.

MISREPORTED — Rosenblat et al. (2019). 'Pooled only four RCTs' is inaccurate: four studies met inclusion for the review, three entered the meta-analysis. The claim that the effect was 'largest for 10 km running, ~40 s greater improvement' is not in the abstract or indexed record and I could not verify it. The paper's own conclusion favours polarized training; 'rated the evidence base as limited' is the research's gloss, not the paper's wording.

SELECTIVELY REPORTED — Oliveira et al. (2024). All quoted numbers are exact, but the research omits that the paper grades the VO2peak finding as HIGH certainty, concludes 'POL is superior to other TIDs for improving VO2peak', and localises that superiority to interventions SHORTER THAN 12 WEEKS (SMD 0.40, CI 0.08–0.71) — i.e. exactly this six-week case, and cutting against the pyramidal choice the research makes. The subgroup that supports the research (highly trained athletes) is reported; the one that undercuts it is not.

UNSUPPORTED ATTRIBUTION — Esteve-Lanao et al. (2007) described as having 'total volume matched'. The paper controlled the proportional contribution of zones 1 and 2, not absolute volume. Related: the paper's conclusion holds only 'provided that the contribution of high-intensity training remains sufficient' (8.3% above the respiratory compensation threshold in both arms) — a caveat this block, with near-zero work above LT2, does not meet.
MISDATED — Kelemen et al. cited as (2024); Crossref gives issue date 2023-12-12, SJSP 3(1):38–46. Substance accurate.

UNSOURCED NUMBER PRESENTED AS CONVENTION — 'MP = threshold pace + 33 s/km, the standard offset'. No such standard exists. Daniels' own threshold-to-marathon gap at VDOT 42 is about 11 s/km. The 33 s/km figure is a defensible judgement call, but it carries no citation and must not enter config wearing one.
UNDER-VERIFIED, NOT WRONG — Jones (2024) is J Physiol 602(17):4113–4128, DOI 10.1113/JP284205. The research says it could not verify volume and pages; they are readily available.
verification.riskForThisAthlete:
Higher than the document lets on, and concentrated in three places the document presents as safe.

FIRST, the peak week is not de-risked. Week 3 (28 Sep–4 Oct, 100 km) is labelled the protected week because it contains no work at the second lactate threshold. It contains the single hardest session in the entire block: 33 km, of which 21.1 km is continuous marathon-pace running at up to 168 bpm, placed at the end of the highest-volume week of his life — roughly four times his 24-week average of 24.4 km and 75% above his all-time peak of 57.1 km. Under any real load measure that is peak volume and peak stress in the same seven days, which is exactly what the plan's own stated principle forbids. The stated risk lever has not actually been pulled.

SECOND, nobody has counted the running days. His most runs in any week on record is four. Week 3 as designed needs seven; weeks 2 and 4 need six. That is a 50–75% jump in session frequency stacked on top of a 3–4x jump in volume, and the risk section discusses only volume. Consecutive-day loading is an independent driver of bone stress injury, and it is the change he has the least history with. It belongs in the week-2 reversal condition alongside resting heart rate.

THIRD, the block starts two days after an all-out half marathon. He races Battersea on 12 September and week 1 — 60 km, his third-biggest week ever, containing a threshold session and a 20 km long run with 6 km at marathon pace — begins on the 14th. There is no recovery allowance anywhere in the document. A flat-out half normally buys 7–10 days before quality resumes.

Two prescriptions are also self-contradictory in ways that will produce bad decisions in the moment. The threshold session pairs a pace 7 s/km faster than his half-marathon race pace with a heart-rate ceiling only 3 bpm above his half-marathon average heart rate, off 60-second recoveries — he will breach the ceiling by rep three every time, and the session's own abort rule will fire in weeks 1 and 2 by construction. The Lincoln Half simultaneously demands a hard ceiling of 168 bpm from the first kilometre and a mean of 168 bpm for the whole race; cardiac drift makes those mutually unsatisfiable, and the plan does not say which rule wins.

Two numbers would put him at real risk if run as written. The 10 km target of 45:30–47:00 rests on a two-minute VDOT miscalculation — his own data support 47:45–48:40 — so he would go out 10–15 s/km too fast in a hard race 13 days before the marathon. And the post-Battersea recalibration takes lactate-threshold heart rate from the final 40 minutes of a flat-out half, which is the most drift-inflated part of it; that inflates the ceiling on every subsequent threshold session, raising intensity across a block whose entire safety argument depends on keeping intensity down.

What survives, and it is a lot: the physiological frame (two thresholds, not one) is correct and every anchor is derivable from data rocket already has. The Daniels VDOT machinery is genuinely verified — I reproduced it independently and it reproduces Daniels' published table. Marathon pace at 5:28/km is conservative and well-triangulated. The refusal to use Garmin's 4:20.9/km threshold pace is correct and correctly supported. The four validation loops (within-session drift, decoupling, resting heart rate, and the two races as calibration events) are the right instruments and are all buildable from data he already produces. The evidence honesty about the Norwegian method's transfer failure is unusually good.

Minimum changes before anything reaches config: rebase the threshold session to a genuine sub-threshold intensity, around 5:10–5:20/km at 168–174 bpm, which is what the source Casado table actually prescribes for a 5 × 6 min session and which will not abort itself; add a recovery week boundary after 12 September; move some of week 3's load off the Lincoln Half day or shorten the marathon-pace segment; correct the 10 km target to 47:45–48:40; take lactate-threshold heart rate from a mid-race 20-minute window rather than the final 40 minutes; widen the easy band to 6:15–6:50/km so it agrees with its own heart-rate cap; and add running-days-per-week to the reversal-condition monitoring.
arithmeticErrors: '~60 s/km SLOWER than the 4:20.9/km Garmin currently reports' — wrong. 4:55/km = 295 s/km, 4:20.9/km = 260.9 s/km, difference 34.1 s/km. Nearly doubles the apparent size of the correction in the sentence whose job is to justify overriding the watch.

'His half-derived VDOT 42 implies 45:35' for the 10 km — wrong by over two minutes. Solving Daniels–Gilbert, a 48:00 10 km returns VDOT 41.97, so VDOT 42 gives ~47:45–48:00. 45:35 corresponds to VDOT ~44.6. This is the anchor for the 45:30–47:00 race target on 11 October and would have him start a hard race 10–15 s/km too fast, 13 days before the marathon. Correct band from his own data: 47:45 (half-derived) to 48:37 (the Garmin-corrected figure the research computes itself).

'From his honest 5 km (22:01, VDOT 44.5) T = 4:44/km' — two errors compounding. (a) That 22:01 was over 5.10 km, not 5.00 km; at the true distance VDOT is 45.6. (b) Even at VDOT 44.5, threshold velocity at 88% is 213.98 m/min = 4:40/km, not 4:44. Both errors shrink the apparent spread between his three race-derived threshold estimates. Correctly computed the fan is 4:37 (5 km) to 4:54 (half) to 5:10 (marathon) — a 33 s/km spread that is itself the important finding.
Week 4 does not balance: 66 easy + 10 marathon-pace + 3.7 at LT2 + 10 km race = 89.7 km inside a week specified as 80 km. Across weeks 1–5 the table sums to 389.8 km against the ratified 380 km.

Week 4 has no session that delivers its marathon-pace kilometres. The distribution table assigns 10 km of marathon pace to week 4; the long-run prescription says week 4 is '24 km all easy' and lists marathon-pace segments only in weeks 1, 2, 3 and 5. Two sections of the same document disagree about what week 4 contains.

Block-average distribution recomputed from the plan's own weekly rows is 78.5% easy / 14.1% marathon-pace / 7.4% at-or-above LT2 (4.8% at LT2 if the 10 km race is excluded), not the stated 80 / 14 / 6.

LT1 'overlap' derivation is invalid: the two stated ranges are 151–161 and 147–152, whose overlap is 151–152; the chosen value of 150 lies outside it. (150 is still a defensible ceiling at 74.6% of maximum — the derivation, not the number, is the problem.)

Strides described as 'roughly 5 km effort' and then as '3:45–4:00/km feel'. His 5 km race pace is 4:19/km; 3:50/km is about 30 s/km faster, nearer mile pace. Harmless over 20 seconds, dangerous if rocket ever converts the 'feel' to a target pace.
Garmin marathon prediction 3:36:12 x 1.118 = 4:01:43, stated as 4:01:47. Trivial, listed only for completeness.

VERIFIED CORRECT, for contrast — VDOT 42.00 from the July half; threshold velocity 204.2 m/min = 4:53.8/km; marathon VDOT 39.25; marathon pace 4:55 + 33 = 5:28/km; 21.1 km at 5:28 = 1:55:21; 5:28/km over 42.195 km = 3:50:40; 177 bpm = 88.1% of 201; 13.80 vs 12.20 km/h and the 1.60 km/h gap; VDOT 51.3 for the excluded April run; 43:29 x 1.118 = 48:37; every repetition-to-kilometre conversion in the weekly tables; and the research's own stated Daniels self-check (VDOT 50 → half 1:31:35 recomputes to 49.96, threshold 4:15/km), which I reproduced exactly. The core pace machinery is sound; the errors are in the cross-checks and the prose around it.

research.tradition: Marathon-specific preparation: Pfitzinger & Douglas (lactate-threshold-centred), Hansons (cumulative fatigue, capped long run), Canova (percentage-of-race-pace specificity)
research.corePrinciple:
A marathon is not an aerobic-power event. For this athlete it will be run at roughly 87-90% of his critical speed for ~3:50 — below VO2max, at or just under the lactate threshold. Two things therefore decide the outcome, and neither is VO2max (his is 53.0 and stable, so it is not the limiter):

(1) FRACTIONAL UTILISATION — how fast he can run while still in a metabolic steady state. This is the lactate threshold, and it is what Pfitzinger's system attacks directly. Raising threshold pace by 10 s/km moves marathon pace by roughly the same amount.

(2) DURABILITY — whether that steady state still exists after 2.5-3 hours. It does not, by default. Two independent mechanisms erode it:
  - Glycogen. Rapoport (2010) modelled the distance at which leg-muscle glycogen empties as a function of running intensity and muscle mass; past that point the runner must burn fat, which cannot support the same power, and pace collapses by ~30%. Smyth (2021), on 4.18 million race records, puts the empirical onset of that collapse at 29.3-29.6 km — the "wall" is a real, dated, locatable event, and 28% of male recreational runners experience it.
  - Decoupling. Smyth et al. (2022), on 82,303 marathoners, measured the ratio of internal load (%HRmax) to external load (%critical speed) and found it rises by a mean factor of 1.16 across a marathon, first detectable at 25.2 km. In the worst third of runners decoupling starts at 19.1 km; in the best third at 33.4 km. Same pace, more heart rate, worse economy — the athlete's whole physiological profile degrades under duration, and by how much varies enormously between individuals.

Generic endurance training addresses neither specifically. Marathon-specific training is the deliberate manufacture of fatigue-resistance AT A DEFINED PACE. That is precisely what all three traditions do, by three different routes to the same place:
  - Pfitzinger: raise the threshold (weekly 20-40 min continuous LT runs), then run long enough to make the raised threshold durable.
  - Hansons: never run further than 16 miles (~26 km), but arrive at every long run already tired from the preceding days, so the long run simulates race kilometres 26-42 rather than 0-26.
  - Canova: express every session as a percentage of goal race pace, and build toward a "specific block" of 20-30 km at 95-105% of race pace — the race rehearsed at race intensity, on pre-fatigued legs.

The three disagree about the long run and agree about everything else: marathon-pace volume, executed under fatigue, is the specific stimulus. That agreement is what this six-week block should be built on.

sources.citation: Doherty C, Keogh A, Davenport J, Lawlor A, Smyth B, Caulfield B (2020). An evaluation of the training determinants of marathon performance: a meta-analysis with meta-regression. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport 23(2):182-188. DOI 10.1016/j.jsams.2019.09.013
sources.claim: Across 85 studies and 137 cohorts, every training covariate examined — average weekly distance, number of weekly runs, peak weekly distance, NUMBER OF RUNS >=32 km in the pre-marathon block, average training pace, DISTANCE OF THE LONGEST RUN, and weekly running hours — showed a negative association with marathon finish time (R2 0.38-0.81, p<0.001). Marathon non-finish rate was 7.27% (95% CI 6.09-8.65%). CAUTION: this is cohort-level meta-regression on observational data. It cannot separate 'long runs cause fast marathons' from 'fast marathoners do long runs'; every covariate is collinear with overall ability and total volume. It establishes association, not a dose requirement.
sources.population: Elite and recreational marathon runners, 137 cohorts, 25% female

sources.citation: Muniz-Pumares D, Hunter B, Meyler S, Maunder E, Smyth B (2024). The Training Intensity Distribution of Marathon Runners Across Performance Levels. Sports Medicine. DOI 10.1007/s40279-024-02137-7
sources.claim: The single most directly applicable dataset for this athlete. 16 weeks of training before 151,813 marathons by 119,452 runners. Mean training volume 45.1 +/- 26.4 km/wk, 3.6 sessions/wk, mean weekly long run 19.6 +/- 9.6 km, mean finish 230.2 min (3:50) — i.e. the average runner in this dataset is almost exactly this athlete's target. Overall intensity distribution was Z1 49.0% / Z2 35.3% / Z3 15.7% of training TIME (zones: Z1 below 82.3% of critical speed; Z2 between that and critical speed; Z3 above critical speed). Faster runners accumulated more volume ALMOST ENTIRELY IN Z1: absolute Z2 and Z3 time was near-constant across all performance levels. Pyramidal distribution (Z1>Z2>Z3) was used by >80% of the fastest runners. OLS regression: each additional percentage point of training time in Z1 predicted -0.30 min finish time; each additional point in Z2 +0.33 min; each additional point in Z3 +0.76 min. The fastest runners still did >20% in Z2, and the authors conclude ~20% Z2 is likely required but has diminishing returns beyond that. Critically for the long-run question: TOTAL DISTANCE covered in long runs across the block carried a coefficient of -0.13 min per km (more long-run km = faster), while NUMBER of long runs carried a positive coefficient (+2.70 min) — consistent with cumulative long-run volume mattering rather than any individual run's length.
sources.population: 119,452 recreational marathon runners, full performance range, mean finish 3:50

sources.citation: Smyth B (2021). How recreational marathon runners hit the wall: a large-scale data analysis of late-race pacing collapse in the marathon. PLOS ONE 16(5):e0251513. DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0251513
sources.claim: 4,183,362 race records, 2.74 million runners, 270 marathons. 'Hitting the wall' defined as slowing >=25% for >=5 km after the 20 km mark, relative to the runner's own km 5-20 pace. 28% of men and 17% of women hit the wall (OR 1.43). Mean onset 29.3-29.6 km. Mean finish-time cost 31.5 min (men) / 33.2 min (women). Most relevant finding for this athlete: incidence rises sharply when a runner is chasing a personal best — 40% of men hit the wall in the three years around a PB versus 26% in other years. Faster runners pay a larger absolute time penalty. The paper offers no specific recommended pace margin.
sources.population: 2.74 million recreational marathon runners, 38 cities, 2005-2019

sources.citation: Smyth B, Maunder E, Meyler S, Hunter B, Muniz-Pumares D (2022). Decoupling of Internal and External Workload During a Marathon: An Analysis of Durability in 82,303 Recreational Runners. Sports Medicine. DOI 10.1007/s40279-022-01680-5
sources.claim: Provides a durability metric computable entirely from a Garmin file. Decoupling = (%HRmax / %critical speed) in the 35-40 km segment divided by the same ratio in the 5-10 km segment. Mean decoupling 1.16 +/- 0.22, first detected at 25.2 +/- 9.9 km. Low-decoupling group (<1.10, 34.5% of runners) raced at 88 +/- 6% of critical speed, finished in 217.3 +/- 33.1 min, and decoupled first at 33.4 +/- 9.0 km. High-decoupling group (>=1.20) raced at only 82 +/- 7% CS, finished in 238.5 +/- 30.7 min, decoupled at 19.1 +/- 6.8 km. Adding decoupling to a critical-speed model cut marathon prediction error from 6.45% to 5.16%.
sources.population: 82,303 recreational marathon runners (13,125 female)

sources.citation: Smyth B, Muniz-Pumares D (2020). Calculation of Critical Speed from Raw Training Data in Recreational Marathon Runners. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 52(12):2637-2645. DOI 10.1249/MSS.0000000000002412
sources.claim: Critical speed can be estimated from ordinary training-file data without lab testing, and predicts marathon performance and pacing. Recreational runners in this dataset completed the marathon at approximately 85% of their critical speed. This is the empirical basis for deriving marathon pace as a fraction of threshold rather than from a race-time equivalence table.
sources.population: >25,000 recreational runners logging to an online fitness platform before big-city marathons

sources.citation: Smyth B, Lawlor A (2021). Longer Disciplined Tapers Improve Marathon Performance for Recreational Runners. Frontiers in Sports and Active Living 3:735220. DOI 10.3389/fspor.2021.735220
sources.claim: Analysis of >158,000 recreational marathoners' training. A strict 3-week taper (disciplined, monotonic volume reduction) was associated with a median finish-time saving of 5 min 32 s versus less disciplined tapers. 64% of recreational runners adopt looser 2-3 week tapers. Observational, so the saving is an association, not a demonstrated causal effect.
sources.population: >158,000 recreational marathon runners

sources.citation: Maunder E, Seiler S, Mildenhall MJ, Kilding AE, Plews DJ (2021). The Importance of 'Durability' in the Physiological Profiling of Endurance Athletes. Sports Medicine 51(8):1619-1628. DOI 10.1007/s40279-021-01459-0
sources.claim: Establishes 'durability' as a distinct trainable quality, defined as the time of onset and magnitude of deterioration in physiological-profile characteristics during prolonged exercise. The key implication for planning: a threshold or VO2max value measured rested does not describe the athlete at 30 km, and using rested values to set race pace systematically over-prescribes.
sources.population: Narrative review; trained and elite endurance athletes

sources.citation: Jones AM, Kirby BS (2025). Physiological Resilience: What Is It and How Might It Be Trained? Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 35(3):e70032. DOI 10.1111/sms.70032
sources.claim: The most direct published statement of the mechanism behind marathon-pace long runs. States that regular prolonged exercise sessions 'especially when these include bouts of high-intensity exercise at race pace or above, or a progressive increase in intensity in the face of developing fatigue' may be an effective means of enhancing resilience; heavy strength and plyometric training also help; and multi-year training consistency promotes resilience. Explicitly notes the physiological underpinnings remain elusive and practical testing protocols are still being developed — this is a reasoned review, not trial evidence that MP-in-long-run beats easy long runs.
sources.population: Narrative review; endurance athletes generally

sources.citation: Rapoport BI (2010). Metabolic Factors Limiting Performance in Marathon Runners. PLoS Computational Biology 6(10):e1000960. DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1000960
sources.claim: A computational model estimating the distance at which a given runner exhausts glycogen as a function of running intensity, VO2max and leg muscle mass. Concludes that more than two-fifths of marathon attempters experience performance-limiting carbohydrate depletion, and that the two levers are (a) setting a personally appropriate pace and (b) mid-race carbohydrate intake. It is a MODEL, validated against physiological literature rather than a prospective trial, and its individual predictions have not been prospectively tested at scale.
sources.population: Modelling study calibrated to marathon runners across ability levels

sources.citation: Jeukendrup A (2014). A Step Towards Personalized Sports Nutrition: Carbohydrate Intake During Exercise. Sports Medicine 44(Suppl 1):S25-S33. DOI 10.1007/s40279-014-0148-z
sources.claim: Exogenous carbohydrate oxidation from a single carbohydrate source saturates at ~60 g/h because intestinal SGLT1 transporters saturate. For exercise of 2-3 h, ~60 g/h is the recommendation; for longer events, ~90 g/h, achievable only by combining glucose and fructose, which use different transporters. Guidelines are duration- and intensity-dependent, and specify carbohydrate TYPE, not just amount.
sources.population: Review of controlled laboratory studies in trained endurance athletes

sources.citation: Jeukendrup A (2017). Training the Gut for Athletes. Sports Medicine 47(Suppl 1):101-110. DOI 10.1007/s40279-017-0690-6
sources.claim: The gastrointestinal tract and its nutrient transporters adapt to habitual intake in a nutrient-specific way. Gastric emptying, stomach comfort and perceptions of fullness can all be trained by progressive exposure to high carbohydrate intake during training. This is the evidence base for rehearsing race-day fuelling rate in training rather than attempting it first on race day.
sources.population: Review; endurance athletes

sources.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM (2016). American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 48(3):543-568. DOI 10.1249/MSS.0000000000000852
sources.claim: Joint ACSM / Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics / Dietitians of Canada position stand. Sets daily carbohydrate at 7-12 g/kg for high-volume endurance training and pre-race loading; 30-60 g/h during exercise of 1-2.5 h and up to 90 g/h beyond 2.5 h using multiple transportable carbohydrates; pre-event meal 1-4 g/kg carbohydrate consumed 1-4 h before.
sources.population: Expert consensus position stand; athletes generally

sources.citation: Bussau VA, Fairchild TJ, Rao A, Steele P, Fournier PA (2002). Carbohydrate loading in human muscle: an improved 1 day protocol. European Journal of Applied Physiology 87(3):290-295. DOI 10.1007/s00421-002-0621-5
sources.claim: Eight endurance-trained men eating 10 g/kg/day of high-glycaemic-index carbohydrate while physically inactive raised muscle glycogen from 95 (5) to 180 (15) mmol/kg wet mass in ONE day; two further days of the same diet added nothing. Maximal glycogen loading takes 24 h, not three days, provided activity is near zero. Small sample (n=8), trained men only.
sources.population: 8 endurance-trained male athletes

sources.citation: Guest NS, VanDusseldorp TA, Nelson MT, et al. (2021). International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: caffeine and exercise performance. Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition 18:1. DOI 10.1186/s12970-020-00383-4
sources.claim: 3-6 mg/kg body mass consistently improves exercise performance; aerobic endurance shows the most consistent moderate-to-large benefit, though magnitude varies substantially between individuals. Typical timing 60 min pre-exercise. Minimum effective dose may be as low as 2 mg/kg. Doses around 9 mg/kg add side effects without added benefit.
sources.population: Expert consensus reviewing controlled trials; trained and recreational athletes

sources.citation: Hew-Butler T, Rosner MH, Fowkes-Godek S, et al. (2015). Statement of the Third International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Development Conference, Carlsbad, California, 2015. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine 25(4):303-320.
sources.claim: 17-expert international consensus. The safest individualised hydration strategy before, during and immediately after exercise is to drink palatable fluids when thirsty. Drinking to thirst will in most cases prevent both dilutional exercise-associated hyponatraemia and performance decrement from excessive dehydration. Directly contradicts fixed-schedule drinking plans.
sources.population: Expert consensus; endurance event participants

sources.citation: Stellingwerff T (2012). Case Study: Nutrition and Training Periodization in Three Elite Marathon Runners. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism 22(5):392-400.
sources.claim: Three elite male marathoners averaged 182 km/wk (peak 231 km/wk) across ~13 sessions/wk. Of 606 training sessions, 74% were Zone 1, 11% Zone 2 (at lactate threshold) and 15% Zone 3. They used 2.5 +/- 2.3 low-carbohydrate-availability sessions per week. On race day they took only 61 +/- 15 g carbohydrate per hour in 604 +/- 156 mL/h (10.1% solution), delivered as ~15 g in ~150 mL every ~15 min. Finish times 2:11:23, 2:12:39 (both PBs) and 2:16:17. n=3; describes elite practice, proves nothing causally.
sources.population: 3 elite male marathon runners

sources.citation: Kenneally M, Casado A, Santos-Concejero J (2018). The Effect of Periodization and Training Intensity Distribution on Middle- and Long-Distance Running Performance: A Systematic Review. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance 13(9):1114-1121.
sources.claim: Systematic review across PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science comparing pyramidal, polarised and threshold intensity distributions in middle- and long-distance runners, calculating zones relative to goal race pace where possible. The honest summary of this literature is that no single distribution is established as superior for the marathon specifically; the evidence base is small and heterogeneous. I did not obtain the full text in this session, so I am citing it for the existence and framing of the question rather than for a specific numeric conclusion.
sources.population: Middle- and long-distance runners, mixed ability levels

sources.citation: Nielsen RO, Parner ET, Nohr EA, Sorensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S (2014). Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries: an association which varies according to type of injury. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy 44(10):739-747. DOI 10.2519/jospt.2014.5164
sources.claim: 874 novice runners followed for one year with GPS watches. Runners progressing weekly distance by more than 30% showed an increased rate of DISTANCE-RELATED injuries (patellofemoral pain, ITB syndrome, medial tibial stress syndrome, gluteus medius injury, greater trochanteric bursitis, TFL injury, patellar tendinopathy) versus those progressing under 10%. IMPORTANT HONESTY NOTE: the hazard ratio was 1.59 with 95% CI 0.96-2.66 and p = .07 — the confidence interval crosses 1 and the result is NOT statistically significant. This is the most-cited evidence against rapid volume ramps and it is weaker than its reputation. It is also a novice cohort, not a runner with a marathon behind him.
sources.population: 874 healthy NOVICE runners on self-structured programmes

sources.citation: Pfitzinger P, Douglas S. Advanced Marathoning, 3rd edition. Human Kinetics, 2019.
sources.claim: The lactate-threshold-centred marathon system. Lactate-threshold runs of at least 20 minutes (progressing to ~40 min) at 15 km-to-half-marathon race pace, or 82-91% of maximum heart rate. States that successful marathoners have lactate thresholds at 84-88% of VO2max and elites at 88-91%. Introduces medium-long runs (19-24 km midweek) and marathon-pace long runs, and places a tune-up race roughly three weeks out. EXPERT PRACTICE, NO TRIAL EVIDENCE — the plans have never been tested against a control programme.
sources.population: Recreational-to-competitive marathon runners; the book's plans are stratified by weekly volume (18/55, 18/70, 18/85 etc.)

sources.citation: Humphrey L, with Hanson K, Hanson K. Hansons Marathon Method, 2nd edition. VeloPress, 2016 (1st ed. 2012).
sources.claim: The explicit counter-position on the long run. Caps the long run at 16 miles (~26 km) and relies on 'cumulative fatigue': the athlete arrives at every long run already tired from the preceding days, so a 16-miler simulates race kilometres 26-42 rather than 0-26. The stated rationale for the cap is recovery cost — after a 35 km run most runners need 7-10 days before returning to quality work, which limits an 18-week block to only 3-4 such runs, whereas shorter long runs permit more total quality work across the block. Prescribes tempo runs AT marathon pace building to 10 miles (16 km). EXPERT PRACTICE, NO TRIAL EVIDENCE — no controlled comparison of a capped versus uncapped long run exists.
sources.population: Recreational marathon runners; the method assumes 6 running days per week

sources.citation: Canova R. Marathon Training: A Scientific Approach. IAAF RDC, 1999.
sources.claim: The percentage-of-race-pace system. Every session is expressed as a percentage of goal marathon race pace: regeneration 70-80%, fundamental 80-90% (high-end aerobic support), special 90-95% (threshold support), specific 95-105% (the race itself). The 'specific block' — repeated every 3-4 weeks in the specific period — is two same-day sessions, classically 10 km at 90% MP plus 20 km at MP in the morning and again in the afternoon, designed to accumulate large volumes of race-pace running on progressively depleted legs. Marathon-pace intervals come in extensive form (e.g. 3 x 7 km at 103-105% MP with 1 km at 98% MP) and intensive form (e.g. 10 x 1 km at 105% MP with 1 km at 100-101% MP). EXPERT PRACTICE, NO TRIAL EVIDENCE, and developed on world-class athletes running 200+ km/wk — the double-session block is not transferable to this athlete.
sources.population: World-class marathon runners (Canova coached multiple world champions and 2:04-2:06 men)

sources.citation: Mujika I, Padilla S (2003). Scientific bases for precompetition tapering strategies. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 35(7):1182-1187.
sources.claim: The classic taper framework: reduce training VOLUME substantially (commonly cited as 41-60%) while MAINTAINING intensity and session frequency. This is the basis for keeping the ASICS 10K as hard running inside the taper while cutting weekly kilometres. HONESTY FLAG: I am confident this paper exists and this is its substance, but my web-search budget was exhausted before I could re-verify the citation details against the source in this session. Treat the volume percentages as approximate until checked.
sources.population: Review of tapering studies in trained endurance athletes

prescriptions.sessionName: Recalibrate every pace from the 12 September Battersea Half — BEFORE anything else
prescriptions.structure:
Not a training session; a mandatory data step on race day, 12 Sep 2026. Take the finish time, normalise to 21.0975 km, then compute three numbers and write them to config/training.ts with their derivation as a comment:
  LT_PACE (= critical speed pace) = half_pace x 0.967
  MP_TARGET = LT_PACE / 0.88
  Z1_CEILING (slowest pace that is still Zone 2) = LT_PACE / 0.823
Every session below is expressed relative to these three. Re-run on 11 Oct after the 10K as a directional check only.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Derived, not asserted. LT_PACE x 0.967: Riegel-extrapolating a half time to the ~12 km / ~58 min distance at which heart rate sits at the lactate threshold gives half_pace x (12/21.0975)^0.06 = half_pace x 0.967. MP as 88% of critical speed comes from Smyth & Muniz-Pumares (2020), who found recreational runners race the marathon at ~85% of CS, and Smyth et al. (2022), whose low-decoupling (best-finishing) group raced at 88 +/- 6% CS. The Zone 1 ceiling at 82.3% of CS is the boundary used by Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024) on 151,813 marathons.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Prevents the single most dangerous error available in this athlete's dataset. Garmin's auto-detected lactate-threshold pace of 4:20.9/km is roughly 30 s/km too fast and MUST NOT be used to set any session. Three independent checks say so: (a) Riegel from his 19 Jul half (1:46:35 for 21.14 km, 5:02/km) puts a 60-minute effort at 4:52/km; (b) his own heart rate — he averaged 174 bpm at 5:02/km for 1:47, and Garmin's own LTHR is 177, so threshold pace cannot be more than ~10 s/km faster than 5:02; (c) 4:20.9/km is almost exactly his 11 Apr 5 km pace (4:19/km), which is what Garmin appears to have fitted to. A 25-minute 'tempo' at 4:21/km would be a near-maximal 10 km effort. On an 80-100 km week that is an overreaching or injury event, and it is the failure mode most likely to end this block.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete:
PROVISIONAL, from the 19 Jul half (5:02.4/km over 21.14 km = 1:46:22 for 21.0975 km); replace on 12 Sep.
  LT / critical-speed pace: 4:52/km (12.33 km/h). HR 172-178 (86-89% of true HRmax 201; his measured LTHR of 177 = 88% sits inside this).
  Zone 1 ceiling: 5:55/km — anything slower than this is Zone 1. Easy running should be 6:10-6:50/km, HR <= 150 (75% HRmax), to sit clearly inside it.
  Zone 3 floor: 4:52/km — anything faster than this is Zone 3. Note this means even his threshold reps are TOP of Zone 2, not Zone 3. He needs almost no Zone 3 at all.
  MARATHON PACE: 5:32/km = 3:53:29. Acceptable band 5:28-5:36/km (89% to 87% of CS) = 3:50:40 to 3:56:20. HR ceiling 168; expect 160-166 (his 10 May marathon averaged 165 bpm at 5:31/km).
  Marathon-pace-minus-10 (for long-run finishes): 5:22/km.
  10 km target for 11 Oct: 4:35-4:45/km (45:50-47:30).
SANITY CHECK ON GARMIN: Garmin predicts 3:36:12 for the marathon. Applying the measured 1.118 over-prediction factor gives 4:01:45. The 5:32/km target sits between that and the Riegel-from-half figure of 3:41, which is where an honest estimate belongs. Do not let Garmin's number set race pace.
DO NOT ATTEMPT A TWO-POINT CRITICAL-SPEED FIT from his 25 Apr 5 km and 19 Jul half: the linear fit returns D' = 1397 m, four to ten times a physiologically plausible value, because the two efforts are three months and a fitness state apart. The fit is invalid; use the single-anchor rule above.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: Once on 12 Sep; directional re-check once on 11 Oct

prescriptions.sessionName: Marathon-pace long run (the spine of the block)
prescriptions.structure:
One long run per week, easy-paced with a continuous marathon-pace block placed at the END so that MP running happens on already-fatigued legs. Progression across the six weeks:
  W1 (14-20 Sep, 60 km): 24 km = 16 km easy + 8 km at MP
  W2 (21-27 Sep, 80 km): 30 km = 20 km easy + 10 km at MP (final 3 km at MP-10 if HR allows)
  W3 (28 Sep-4 Oct, 100 km): the Lincoln session, described separately
  W4 (5-11 Oct, 80 km): 26 km = 18 km easy + 8 km at MP, placed WEDNESDAY 7 Oct (never the day before the 10K)
  W5 (12-18 Oct, 60 km): 21 km = 13 km easy + 8 km at MP
  W6 (race week): 12 km = 8 km easy + 4 km at MP, Tuesday 20 Oct
HARD CEILING: no single run may exceed 3 h 15 min on feet. That is the binding constraint, not distance.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Easy portion: slower than Z1_CEILING (LT_PACE / 0.823), targeted 20-40 s/km slower still, HR <= 75% HRmax. MP portion: MP_TARGET = LT_PACE / 0.88, with an absolute HR ceiling of 84% HRmax; if HR exceeds that at target pace, slow down and record it — that is a durability reading, not a discipline failure.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Attacks durability, the half of the marathon problem that easy long runs do not reach. Jones & Kirby (2025) state that prolonged sessions containing bouts at race pace or above are the mechanism-level recommendation for training physiological resilience. Placing the MP block last is Hansons' cumulative-fatigue logic and Canova's specific-block logic in a single session: the MP kilometres land in the 16-33 km window where Smyth et al. (2022) find decoupling begins (mean onset 25.2 km) and where Smyth (2021) finds the wall (mean onset 29.3-29.6 km). It is also the block's main Zone 2 supply — Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024) find the fastest recreational runners still complete >20% of training in Zone 2, and marathon pace at 90% of this athlete's critical speed sits squarely in upper Zone 2.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete:
MP block paces (provisional): 5:32/km, HR ceiling 168, target 160-166. Easy portions 6:20-6:40/km, HR <= 150. MP-10 finish: 5:22/km.
W1 duration: 16 km x 6:30 + 8 km x 5:32 = 1:44 + 0:44 = 2:28.
W2 duration: 20 x 6:30 + 10 x 5:32 = 2:10 + 0:55 = 3:05.
W4 duration: 18 x 6:30 + 8 x 5:32 = 1:57 + 0:44 = 2:41.
Total long-run distance across the block: 24 + 30 + 33 + 26 + 21 + 12 = 146 km, with two runs >= 30 km. That is the realistic ceiling given the six weeks, and it is what Muniz-Pumares et al.'s -0.13 min-per-long-run-km coefficient rewards. Total marathon-pace volume across the block: 8 + 10 + 21.1 + 8 + 8 + 4 = 59.1 km.
His 10 May marathon (3:55:54) came off a longest run of 30.11 km four weeks out. He has already demonstrated that ~30 km is sufficient long-run stimulus for a sub-4 marathon. The variable being changed this block is not longest-run distance — it is MP volume and total long-run kilometres.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: 1x per week, every week of the block

prescriptions.sessionName: The Lincoln Half specific block, 4 October — 33 km, NOT raced
prescriptions.structure:
12 km easy, run BEFORE the half-marathon start (a genuine 75-80 min pre-load, not a warm-up), then the Lincoln Half itself, all 21.0975 km, at marathon pace. No cool-down. Total 33.1 km, approximately 3 h 12 min. Full dress rehearsal: race-day shoes, race-day breakfast at race-day timing, race-day fuel at race-day rate, race-day caffeine dose.
ABORT RULES, written down before the start and non-negotiable:
  - If HR exceeds 168 at MP for 2 consecutive kilometres, slow to 5:45/km and finish there.
  - If decoupling (see validation) exceeds 1.20 by 25 km, stop the MP block and jog the remainder.
  - Under no circumstance run faster than 5:25/km. The failure mode of this session is racing it.
If the week-2 gate (see validation) failed on 27 Sep, cut the pre-load from 12 km to 8 km and cap the total at 29 km.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: The MP block runs at MP_TARGET exactly, with an HR ceiling at 84% HRmax. The pre-load runs slower than Z1_CEILING minus 25 s/km — genuinely easy, because a pre-load run too hard will make the MP block fail and convert the session into a race.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: This is Canova's specific block, scaled from a world-class double session to what a 6-week amateur block can absorb. The MP portion FINISHES at 33.1 km cumulative — precisely on the 29.3-29.6 km wall onset that Smyth (2021) measured across 4.18 million races, and past the 25.2 km mean decoupling onset of Smyth et al. (2022). Running marathon pace through that window, three weeks out, is the single most specific stimulus available to him and the only rehearsal of the exact problem the race will pose. Pfitzinger places a tune-up race roughly three weeks out for the same reason; 4 Oct is 20 days from 24 Oct. Running it at MP rather than racing it converts a session that would cost 7-10 days of recovery into one that costs 3-4.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete:
Pre-load: 12 km at 6:30-6:50/km = 78-82 min, HR <= 145.
MP block: 21.0975 km at 5:32/km = 1:56:47, HR 160-166, ceiling 168.
Total: 33.1 km, 3:15. That is 83% of his projected race duration (3:53) — at the very top of what is defensible, and the reason the 3:15 ceiling exists. Pfitzinger caps long runs near 3 h; this deliberately exceeds it by 15 min once, in the peak week, and never again.
Fuel: this session must be run at the full race rate reached by this point in gut training (target 70-80 g CHO/h from 40 min onward), plus 3 mg/kg caffeine (~255 mg at 85.5 kg) 60 min before the start. If the caffeine or the fuelling rate causes GI trouble here, there is still time to change it. There is not, on 24 October.
CONFLICT TO FLAG: this session sits on the last day of the 100 km week, which is the highest-risk day of the entire block. The 100 km is the athlete's ratified risk; stacking the block's hardest session on its final day compounds it. If anything must be moved to protect the block, move the 100 km target down to 90 km — not this session.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: Once, 4 October 2026

prescriptions.sessionName: Lactate-threshold run (Pfitzinger)
prescriptions.structure:
20-30 minutes of work at threshold pace, plus 3 km easy warm-up and 2 km easy cool-down.
  W1: 20 min continuous
  W2: 25 min continuous
  W3: OMITTED — the Lincoln session supplies the week's entire Zone 2 load
  W4: 2 x 12 min with 2 min jog (broken, because the week also contains a hard 10K)
  W5: 20 min continuous
  W6: 12 min continuous, Wednesday 21 Oct, then nothing hard until race day
Broken rather than continuous whenever the week's volume exceeds 80 km: the lactate stimulus is equivalent and it is far more likely to be completed at correct pace when the athlete arrives tired.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: LT_PACE exactly, derived as half_pace x 0.967 — NOT Garmin's threshold pace. Heart rate cross-check 82-91% HRmax (Pfitzinger & Douglas's stated range), narrowed to 86-89% given his measured LTHR. If pace and HR disagree, the HR wins; that means the pace anchor needs re-deriving.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Raises fractional utilisation — the fraction of VO2max sustainable without lactate accumulation. Pfitzinger & Douglas note successful marathoners run at 84-88% of VO2max and elites at 88-91%; his VO2max of 53.0 is already adequate for a sub-3:30 marathon, so utilisation, not aerobic power, is where his time is. This is the cheapest session in the block: 5 km of work per week for the lever that most moves a 3:5x marathon. It is also why VO2max intervals are omitted — his 25 Apr 5 km at 3:54/km against a 5:02/km half shows a 17.8% endurance deficit relative to Riegel, i.e. abundant speed and absent endurance. Adding Zone 3 work would train the quality he already has, at the cost of the volume ramp.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete:
Threshold pace 4:52/km (provisional), HR 172-178. Session totals: W1 4.1 km of work, W2 5.1 km, W4 4.9 km, W5 4.1 km, W6 2.5 km. With warm-up and cool-down: 9-11 km sessions.
NOTE THE 5 km IS AT THE ZONE 2 / ZONE 3 BOUNDARY, not above it — 4:52/km IS his critical speed. This session therefore contributes to the ~20% Zone 2 budget, not to a Zone 3 budget. That is deliberate: it means the entire block contains almost no Zone 3 running outside the 11 Oct 10K.
IF GARMIN'S 4:20.9/km IS EVER USED FOR THIS SESSION, STOP THE BLOCK. A 25-minute effort at 4:21/km is a 10 km race. Run weekly on an 80-100 km ramp it will produce injury or non-functional overreaching within three weeks.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: 1x per week in weeks 1, 2, 4, 5, 6; omitted in week 3

prescriptions.sessionName: Zone 1 easy volume — where the 60-to-100 km actually comes from
prescriptions.structure:
Everything that is not the long run or the threshold session. Six running days per week, adding a second run on two days in the 80 and 100 km weeks rather than lengthening single runs.
  W1 60 km: long run 24, threshold session 10, easy 26 across 4 days
  W2 80 km: long run 30, threshold 11, easy 39 across 4 days + 1 double
  W3 100 km: Lincoln 33, easy 67 across 5 days + 2 doubles (no threshold session)
  W4 80 km: long run 26, threshold 11, 10K day 16 (incl. warm-up/cool-down), easy 27
  W5 60 km: long run 21, threshold 10, easy 29
  W6 race week: ~30 km pre-race + the marathon
The 2-hour weekly swim stays and does not count toward the running total.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Slower than Z1_CEILING (= LT_PACE / 0.823), with a heart-rate ceiling at 75% of true HRmax. Recovery-day runs slower again, HR <= 70% HRmax.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: This is the finding from the largest applicable dataset, and it is unambiguous. Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024), across 151,813 marathons: faster runners accumulate more total volume ALMOST ENTIRELY IN ZONE 1 — absolute Zone 2 and Zone 3 time is near-constant across every performance level. Their regression: each additional percentage point of training time in Zone 1 predicts a 0.30 min faster marathon; each additional point in Zone 2 predicts 0.33 min slower and in Zone 3 0.76 min slower. Stellingwerff's (2012) three elite marathoners ran 74% of sessions in Zone 1 at 182 km/wk. Zone 1 running also carries the lowest mechanical loading rate per kilometre, which is the entire argument for building an unprecedented volume ramp out of it rather than out of anything faster.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete:
Easy pace 6:10-6:50/km, HR <= 150 (75% of 201). Recovery pace 7:00+/km, HR <= 141.
CONTEXT FOR THE RAMP: his last four complete weeks were 27.2 / 34.8 / 0 / 14.8 km — a four-week mean of 19.2 km. Week 1's 60 km is a 4-fold increase on that mean and a 5% increase on the highest week he has ever run (57.1 km, which contained a marathon). Week 3's 100 km is 75% above his all-time peak week and 5.2x his recent mean. His CTL of 52.2 is down from a 72.3 peak on 2 Aug; TSB +24.7 says he is very fresh but detrained relative to his own best.
Nielsen et al. (2014) is the usual citation against this, and it is weaker than its reputation: HR 1.59 for distance-related injury above 30% weekly progression, but 95% CI 0.96-2.66 and p = .07 — not statistically significant, and in a NOVICE cohort. The honest statement is that there is no good evidence establishing a safe ceiling on volume progression, and none establishing that this ramp is safe either. The ramp is unratified by evidence in both directions; it is the athlete's judgement call, already made in writing.
What the intensity design CAN control is not adding to the risk: two quality sessions per week, never three; Zone 3 confined to a single race; volume added as Zone 1 doubles rather than longer single runs.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: 4-6 sessions per week, ~80% of weekly volume

prescriptions.sessionName: ASICS LDNX 10K, 11 October — raced hard, and treated as a measurement
prescriptions.structure: 3 km easy warm-up, 4 x 100 m strides, race 10 km flat out, 3 km easy cool-down. Approximately 16 km for the day. It is the last day of the 80 km week and the only Zone 3 running in the entire block. The three days after it are Zone 1 only.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Raced by effort, not by prescribed pace. Predicted from the September half: 10 km pace ~= half_pace x 0.957 (Riegel to 10 km). Post-race, use the result only as a DIRECTIONAL check on marathon pace — if he beats prediction by x%, marathon pace can move x/2% faster; if he misses it by x%, move marathon pace x% slower. Never let a 10 km result move marathon pace faster by more than 5 s/km.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Two jobs. (1) Taper physiology: Mujika & Padilla's framework is to cut volume sharply while MAINTAINING intensity and frequency, and a hard 10K is the cleanest way to hold high-intensity exposure through a period of falling volume. (2) A real fitness measurement 13 days out, which is more informative than any Garmin estimate and arrives in time to adjust race pace. Smyth & Lawlor (2021) found a strict 3-week taper worth a median 5 min 32 s to recreational marathoners; volume here declines 100 -> 80 -> 60 -> race week, which IS a three-week monotonic reduction, with this one hard effort inside it.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete:
Predicted 45:50-47:30 (4:35-4:45/km) from the July half. DO NOT chase the ~41:00 that Riegel-from-his-April-5 km suggests — that projection ignores the 17.8% endurance deficit his own half already demonstrated, and chasing it will produce a blow-up that costs recovery days he cannot spare 13 days out.
CALENDAR RISK TO FLAG: this race sits on the final day of the 80 km week, meaning the athlete's genuinely undisturbed taper runs only from 12 Oct — 12 days. Smyth & Lawlor's best-performing group tapered for three weeks with no hard racing inside it. Moving the 10K to 4 Oct is impossible (Lincoln), so the compromise is to accept a 12-day clean taper and make week 5 strictly Zone 1 apart from one 20-min threshold run. Flag to the athlete that this costs some fraction of that median 5:32 taper benefit; it is a real, quantified trade, not a technicality.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: Once, 11 October 2026

prescriptions.sessionName: Gut training and race-day fuelling protocol
prescriptions.structure:
Progressive carbohydrate exposure on every long run, starting immediately. Rate per hour of running, taken from 40 minutes onward in equal doses every 15-20 minutes, always with the same products that will be used on race day:
  W1 long run: 45 g/h
  W2 long run: 55 g/h
  W3 (Lincoln, 4 Oct): 75 g/h — full race rate, full dress rehearsal
  W4 long run: 75 g/h
  W5 long run: 75 g/h
  Race day: 75 g/h from 40 min = ~4 h x 75 = ~285 g total
Fluid: drink to thirst, from what is on the course. Do NOT run a fixed-volume drinking schedule.
Carbohydrate load: 8-10 g/kg/day for the 36 hours before the race, with activity near zero on the day before.
Caffeine: 3 mg/kg 60 min before the start — trialled at Lincoln on 4 Oct, never first on race day.
Log for every long run: grams per hour actually achieved, and any GI symptom on a 0-10 scale. If symptoms exceed 4, hold the rate rather than advancing it.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Carbohydrate rate is anchored to expected race duration, not to bodyweight: Jeukendrup (2014) and the ACSM/AND/DC position stand (Thomas, Erdman & Burke, 2016) both set ~60 g/h for 2-2.5 h and up to ~90 g/h beyond 2.5 h, achievable only with a glucose:fructose blend because single-source carbohydrate saturates SGLT1 at ~60 g/h. A 3:53 marathon sits in the upper band. Caffeine at 3 mg/kg is the lower end of the ISSN's consistently effective 3-6 mg/kg range (Guest et al., 2021), chosen low because it is untested in this athlete.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Fuelling changes the outcome more than any single session, because glycogen depletion is one of the two things that actually breaks at 32 km. Rapoport (2010) models the depletion distance as a direct function of intensity and mid-race carbohydrate intake; Smyth (2021) locates the resulting collapse at 29.3-29.6 km with a mean cost of 31.5 minutes. The 75 g/h is not optional detail — it is worth substantially more than any marginal training session in this block. The progressive build exists because the gut is trainable and untrained: Jeukendrup (2017) shows intestinal transporters, gastric emptying and subjective fullness all adapt to habitual intake, and attempting 75 g/h cold on race day is a common cause of the GI failure that ends races. The 1-day carbohydrate load is Bussau et al. (2002): 10 g/kg with near-zero activity took muscle glycogen from 95 to 180 mmol/kg wet mass in 24 hours, with two further days adding nothing. Drink-to-thirst is the Third International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus (Hew-Butler et al., 2015) — a fixed schedule risks dilutional hyponatraemia, which kills people and a fixed schedule does not outperform thirst.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete:
At 85.5 kg (STALE — typed once in March, and his resting HR has fallen from 84 to 50 since, so he is probably lighter; reweigh before the load, this number scales two prescriptions):
  Caffeine: 3 x 85.5 = 257 mg, 60 min pre-start. One strong coffee plus a 100 mg gel, or two caffeinated gels.
  Carbohydrate load: 8-10 g/kg = 684-855 g/day for 36 h before the race. Practically: Thursday 22 Oct normal-plus, Friday 23 Oct ~800 g with minimal running.
  Race fuel: 285-300 g total. At ~25 g per gel that is 11-12 gels, or a mix of gels and on-course sports drink. This is roughly five times what most 3:50 runners actually take, which is exactly why it needs six weeks of rehearsal.
Contrast honestly: Stellingwerff's (2012) three elite marathoners took only 61 +/- 15 g/h — but they were racing for 2:11-2:16, not 3:53, and finished before glycogen became decisive. Longer race, more carbohydrate. Do not copy the elite number.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: Every long run; full rehearsal 4 Oct; executed 24 Oct

prescriptions.sessionName: Race-day pacing protocol, 24 October
prescriptions.structure:
Written on the wrist before the start, in three segments:
  km 0-5: MP + 8 s/km. It will feel absurdly easy. That is the point.
  km 5-32: MP exactly. Do not bank time. Do not respond to other runners.
  km 32-42.2: whatever is left. If the legs are there, MP or faster. If not, hold.
Hard rule: no kilometre in the first half faster than MP. Not one.
Heart-rate abort: if HR exceeds 84% HRmax before 25 km at target pace, slow by 8 s/km immediately — that is decoupling arriving early and it will not resolve by pushing.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: MP = LT_PACE / 0.88, where LT_PACE is re-derived from the 12 Sep half and sanity-checked against the 11 Oct 10K. The 88% figure is the fractional utilisation of critical speed observed in the best-finishing (low-decoupling) third of Smyth et al.'s (2022) 82,303 marathoners.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: The pacing decision is worth more than any training decision remaining in this block. Smyth (2021): 28% of male recreational marathoners slow by >=25% for >=5 km after 20 km, at a mean cost of 31.5 minutes — and the incidence rises to 40% among men in the years they are chasing a personal best, which is exactly this athlete's situation. The +8 s/km opening is not superstition: Rapoport's (2010) model shows glycogen depletion distance is highly sensitive to early intensity, so a few seconds per kilometre spent early is repaid several-fold in the last 10 km. His 10 May marathon shows he can already execute discipline — 42.67 km with only 2:37 of stopped time is genuinely well-controlled running, and that is a real asset.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete:
Provisional, from the July half:
  km 0-5 at 5:40/km (28:20)
  km 5-32 at 5:32/km (2:29:24)
  km 32-42.2 at 5:32/km (56:29)
  Projected finish 3:54:13; on an even 5:32 throughout, 3:53:29.
The realistic band is 3:50 to 3:58 depending on the 12 Sep half. Anything faster than 3:50 requires racing above 89% of critical speed, which for a runner with a 6-week block and a 19 km/week four-week base going in is the profile Smyth et al. (2022) associate with early decoupling and a high-decoupling finish.
What improvement to expect, honestly: 3:55:54 to roughly 3:52 is a ~4-minute gain. That is small for the risk taken, and most of it comes from fuelling and pacing rather than from the 100 km week. If the athlete wants a number that justifies the block, it is not the marathon time — it is that this block builds the base that makes a genuinely fast marathon possible in spring 2027.
SANITY CHECK AGAINST GARMIN: Garmin says 3:36:12. It over-predicts THIS athlete by a median factor of 1.118 across three realised efforts and missed his May marathon by 27 minutes. 3:36:12 x 1.118 = 4:01:45. If he sets off at 5:07/km chasing Garmin's number, Smyth's 28%-of-men wall statistic becomes a near-certainty.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: Once, 24 October 2026

research.intensityDistribution:
TARGET: Zone 1 >= 80% of training TIME, Zone 2 18-20%, Zone 3 <= 2%. Pyramidal (Z1 > Z2 > Z3), never polarised, never threshold-dominant.

ZONE BOUNDARIES, derived not asserted, using the three-zone model of Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024):
  Z1/Z2 boundary = 82.3% of critical speed. For this athlete (provisional CS pace 4:52/km): 5:55/km. Anything slower is Zone 1.
  Z2/Z3 boundary = critical speed itself = 4:52/km. Anything faster is Zone 3.
