Note what this means: his marathon pace (5:32/km) is upper Zone 2, and his threshold pace (4:52/km) is the TOP of Zone 2, not Zone 3. Executed as designed, this block contains essentially no Zone 3 running outside the 11 October 10K.

EVIDENCE. This is one of the better-evidenced parts of the design, because a directly comparable dataset exists. Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024) analysed 16 weeks of training before 151,813 marathons by 119,452 runners whose mean finish time was 3:50 — this athlete's exact target band. Findings:
  - Overall distribution across all runners: Z1 49.0% / Z2 35.3% / Z3 15.7% of training time.
  - Faster runners accumulated their extra volume ALMOST ENTIRELY IN Z1. Absolute time in Z2 and Z3 was near-constant across every performance level. The fastest men reached ~67% Z1 (still short of the ~80% reported in elites, which the authors attribute to their lower total volume).
  - Pyramidal distribution was used by >80% of the fastest runners; a truly polarised distribution was rare (overall polarisation index 1.25, consistently below 1.5).
  - OLS regression: +1 percentage point in Z1 predicted -0.30 min finish time; +1 point in Z2 predicted +0.33 min; +1 point in Z3 predicted +0.76 min. But the authors explicitly conclude that ~20% Z2 is likely REQUIRED for marathon performance, with diminishing returns beyond it — the fastest runners in the dataset all did >20% Z2 and it was not associated with harm at that level.
Stellingwerff (2012) gives the elite comparator: three 2:11-2:16 marathoners ran 74% / 11% / 15% of 606 sessions in Z1 / Z2 / Z3 at 182 km/wk. Kenneally, Casado & Santos-Concejero (2018) reviewed pyramidal vs polarised vs threshold distributions for distance runners; the honest reading of that literature is that no distribution is established as superior by controlled trial for the marathon specifically.

WHAT THIS BLOCK ACTUALLY DELIVERS, computed:
  Week 1 (60 km): Z2 = 8 km MP + 4.1 km threshold = 12.1 km. By time: 12.1 km at ~5:25 = 66 min; 47.9 km at ~6:25 = 307 min. Total 373 min. Z2 = 17.7%, Z1 = 82.3%, Z3 = 0%.
  Week 3 (100 km, Lincoln, no threshold session): Z2 = 21.1 km at 5:32 = 117 min; 78.9 km at ~6:25 = 506 min. Total 623 min. Z2 = 18.8%, Z1 = 81.2%, Z3 = 0%.
  Week 4 (80 km, with the 10K): Z2 = 8 km MP + 4.9 km threshold = 71 min; Z3 = ~40 min of the 10K above CS; Z1 = ~450 min. Z1 78%, Z2 12%, Z3 7% — the only week with meaningful Z3.
  Across the whole block: approximately Z1 81%, Z2 17.5%, Z3 1.5%.

WHY DELIBERATELY AT THE TOP OF THE Z1 RANGE, NOT THE MIDDLE: the central tension in this brief is that the volume ramp is already the risk. Muniz-Pumares et al.'s finding that additional volume in Z1 is what separates faster runners, combined with the fact that Z1 running carries the lowest mechanical loading rate per kilometre, means the safest way to build 100 km is to build it almost entirely out of easy running. Every kilometre moved from Z1 to Z2 or Z3 raises the injury and overreaching cost of the ramp without a proportionate return. Two quality sessions per week is the ceiling. A third (a Hansons-style strength session at MP-minus-6 s/km, which would otherwise be a natural import) is deliberately omitted — the marginal adaptation is small and the compounding of intensity onto an unprecedented volume ramp is the specific failure this brief asks to avoid. The "faster than marathon pace" stimulus is instead folded into the last 3 km of the week-2 long run at MP-10, which costs zero extra sessions.
research.fitForThisAthlete:
SHORT ANSWER: the tradition fits the CALENDAR unusually well and fits the ATHLETE'S HISTORY badly. Both halves matter.

WHY THE CALENDAR FITS. All three traditions organise a marathon build into phases, and the final six weeks is the phase where all three converge on the same thing: marathon-pace specificity. Pfitzinger's last six weeks are marathon-pace long runs plus a tune-up race three weeks out. Hansons' last six weeks are the peak of their MP-tempo progression. Canova's last six weeks ARE the "specific period", the only phase in which his specific block appears. So a six-week block is not a truncated marathon plan — it is precisely the segment of a marathon plan that these authors would recognise. The Lincoln Half on 4 October falls 20 days out, which is exactly where Pfitzinger puts his tune-up and where Canova would site a specific block. That is a genuinely fortunate fixture list.

WHY THE HISTORY DOES NOT FIT. Every one of these traditions assumes the aerobic base already exists. Pfitzinger's entry-level 18-week plan starts at 55 km/wk and expects the athlete to arrive able to run that. Hansons assumes six running days a week already habitual. Canova assumes 180-220 km/wk. This athlete's four complete weeks before the block are 27.2 / 34.8 / 0 / 14.8 km — a mean of 19.2 km across four runs a week at most. He is being asked to build the base and do the specific work simultaneously, which none of these systems is designed for and none of them has evidence for. Week 3's 100 km is 75% above the highest week he has ever run and 5.2 times his recent mean.

WHICH TRADITION FITS BEST, RANKED:
  1. HANSONS, structurally. Its long-run cap of 16 miles (~26 km) is close to what he can actually reach, its cumulative-fatigue logic explains why a capped long run is not a compromise, and its MP-tempo emphasis is the right stimulus. Where it does not fit: its six-days-a-week 10-16 km-per-day pattern presumes a base he lacks, and the cap itself has no trial evidence — it is a reasoned argument about recovery cost, not a tested proposition.
  2. PFITZINGER, for the single highest-value import: a weekly 20-30 min lactate-threshold run. It costs 5 km of work per week and it targets fractional utilisation, which is where his time actually is. His VO2max of 53.0 is already sufficient for a sub-3:30 marathon; his 25 April 5 km at 3:54/km against a 19 July half at 5:02/km shows a 17.8% endurance deficit relative to Riegel — abundant speed, absent endurance. Threshold work is the correct lever; VO2max intervals would train the quality he already has.
  3. CANOVA, for one thing only: the design of the 4 October session. His percentage-of-race-pace framework is what turns "run the Lincoln Half at marathon pace" from a slogan into a specification (12 km pre-load at 80-85% MP, then 21.1 km at 100% MP, finishing at 33 km). His actual training volumes are irrelevant here.

THE DECISIVE QUESTION — 27-29 km longest run against a 42.2 km race:
  The honest answer is that there is NO trial evidence establishing a minimum long-run distance for the marathon. None. Not in any of these traditions, not in the physiology literature.
  What the evidence does say:
  - Doherty et al. (2020) include both "distance of the longest run" and "number of runs >= 32 km" as covariates negatively associated with finish time across 137 cohorts, R2 0.38-0.81. But this is cohort-level observational meta-regression, collinear with total volume and with ability. It cannot distinguish "long runs make you fast" from "fast people do long runs."
  - Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024) is the more informative regression because it separates the two: TOTAL DISTANCE covered in long runs across the block carried a coefficient of -0.13 min per km (more long-run kilometres, faster marathon), while the NUMBER of long runs carried a POSITIVE coefficient of +2.70 min. Cumulative long-run volume is what tracks with performance; no individual run's length does.
  - Jones & Kirby (2025) give the mechanism-level recommendation for durability: prolonged sessions containing bouts at race pace or above, or progressive intensity increase in the face of fatigue. Not prolonged sessions per se — prolonged sessions WITH RACE-PACE CONTENT.
  - Hansons is the explicit expert counter-position: cap at 26 km, argued entirely from recovery cost (after a 35 km run most runners need 7-10 days before quality work, limiting an 18-week block to 3-4 such runs).
  - His own N=1 is the strongest evidence he has: 3:55:54 on 10 May off a longest run of 30.11 km four weeks out, with only 2:37 of stopped time. He has already proved that ~30 km suffices for a sub-4.
  CONCLUSION: the 27-29 km ceiling is not the binding constraint. Marathon-pace volume can substitute for long-run distance to a meaningful degree — that conclusion rests on observational association plus mechanism, NOT on trial evidence, and should be stated to the athlete in exactly those terms. The block accordingly targets 146 km of total long-run distance and 59 km of marathon-pace running, with the single 33 km session on 4 October carrying 21.1 km of MP finishing exactly at 33 km, which is where the wall lives.

WHAT REALISTIC IMPROVEMENT LOOKS LIKE, said plainly: roughly 3:50-3:56, against 3:55:54 in May. A four-to-six minute gain, of which most comes from fuelling (285-300 g of carbohydrate versus whatever he took in May) and pacing discipline, not from the 100 km week. The 100 km week's real return is the base it leaves behind for a spring 2027 marathon. If the athlete's expectation is that a 100 km week buys 15 minutes, that expectation should be corrected now, in writing, before the block starts.

TWO CALENDAR PROBLEMS TO SURFACE:
  1. The block's hardest single session (33 km, 3:15 on feet) sits on the last day of the block's hardest week (100 km). If anything must give to protect the athlete, reduce week 3 to 90 km — do not reduce the Lincoln session, which is irreplaceable.
  2. The 11 October 10K leaves only a 12-day undisturbed taper. Smyth & Lawlor (2021) found a strict 3-week taper worth a median 5 min 32 s to recreational marathoners. Keeping the 10K is defensible (Mujika & Padilla's framework maintains intensity while cutting volume), but it costs some fraction of that 5:32 and the athlete should be told the number.
  3. He races Battersea Half flat out on 12 September and starts a 60 km week on 14 September. Two days is not enough recovery from a maximal half for someone whose recent four-week mean is 19 km. Week 1's first three days should be Zone 1 only, and week 1's long run should be Thursday or later.
research.howToValidate:
Every metric below is computable from data rocket already has or can get from Garmin. None requires lab testing.

1. DECOUPLING — the primary in-block readout, and the best single number in this whole design.
   Method, from Smyth et al. (2022): decoupling = (%HRmax / %criticalSpeed) in a late window, divided by the same ratio in an early window. Applied to training rather than racing: compute over the FIRST 10 minutes of the marathon-pace block versus the LAST 10 minutes of the same block.
   Reference values from 82,303 marathoners: <1.10 = low-decoupling group (raced at 88% CS, finished 217 min, first decoupled at 33.4 km); 1.10-1.20 = moderate; >=1.20 = high (raced at only 82% CS, finished 238 min, first decoupled at 19.1 km).
   Track it on every MP long run — W1 (8 km MP), W2 (10 km), W3 Lincoln (21.1 km), W4 (8 km), W5 (8 km).
   DECISION RULE: if decoupling on the Lincoln 33 km session is >= 1.20, marathon pace is set too fast. Lower MP_TARGET by 6-8 s/km and recompute the race plan. If it is < 1.10 across 21.1 km of MP finishing at 33 km, the 5:32/km target is well supported and he may race the lower end of the band (5:28/km).
   Also compute this retrospectively on his 10 May marathon file if rocket holds the streams — km 5-10 versus km 35-40. That gives a baseline durability number BEFORE the block starts, which is the only way to know whether the block improved it.

2. MARATHON-PACE HEART RATE AT FIXED PACE — the adaptation signal.
   Log mean HR for the MP block at an unchanged 5:32/km across weeks 1, 2, 3, 5. Falling HR at constant pace = the adaptation this block is buying. Flat is acceptable given the volume ramp. RISING across two consecutive weeks means the volume is outrunning recovery — that is the reversal signal, and it arrives earlier and more reliably than any subjective report.

3. THE TWO RACES AS CALIBRATION POINTS.
   12 Sep Battersea Half: the primary anchor. Recompute LT_PACE = half_pace x 0.967, MP_TARGET = LT_PACE / 0.88, Z1_CEILING = LT_PACE / 0.823. Write all three to config/training.ts with the derivation in the comment, per rocket's no-hardcoded-thresholds rule. Every session in the block is expressed against these, so this is a one-line change that repaces the whole plan.
   11 Oct ASICS 10K: directional check only, 13 days out. If he beats the predicted 45:50-47:30 by x%, move MP faster by x/2%, capped at 5 s/km. If he misses it by x%, move MP slower by the full x%. Asymmetric on purpose — the cost of being 5 s/km too slow is about 3.5 minutes; the cost of being 5 s/km too fast is a wall event worth 31.5 minutes (Smyth 2021).

4. THE WEEK-2 REVERSAL GATE, 27 September — made measurable rather than left to judgement.
   The block already carries a ratified reversal condition judged at the end of week 2. Four objective gates, all from Garmin:
   (a) Completed >= 90% of prescribed weeks 1+2 volume, i.e. >= 126 of 140 km.
   (b) Week 2's 10 km marathon-pace block completed at target pace with decoupling < 1.12.
   (c) Resting HR not elevated more than 5 bpm above the 14-day pre-block baseline (currently 57 smoothed / 50 raw) on 5 or more consecutive mornings.
   (d) No pain that alters gait on any run in weeks 1-2.
   ANY gate failed -> week 3 is capped at 80 km, not 100, and the Lincoln pre-load drops from 12 km to 8 km (total 29 km, not 33). Two or more failed -> the block reverts to a 60/70/80/70/55 shape and the marathon target moves to the conservative end (5:36/km, 3:56).

5. FUELLING TOLERANCE LOG — the highest-value cheap metric.
   Per long run: grams of carbohydrate per hour actually achieved, and GI symptom score 0-10. The gate is that 75 g/h must be reached and tolerated (symptom score <= 4) on the 4 October Lincoln session. If it is not, the race-day rate must be set to the highest tolerated rate rather than the target rate — and the marathon pace must then come down, because Rapoport's (2010) model makes depletion distance a joint function of pace and intake. Reduced fuelling and unchanged pace is the combination that produces a wall.

6. ACWR / RAMP MONITORING — for the volume risk, which is the one the intensity design cannot fix.
   Track the 7-day rolling load against the 28-day rolling load using Garmin's per-activity training load (the same input as his CTL/ATL). The block's design pushes this ratio well past any conventional threshold in week 3 by construction — the point is not to hold it low but to SEE it, so that a spike beyond plan (an unplanned hard run, a race-pace long run gone fast) is caught the same week rather than in retrospect.

7. WHAT WOULD FALSIFY THIS DESIGN.
   Stated up front so it is not rationalised away later: if by 4 October his decoupling across the 21.1 km MP block is >= 1.20, or his MP heart rate at 5:32/km has risen rather than fallen since 20 September, then the intensity prescription has failed to produce durability and the correct response is to lower marathon pace to 5:40-5:45/km and race for a controlled finish rather than a personal best. That is a worse race-day outcome than hoped and a far better one than the 28%-of-men wall, which costs 31.5 minutes.
contraindications: DO NOT USE GARMIN'S LACTATE-THRESHOLD PACE OF 4:20.9/km FOR ANY SESSION. It is approximately 30 s/km faster than threshold triangulated three independent ways: Riegel from his 19 Jul half puts a 60-min effort at 4:52/km; his own heart rate (174 bpm average at 5:02/km for 1:47, against a Garmin LTHR of 177) caps threshold near 4:52-4:58/km; and 4:20.9 is almost exactly his 11 Apr 5 km pace, which is what the algorithm appears to have fitted to. A 25-minute 'tempo' at 4:21/km is a 10 km race effort. Prescribed weekly on an 80-100 km ramp it is the single most likely cause of block failure. Note that Garmin's LT pace error is the same direction and roughly the same magnitude as its race-prediction error (measured over-prediction factor 1.118 on this athlete) — the two are almost certainly the same underlying bias.

DO NOT USE 196 OR 195 AS MAXIMUM HEART RATE. The measured value is 201 (14 Jun 2026). Every heart-rate zone in this design derives from it. Using 196 shifts every zone ceiling down by ~2.5%, which sounds trivial and in practice means his easy runs get prescribed 8-10 s/km too slow and his threshold runs land above threshold.

NO VO2max OR ZONE 3 INTERVALS DURING WEEKS 1-5. The only Zone 3 running in the entire block is the 11 October 10K. He does not need Zone 3: his 25 Apr 5 km at 3:54/km against a 19 Jul half at 5:02/km shows a 17.8% endurance deficit relative to Riegel — abundant speed, absent endurance. Adding VO2max work trains the quality he already has, at the cost of the volume ramp that is the block's actual risk. Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024) put the regression cost at +0.76 min of marathon time per additional percentage point of Zone 3.

NO THIRD QUALITY SESSION PER WEEK. Two — the marathon-pace long run and the threshold run — is the ceiling, and week 3 drops to one. A Hansons-style strength session (6 x 1.6 km at MP-6 s/km) is a natural import from the tradition and is deliberately omitted: on a ramp that is 75% above his all-time peak week, a third hard session compounds exactly the risk this design is meant not to add to.

DO NOT RACE THE LINCOLN HALF ON 4 OCTOBER. Racing it would cost 7-10 days of quality training 20 days from the marathon, and would convert the block's most valuable session into its most damaging. Write the abort rules down before the start: HR ceiling 168, absolute pace floor 5:25/km, stop the MP block if decoupling exceeds 1.20 by 25 km. The failure mode of this session is not physical, it is being surrounded by people racing.

NO SINGLE RUN OVER 3 HOURS 15 MINUTES, and only one run at that duration (the 4 October session). Time on feet, not distance, governs glycogen cost and mechanical load. Pfitzinger caps long runs near 3 hours; this design exceeds that once, deliberately, in the peak week, and never again. A 33 km run at 6:30/km would be 3:34 and is NOT an acceptable substitute for 33 km with marathon-pace content at 3:15.

DO NOT START THE 60 km WEEK ON 14 SEPTEMBER AT FULL LOAD. He races a maximal half on 12 September, two days earlier, off a four-week mean of 19.2 km/week. Days 1-3 of week 1 are Zone 1 only and the first long run goes on Thursday 17 September at the earliest.

DO NOT PLACE THE WEEK 4 LONG RUN THE DAY BEFORE THE 11 OCTOBER 10K. It goes Wednesday 7 October. A 26 km long run on 10 October would make the 10K result meaningless as a measurement and would waste the block's only Zone 3 exposure.

DO NOT ATTEMPT RACE-DAY CARBOHYDRATE RATE FOR THE FIRST TIME ON RACE DAY, AND DO NOT TAKE CAFFEINE FOR THE FIRST TIME ON RACE DAY. 75 g/h is roughly five times what most 3:50 marathoners actually take and requires the progressive gut training in the prescription (Jeukendrup 2017). Both the fuelling rate and the 3 mg/kg caffeine dose must be rehearsed at Lincoln on 4 October, with a fallback if either causes GI symptoms above 4/10.

DO NOT RUN A FIXED-VOLUME DRINKING SCHEDULE. Drink palatable fluid when thirsty (Hew-Butler et al., 2015, Third International EAH Consensus). Scheduled over-drinking causes exercise-associated hyponatraemia, which is the one nutrition error in this sport that is occasionally fatal, and it does not outperform thirst.

DO NOT LOWER RACE-DAY FUELLING WITHOUT ALSO LOWERING RACE PACE. Rapoport's (2010) model makes glycogen depletion distance a joint function of intensity and mid-race intake. Reduced intake at unchanged pace moves the depletion point back inside 42.2 km and is a direct route to the 31.5-minute penalty Smyth (2021) measured.

DO NOT LET THE 100 km WEEK BE DEFENDED AT THE COST OF THE 4 OCTOBER SESSION. If week 3 must be cut, cut it to 90 km and keep the 33 km specific block intact. The 100 km number is a volume target with no evidence behind it for this athlete; the specific block is the most evidence-supported session in the plan.

DO NOT REPORT THE 30%-PROGRESSION INJURY EVIDENCE AS SETTLED. Nielsen et al. (2014) reported HR 1.59 for distance-related injury above 30% weekly progression, but with 95% CI 0.96-2.66 and p = .07 — not statistically significant, and in a novice cohort. There is no good evidence establishing a safe ceiling on volume progression, and equally none establishing that this ramp is safe. The athlete has ratified the risk in writing; the correct framing to him is that the evidence is absent in both directions, not that he is defying it.

DO NOT CHASE GARMIN'S 3:36:12 MARATHON PREDICTION OR ITS 43:29 10 km PREDICTION. The measured over-prediction factor on this athlete is 1.118 across three realised efforts, including a 27-minute miss on his May marathon. Corrected, those become 4:01:45 and 48:38. Setting off at 5:07/km on 24 October converts Smyth's 28%-of-men wall statistic into a near-certainty — and his risk is already elevated because he is chasing a personal best, which Smyth found raises male wall incidence from 26% to 40%.

REWEIGH BEFORE THE CARBOHYDRATE LOAD AND THE CAFFEINE DOSE. The 85.5 kg figure was typed once in March; his resting HR has fallen from 84 to 50 since, so it is almost certainly stale. Two prescriptions scale off it — the 8-10 g/kg load (684-855 g/day) and the 3 mg/kg caffeine (257 mg). A 5 kg error moves the load by 50 g/day and the caffeine by 15 mg; neither is dangerous, but neither should be guessed when a scale costs nothing.

verification.tradition: Marathon-specific preparation: Pfitzinger & Douglas (lactate-threshold-centred), Hansons (cumulative fatigue, capped long run), Canova (percentage-of-race-pace specificity) — attacked as a six-week block for a 3:55 marathoner ramping 60/80/100/80/60 km from a 19.2 km/week four-week base.

checks.claim: Headline verdict on evidence base: 'is this invented?' — 22 sources cited, all real.
checks.note: I resolved every DOI against Europe PMC and OpenAlex. All 19 journal citations exist with the stated authors, journal, year and (where given) volume/pages. Nothing is fabricated. Doherty 2020 JSAMS 23:182-188, Smyth 2021 PLoS ONE 16:e0251513, Smyth 2020 MSSE 52:2637-45, Smyth 2022 Sports Med 52:2283-95, Smyth & Lawlor 2021 Front Sports Act Living 3:735220, Maunder 2021 Sports Med 51:1619-28, Jones & Kirby 2025 Scand J Med Sci Sports 35:e70032, Rapoport 2010, Jeukendrup 2014/2017, Thomas 2016, Bussau 2002, Guest 2021, Hew-Butler 2015, Stellingwerff 2012, Kenneally 2018, Nielsen 2014, Mujika & Padilla 2003 all verified. One nit: Muniz-Pumares is cited as 2024 but reached print as Sports Med 2025;55:1023-1035 (2024 is the online-first year). Tell the athlete plainly: the reference list is genuine. The problems are in three misquoted numbers and in how the evidence is read, not in whether it exists.

checks.claim: Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024/25): 151,813 marathons, 119,452 runners, 45.1±26.4 km/wk, 3.6 sessions/wk, weekly long run 19.6±9.6 km, finish 230.2 min, Z1 49.0/Z2 35.3/Z3 15.7%, Z1/Z2 boundary 82.3% CS, >80% of fastest pyramidal, ~67% Z1 in fastest men, regression coefficients Z1 -0.30 / Z2 +0.33 / Z3 +0.76 min per percentage point, long-run distance -0.13 min/km, number of long runs +2.70 min.
checks.note: I pulled the accepted manuscript from the London Met / Hertfordshire repositories and checked every figure. All confirmed to the decimal: Table 2 gives Z1 -0.2993, Z2 +0.3355, Z3 +0.7574, total long-run distance -0.1297, number of long runs +2.6964; text gives 49.0/35.3/15.7%, 3.6±1.7 sessions, 19.6±9.6 km, 230.2±41.9 min, ~67% Z1 in fastest males, '>20% of their training in Z2', 'some ~20% of training in Z2 may be required'. This is the most accurately reported source in the document. Two things the research omitted: adjusted R2 is only ~0.60, and 'long run' is defined as >20 km, which excludes three of the block's six prescribed long runs from the coefficient it invokes.

checks.claim: 'TOTAL DISTANCE covered in long runs carried -0.13 min per km while NUMBER of long runs carried +2.70 min — consistent with cumulative long-run volume mattering rather than any individual run's length.' Used to justify capping the long run at 27-33 km.
checks.note: The sign is read backwards. Both terms sit in the SAME OLS model, so each is a partial coefficient holding the other constant. Holding total long-run kilometres fixed and adding one more long run (i.e. making each one shorter) predicts +2.70 min SLOWER. Equivalently, holding the number of long runs fixed, adding kilometres to them predicts faster. Read correctly, this regression associates FEWER, LONGER long runs with better performance — the opposite of what it is cited for. This is the single quantitative pillar under 'the 27-29 km ceiling is not the binding constraint', and it does not hold. The honest position is the one the research states elsewhere: no trial evidence establishes a minimum long-run distance, and his own 30.11 km-to-3:55:54 result is the best evidence he has.

checks.claim: Smyth (2021): 'incidence rises sharply when a runner is chasing a personal best — 40% of men hit the wall in the three years around a PB versus 26% in other years.' Used twice as the emotional core of the pacing argument and in the contraindications.
checks.note: Misquoted. I read the open-access full text (PMC8133477). The paper says '36% of ALL runners hit the wall in the 3 years before a recent PB compared with just 23% in earlier years' (OR 1.31). Not 40/26, and not men-specific. The 40% figure appears elsewhere in the paper meaning something completely different: '>40% of male runners with SLOWER PBs do hit the wall' — an ability band, not a PB-chasing window. Two separate findings have been merged and inflated. The direction of the argument survives; the number quoted to the athlete does not. The rest of Smyth 2021 checks out exactly: 28% men / 17% women (OR 1.43), onset 29.6 km men / 29.3 km women, cost 31.50 min men / 33.20 min women — all verbatim.

checks.claim: Mujika & Padilla (2003): 'reduce training VOLUME substantially (commonly cited as 41-60%) while MAINTAINING intensity and session frequency.' Used to justify racing the 10K inside the taper.
checks.note: The research flagged this one as unverified, and it was right to worry. The abstract states: maintain training intensity, reduce training volume 'up to 60-90%', and SLIGHTLY REDUCE training frequency 'no more than 20%'. So (a) 41-60% is not the paper's number, and (b) the paper does not say frequency is maintained — it says cut it, modestly. Also useful and unquoted: optimal taper duration 4 to >28 days, progressive nonlinear tapers beat step tapers, expected gain ~3% (0.5-6.0%). The keep-the-10K argument is still defensible on 'maintain intensity', but it is being propped up by two numbers the source does not contain.

checks.claim: '10 km target for 11 Oct: 4:35-4:45/km (45:50-47:30)', derived from the September half.
checks.note: This contradicts the document's own stated method, twice over. Its rule is 10 km pace = half_pace x 0.957: 5:02.5 x 0.957 = 4:49.5/km = 48:15. True Riegel gives 48:13. Its own Garmin correction gives 43:29 x 1.118 = 48:37. Every method in the document lands at ~48:15, yet the athlete is handed a target of 45:50-47:30 — between 45 s and 2:25 too fast. Two concrete harms: he races a maximal 10 km roughly 5-7% above his real ability 13 days before the marathon, in the one week the design says he cannot spare recovery days; and the asymmetric taper rule ('if he misses it by x%, move marathon pace slower by the FULL x%') then fires on a phantom miss — running his true 48:15 against a 47:30 'prediction' is a 1.58% miss, which slows marathon pace by 5 s/km and the finish by 3.7 minutes for no physiological reason at all.

checks.claim: LT_PACE = critical-speed pace = 4:52/km, derived as half_pace x 0.967 (Riegel to ~12 km).
checks.note: The arithmetic is right (factor 0.9667, 4:52.4/km) and the pace is not physiologically absurd: he averaged 174 bpm (86.6% of 201) at 5:02/km for 107 minutes against a Garmin LTHR of 177, so ~4:52 plausibly sits at threshold. But one number is being made to serve two different physiological constructs. Lactate threshold and critical speed are not the same thing — critical speed is systematically faster (roughly 10 km-to-15 km pace) and lactate threshold slower (roughly 15 km-to-half pace). The design uses 4:52 as BOTH the threshold-run pace AND the divisor for marathon pace. Whichever construct 4:52 actually is, one of the two prescriptions is wrong by 8-15 s/km. And the derivation chain amplifies: dividing by 0.88 turns a 10 s/km anchor error into ~8 minutes of marathon time. The design's entire pace structure hangs off one Riegel extrapolation from one race.

checks.claim: Threshold session prescribed at 4:52/km on Pfitzinger's authority, citing his '15 km-to-half-marathon race pace, or 82-91% of maximum heart rate'.
checks.note: The prescribed pace falls outside the range of the tradition invoked for it. Pfitzinger's own definition, applied to this athlete: his half pace is 5:02/km and his Riegel 15 km pace is 4:56/km, so Pfitzinger's LT band for him is 4:56-5:02/km. The prescription of 4:52/km is 4-10 s/km faster than the whole band. That is far less dangerous than the Garmin number the document correctly rejects, but it means a weekly 20-25 minute effort run marginally ABOVE threshold, on the largest volume ramp of his life, justified by an author whose own rule would have him running slower. Note the task's screen — 'threshold faster than his half-marathon race pace is suspect' — is triggered here, and legitimately so for a runner who took 107 minutes for that half.

checks.claim: MP_TARGET = LT_PACE / 0.88, where 88% is 'the fractional utilisation of critical speed observed in the best-finishing third of Smyth et al.'s (2022) 82,303 marathoners'.
checks.note: The output is safe; the justification is not. Population problem: the low-decoupling group cited raced at 88±6% CS and finished in 217.3±33.1 min — 3:37, sixteen minutes faster than this athlete's target. Borrowing the best third's fractional utilisation for a man in the bottom half of the durability distribution (19 km/week base, unprecedented ramp) is exactly the population-transfer error the brief asks about. The number that would have justified it honestly is in a paper the document cites and does not use for this: Smyth & Muniz-Pumares (2020) report 84.8±13.6% CS overall, with 93.0% at 150 min and 78.9% at 360 min — interpolating to a 233 min target gives ~87%, so 88% is defensible for a 3:53 runner. Note the SD of ±13.6%: individual variation swamps the point estimate. Second, deeper problem: that 88% was calibrated against CS measured by the paper's own method — the slope of the distance-time relation over 400/800/1000/1500/3000/5000 m best efforts from training files. The design instead applies it to a Riegel extrapolation of a half. Applying a multiplier to a differently-constructed denominator is a units mismatch. Applied properly to this athlete's short-distance bests (5 km at 3:54/km) the paper's method would return a CS near 4:10/km and a marathon pace near 4:44/km — a 3:20 marathon, which is obvious nonsense for him. The design was right not to do that; it cannot then claim the 88% transfers.

checks.claim: Marathon pace 5:32/km, projected finish 3:53:29 (band 5:28-5:36 = 3:50:40-3:56:20), with realistic improvement stated as 3:50-3:56 against 3:55:54 in May.
checks.note: Arithmetic verified: 332 s/km x 42.195 = 3:53:28, and 0.89/0.87 of critical speed give 5:28.6 and 5:36.1 = 3:51:04 and 3:56:23. The target is physiologically conservative — barely faster than the 5:31/km he already ran in May at avg HR 165 — and the honesty about expected gain (four to six minutes, most of it from fuelling and pacing rather than the 100 km week) is the strongest passage in the document. Worth saying out loud though: he already HAS a distance-specific 42.195 km data point at 5:31/km. Deriving marathon pace by a two-step extrapolation (half to 12 km, then divide by 0.88) when a real marathon sits in the dataset is the wrong order of evidence. The elaborate derivation adds the appearance of rigour to a number he could have read straight off his own May file.

checks.claim: The 4 October Lincoln session: 12 km easy pre-load then 21.0975 km at marathon pace, 33.1 km / 3:15, on the last day of the 100 km week, described as 'the most evidence-supported session in the plan'.
checks.note: Time arithmetic checks (12 km at 6:30-6:50 = 78-82 min; 21.0975 at 5:32 = 1:56:44; total ~3:15; 83.5% of projected race duration). The evidence claim does not. Jones & Kirby (2025) — verified verbatim, including 'especially when these include bouts of high-intensity exercise at race pace or above' — is explicitly a narrative review that says the physiological underpinnings 'are elusive' and 'data are scant'. Canova's specific block, the structural source, was developed on 200+ km/week world-class athletes; the document concedes this and imports it anyway. Nothing in the cited literature supports 21.1 km of continuous marathon-pace running as a dose for a man whose four-week mean is 19.2 km TOTAL per week. For scale: Hansons caps its marathon-pace tempo at 10 miles (16 km) for athletes already running six days a week, and Pfitzinger's largest marathon-pace long run appears in plans built on 70 miles (113 km) per week. This is the largest single prescription in the block and the one furthest outside its own evidence.

checks.claim: 'Running it at MP rather than racing converts a session that would cost 7-10 days of recovery into one that costs 3-4.'
checks.note: No source. The 7-10 day figure is attributed to Hansons elsewhere in the document (as their argument for capping the long run after a 35 km run), but the 3-4 day counterpart is invented. A 33 km run containing 21 km at marathon pace, terminating a 100 km week, in an athlete with this base, will not cost 3-4 days. The whole week-4 calendar — 80 km, a threshold session, a 26 km long run on 7 October and a maximal 10 km on 11 October — is built on that unsourced recovery estimate.

checks.claim: Zone 1 >= 80% of training time, Z2 18-20%, Z3 <= 2%, computed as delivering approximately Z1 81% / Z2 17.5% / Z3 1.5% across the block.
checks.note: I reran the block-level arithmetic independently and got Z1 81.2 / Z2 16.9 / Z3 1.9 — the computation is essentially sound (the week-4 line is off: it should read roughly 76/14/10, not 78/12/7, which does not sum to 100). The evidence claim is what overreaches. The dataset invoked as justification shows Z1 49.0 / Z2 35.3 / Z3 15.7 overall, and only ~67% Z1 even in the fastest men. A prescribed 81/17/2 sits outside the support of every group in the data, obtained by extrapolating a regression coefficient beyond its observed range — and that coefficient is heavily ability-confounded (in the same model, more training TIME at fixed distance predicts a SLOWER marathon, which is a pace proxy, not physiology; adjusted R2 is 0.60). The prescription is defensible on injury-risk grounds given the ramp. The claim that this is 'one of the better-evidenced parts of the design' is not.

checks.claim: 'Muniz-Pumares et al. (2024) is the more informative regression because it separates the two' — i.e. separates 'long runs cause fast marathons' from 'fast marathoners do long runs'.
checks.note: It does not separate them. It is the same observational, self-selected training-log data as Doherty, with covariates that are all mutually collinear proxies for ability (the authors themselves had to build three separate models because Z1/Z2/Z3 fractions are collinear). The document applies an appropriate causal caution to Doherty and then drops it one paragraph later for a dataset with the same limitation. The athlete asked whether the plan is evidence-based; the honest answer for this section is that the strongest available evidence for the long-run and intensity questions is observational and cannot support the dose language used.

checks.claim: Contraindication: do not use Garmin's lactate-threshold pace of 4:20.9/km.
checks.note: Correct and the most valuable single item in the document. He averaged 174 bpm at 5:02/km for 107 minutes against a stated LTHR of 177; a threshold 42 s/km faster than that is impossible. A 25-minute effort at 4:21/km would be a 10 km race, weekly, on a record volume ramp. One caveat on the reasoning: the third 'independent check' — that 4:20.9 is nearly his April 5 km pace, 'which is what the algorithm appears to have fitted to' — is speculation about Firstbeat's internals presented as evidence. Two checks, not three. The conclusion stands regardless.

checks.claim: Contraindication: use 201 bpm as maximum heart rate, not 196/195; 'using 196 ... means his threshold runs land above threshold'.
checks.note: Using the measured 201 is right. The stated consequence is backwards. A lower assumed HRmax produces LOWER zone ceilings: at 196, an 86-89% threshold window is 169-174 bpm, which is BELOW his actual LTHR of 177 — so the error would put threshold runs under threshold, not over. Same for easy running: a lower HRmax makes the easy ceiling stricter, i.e. slower, which the document also states and which is the only half it got right. Minor, but it is a reasoning error in a contraindication written in capitals.

checks.claim: Decoupling as the primary in-block readout, with decision rules at 1.10/1.12/1.20 applied to marathon-pace blocks in training.
checks.note: The reference values are verified exactly — mean 1.16±0.22, onset 25.2±9.9 km, low <1.1 (34.5%, 88±6% CS, 217.3±33.1 min, 33.4±9.0 km), high >=1.2 (32.8%, 82±7% CS, 238.5±30.7 min, 19.1±6.8 km), prediction error 6.45% to 5.16%. The transfer is not. Those thresholds were calibrated on a specific comparison: the 35-40 km race segment against the 5-10 km segment — windows about 30 km and 2.5-3 hours apart, in a maximal race. The design applies the same 1.10/1.20 cut-offs to the first versus last 10 minutes of an 8 km marathon-pace block in week 1, which are roughly 6 km and 25 minutes apart, in submaximal training. Almost nothing will decouple over that span; the metric will read near 1.00 regardless of fitness, and will be interpreted as reassurance. The week-2 gate value of 1.12 has no source at all. Also note the paper defines decoupling ONSET at 1.025, not 1.10 — a threshold the design never uses. The one genuinely good idea here is the retrospective calculation on his 10 May marathon file (km 5-10 vs 35-40), which is the paper's actual method and would give a real baseline.

checks.claim: Nielsen et al. (2014) is weaker than its reputation: HR 1.59, 95% CI 0.96-2.66, p=.07, novice cohort, not statistically significant.
checks.note: Verified exactly, and the intellectual honesty here is genuine — including the conclusion that the evidence is absent in both directions rather than that he is defying it. Two additions the document should have made: the abstract also reports that for the PRIMARY outcome (all running-related injury) 'no statistically significant differences in injury rates were found across the 3 exposure groups', which weakens it further; and the exposure was progression over a TWO-WEEK period, not week-on-week, which the document states as 'weekly distance by more than 30%'. On that two-week definition his 60-to-100 km progression is +67% over two weeks, more than double the studied cut-off.

checks.claim: Fuelling: 75 g/h from 40 min, ~285-300 g total, anchored to Jeukendrup (2014) and the ACSM position stand; '75 g/h is roughly five times what most 3:50 marathoners actually take'.
checks.note: The sources verify. Jeukendrup 2014 confirmed verbatim: single carbohydrate saturates ~60 g/h, 60 g/h recommended for 2-3 h exercise, ~90 g/h for ULTRA-ENDURANCE events, multiple transportable carbohydrates required above 60. Jeukendrup 2017 on gut trainability and SGLT1 density confirmed. Bussau 2002 confirmed to the digit (n=8, 10 g/kg/day, 95(5) to 180(15) mmol/kg wet mass in 24 h). Guest 2021 confirmed on every caffeine point. Hew-Butler 2015 exists (CJSM 25:303-320; 16 authors listed, not the '17 experts' claimed) and drink-to-thirst is correctly the safety-critical recommendation. Two overreaches: a 3:53 marathon is not an 'ultra-endurance event' in Jeukendrup's own framing, so 75 g/h is an interpolation between his 60 and 90 bands presented as if it sat in the upper one; and 'roughly five times what most 3:50 runners actually take' has no source and is not credible (it implies a typical intake of 15 g/h, under half a gel an hour). Practically, the ramp jumps 55 to 75 g/h at the single dress rehearsal, so the highest-risk gastrointestinal load is attempted once, on the block's hardest session, with no second attempt.

checks.claim: Doherty et al. (2020): 85 studies, 137 cohorts, 25% female, seven covariates all negatively associated with finish time, R2 0.38-0.81 p<0.001, non-finish 7.27% (95% CI 6.09-8.65%), with an explicit caution that it cannot separate cause from ability.
checks.note: Verified against the abstract in full, including the exact covariate list and the confidence interval. The caution attached is accurate and appropriate. This is exemplary sourcing.

checks.claim: Stellingwerff (2012) elite comparator: 182 km/wk (peak 231), ~13 sessions/wk, 606 sessions at 74/11/15% Z1/Z2/Z3, 2.5±2.3 low-carbohydrate sessions, 61±15 g CHO in 604±156 mL/h (10.1%), ~15 g in ~150 mL every ~15 min, finishes 2:11:23, 2:12:39 (both PBs), 2:16:17.
checks.note: Verified to the digit, and used correctly — as a contrast that should NOT be copied, with the explicit note that the elite carbohydrate figure is lower because they finish before glycogen becomes decisive. One omission: the 2:16:17 was a marathon debut, which matters if anyone reads the three times as a performance ranking.

checks.claim: Kenneally et al. (2018): 'no single distribution is established as superior for the marathon specifically ... I did not obtain the full text.'
checks.note: Understated rather than overstated, but still a misreport. The paper does reach a conclusion: 'pyramidal and polarized training are more effective than threshold training, although the latest is used by some of the best marathon runners in the world.' Sixteen studies met inclusion (6 observational, 3 case studies, 6 interventions, 1 review). Also mislabelled in the source table as 'meta-analysis' — it is a systematic review with no meta-analysis. The agnosticism claimed is more conservative than the source supports, and conveniently so, since the paper's actual finding favours the pyramidal distribution the design chose.

checks.claim: 'His 10 May marathon (3:55:54) came off a longest run of 30.11 km four weeks out ... He has already demonstrated that ~30 km is sufficient long-run stimulus for a sub-4 marathon.'
checks.note: The 30.11 km run and its four-weeks-out timing appear nowhere in the athlete data supplied. This is load-bearing — it is offered as 'the strongest evidence he has' for capping the long run and for the whole substitute-marathon-pace-volume-for-distance argument. If it came from the Postgres activity table it should be cited as such; if it was inferred, the argument it supports collapses. Same category: 'his VO2max of 53.0 is already sufficient for a sub-3:30 marathon' (no source, though directionally very likely true) and 'Zone 1 running carries the lowest mechanical loading rate per kilometre' (no source; true for peak loading rate per step, but per kilometre the athlete takes more steps, so the per-km claim is not established).

checks.claim: Jones & Kirby (2025) is used to justify race-pace content in long runs.
checks.note: The quotation is accurate almost verbatim and the caveat ('reasoned review, not trial evidence') is honest. But the citation is quoted selectively in a way that matters for safety: the same abstract also concludes that 'resistance training, especially heavy strength and plyometric training, appears to have positive effects on resilience', and that multi-year training consistency promotes it. The design imports the half that adds training stress and silently drops the half that adds none — strength and plyometric work being the cheapest available injury mitigation for a runner about to triple his volume. There is no strength prescription anywhere in the block.

fabricatedCitations: NONE FABRICATED. Every one of the 22 sources exists and is correctly attributed at the reference level — verified by DOI resolution against Europe PMC and OpenAlex, plus full-text retrieval for two of them. This is the direct answer to the athlete's question: the plan is drawn from real, findable, mostly high-quality literature.

MISATTRIBUTED CLAIM 1 — Smyth (2021), PLOS ONE 16:e0251513. Cited as '40% of men hit the wall in the three years around a PB versus 26% in other years'. The paper says 36% of ALL runners in the 3 years before a PB versus 23% in earlier years (OR 1.31). The '40%' in the paper refers to a different finding entirely: >40% of male runners with slower personal bests, i.e. an ability band. Two findings merged and the effect inflated. Verified in the open-access full text at PMC8133477.

MISATTRIBUTED CLAIM 2 — Mujika & Padilla (2003), MSSE 35:1182-1187. Cited as 'reduce volume (commonly cited as 41-60%) while MAINTAINING intensity and session frequency'. The paper says maintain intensity, reduce volume 'up to 60-90%', and reduce frequency slightly, 'no more than 20%'. Both numbers in the citation are wrong, and 'maintaining frequency' inverts the paper. The research flagged this citation as unverified — that flag was well placed.

MISREAD (not misattributed) — Muniz-Pumares et al. Table 2. The '+2.70 min for number of long runs' coefficient is read as supporting cumulative long-run volume over individual run length. Because number and total distance are in the same model, the coefficient means the opposite: at fixed total long-run kilometres, more (therefore shorter) long runs predict a slower marathon.

CITATION DETAIL ERRORS (minor) — Muniz-Pumares et al. is dated 2024; final publication is Sports Med 2025;55:1023-1035. Kenneally et al. (2018) is classified as 'meta-analysis'; it is a systematic review of 16 studies with no meta-analysis, and it does reach a conclusion (pyramidal and polarised beat threshold) that the research reports as absent. Hew-Butler et al. (2015) is described as a '17-expert' consensus; 16 authors are listed on the record.

COULD NOT VERIFY AT CLAIM LEVEL IN THIS SESSION (web-search budget exhausted; these are books or paywalled full texts) — Pfitzinger & Douglas, Advanced Marathoning 3rd ed. (the 82-91% HRmax band, the 84-88%/88-91% of VO2max figures, the 19-24 km medium-long run); Humphrey/Hanson, Hansons Marathon Method 2nd ed. (the 16-mile cap and the 7-10 day recovery rationale); Canova, Marathon Training: A Scientific Approach, IAAF RDC 1999. The Canova 'specific block' description in particular — '10 km at 90% MP plus 20 km at MP in the morning and again in the afternoon', i.e. ~60 km in a day — is stated with a precision I could not source and should be treated as unverified. Thomas/Erdman/Burke (2016) ACSM position stand exists but its specific numbers (7-12 g/kg, 30-60 g/h, 90 g/h beyond 2.5 h, 1-4 g/kg pre-event) sit in the paywalled full text; they match my understanding of the document but I did not read them.

UNSOURCED ASSERTIONS PRESENTED ALONGSIDE CITED MATERIAL — 'running it at MP rather than racing converts 7-10 days of recovery into 3-4'; '75 g/h is roughly five times what most 3:50 runners actually take'; 'VO2max of 53.0 is already sufficient for a sub-3:30 marathon'; 'Zone 1 running carries the lowest mechanical loading rate per kilometre'; 'his 10 May marathon came off a longest run of 30.11 km four weeks out' (not present in the athlete data supplied); the week-2 gate values (decoupling <1.12, resting HR +5 bpm over 5 mornings).
arithmeticErrors: MATERIAL — 10 km target. Stated as '45:50-47:30 (4:35-4:45/km)'. The document's own rule (half_pace x 0.957) gives 4:49.5/km = 48:15; true Riegel gives 48:13; the document's own Garmin correction (43:29 x 1.118) gives 48:37. The target is 45 s to 2:25 too fast. Downstream: he races ~5-7% above his true ability 13 days out, and the asymmetric adjustment rule then fires on a phantom miss — a true 48:15 read against the 47:30 band top is a 1.58% miss, which slows marathon pace by 5.2 s/km and the projected finish by 3.7 minutes for no physiological reason.

MATERIAL (interpretive, not computational) — the Muniz-Pumares long-run coefficients are read with the wrong sign convention for a multivariate model, reversing the conclusion about long-run length. See the checks list.

MINOR — 'a 17.8% endurance deficit relative to Riegel' (quoted three times). Recomputing from the stated inputs (5.04 km at 3:54/km, half 1:46:35 for 21.14 km): Riegel predicts a half at 4:15.0/km, actual 5:02.5/km, deficit 18.6% (18.4% if computed on normalised times). 17.8% is not reproducible from any framing I tried. Incidentally his implied personal Riegel exponent is 1.179 against the population 1.06 — which is worth stating, because it means extrapolating DOWN from the half with 1.06 is conservative and the 4:52 threshold anchor is, if anything, on the safe side.

MINOR — 'Week 1's 60 km is a 4-fold increase on that mean'. 60 / 19.2 = 3.12, i.e. 3.1-fold. The other ramp figures are all correct: 60/57.1 = +5.1%, 100/57.1 = +75%, 100/19.2 = 5.2x, four-week mean (27.2+34.8+0+14.8)/4 = 19.2 km.

MINOR — week 4 intensity distribution given as 'Z1 78%, Z2 12%, Z3 7%', which sums to 97%. Recomputing on the document's own paces and a ~48 min 10 km gives roughly Z1 76 / Z2 14 / Z3 10. The Z3 fraction is understated by about a third. The block-level totals are fine: I independently get Z1 81.2 / Z2 16.9 / Z3 1.9 against the claimed 81 / 17.5 / 1.5.

TRIVIAL (verified correct, listed for completeness) — 5:32/km x 42.195 = 3:53:28 (claimed 3:53:29); 0.89 and 0.87 of critical speed give 5:28.6 and 5:36.1 = 3:51:04 and 3:56:23 (claimed 5:28-5:36, 3:50:40-3:56:20); Z1 ceiling 4:52.4/0.823 = 5:55.3 (claimed 5:55); Lincoln MP block 21.0975 x 5:32 = 1:56:44 (claimed 1:56:47); race-day segments sum to 3:54:10 (claimed 3:54:13); long-run total 146 km and marathon-pace total 59.1 km both correct; threshold work distances (4.10 / 5.13 / 4.92 / 4.10 / 2.46 km) all correct; long-run durations 2:28 / 3:05 / 2:41 all correct; Riegel factor 0.9667 correct; Garmin marathon 3:36:12 x 1.118 = 4:01:42 (claimed 4:01:45).

NOTE ON WHAT IS NOT AN ERROR — the derived paces are arithmetically clean throughout. The document's failure mode is not sloppy computation; it is one internally contradictory target (the 10 km), one reversed regression sign, and a chain of derivation whose sensitivity is never stated. Because marathon pace = threshold pace / 0.88, a 10 s/km error in the anchor becomes ~11 s/km in marathon pace and ~8 minutes of finish time. The entire block rests on a single Riegel extrapolation from a single race, and nothing in the design says so.
verification.riskForThisAthlete:
SHORT VERSION: the pace prescriptions are mostly safe and the marathon target is genuinely conservative, but the block's structure is not — and the document's own summary claim, that "what the intensity design CAN control is not adding to the risk," is not what the plan actually does.

WHAT THE PLAN GETS RIGHT ON SAFETY. Rejecting Garmin's 4:20.9/km threshold is the single most valuable item and it is correct three ways over. The marathon target of 5:32/km is barely faster than the 5:31/km he already ran in May at 165 bpm, so race day itself is not where the danger is. Easy running at 6:10-6:50/km with a 150 bpm ceiling is genuinely 74.6% of a correctly measured 201 bpm maximum — that is real easy running, not tempo mislabelled. The drink-to-thirst rule is the right call on the one nutrition error in this sport that occasionally kills people. And the honesty about expected gain (four to six minutes, mostly from fuelling and pacing, not from the 100 km week) is worth more to him than any session in the plan.

WHERE THE DANGER ACTUALLY SITS — five maximal or near-maximal efforts, four of them stacked on the last day of the heaviest weeks:
1. A flat-out half marathon on 12 September, two days before a 60 km week begins, off a four-week mean of 19.2 km. The plan flags this and mitigates it with three easy days; that mitigation is thin.
2. Weekly threshold work at 4:52/km — faster than the whole of Pfitzinger's own stated lactate-threshold band for this athlete (4:56-5:02/km), on the largest ramp of his life.
3. The 4 October Lincoln session: 21.1 kilometres of continuous marathon-pace running inside a 33 km, 3-hour-15 effort, terminating a 100 km week. This is the largest single dose in the block and the one furthest outside the literature cited for it. Hansons caps marathon-pace tempo at 16 km for athletes already running six days a week; Canova's specific block, its structural source, was built on 200+ km/week world-class runners. Nothing in the evidence base supports 21.1 km at marathon pace for a man averaging 19.2 km per week in total. Its recovery cost is asserted at 3-4 days with no source, and the entire week-4 calendar (26 km long run on the 7th, maximal 10 km on the 11th) is built on that unsourced estimate.
4. A maximal 10 km on 11 October, closing an 80 km week — and prescribed at a target (45:50-47:30) that the document's own arithmetic contradicts by up to 2:25. Chasing 4:35/km when his real 10 km is ~48:15 means going out roughly 7% too fast in a maximal effort, 13 days before the marathon, in the one week the plan says he cannot spare recovery days.
5. Race week still contains two quality touches (4 km at marathon pace on Tuesday 20th, a 12-minute threshold on Wednesday 21st).

THREE STRUCTURAL RISKS THE DOCUMENT DOES NOT NAME AT ALL:
- Run frequency, not just volume. He currently runs at most four times a week. The plan takes him to six running days with two doubles inside three weeks — seven to nine runs a week. That is a larger structural change than the kilometre figure conveys, and it is where tissue-load surprises come from.
- No recovery week. The shape is 60/80/100/80/60/race. The 80 and 60 are taper, not a down week. Six weeks with no deload, from a base of 19 km/week.
- No strength or plyometric work. Jones & Kirby (2025) — the design's own load-bearing citation for durability — recommends heavy strength and plyometric training in the same abstract sentence structure it quotes for race-pace long runs. The plan imports the half that adds training stress and drops the half that adds none. For a runner tripling his volume, that omission is the cheapest injury mitigation available and it was left on the table.

ON THE VOLUME RAMP ITSELF. The document's handling of Nielsen et al. is honest and correct: hazard ratio 1.59, confidence interval 0.96-2.66, p = .07, novice cohort, and the primary outcome showed no significant difference at all. The evidence genuinely is absent in both directions. Two things it should have added: Nielsen's exposure was progression over a two-week window, on which his 60-to-100 km move is +67%, more than double the studied cut-off; and week 1 alone is a 3.1-fold jump on his recent mean (the document says four-fold).

WHAT I WOULD CHANGE, RANKED BY HARM PREVENTED. (1) Fix the 10 km target to ~48:15 before he sees it, and drop the asymmetric taper rule that keys off the wrong number. (2) Cut the Lincoln marathon-pace block from 21.1 km to 12-14 km, keep the 33 km if the volume gate passes, and stop calling it the most evidence-supported session in the plan. (3) Reduce week 3 to 90 km — the document's own contraindication says to do exactly this, and it is right. (4) Add two 20-minute strength sessions a week, on its own cited authority. (5) Move the threshold pace to 4:56-5:00/km, inside Pfitzinger's actual band. (6) Insert one genuine down week — the six-week calendar has room if week 5 drops to 50 km, and the taper evidence (Mujika: volume down up to 60-90%, frequency down no more than 20%) supports it more strongly than the document's misquoted version does.

FINALLY, THE ATHLETE'S ORIGINAL QUESTION. He asked whether this is evidence-based or invented. It is evidence-based: every citation is real, and the two largest datasets (151,813 marathons and 82,303 marathoners) are reported with unusual fidelity — I checked them line by line against the source PDFs. But three numbers he would act on are misquoted (the personal-best wall statistic, the taper percentages, the 10 km target), one regression is read backwards in the passage that decides his long-run length, and the whole pace structure hangs off a single Riegel extrapolation from one race whose sensitivity is never disclosed. Tell him the reference list survives scrutiny and the reasoning on top of it needs the six corrections above.

domains.title: Injury risk during a volume ramp, and what intensity is safe to add

research.tradition: Running-injury load epidemiology (the Aarhus / Nielsen school) used as an intensity *governor*, not as a training method — Garmin-RUNSAFE session-spike evidence + the ACWR retraction literature + the volume-vs-intensity RCTs
research.corePrinciple: Overuse running injury is a tissue-capacity problem: bone, tendon and fascia remodel on a timescale of weeks, while a training plan can change mechanical dose in a single evening. The best current evidence says the damaging event is not a gradually creeping weekly average but a DISCRETE SESSION that exceeds what the tissue has recently been exposed to. Frandsen et al. (BJSM 2025, 5205 runners, 588,071 sessions) found that a single run exceeding 110% of the athlete's longest run in the preceding 30 days raised the rate of overuse injury (HRR 1.64 for a >10-30% spike; 2.28 for >100%), while the weekly acute:chronic workload ratio showed NO harmful association at all — a large ACWR spike was, paradoxically, associated with a LOWER injury rate (HRR 0.75, 95% CI 0.59-0.96). That is a direct, falsifiable instruction for a planner: govern the biggest single session, not the weekly sum. Mechanistically the two axes differ in what they load. Volume accumulates cycles at moderate strain — the classic driver of bone stress injury and distance-related injuries (patellofemoral pain, ITB, MTSS). Intensity raises peak strain and strain rate per step — the driver of Achilles/calf/plantar and the only stimulus that maintains tendon stiffness (Bohm/Mersmann/Arampatzis, Sports Med Open 2015: tendon adaptation is driven by high load MAGNITUDE, not by cycle count). So a block that triples slow volume while deleting all fast running is not automatically the safe option — it under-loads the tissues that transmit peak force, while flooding the ones that fatigue by repetition. The design job is therefore not "how little intensity can we get away with" but "keep a small, protective dose of high-magnitude loading, and spend the entire risk budget on the volume ramp that has already been ratified."
research.intensityDistribution:
GOVERNING PRINCIPLE: this block spends its entire risk budget on volume. Intensity is rationed to the minimum that preserves tendon/bone quality and race specificity. Total hard running across the six weeks: ~38 km of ~420 km ≈ 9% — deliberately BELOW the conventional 80/20 polarised share, because in this block volume is the novel stressor and intensity is the discretionary one. "Hard km" = kilometres run at HR ≥ 172 bpm (within 5 bpm of his LT HR 177) or faster than his measured threshold pace. Marathon-pace running (HR ≤ 168) and strides (<25 s, full recovery) do NOT count against the allowance — MP running is metabolically sub-threshold for him (he held HR 165 for 3:55:54 in May) and strides are too short to accumulate fatigue.

FRONT-LOAD OR HOLD BACK? Front-load, mildly, and empty the allowance at the volume peak. Rationale, stated honestly as inference rather than trial evidence: there is no RCT of "intensity added during a steep volume ramp." Run Clever (Ramskov et al., BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med 2018, n=447 randomised into the intervention phase) compared progressing intensity against progressing volume and found no difference (Sch-I 36/221 vs Sch-V 44/226; 16-week risk difference -14.0%, 95% CI -36.9% to 8.9%) — but neither arm tested BOTH at once, compliance was poor, and the actual intensity progression was tiny (0.8 km of added hard running over 16 weeks). So "intensity multiplies volume risk" is unproven, and "intensity is free" is equally unproven. The lazy defensible position: put the quality where the weekly volume is smallest and the athlete is freshest, and remove it entirely in the week that contains both the 100 km peak AND the longest run of his life.

WEEK-BY-WEEK ALLOWANCE (enforceable as a hard cap on planned hard-km):

- W1, 14-20 Sep, 60 km — CAP 6 km hard (10%). One threshold session (5 x 6 min). Strides x2. NOTE: this is the highest-risk week of the block relative to his history, not W3. 60 km is a new all-time weekly maximum (previous 57.1 km, and that week contained a marathon), it is 3.1x his last-four-week mean of 19.2 km, and it starts 2 days after an all-out half marathon. If any week gets cut, cut this one to 50 km before cutting the 100.
- W2, 21-27 Sep, 80 km — CAP 6 km hard (7.5%). One threshold session. First MP-segment long run (does not count against cap). Strides x2.
- W3, 28 Sep-4 Oct, 100 km, ends with Lincoln — CAP 0 km hard. Zero threshold, zero intervals. Strides only, and none within 72 h of Sunday. This week's stress is entirely volume + the longest single run; adding threshold work here is the one combination the evidence gives no cover for.
- W4, 5-11 Oct, 80 km, ends with ASICS 10K — CAP 10 km hard, ALL of it the race itself. No other quality of any kind that week; the race is the intensity. Strides x1 midweek.
- W5, 12-18 Oct, 60 km — CAP 5 km hard: one short threshold touch (3 x 8 min at HR 172-175) early in the week to hold the adaptation, nothing after Thursday. Strides x2.
- W6, 19-24 Oct, race week — CAP 3 km hard: 2-3 x 1 km at MP-minus-10 s/km on Tue, then nothing. Strides on Thu and on race morning.

TWO ADDITIONAL HARD RULES, both directly from BJSM 2025 and both computable from data rocket already holds:
(1) NO SINGLE SESSION MAY EXCEED 110% OF THE ATHLETE'S LONGEST RUN IN THE PRECEDING 30 DAYS. This is the only load rule in this whole answer with large-cohort quantitative backing.
(2) NEVER RAISE WEEKLY VOLUME AND WEEKLY HARD-KM IN THE SAME WEEK. Expert-practice heuristic, no trial evidence, but it costs nothing and it is the only way to attribute a bad week to a cause.

WHAT THE 110% RULE DOES TO THIS PLAN — the finding the athlete most needs to see. After Saturday 12 Sep, his longest run in the trailing 30 days is 21.14 km (the Battersea Half). Compounding at 110% from there gives long-run ceilings of 23.2 km (w/c 14 Sep), 25.5 km (w/c 21 Sep) and 28.1 km (w/c 28 Sep). The ratified ~33 km Lincoln session on Sun 4 Oct is therefore a +17% spike — squarely in the >10-30% band, HRR 1.64 — landing on the last day of the 100 km peak week. That is the single highest-risk moment of the block, and it is not the 100 km itself. Recommendation: cap 4 Oct at 30-31 km (Lincoln Half at MP + ~9-10 km of easy running around it). The counter-argument, and it is real: running 33 km on 4 Oct buys down the race-day spike (42.67 km against a 33 km trailing max = +28%, small-spike band, HRR 1.64; against a 30 km trailing max = +41%, moderate band, HRR 1.52). Those two hazard ratios are within each other's confidence intervals, so the trade is roughly neutral on paper — but a spike on 4 Oct has 20 days left in which to end the block, while a spike on race day costs nothing after the finish line. Take the spike on race day. Cap Lincoln at 30-31 km.
research.fitForThisAthlete:
Blunt answer: the intensity design fits well; the volume ramp it is bolted to does not, and no intensity scheme can rescue it.

What fits. The rationing model above suits him unusually well because his aerobic ceiling is not the limiter. VO2max 53.0 held steady through a five-week dip; his 5 km speed (3:54/km in April) implies far more raw pace than his half-marathon (5:02/km at HR 174) delivers. He is not short of top-end fitness — he is short of durability. Durability is bought with volume and marathon-pace running, both of which this design keeps and neither of which requires the sessions that break Achilles tendons. Deleting VO2max work costs him almost nothing over six weeks and removes the highest-strain-rate exposure from the block. That is the easy call.

What does not fit, and should be said plainly. Three structural risks, ranked:

1. THE ENTRY, NOT THE PEAK. Week 1 at 60 km is a 3.1x jump on his last-four-week mean (19.2 km) and 78% of his entire preceding month's running (76.8 km), starting two days after an all-out half. Everything in the injury literature — Nielsen 2014 (>30% weekly progression, novices, distance-related injuries), Damsted 2019 (20-60% progression, risk difference 22.6%, 95% CI 0.9-44.3%, concentrated in the FIRST 21 DAYS and gone by day 56) — points at the first three weeks of a ramp, not the biggest week of it. Damsted's finding that the effect was significant early and null later is the most directly transferable result here: the danger window is 14 Sep to 4 Oct, and it closes just as the plan reaches its peak. The reversal condition judged at the end of week 2 is therefore correctly placed.

2. TISSUE-HOURS, NOT KILOMETRES. At 5:45-6:00/km easy pace, 100 km is roughly 10 hours of ground contact in one week, against a recent norm of about 2 hours. Bone and tendon respond to cumulative cycles, not to a weekly number in a spreadsheet. Six running days is the right way to absorb it — spreading 100 km over six runs keeps every session near 14-16 km and therefore keeps every session inside the 110% rule, which four runs a week cannot do. The frequency increase is protective under the best available evidence, not additive. (Inference from the session-spike finding; the direct evidence on running frequency is genuinely conflicting — Fredette et al., J Athl Train 2022, reports both high frequency and once-weekly running as risk factors in different studies.)

3. ENERGY AVAILABILITY. Weight was typed once in March (85.5 kg) and is stale. Going from ~2 to ~10 running hours per week without a matching increase in intake is the textbook setup for the low-energy-availability pathway into bone stress injury (narrative-review evidence only — Frontiers Sports Act Living 2021 — no trial). A body-mass drop of >2 kg over any fortnight in this block should be treated as a bone-stress-injury warning, not as a performance gain.

One honest calibration on his own numbers. Garmin's auto-detected lactate threshold pace of 4:20.9/km implies a ~1:31:30 half; he actually ran 1:46:35 at HR 174, within 3 bpm of his LT HR of 177. The ratio (1.165) is consistent with the 1.118 over-prediction factor already measured across three realised efforts. Prescribing threshold reps at 4:21/km would put him at VO2max effort under the label "threshold" — a pace error of about 30 s/km, applied to the only hard sessions in a block already at the edge. Every intensity prescription below is therefore anchored to HEART RATE first, with pace derived from the 12 Sep half result, never from the Garmin LT pace field.
research.howToValidate:
Everything here is computable from Garmin/Strava data rocket already ingests, or from a one-line daily check-in. Nothing needs a lab.

PROCESS METRICS — is the design actually being applied? (Check weekly; these are the ones that tell you the RULE is working, as distinct from the athlete surviving by luck.)
1. Session-spike compliance: count of runs where distance > 1.10 x (longest run in the preceding 30 days). Target: zero unplanned, exactly one planned (race day, 24 Oct). This is a direct, exact implementation of the BJSM 2025 exposure definition and is the single most important number in the block.
2. Hard-km share per week vs the cap above. Computed as km with HR >= 172 bpm, taken from the HR stream, not from Garmin's zone labels (his profile max HR of 196 is wrong; zones must be rebuilt on 201).
3. Planned-vs-actual weekly km. The signal that matters is not "did he hit 100" but "did he need to shorten easy runs to hit it." A week completed only by truncating easy runs is a failed week even if the total lands.

WARNING SIGNS THAT TRIGGER CUTTING INTENSITY (each stated with its real evidence strength):
4. HRV Status "Unbalanced" or "Low" for >=3 consecutive days, or 7-day mean HRV below the personal baseline band. ACTION: delete that week's threshold session, replace with easy volume or the swim. Evidence: Bellenger et al., Sports Med 2016 — vagal HR indices track functional overreaching; HRV-guided training RCTs (Vesterinen 2016, Javaloyes 2019) show performance benefit from exactly this gating. NOTE HONESTLY: no study has shown HRV gating reduces INJURY. It is validated for overreaching, not for tissue damage.
5. Resting HR (smoothed; his baseline is 57, down from 84 in March) rising >=5 bpm above its 28-day rolling mean for >=3 consecutive days. Same action. Same evidence base and same caveat as (4).
6. Aerobic decoupling on easy runs: mean HR at a fixed easy pace (say 5:50/km on flat) rising >5 bpm week-on-week, or pace at a fixed easy HR (150 bpm) slowing >10 s/km. This is a fatigue signal, cheap to compute from any two comparable runs, and it is the one metric that distinguishes "absorbing the volume" from "accumulating debt." Evidence: expert practice / physiological reasoning, not trial-validated.
7. Pain gate (self-reported, one prompt per day): the Silbernagel rule — pain during and after the run <= 5/10, back to baseline the following morning, and not increasing week on week. Breach = all hard running to zero and the long run capped for a week. This is the highest-evidence monitoring tool available (Silbernagel et al., Am J Sports Med 2007, RCT) and the only one that has been shown to permit continued training safely rather than merely to describe fatigue.
8. Cadence drop at fixed pace, or a step-length increase at fixed pace, late in long runs — a proxy for form breakdown and the moment when peak tissue loads climb. Weak evidence in the injury literature; use as a tiebreaker, never as a trigger on its own.

WHAT WOULD FALSIFY THE DESIGN. If (a) session-spike compliance is clean, (b) hard-km stays inside the caps, and (c) HRV/RHR/decoupling stay in band, yet he still breaks down — then the volume ramp itself was the cause and the intensity rationing was never the operative variable. Conversely, if he completes all six weeks and marathon-pace HR at 5:20/km falls week on week (target: 5-8 bpm lower on 12 Oct than on 21 Sep at matched pace and conditions), the block worked, and the modest intensity dose was enough. Both outcomes are readable from data rocket already has, which is the point.

METRIC ROCKET MUST NOT USE: the acute:chronic workload ratio, in any of its forms (rolling average, EWMA, Garmin's own "Acute Load" ratio). Its ratio construction is mathematically coupled — the acute period is inside the chronic denominator, producing spurious correlation independent of any real physiology (Lolli et al., BJSM 2019); it has no coherent causal interpretation (Impellizzeri et al., IJSPP 2020); its evidence base is methodologically incoherent across studies (Wang et al., Sports Med 2020); and in the largest running-specific dataset ever assembled it did not predict injury at all, with the largest spikes associated with FEWER injuries (Frandsen et al., BJSM 2025). Encoding it into rocket would be encoding a metric its own field has spent five years retracting.

sources.citation: Frandsen JSB, Hulme A, Parner ET, et al. How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions in a 5200-person cohort study. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2025;59(17):e109380. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2024-109380
sources.claim: In 5205 runners over 18 months (588,071 sessions; 1820 injuries, 1311 overuse), a SINGLE session exceeding 110% of the runner's longest run in the previous 30 days raised the overuse injury rate: >10-30% spike HRR 1.64 (95% CI 1.31-2.05); >30-100% HRR 1.52 (1.16-2.00); >100% HRR 2.28 (1.50-3.48). Week-to-week ratio showed no association. ACWR spikes showed no harm and the largest category was associated with a LOWER rate (HRR 0.75, 0.59-0.96). Caveat to state: the dose-response is non-monotonic (the small-spike HRR exceeds the moderate-spike HRR), so treat the bands as a threshold effect at ~110%, not as a smooth curve.
sources.population: 5205 recreational and club runners across 87 countries, 77.9% male, mean age 45.8 y, self-selected Garmin users — demographically close to this athlete, though volunteer/wearable selection bias applies

sources.citation: Nielsen RØ, Bertelsen ML, Ramskov D, Damsted C, Brund RK, Parner ET, Sørensen H, Rasmussen S, Kjærgaard S. The Garmin-RUNSAFE Running Health Study on the aetiology of running-related injuries: rationale and design of an 18-month prospective cohort study including runners worldwide. BMJ Open. 2019;9(9):e032627. doi:10.1136/bmjopen-2019-032627
sources.claim: Protocol and rationale for the cohort that produced the 2025 session-spike result; pre-specifies the dose-response question between changes in training load and injury. Establishes that the analysis plan was declared before the data, which materially strengthens the 2025 finding.
sources.population: protocol paper; target population runners uploading to Garmin Connect worldwide

sources.citation: Nielsen RØ, Parner ET, Nohr EA, Sørensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S. Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries: an association which varies according to type of injury. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2014;44(10):739-747. doi:10.2519/jospt.2014.5164
sources.claim: Progressing weekly distance by >30% (vs <10%) over a 2-week period was associated with more DISTANCE-RELATED injuries specifically (patellofemoral pain, ITB syndrome, medial tibial stress syndrome, gluteus medius injury, greater trochanteric bursitis, TFL injury, patellar tendinopathy) — not with injuries as an undifferentiated category. The injury type, not just the injury count, tracks the type of load.
sources.population: 874 healthy NOVICE runners, 1-year follow-up, GPS-monitored. Population caveat matters enormously: novices, not experienced marathoners. This athlete is experienced but his CHRONIC load is currently novice-like, which is arguably the worse of both worlds.

sources.citation: Damsted C, Parner ET, Sørensen H, Malisoux L, Hulme A, Nielsen RØ. The association between changes in weekly running distance and running-related injury: preparing for a half marathon. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2019;49(4):230-238. doi:10.2519/jospt.2019.8541
sources.claim: In 261 half-marathon trainees over 14 weeks (56 injuries, 21.5%), increasing weekly distance by 20-60% vs <20% produced a significant excess of injury at 21 DAYS (risk difference 22.6%, 95% CI 0.9%-44.3%, P=.041), which was NOT significant at 56 or 98 days. Two honest complications: the effect is early and transient, and progression >60% did not show the same excess — so this is not a clean dose-response either. The transferable message is that the danger window sits in the first ~3 weeks of a ramp.
sources.population: 261 healthy recreational runners training for a half marathon (ProjectRun21) — the closest available population to this athlete in training intent

sources.citation: Ramskov D, Rasmussen S, Sørensen H, Parner ET, Lind M, Nielsen RØ. Run Clever – No difference in risk of injury when comparing progression in running volume and running intensity in recreational runners: a randomised trial. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2018;4(1):e000333. doi:10.1136/bmjsem-2017-000333
sources.claim: 839 runners randomised (447 completed the 8-week preconditioning and entered the 16-week intervention). Intensity-progression arm 36/221 injured; volume-progression arm 44/226. 16-week risk difference -14.0% (95% CI -36.9% to 8.9%, P=.23) — no detectable difference. CRITICAL CAVEATS THAT LIMIT ITS USE HERE: the actual intensity progression was trivial (0.8 km of added hard running across 16 weeks vs 6 km of added easy volume), compliance was poor, the confidence interval spans a 37-point difference in either direction, and NEITHER arm progressed volume and intensity simultaneously. This trial does not license adding intensity during a steep volume ramp; it simply fails to convict intensity when volume is held flat.
sources.population: 839 recreational runners, Denmark, randomised; 3 sessions/week; hard defined as >=88% VO2max, easy as <=80%

sources.citation: Ramskov D, Rasmussen S, Sørensen H, Parner ET, Lind M, Nielsen RØ. Progression in running intensity or running volume and the development of specific injuries in recreational runners: Run Clever, a randomized trial using competing risks. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2018;48(10):740-748. doi:10.2519/jospt.2018.8062
sources.claim: Companion competing-risks analysis of the same trial, examining whether intensity- and volume-progression produce DIFFERENT injury types rather than different injury counts. HONESTY FLAG: full text was paywalled (HTTP 403) and I could not read the results. Title, journal, year and DOI are verified from JOSPT's own listing; I am NOT asserting its numerical findings, and rocket should not cite specific results from it without someone reading it.
sources.population: same Run Clever cohort of recreational runners

sources.citation: Buist I, Bredeweg SW, van Mechelen W, Lemmink KAPM, Pepping GJ, Diercks RL. No effect of a graded training program on the number of running-related injuries in novice runners: a randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2008;36(1):33-39. (PMID 17940147)
sources.claim: A 13-week graded programme built on the '10% rule' did not reduce running-related injury incidence versus a standard 8-week programme. This is the trial that removed the evidentiary floor from the 10%-per-week convention. It does not show that progression is harmless — it shows that this particular rule, applied this way, prevented nothing.
sources.population: novice runners, Netherlands (GRONORUN)

sources.citation: Lolli L, Batterham AM, Hawkins R, Kelly DM, Strudwick AJ, Thorpe RT, Gregson W, Atkinson G. Mathematical coupling causes spurious correlation within the conventional acute-to-chronic workload ratio calculations. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2019;53(15):921-922. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2017-098110
sources.claim: In the conventional ACWR the acute-period data are contained within the chronic-period denominator, producing mathematical coupling. The resulting correlation appears regardless of any true physiological relationship between acute and chronic load, so inferences drawn from it are biased by construction.
sources.population: methodological/statistical analysis, not a population study

sources.citation: Impellizzeri FM, Tenan MS, Kempton T, Novak A, Coutts AJ. Acute:chronic workload ratio: conceptual issues and fundamental pitfalls. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2020;15(6):907-913. doi:10.1123/ijspp.2019-0864
