sources.claim: The ACWR lacks a coherent causal interpretation; the ratio distorts data when chronic load is low (inflating and destabilising the index — precisely this athlete's situation); and no study has properly estimated a causal effect, so manipulating ACWR to change injury rates is conjecture rather than evidence-based practice.
sources.population: conceptual/methodological critique across team sports

sources.citation: Wang C, Vargas JT, Stokes T, Steele R, Shrier I. Analyzing activity and injury: lessons learned from the acute:chronic workload ratio. Sports Medicine. 2020;50(7):1243-1254. doi:10.1007/s40279-020-01280-1
sources.claim: Systematic review of ACWR methodology: acute/chronic window choices and calculation models (rolling average vs EWMA) vary so widely between studies that the literature cannot be pooled, and the evidence is insufficient to determine any best method of application. Combined with Lolli and Impellizzeri, this is why an ACWR gate should not be written into a planner.
sources.population: professional team-sport athletes (systematic review) — not runners, which is itself part of the problem when the metric is applied to running

sources.citation: Fredette A, Roy JS, Perreault K, Dupuis F, Napier C, Esculier JF. The association between running injuries and training parameters: a systematic review. Journal of Athletic Training. 2022;57(7):650-671. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-0195.21
sources.claim: Conflicting evidence across the board: the 10% rule is 'not justified'; intensity findings conflict (one study found tempo runs in the initial phase raised injury odds, OR 3.96; another found regular speed intervals protective against knee injury); frequency findings conflict (7 days/week raised risk vs 0-2 days, yet running only once weekly was itself a risk factor); weekly distance thresholds reported at >30 km (HR 3.28) and >64 km (adjusted RR 2.88). Directly relevant caution: >64 km/week is itself an elevated-risk zone in the literature, and three of this athlete's six weeks sit above it.
sources.population: systematic review across recreational, novice and competitive runners — heterogeneity is the headline finding

sources.citation: Lauersen JB, Andersen TE, Andersen LB. Strength training as superior, dose-dependent and safe prevention of acute and overuse sports injuries: a systematic review, qualitative analysis and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;52(24):1557-1563. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2018-099078
sources.claim: Strength training reduced overall sports injuries to roughly one third (RR ~0.34) and approximately halved overuse injuries, with a dose-response relationship and no evidence of harm. This is the strongest injury-prevention evidence in the entire answer, and it is the one intervention that adds protective high-magnitude loading without adding a single running kilometre.
sources.population: RCTs across multiple sports and ages (adolescent to adult); not running-specific, which is the main transferability caveat

sources.citation: Bohm S, Mersmann F, Arampatzis A. Human tendon adaptation in response to mechanical loading: a systematic review and meta-analysis of exercise intervention studies on healthy adults. Sports Medicine - Open. 2015;1(1):7. doi:10.1186/s40798-015-0009-9
sources.claim: Tendon stiffness and material adaptation are driven principally by high LOAD MAGNITUDE (contraction intensity), with longer intervention durations (>12 weeks) more effective; cycle count alone is a weak stimulus. Mechanistic basis for retaining a small dose of high-magnitude loading (strides, heavy strength) during a block that is otherwise a flood of low-magnitude repetitions. NOTE: this is adaptation evidence, NOT injury-outcome evidence — no trial has shown that maintaining tendon stiffness during a volume ramp reduces injuries in runners.
sources.population: healthy adults in exercise-intervention studies; tendon mechanical/material/morphological outcomes, not injury outcomes

sources.citation: Bellenger CR, Fuller JT, Thomson RL, Davison K, Robertson EY, Buckley JD. Monitoring athletic training status through autonomic heart rate regulation: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2016;46(10):1461-1486. doi:10.1007/s40279-016-0484-2
sources.claim: Vagal-related HRV indices, post-exercise heart-rate recovery and HR acceleration are sensitive to training status and, once methodological factors are controlled, to functional overreaching. Basis for using Garmin HRV Status and resting-HR drift as the trigger to cut intensity. CAVEAT TO STATE IN ROCKET: validated against OVERREACHING and performance, never against injury.
sources.population: endurance-trained athletes

sources.citation: Silbernagel KG, Thomeé R, Eriksson BI, Karlsson J. Continued sports activity, using a pain-monitoring model, during rehabilitation in patients with Achilles tendinopathy: a randomized controlled study. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2007;35(6):897-906. doi:10.1177/0363546506298279
sources.claim: Continuing to run while symptomatic is safe and non-inferior provided pain stays <=5/10 during and after activity, returns to baseline by the next morning, and does not increase week to week. Gives rocket a validated, self-reportable gate that permits training to continue rather than only telling the athlete to stop.
sources.population: patients with Achilles tendinopathy; the rule has since been generalised well beyond that population by clinical convention rather than by trial

sources.citation: Nielsen RØ et al. (title verified) A paradigm shift in understanding overuse running-related injuries: findings from the Garmin-RUNSAFE study point to a sudden not gradual onset. JOSPT Open. doi:10.2519/josptopen.2024.0075
sources.claim: Argues the conceptual shift from gradual accumulation to sudden, session-level onset. HONESTY FLAG: full text returned HTTP 403 and I could not read it. Title, journal and DOI are verified from JOSPT's listing; the AUTHOR LIST IS NOT VERIFIED and I have attributed it to the RUNSAFE group by inference only. Rocket should not cite this without someone opening it.
sources.population: commentary on the Garmin-RUNSAFE cohort

prescriptions.sessionName: Long-run ladder governed by the 110% session-spike rule (the block's primary safety mechanism)
prescriptions.structure: The long run's distance is COMPUTED, not chosen: distance_cap = 1.10 x (longest single run in the preceding 30 days). Run continuous, no walk breaks, on the flattest surface available. One per week, Saturday or Sunday. The planner refuses to emit a long run above the cap; if the plan's weekly km target cannot be met under the cap, the excess is redistributed to midweek runs, never to the long one.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Distance derived from a rolling 30-day maximum computed from his own activity history — not from a percentage of weekly volume and not from a coach's judgement. Effort anchor: HR <= 157 bpm (LT HR 177 minus 20) for the easy portions.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Directly implements the only quantitatively-backed load rule in the running-injury literature (Frandsen et al., BJSM 2025). Keeps every session inside the exposure band where the overuse-injury hazard ratio is 1.0, rather than 1.64-2.28. Secondary effect: it forces the weekly volume to be spread across more runs, which is the only way to build 100 km without manufacturing spikes.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: Trailing 30-day maximum after Sat 12 Sep = 21.14 km (the Battersea Half). Caps: w/c 14 Sep 23.2 km; w/c 21 Sep 25.5 km; w/c 28 Sep 28.1 km; w/c 5 Oct 30.9 km. The ratified ~33 km Lincoln session on Sun 4 Oct exceeds its cap by 17% (HRR 1.64) and lands on the last day of the 100 km peak week — RECOMMEND CAPPING AT 30-31 km. The marathon on 24 Oct will be a +38-41% spike against a 30-31 km trailing max (moderate band, HRR 1.52); that is unavoidable, it is the point of the block, and it is the one spike the rule should be allowed to break.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: 1 per week, 6 total

prescriptions.sessionName: Threshold cruise intervals, heart-rate capped
prescriptions.structure: 5 x 6 min with 90 s easy jog float, on flat tarmac or a well-drained path. Total 30 min / ~6 km at intensity. 15 min easy warm-up, 10 min easy cool-down. Placed Tuesday or Wednesday, never within 72 h of the long run.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: HEART RATE IS THE ANCHOR: 172-177 bpm, hard ceiling 177 (his Garmin-detected LT HR of 177, measured 2026-08-08). Pace is an OUTPUT, capped at (12 Sep half-marathon pace minus 12 s/km) so that a good-feeling day cannot turn a threshold session into a 5 km time trial. Zones must be rebuilt on max HR 201 (measured 14 Jun), not the 196 in his Garmin profile or the 195 he believes.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Maintains lactate-clearance capacity and running economy through a block whose volume would otherwise flatten his top end, at the lowest tissue cost per unit of adaptation — sub-maximal ground contact forces, moderate strain rate, no sprint mechanics. Six-minute repetitions rather than short fast reps deliberately avoid the high strain-rate exposure that drives Achilles, calf and plantar injuries.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: Do NOT use Garmin's LT pace field of 4:20.9/km. That value implies a ~1:31:30 half; he ran 1:46:35 (5:02/km) at HR 174 in July, and Garmin over-predicts him by a median factor of 1.118. His true durable threshold pace is approximately 4:45-4:55/km. Re-derive it on 13 Sep from the Battersea Half: threshold pace ~= half-marathon pace minus 10-15 s/km. If he runs 1:44 (4:56/km), threshold = 4:43-4:46/km at HR 172-177.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: Once in W1 (14-20 Sep), once in W2 (21-27 Sep), once in W5 (12-18 Oct, shortened to 3 x 8 min and placed before Thursday). ZERO in W3 (peak volume week) and ZERO in W4 (the 10K race is that week's only intensity). 3 sessions in the whole block.

prescriptions.sessionName: Marathon-pace segments inside the long run
prescriptions.structure: Long run with 2-3 x 20-25 min at marathon pace, separated by 8-10 min easy. Segments placed in the SECOND half of the run so the pace is executed on tired legs. Does not count against the weekly hard-km allowance.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: HR ceiling 168 bpm — he averaged 165 bpm for the 3:55:54 marathon in May, so this is a genuinely sub-threshold effort for him (9-12 bpm below LT HR 177). Pace derived from his realised half (5:02/km) via Riegel (1.06 exponent), giving ~3:45-3:47 marathon = 5:20/km, cross-checked against his actual May marathon at 5:31/km.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: The highest-specificity, lowest-injury-cost quality available. Trains substrate utilisation, pacing discipline and fatigue-resistance at exactly the mechanics he will use on 24 Oct, at ground reaction forces barely above easy running. It is also the enforcement mechanism for 'do not race Lincoln': an HR ceiling is checkable after the fact, a verbal instruction is not.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: Marathon pace 5:15-5:25/km at HR 160-168. LINCOLN HALF, Sun 4 Oct: run the 21.1 km at 5:20/km with a hard HR ceiling of 168, inside a session of 30-31 km total (recommended) rather than 33. If his HR exceeds 172 for more than 3 continuous minutes at any point, the session is logged as a race, not a workout, and the following week's threshold session is deleted.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: 1 in W2, 1 in W3 (Lincoln), 1 short version in W5, 1 token version in race week. 4 total.

prescriptions.sessionName: Strides (the tendon-and-bone insurance policy)
prescriptions.structure: 6 x 20 s at controlled fast pace on flat ground, walk-back recovery of 60-90 s, appended to the end of an easy run. Total intensity exposure ~2 min. Stop immediately if form degrades.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Effort-anchored, not HR-anchored (20 s is too short for HR to respond): roughly 3:50-4:00/km, i.e. his measured 5 km speed, run relaxed and never maximal. This is the only session in the block that deliberately produces high strain rate.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Preserves tendon stiffness and neuromuscular coordination through a block dominated by low-magnitude repetition. Bohm/Mersmann/Arampatzis (Sports Med Open 2015) established that tendon adapts to load MAGNITUDE, not cycle count — so tripling slow volume while removing all fast running plausibly leaves the Achilles under-prepared. HONESTY: the adaptation evidence is solid; the claim that this PREVENTS INJURY during a volume ramp is mechanistic inference with no trial behind it. It is included because the cost is ~2 minutes a week and the mechanism is coherent.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: 6 x 20 s at ~3:55/km. He has demonstrated 3:54/km over 5.04 km, so this pace is comfortably sub-maximal for him and carries no sprint-strain risk. Never within 48 h of the long run; never in the 72 h before Lincoln or the 10K.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: 2x/week in W1, W2, W5; 1x/week in W3 (early in the week only) and W4; twice in race week including race-morning activation.

prescriptions.sessionName: Heavy slow strength (the highest-evidence item in this entire answer)
prescriptions.structure: 3 exercises, 3 sets of 6 at RPE 8, ~35 minutes: (1) straight-knee calf raise, (2) bent-knee (soleus) calf raise, (3) split squat or single-leg Romanian deadlift. Loaded, slow tempo (3 s down, 3 s up). Placed on the same day as a quality run or an easy run — never on a rest day, never the day before the long run.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Load anchored to RPE 8 (2 reps in reserve) at 6 reps, progressed by adding load whenever all 3 sets complete at RPE <= 7. No 1RM testing required — the anchor is a self-reported effort scale, which is exactly the kind of measurement that survives contact with a runner who has no gym history.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Lauersen et al. (BJSM 2018) is the strongest injury-prevention finding in sports medicine: strength training cut overall sports injuries to roughly one third (RR ~0.34) and approximately halved overuse injuries, dose-dependently and safely. Calf/soleus work specifically targets the tissue most exposed by a large easy-volume ramp. It adds protective high-magnitude loading at zero running kilometres — the single best risk-adjusted intervention in this block.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: At ~85.5 kg he is a heavy runner by recreational-marathon standards, which raises absolute tissue loading per step at every pace. He also has no cycling and one 2-hour swim per week, so there is no competing lower-body load to manage. Start conservatively: bodyweight-plus-dumbbell in W1, progressing load through W3, then hold load flat and drop to 2 sets from W4 and 1 maintenance session in race week.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: 2x/week W1-W3, 2x/week W4-W5 at reduced volume, 1x in race week (Mon or Tue only).

prescriptions.sessionName: ASICS LDNX 10K — the taper's only hard session, and its entire intensity budget
prescriptions.structure: Race it. 3 km easy warm-up including 4 strides, 10 km hard, 2 km easy cool-down. Total ~15 km. NO other quality of any kind that week — no threshold, no marathon-pace work, no long fast finish.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Raced on feel; no HR cap (this is the one session where a cap would be counterproductive). Expect HR to reach 190-196 given max 201. Pace: Garmin predicts 43:29 for 10 km; applying his measured over-prediction factor of 1.118 gives a realistic ~48:37 (4:52/km), which is also consistent with his half at 5:02/km.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Provides the block's sharpest neuromuscular and VO2max stimulus in a context where he will self-limit sensibly (a race with people around him and a finish line) rather than in an interval session where a planner's prescribed pace could be 30 s/km too fast. Also functions as a clean, free fitness measurement 13 days out from the marathon — see validation.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: Sun 11 Oct, the last day of the 80 km week. Cap that week's total at 80 km INCLUDING the 15 km race day, and cap its long run at 24-26 km on the previous weekend rather than letting a long run and a race coexist. Expected finish ~48-49 min; if he runs under 47:00 the marathon-pace band should be revised downward by ~5 s/km before race week.
prescriptions.weeklyFrequency: Once, W4 (5-11 Oct). This is the block's only maximal effort before 24 Oct.

contraindications: NO VO2max INTERVALS AT ANY POINT IN THIS BLOCK. No sessions at HR >185 bpm (>92% of his 201 max) other than the 10K race on 11 Oct and the marathon itself. Short fast repetitions carry the highest strain rate per step and are the classic route into Achilles, calf and plantar injury; over six weeks they add almost nothing to a marathon that his existing VO2max of 53.0 does not already cover. This is the cheapest risk reduction available and it costs him nothing he needs.

NO QUALITY WORK IN THE 100 km WEEK (28 Sep - 4 Oct). Zero threshold, zero intervals, strides only and none within 72 h of Sunday. That week already contains the highest weekly volume of his life AND the longest run of his life; adding a third novel stressor is the one combination for which the literature offers no cover at all.
NEVER RAISE WEEKLY VOLUME AND WEEKLY HARD-KM IN THE SAME WEEK. Expert-practice rule, no trial evidence — but it is the only way to attribute a bad week to a cause, and it costs nothing.

DO NOT PRESCRIBE PACES FROM GARMIN'S LT PACE FIELD (4:20.9/km). It implies a ~1:31:30 half against his realised 1:46:35 at HR 174, and Garmin over-predicts him by a median factor of 1.118 across three realised efforts. A ~30 s/km pace error applied to the only hard sessions in an already-maximal block is a foreseeable injury, not a training stimulus. Anchor to HR; re-derive pace from the 12 Sep half result.

DO NOT ENCODE THE ACUTE:CHRONIC WORKLOAD RATIO AS A GATE — in any form, including Garmin's own Acute Load ratio. It is mathematically coupled (Lolli, BJSM 2019), causally uninterpretable (Impellizzeri, IJSPP 2020), methodologically incoherent across the literature (Wang, Sports Med 2020), and in the largest running dataset ever assembled it did not predict injury, with the largest spikes associated with FEWER injuries (Frandsen, BJSM 2025, HRR 0.75). It is also maximally unstable in exactly his situation, where chronic load is very low: his ACWR in week 1 will read as catastrophic and mean nothing.

DO NOT APPLY THE 110% SESSION RULE TO THE MARATHON. Race day will be a +38-41% spike over his trailing 30-day maximum. That is the goal of the block, and post-race injury risk is not a reason to shorten the race. The rule governs training, not the event.

DO NOT RACE LINCOLN (4 Oct). Enforce with an HR ceiling of 168 bpm, not with a verbal instruction — a ceiling is checkable in the file afterwards. If HR exceeds 172 for more than 3 continuous minutes, log it as a race and delete the following week's quality.

PAIN STOP RULE. Any lower-limb pain above 5/10 during or after a run, or pain not back to baseline the following morning, or pain increasing week on week (Silbernagel et al., AJSM 2007): hard running to zero, long run capped at the previous week's distance, substitute the 2-hour swim. This overrides every other rule in this document, including the ratified weekly kilometres.

BONE-STRESS-INJURY FLAG: body mass falling more than 2 kg in any fortnight, or persistent focal bony tenderness (shin, metatarsal, femoral neck, sacrum). His 85.5 kg is a stale March figure and his running hours are going from roughly 2 to roughly 10 per week; low energy availability plus a fivefold increase in loading cycles is the textbook setup. Evidence here is narrative-review only — no trial — but the failure mode is a six-week absence, so treat it as a hard stop, not a nudge.

THE ENTRY IS THE DANGER, NOT THE PEAK. Week 1 at 60 km is a new all-time weekly maximum, 3.1x his last-four-week mean of 19.2 km, 78% of his entire preceding month's running, starting two days after an all-out half marathon. Damsted et al. (JOSPT 2019) found the excess injury risk from a ramp concentrated in the first 21 days and gone by day 56. If any week must be cut, cut week 1 to 50 km before touching the 100 — and the reversal condition judged at the end of week 2 is correctly placed, because that is precisely when the evidence says the damage shows up.

SIX RUNNING DAYS IS A CHANGE TOO. He has never run more than 4 times in a week. Adding two running days is itself novel, though the session-spike evidence says it is the RIGHT way to absorb 100 km (six runs of ~14 km contain no spikes; four runs of ~25 km do). Introduce the sixth day in week 2, not week 1, and make it the shortest run of the week.

HRV AND RESTING-HR GATES ARE VALIDATED FOR OVERREACHING, NOT FOR INJURY. Use them to cut intensity, and say so honestly in rocket's UI. Do not let a green HRV reading override the pain rule or the 110% session rule — those rest on stronger ground.

verification.tradition: Aarhus/Nielsen running-injury load epidemiology (Garmin-RUNSAFE cohort + the ACWR-retraction literature), used as an intensity governor rather than a training method. The tradition is correctly identified and the primary sources are real. But the piece silently borrows a second tradition it never names — Daniels/Riegel pace-prescription methodology — for every actual number an athlete would run (threshold pace, marathon pace, stride pace, 10 K target). The epidemiology is well sourced; the pace prescriptions have no source at all, and they are the part that becomes a session.

checks.claim: Frandsen et al. BJSM 2025: 5205 runners, 588,071 sessions, 1820 injuries of which 1311 overuse; single-session spike >110% of longest run in prior 30 days gives HRR 1.64 (1.31-2.05), 1.52 (1.16-2.00), 2.28 (1.50-3.48); week-to-week ratio null; largest ACWR spike HRR 0.75 (0.59-0.96).
checks.note: Verified against the paper itself (PMID 40623829, PMC12421110). Every figure matches exactly, including the 1311 overuse count, the 87 countries, 22% female, mean age 45.8, and the ACWR row 0.75 (0.59-0.96) from Table 2. Citation formatting is wrong though: the paper is Br J Sports Med 2025;59(17):1203-1210, not 59(17):e109380, and the first author indexes as Schuster Brandt Frandsen J, not Frandsen JSB. Also unmentioned: median time at risk was only 80 running sessions (IQR 31-161), so the cohort is not observed across a marathon build.

checks.claim: The 110% session rule is 'the only load rule in this whole answer with large-cohort quantitative backing' and 'a direct, falsifiable instruction for a planner'.
checks.note: Two problems. (1) Causal double standard: the piece rejects ACWR partly by citing Impellizzeri 2020 ('no studies have even tried to estimate causal effects properly... manipulating ACWR remains a conjecture') and then exempts its favoured finding from the identical test. Frandsen is an observational multistate Cox model. Manipulating session distance to change injury rates is exactly as much a conjecture. (2) Confounding by session type: the reference state is 'regression or progression up to 10%', which contains every short recovery run in the cohort; the spike states are, by construction, the long runs. Part of the HRR is 'long runs are when overuse injury becomes noticeable', reported same-day or 1-2 days after per the paper's own supplement.

checks.claim: Nielsen 2014 (JOSPT 44(10):739-747): progressing weekly distance >30% vs <10% was associated with more distance-related injuries (PFP, ITB, MTSS, etc.).
checks.note: The result was NOT statistically significant. Verified abstract (PMID 25155475): hazard ratio 1.59, 95% CI 0.96 to 2.66, P = .07 — the CI crosses 1. The paper's primary analysis found 'no statistically significant differences in injury rates across the 3 exposure groups', and the authors call the study explorative and ask for RCTs to verify. The research states the association as established fact and omits the CI and p-value entirely. This is one of the two pillars holding up 'the entry is the danger', and it does not hold weight.

checks.claim: Damsted 2019 (JOSPT 49(4):230-238): 261 half-marathon trainees, 56 injuries (21.5%), 20-60% progression vs <20% gave risk difference 22.6% (0.9-44.3), P=.041 at 21 days, null at 56 and 98 days.
checks.note: Verified exactly (PMID 30526231). But transferability is weaker than presented: the CI lower bound is 0.9% and p=.041, i.e. barely significant with one degree of fragility; and the studied exposure band tops out at 60% week-on-week. This athlete's week 1 is a +213% jump (19.2 -> 60 km). Damsted contains no data on jumps of that size, so 'the danger window is 14 Sep to 4 Oct' is an extrapolation well outside the fitted range, not a finding.

checks.claim: Run Clever (Ramskov, BMJ Open SEM 2018;4:e000333): 839 randomised, 447 entered intervention, Sch-I 36 vs Sch-V 44 injured, 16-week risk difference -14.0% (-36.9% to 8.9%).
checks.note: Verified exactly (PMID 29527322), including the RD and CI. The research's caveats are honest and correct. Two sub-claims could not be verified from the abstract and are not sourced to a page: 'P=.23', 'the actual intensity progression was trivial (0.8 km of added hard running across 16 weeks vs 6 km of added easy volume)', and 'compliance was poor'. Those are load-bearing for the argument that the trial does not license adding intensity during a ramp — they should be page-cited or dropped.

checks.claim: Ramskov JOSPT 2018;48(10):740-748 — 'full text was paywalled (HTTP 403) and I could not read the results... I am NOT asserting its numerical findings.'
checks.note: The results and conclusion are freely readable on PubMed (PMID 29895234) and were retrieved in one call. They matter because they contradict the answer's own corePrinciple. The trial explicitly tested whether intensity progression produces Achilles/gastrocnemius/plantar injuries while volume progression produces PFP/ITB/patellar tendinopathy. Conclusion: 'No difference in risk of hypothesized intensity- and volume-specific running-related injuries exists between the 2 running schedules.' All risk differences straddle zero. The mechanistic tissue-partition argument that justifies keeping strides and deleting VO2max work is the one claim in the piece that has been directly tested, and the test was null. Declaring the paper unreadable removed the only disconfirming evidence in the source list.

checks.claim: Lauersen 2018 (BJSM 52(24):1557-1563): strength training cut overall sports injuries to roughly one third (RR ~0.34) and approximately halved overuse injuries, dose-dependently.
checks.note: Half right, half misattributed. Verified (PMID 30131332): RR 0.338 (0.238-0.480) for strength-training RCTs — the 'one third' is correct. But 'approximately halved overuse injuries' is from Lauersen 2014 (BJSM 48(11):871-7, PMID 24100287), where overuse RR 0.527 (0.373-0.746) refers to physical-activity programmes generally. The 2018 paper reports no separate overuse RR of ~0.5. Also, 'the strongest injury-prevention evidence in sports medicine' rests on six trials, 7738 participants and 177 total injuries, none of them running-specific. The dose-response ('10% more volume, 4 percentage points less risk') is post-hoc meta-regression over six studies.

checks.claim: Bohm/Mersmann/Arampatzis 2015 (Sports Med Open 1(1):7): tendon adaptation is driven by high load magnitude, not cycle count — justifying strides as tendon insurance.
checks.note: The paper is real and the headline is right (PMID 27747846: stiffness adaptation depends significantly on loading intensity, not contraction type; SMD 0.70 for stiffness). But the inclusion criteria were longitudinal interventions of >=8 weeks (>=12 weeks more effective) using sustained resistance-type loading. Nothing in it concerns 20-second running strides across a 6-week block. The one prescription Bohm actually supports is the heavy slow strength work; the strides ride on its coat-tails. The research flags that this is adaptation not injury evidence, which is honest, but does not flag the duration and contraction-type mismatch.

checks.claim: Bellenger 2016 (Sports Med 46(10):1461-86) supports gating on HRV Status 'Unbalanced/Low' and resting-HR drift to cut intensity.
checks.note: The paper points the other way for the metric being gated on. Verified abstract (PMID 26888648): studies inducing performance DECREASES (i.e. overreaching) showed 'a small increase in resting RMSSD (SMD = 0.26; P = 0.01)' and trivial changes in resting HFP. Pooled, vagal HRV rises with functional overreaching. A rule that fires on LOW HRV therefore does not follow from this citation and may fail to fire, or fire on the wrong sign. Separately, Vesterinen 2016 and Javaloyes 2019 are invoked in the validation section with no author-journal-DOI entry in the source list at all — unverifiable as given.

checks.claim: Wang et al. Sports Med 2020;50(7):1243-1254 is a 'systematic review of ACWR methodology' finding that window choices vary so widely the literature cannot be pooled.
checks.note: The paper exists exactly as cited (PMID 32125672, DOI 10.1007/s40279-020-01280-1) and does conclude that ACWR limitations 'should discourage its use'. But it is a narrative/methodological review, not a systematic review and certainly not a meta-analysis — the research tags its strength as 'meta-analysis' and its population as 'professional team-sport athletes (systematic review)', both wrong. The specific 'cannot be pooled / insufficient to determine any best method' wording is not in the paper; its actual content is ratio-construction problems, the EWMA initial-load problem, discretization, bias in injured athletes, and confounding.

checks.claim: Silbernagel 2007 (AJSM 35(6):897-906) is 'the highest-evidence monitoring tool available' and 'the only one shown to permit continued training safely'.
checks.note: Real and correctly cited (PMID 17307888). But it is n=38 Achilles tendinopathy patients in rehabilitation, and the result was 'no significant differences in the rate of improvements were found between the groups' — a null in a 38-patient trial, which is not evidence of safety, it is absence of power to detect harm. The 5/10 threshold is one component of a study protocol, never independently validated. The research honestly notes the generalisation is by clinical convention, then calls it the highest-evidence tool anyway.

checks.claim: Nielsen 2019 BMJ Open protocol 'establishes that the analysis plan was declared before the data, which materially strengthens the 2025 finding'.
checks.note: The protocol is real and correctly cited (PMID 31494626). But it pre-specifies the general dose-response question with exposures defined as 'change in training load (eg, running distance and the cumulative training load based on the number of strides, ground contact time, vertical oscillation and body weight)'. It does not pre-specify the session-relative-to-30-day-longest-run operationalisation, nor the four spike bands (>10-30 / >30-100 / >100%), which are where all the reported effects live. It also targets 'a minimum of 20,000 consenting runners'; 5205 were analysed.

checks.claim: Total hard running across six weeks is ~38 km of ~420 km, about 9%.
checks.note: Arithmetic error against its own table. The stated weekly caps are 6 + 6 + 0 + 10 + 5 + 3 = 30 km, not 38. Against 420 km that is 7.1%, not 9%. The direction is safe (the plan is more conservative than advertised), but a planner that encodes '9% of weekly volume' as the cap would licence 25% more hard running than the week-by-week table permits — the two numbers must not both be written into config/training.ts.

checks.claim: The ~33 km Lincoln session on 4 Oct is a '+17% spike, squarely in the >10-30% band'.
checks.note: Wrong denominator. The BJSM exposure is the session distance divided by the LONGEST RUN in the previous 30 days, not divided by 1.10x it. Trailing max before 4 Oct under the ladder is 25.58 km, so 33 km is 33/25.58 = 1.290, a +29.0% spike. The +17.3% figure is 33/28.14, i.e. the overshoot of the cap, mislabelled as the spike. This matters twice over: 29.0% is one percentage point from tipping into the >30-100% band, so any shortfall in the 21 Sep long run (25.0 km instead of 25.6) moves Lincoln into a different hazard state.

checks.claim: Capping Lincoln at 30-31 km is the right trade because it moves the spike to race day, where it costs nothing.
checks.note: By the study's own point estimates the trade is close to a wash and may be negative. Recomputed: 33 km on 4 Oct = +29.0% (small spike, HRR 1.64) and then race day vs 33 = +29.3% (small spike, HRR 1.64). Capping at 30 km = +17.3% on 4 Oct (still small spike, HRR 1.64) and race day vs 30 = +42.2% (moderate spike, HRR 1.52). So the recommendation does not remove a spike on 4 Oct — it leaves the same hazard band — and moves race day into a band whose point estimate is LOWER because the dose-response is non-monotonic. The research notes the non-monotonicity elsewhere and then reasons as if the curve were smooth. Also unaddressed: capping Lincoln at 30-31 leaves no long run at all between 4 Oct and 24 Oct under the plan as written.

checks.claim: Threshold pace is ~4:45-4:55/km, worked example 4:43-4:46/km at HR 172-177, derived as half-marathon pace minus 10-15 s/km.
checks.note: Trips the stated red line and contradicts his own file. He ran 21.14 km at 5:02/km with average HR 174 — within 3 bpm of the LT HR the prescription uses as its anchor. His demonstrated pace at HR 174 is therefore ~5:02/km, not 4:43-4:46. The worked example is 16-19 s/km faster than any pace he has ever held at that heart rate. Some of the gap is real (HR lags in a 6-min rep) but none of it is derived — no lag correction is shown. The piece correctly kills a 30 s/km error from Garmin's LT field and then reintroduces a 17 s/km one from an unsourced coaching heuristic. For reference, Daniels' tables put threshold near 4:55-5:00/km for a 1:46 half. The HR ceiling must be binding and the pace band advisory and slower — ~4:55-5:05/km.

checks.claim: Marathon pace 5:15-5:25/km at HR 160-168, derived via Riegel (1.06) from the realised half, cross-checked against May's marathon.
checks.note: Riegel arithmetic is defensible only on his GPS distances: 6395 s over 21.14 km projected to 42.67 km gives 3:44:23 = 5:19/km. On standard distances (21.0975 -> 42.195) it gives 3:42:13 = 5:16/km, so the stated '3:45-3:47' is 2-4 minutes slow relative to its own method. The real problem is the HR/pace pair: he ran 5:31/km at average HR 165 in May, so 5:20/km will very likely sit at or above 168 on tired legs in the back half of a long run. The plan then punishes that with 'if HR exceeds 172 for more than 3 continuous minutes, log it as a race and delete the following week's threshold' — penalising him for an incompatibility the planner authored. Prescribe the HR ceiling or the pace, not both.

checks.claim: ASICS 10K realistic time ~48:37 (4:52/km), from Garmin's 43:29 times his measured 1.118 over-prediction factor.
checks.note: The arithmetic is right (2609 s x 1.118 = 48:36) and the method is not. The 1.118 factor was measured on half and marathon efforts; Garmin's 5 km prediction of 20:11 UNDER-predicts his realised 5.04 km at 3:54/km (19:39), so the correction has the wrong sign at short distances. 4:52/km for 10 K is also only 10 s/km faster than his 5:02/km half, where 20-30 s/km is the normal differential — physiologically implausible. This is not dangerous (a slow target is safe) but it is wired into a decision rule: 'if he runs under 47:00, revise marathon pace down by 5 s/km' will fire almost certainly and spuriously.

checks.claim: Strides at ~3:55/km are 'the only session in the block that deliberately produces high strain rate' and 'carry no sprint-strain risk'.
checks.note: Self-contradictory, and the two halves cannot both be true. 3:54/km is his all-out 5 km race pace — roughly threshold-plus mechanics, not a high-strain-rate stimulus. Genuine strides sit near mile pace or faster. So either the session delivers the Bohm load-magnitude mechanism it is justified by (and is faster and not risk-free), or it is safe at 5 km pace (and does not deliver the mechanism). As written it does neither, and it is the entire stated rationale for keeping any fast running at all.

checks.claim: 'NEVER RAISE WEEKLY VOLUME AND WEEKLY HARD-KM IN THE SAME WEEK' — presented as a hard rule.
checks.note: Broken in the plan's own week 1. Volume goes 14.8 km (last complete week) to 60 km, a +306% rise, while hard-km goes 0 to 6 and heavy slow strength starts from zero at 2x/week. That is three simultaneous novel stressors in the week the piece itself names as the highest-risk of the block. A rule violated by the very first row of the table it governs cannot be encoded as a gate.

checks.claim: 'Six runs of ~14 km contain no spikes' and the frequency increase is protective, so 100 km should be spread over six days.
checks.note: The distance arithmetic works (30 km long + 5 x 14 km = 100). Two gaps. First, 'protective under the best available evidence' is contradicted in the same paragraph by the piece's own citation of Fredette 2022, whose verified abstract concludes the evidence on frequency (and on distance, duration and intensity) is 'conflicting' and that 'caution should be taken when recommending optimal parameters or progressions'. Second, the frequency change is itself unprecedented for him (max 4 runs/week ever), and five weekly runs at 14 km each is roughly his current longest typical run repeated five times — not a soft landing.

checks.claim: Fredette 2022: >64 km/week is an elevated-risk zone (adjusted RR 2.88) and three of this athlete's six weeks sit above it.
checks.note: The paper is real and correctly cited (J Athl Train 2022;57(7):650-671, PMID 34478518) and its 'conflicting evidence' headline is confirmed. The specific figures — OR 3.96 for tempo runs, HR 3.28 for >30 km, RR 2.88 for >64 km — sit in the full text, which returned nothing through open access. The three-weeks-above-64-km arithmetic is correct (80, 100, 80). Note that this is the one danger figure the research surfaces and then drops: it appears only in a source annotation, never in the contraindications list, even though the plan spends half the block above the threshold it names.

checks.claim: Long-run effort anchor HR <= 157 bpm ('LT HR 177 minus 20') for the easy portions.
checks.note: 157 bpm is 78.1% of his measured max of 201 — above the ~75% line that separates easy from steady. The plan is also internally inconsistent about it: the validation section proposes tracking 'pace at a fixed easy HR (150 bpm)' and 'mean HR at 5:50/km', i.e. 74.6% of max. Prescribe 150 and monitor 150, or prescribe 157 and monitor 157. During a tripling of weekly volume the difference is the difference between absorbing the ramp and accumulating debt, which is precisely what the piece says it wants to measure.

checks.claim: Heavy slow strength (calf raises, split squats) 'adds protective high-magnitude loading at zero running kilometres — the single best risk-adjusted intervention in this block'.
checks.note: Zero running kilometres is not zero tissue load. Heavy slow bent- and straight-knee calf raises at RPE 8 load the Achilles and soleus hard, and this athlete has no gym history. Lauersen's RR 0.338 comes from programmes run across a season in already-participating athletes, not from a cold start in the 21-day window the piece itself identifies as the block's most dangerous. Starting a novel eccentric calf stimulus in week 1, alongside a +306% volume jump and the first threshold session, is exactly the compounding the answer forbids elsewhere. The intervention is right; the timing contradicts the answer's own risk model. Introduce it at low load in week 1 only if the running load is cut, or start it in week 2.

checks.claim: Validation metric: 'session-spike compliance: target zero unplanned spikes, exactly one planned (race day)'.
checks.note: Unachievable as specified, and it will read as breached almost every week. The prescribed long-run ladder increments by exactly 10% (23.25, 25.58, 28.14, 30.95), which places every long run precisely on the boundary of the study's reference state (ratio <= 1.1). Any GPS variance, route overshoot, or a lap around the block tips it into the >10% spike state. If this is to be a gate rather than an alarm generator, the planner's cap must sit below the exposure threshold — 1.05 gives margin; 1.10 gives none. Verified against the paper's own state definition ('Change from 0 to 1.1' = reference).

checks.claim: The JOSPT Open 'paradigm shift' commentary — 'author list is NOT verified... attributed to the RUNSAFE group by inference only'.
checks.note: The honesty flag was appropriate but the uncertainty is resolvable in one Crossref call. Confirmed: Frandsen JSB, Simonsen NS, Hulme A, Jacobsen JS, Nielsen RØ. 'A Paradigm Shift in Understanding Overuse Running-Related Injuries: Findings From the Garmin-RUNSAFE Study Point to a Sudden Not Gradual Onset.' JOSPT Open 2025;3:85-92, doi 10.2519/josptopen.2024.0075. It is a commentary by the same group on their own cohort, so it is not independent corroboration of the 2025 finding and should not be counted as a second source.

checks.claim: Garmin's LT pace of 4:20.9/km implies a ~1:31:30 half, a ratio of 1.165 to his realised 1:46:35, 'consistent with the 1.118 over-prediction factor'.
checks.note: Arithmetic: 260.9 s/km x 21.0975 km = 1:31:44 (not 1:31:30), and 6395/5504 = 1.162. But 1.162 and 1.118 are not the same quantity — one is the ratio of a realised half to an LT-pace extrapolation, the other the median error of Garmin's race predictor across three efforts. A 4-point gap between two differently-constructed ratios is not corroboration. Garmin's current half prediction is 1:38:25, which against his 1:46:35 gives 1.083. Three different numbers are in play; the piece picks whichever supports the sentence.

checks.claim: Racing the ASICS 10K flat out on 11 Oct is 'the block's only maximal effort' and is safe because he will self-limit in a race.
checks.note: It is the single highest strain-rate exposure in a block whose entire thesis is minimising strain-rate exposure, it is exempted by name from the answer's own 'no sessions above HR 185' contraindication, it lands on the last day of an 80 km week, and it is 13 days from the goal race. The stated justification is behavioural, not physiological ('he will self-limit sensibly'). The counter-evidence is in his own file: he raced his best half three days into a period the plan treats as recovery, and the plan elsewhere assumes he will breach an HR ceiling at Lincoln unless one is enforced in software. If he cannot be trusted to hold 168 at Lincoln, he cannot be assumed to self-limit at a 10 K.

checks.claim: Week 4 guidance: 'cap that week's total at 80 km INCLUDING the 15 km race day, and cap its long run at 24-26 km on the previous weekend'.
checks.note: Internally incoherent. The previous weekend is Sunday 4 October, which is Lincoln at the recommended 30-31 km, in week 3, not 24-26 km in week 4. Read literally, week 4 has no long run at all. Combined with the recommendation to cap Lincoln, the plan as written leaves the 20 days from 4 October to race day with no run longer than about 26 km, which both worsens the race-day spike it chose to accept and removes the last specific long effort of the build.

fabricatedCitations: None of the sixteen sources is fabricated. All sixteen exist and were verified by DOI, PMID or Crossref. The failures are misattribution, misdescription and misstatement of findings, listed below.

MISSTATED FINDING - Nielsen 2014 (JOSPT 44(10):739-747, PMID 25155475). Presented as an established association between >30% weekly progression and distance-related injuries. The actual result is HR 1.59, 95% CI 0.96 to 2.66, P = .07 - not significant - inside a study whose primary analysis found no significant difference across exposure groups and which its authors label explorative. The CI and p-value are omitted from both the source annotation and the prose. This citation is load-bearing for the 'the entry is the danger, not the peak' conclusion.

MISATTRIBUTED FIGURE - Lauersen 2018 (BJSM 52(24):1557-1563, PMID 30131332). The 'approximately halved overuse injuries' figure belongs to Lauersen 2014 (BJSM 48(11):871-7, PMID 24100287, overuse RR 0.527), not to the 2018 dose-response paper, which reports RR 0.338 for strength-training RCTs overall and no separate overuse estimate. The 'roughly one third' half of the claim is correct for 2018.

MISSTATED FINDING (wrong direction) - Bellenger 2016 (Sports Med 46(10):1461-86, PMID 26888648). Cited to justify cutting intensity when HRV is Low or Unbalanced. The paper's pooled result for performance decrements (functional overreaching) is a small INCREASE in resting RMSSD (SMD 0.26, P = 0.01) with trivial change in resting HFP. The cited evidence does not support a low-HRV gate and arguably points the other way.

MISDESCRIBED - Wang 2020 (Sports Med 50(7):1243-1254, PMID 32125672). Tagged 'meta-analysis' and described as a 'systematic review of ACWR methodology' with a finding that the literature 'cannot be pooled'. It is a narrative methodological review; that pooling claim is not in it. Its actual conclusion (ACWR limitations should discourage its use) does support the broader point.

OVERSTATED PROVENANCE - Nielsen 2019 protocol (BMJ Open 9(9):e032627, PMID 31494626). Claimed to pre-register the 2025 analysis plan. It pre-specifies a general dose-response question with exposures defined as running distance and cumulative load from strides/ground contact/vertical oscillation/body weight. The 110%-of-30-day-longest-run session exposure and its four spike bands are not in the protocol. It also targets >=20,000 runners against 5205 analysed.

WRONGLY DECLARED UNREADABLE - Ramskov 2018 JOSPT 48(10):740-748 (PMID 29895234). The research says the full text returned 403 and refuses to assert its findings. Results and conclusion are freely on PubMed and they contradict the answer's central mechanism: the trial tested exactly the volume-injuries-vs-intensity-injuries partition and concluded 'No difference in risk of hypothesized intensity- and volume-specific running-related injuries exists between the 2 running schedules.' All risk differences straddle zero. This is the only disconfirming source in the list and it was set aside as unreadable.

CITATION FORMATTING - Frandsen 2025. Given as 'Br J Sports Med. 2025;59(17):e109380'. Actual: Br J Sports Med 2025;59(17):1203-1210, PMID 40623829. First author indexes as Schuster Brandt Frandsen J. Content of the claim is otherwise exact.

UNCITED ENTIRELY - 'Vesterinen 2016' and 'Javaloyes 2019' are invoked in the validation section as HRV-guided training RCTs with no authors, journal, volume or DOI anywhere in the source list. Unverifiable as given.

UNVERIFIABLE SUB-CLAIMS - Fredette 2022's specific figures (OR 3.96 for tempo runs, HR 3.28 for >30 km/week, adjusted RR 2.88 for >64 km/week) sit in a full text that returned nothing through open access; only the 'conflicting evidence' headline is confirmed. Run Clever's 'P=.23', 'compliance was poor' and '0.8 km of added hard running across 16 weeks' are likewise not in the abstract and are not page-cited.
verification.riskForThisAthlete:
The epidemiology is real and the governing instinct is right: spend the risk budget on volume, ration intensity, govern the biggest single session. Where it fails is at the boundary between the literature and the numbers a person actually runs.

WHAT IS GENUINELY DANGEROUS

1. Threshold pace 4:43-4:55/km is the sharpest risk. He ran 21.14 km at 5:02/km with average HR 174, three beats under the LT HR the prescription anchors to. His demonstrated pace at that heart rate is 5:02/km. Prescribing 4:43-4:46 asks for 17-19 s/km faster than anything he has held there, in the only hard sessions of a block already at its ceiling. The piece correctly refuses Garmin's 4:20.9 and then substitutes an unsourced heuristic that reintroduces half the error it removed. Make the HR ceiling binding and the pace band advisory at 4:55-5:05/km.

2. Week 1 is three novel stressors at once, and it violates the answer's own rule. Volume goes 14.8 to 60 km (+306%), hard running goes 0 to 6 km, and heavy slow calf work starts from zero at twice a week - in the week the answer itself names as the highest-risk of the block, two days after a raced half. Its own stated rule ('never raise weekly volume and weekly hard-km in the same week') is broken by the first row of its own table. If anything moves, move the threshold session and the strength start to week 2 and cut week 1 to 50 km, which the answer half-recommends and then does not apply.

3. Marathon-pace segments carry a built-in contradiction that then triggers a penalty. He ran 5:31/km at HR 165 in May. Asking for 5:15-5:25/km under a 168 ceiling on tired legs in the back half of a long run will either miss the pace or breach the ceiling, and breaching the ceiling is defined to cost him the following week's quality. Specify one anchor.

4. The 10K on 11 Oct is the block's largest peak-strain exposure, exempted by name from the answer's own >185 bpm contraindication, on the last day of an 80 km week, 13 days out. The safety argument for it is behavioural ('he will self-limit') from a document that elsewhere assumes he cannot be trusted with a verbal instruction at Lincoln.

5. Three of six weeks sit above 64 km/week, which the answer's own Fredette citation flags as an elevated-risk zone (RR 2.88). It appears in a footnote and never reaches the contraindications.

WHAT IS WORTH KEEPING
The 110% session rule, the refusal of ACWR, the pain gate, the deletion of VO2max intervals, the HR ceiling at Lincoln as an after-the-fact check rather than an instruction, and the bone-stress/energy-availability flag. Those are sound, and the ACWR refusal is the best-evidenced call in the document.

WHAT MUST CHANGE BEFORE ANYTHING REACHES config/training.ts
- Hard-km budget: the table sums to 30 km, not the stated 38; 7.1%, not 9%. Do not encode both.
- Session-spike cap: set the planner's ceiling at 1.05, not 1.10. At 1.10 every long run sits exactly on the study's reference boundary and any route variance reads as a breach, so the block's headline safety metric will alarm continuously and be ignored.
- Lincoln spike: correctly computed it is +29.0% against the trailing 30-day maximum, not +17%. And the recommended cap at 30-31 km leaves it in the same hazard band (1.64) while moving race day into a band with a lower point estimate (1.52). The trade the answer presents as decisive is, on its own numbers, a wash.
- Week 4 as written has no long run, and capping Lincoln leaves 20 days with nothing above 26 km before a marathon.
- Every pace in the document needs a source comment naming its derivation, since none of the six sources supports any pace. The epidemiology governs how much; nothing cited governs how fast.

POPULATION VALIDITY
The Frandsen cohort is the closest match in the literature to this athlete (mean age 45.8, 78% male, self-selected Garmin users, median 9.5 years running). But median time at risk was 80 sessions, and it is a general running population, not marathon builders mid-ramp. Damsted's cohort is the closest by intent (half-marathon trainees) but its studied progression band tops out at 60% week-on-week against this athlete's +306%. Nielsen 2014 is novices. Lauersen is not running-specific. Bohm is resistance-training adaptation, not injury, in >=8-week interventions. No cited study observed anyone doing what this athlete is about to do, and the answer's confident week-by-week caps read as though one had.

domains.title: How to know the plan is working — measurement and falsification

research.tradition: Athlete monitoring and per-athlete model calibration — the measurement layer, drawn from (a) large-scale observational running-performance modelling (Riegel-family power laws with individually fitted exponents; the UCD/Hertfordshire critical-speed and durability work on 25k–120k Strava marathoners), and (b) the sports-science athlete-monitoring literature (submaximal heart-rate indices, weekly-averaged vagal HRV, subjective wellness, overreaching consensus criteria). This is not a training tradition; it is the falsification apparatus that turns the 60/80/100/80/60 block from an assertion into a hypothesis.
research.corePrinciple:
Three mechanisms, kept separate because they move on different timescales and fail in different ways.

(1) PREDICTION IS A TWO-PARAMETER PROBLEM, NOT ONE. Any race-time predictor has a LEVEL (how fast at one distance) and a DECAY (how much slower per doubling of distance — the Riegel exponent k, or equivalently the fraction of critical speed you can hold). Garmin's over-prediction for this athlete is almost entirely a LEVEL error, not a decay error: Garmin's own 2026-09-07 numbers imply a half→marathon exponent of 1.135, close to this athlete's own measured 1.13–1.18. What is wrong is the anchor — Garmin asserts a threshold pace of 4:20.9/km that his own race heart-rate/pace data cannot support. A single scalar "Garmin ×1.118" correction is therefore the wrong object: it conflates two independent errors and is distance-dependent (Garmin is roughly right at 5 km and ~12% optimistic at the marathon). Calibrate the two parameters separately.

(2) DURABILITY IS THE OUTCOME THE BLOCK IS ACTUALLY BUYING. In 82,303 recreational marathoners, internal:external decoupling (%HRmax ÷ speed-relative-to-critical-speed, 35–40 km window versus the 5–10 km window) averaged 1.16 ± 0.22 and predicted finish time beyond critical speed alone (Smyth 2022). Six weeks is too short to move VO2max meaningfully, but it is exactly the right length to move the fraction of critical speed a runner can hold to 42 km. So decoupling — not VO2max, not Endurance Score — is the primary in-block outcome, and it is computable from per-second HR and pace on runs he is already doing.

(3) MONITORING SIGNAL LIVES IN 7-DAY AVERAGES AND IN CONCORDANCE, NOT IN SINGLE READINGS. Single-day resting HR and single-day HRV correlate weakly with training adaptation; the 7-day means correlate strongly (r = .35 → −.62 and −.21 → −.77 in Plews 2013). Subjective self-report outperformed objective markers for sensitivity to load in a 56-study systematic review (Saw 2016). And in the closest-matched study that exists — 24 recreational runners put through a deliberate 2-week overload — nocturnal HR, subjective readiness-to-train, and an exercise-derived HR:running-speed index each reached ≥85% positive and negative predictive value for separating the overreached from the responders (Nuuttila 2024). Those are precisely the three channels rocket already holds. Require two of three to agree before acting.

sources.citation: Riegel PS. Athletic records and human endurance. American Scientist. 1981;69(3):285-290. (The T2 = T1 x (D2/D1)^1.06 form was popularised in Runner's World, 1977.)
sources.claim: Endurance performance decays as a power law of distance; a fatigue exponent near 1.06 fits pooled trained-athlete record data across running, swimming and cycling. Establishes the FORM of the model, not its per-athlete parameter.
sources.population: Pooled competitive/record performances, not individual recreational runners. Not a controlled study.

sources.citation: Vickers AJ, Vertosick EA. An empirical study of race times in recreational endurance runners. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2016;8:26. doi:10.1186/s13102-016-0052-y
sources.claim: The single most important source here. Riegel with the fixed 1.06 exponent is well calibrated up to the half marathon but dramatically underestimates marathon time — at least 10 minutes too fast for half of recreational runners. Their regression models using sex, age, BMI, weekly mileage, interval/tempo volume and one or two prior races achieved MSE 228 and 208 min^2 respectively versus 381 for Riegel. Weekly mileage and interval training predicted velocity at all distances; tempo running predicted more strongly at shorter distances.
sources.population: 2,303 recreational endurance runners, internet survey, split 2:1 into training and validation sets. Internally validated only — never externally replicated. Self-reported data.

sources.citation: Blythe DAJ, Kiraly FJ. Prediction and Quantification of Individual Athletic Performance of Runners. PLoS ONE. 2016;11(6):e0157257. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0157257
sources.claim: A power-law model with a PER-RUNNER exponent fits substantially better than any fixed-exponent law, and a three-parameter-per-runner model beat the state of the art in prediction error by ~30% RMSE. Direct evidence that fitting k per athlete is the right move rather than a refinement.
sources.population: 164,746 British runners, 1,417,432 performances from the Power of 10 database — club and competitive runners, i.e. faster and higher-volume than this athlete.

sources.citation: Smyth B, Muniz-Pumares D. Calculation of Critical Speed from Raw Training Data in Recreational Marathon Runners. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2020;52(12):2637-2645. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002412
sources.claim: Critical speed can be estimated from ORDINARY TRAINING FILES — the fastest grade-adjusted pace achieved over 400, 800, 1000, 1500, 3000 and 5000 m, fitted as the slope of the distance-time relationship — with no dedicated test, and this CS predicts marathon performance and pacing. This is what makes the whole durability measurement free for rocket: no lab, no test session.
sources.population: >25,000 recreational athletes logging to an online fitness platform before big-city marathons. Same population type as this athlete.

sources.citation: Smyth B, Maunder E, Meyler S, Hunter B, Muniz-Pumares D. Decoupling of Internal and External Workload During a Marathon: An Analysis of Durability in 82,303 Recreational Runners. Sports Med. 2022;52(9):2283-2295. doi:10.1007/s40279-022-01680-5
sources.claim: Decoupling (%HRmax / (speed/CS) at 35-40 km relative to 5-10 km) averaged 1.16 +/- 0.22, onset at 25.2 +/- 9.9 km. Low decouplers (<1.1) held 88 +/- 6% of CS and finished in 217 +/- 33 min; high decouplers (>=1.2) held 82 +/- 7% CS and finished in 239 +/- 31 min. Adding decoupling magnitude and onset to CS and curvature constant cut marathon prediction error from 6.45% to 5.16%. Gives both the metric definition and the reference distribution to score this athlete against.
sources.population: 82,303 recreational marathon runners (13,125 female). Exactly this athlete's population. Cross-sectional — it does not show that training changes decoupling.

sources.citation: Muniz-Pumares D, Hunter B, Meyler S, Maunder E, Smyth B. The Training Intensity Distribution of Marathon Runners Across Performance Levels. Sports Med. 2025;55:1023-1035. doi:10.1007/s40279-024-02137-7
sources.claim: 16 weeks of training before 151,813 marathons. Mean volume 45.1 +/- 26.4 km/week. Time in Zone 2 and Zone 3 was roughly CONSTANT across all performance levels; what rose with performance was Zone 1 volume. >80% of the fastest group used a pyramidal distribution. Marathon time correlated with volume markers and with the proportion of volume in Z1 at R^2 >= 0.90; not with Z2 or Z3 proportions. Also supplies usable zone boundaries: Z2/Z3 at critical speed, Z1/Z2 at 82.3% of CS.
sources.population: 119,452 recreational-to-fast marathoners. Correlational; faster runners may run more easy volume because they are faster, not the reverse.

sources.citation: Maunder E, et al. The Importance of 'Durability' in the Physiological Profiling of Endurance Athletes. Sports Medicine. 2021. (I verified the title, lead author, journal and year; I did NOT verify the full co-author list, volume or page numbers — check before quoting them.)
sources.claim: Argues that fresh-state physiological profiling (VO2max, threshold) is insufficient, and that resilience of those parameters under accumulated fatigue — 'durability' — is a separate, trainable, performance-relevant trait. The conceptual justification for making decoupling the primary in-block marker rather than VO2max.
sources.population: Narrative/conceptual review of endurance athletes. Not an experiment.

sources.citation: Lamberts RP, Lemmink KAPM, Durandt JJ, Lambert MI. Variation in heart rate during submaximal exercise: implications for monitoring training. J Strength Cond Res. 2004;18(3):641-645.
sources.claim: 44 subjects ran a submaximal test at the same time of day on 5 consecutive days. Day-to-day ICC 0.94-0.99; the standard error of measurement of submaximal heart rate is 1.1-1.4%. This is the number that sets the noise floor for every fixed-pace HR threshold below: at 150 bpm, SEM is 1.7-2.1 bpm, so a change under ~4 bpm on a 7-day mean is not a signal.
sources.population: 44 healthy adults, mean age 26.5. Reliability study, not an intervention.

sources.citation: Buchheit M. Monitoring training status with HR measures: do all roads lead to Rome? Front Physiol. 2014;5:73. doi:10.3389/fphys.2014.00073
sources.claim: Review concluding that ~5-minute near-daily resting HR recordings and 30-60 s averaged submaximal exercise HR are the most useful practical monitoring tools, and that most contradictory findings in the literature stem from methodological inconsistency rather than a failure of HR measures. Crucially also warns that a FALLING submaximal HR is ambiguous — it can indicate fitness or accumulating fatigue — which is why it must never be read alone.
sources.population: Review across trained and elite endurance athletes.

sources.citation: Vesterinen V, Nummela A, Laine T, Hynynen E, Mikkola J, Hakkinen K. A Submaximal Running Test With Postexercise Cardiac Autonomic and Neuromuscular Function in Monitoring Endurance Training Adaptation. J Strength Cond Res. 2017;31(1):233-243. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001458
sources.claim: 35 endurance-trained men and women, 18 weeks. Submaximal running test = 6 min at 70% HRmax, 6 min at 80% HRmax, 3 min at 90% HRmax, then 2 min recovery. The high responders improved running SPEED at the 80% and 90% HRmax stages; the low responders did not. Speed at the 90% HRmax stage correlated most strongly with change in maximal endurance performance. Post-exercise HRR and HRV added little. Supports pace-at-fixed-HR as an adaptation marker — but note the sampling interval was every 4 weeks over 18, so it is calibrated to a longer horizon than 6 weeks.
sources.population: 35 recreational-to-trained endurance runners. Longitudinal within a training intervention; not a randomised comparison of monitoring methods.

sources.citation: Nuuttila OP, Uusitalo A, Kokkonen VP, Weerarathna N, Kyrolainen H. Monitoring fatigue state with heart rate-based and subjective methods during intensified training in recreational runners. Eur J Sport Sci. 2024;24(6):857-869. doi:10.1002/ejsc.12115
sources.claim: The closest analogue in the literature to what this athlete is about to do. 24 recreational runners: 3-week baseline, 2-week deliberate overload, 1-week recovery; 3000 m test after each block. Responders improved 3000 m by 2.5 +/- 1.0%; the overreached group got 0.6 +/- 1.2% WORSE. Nocturnal HR rose 3.2 +/- 3.1% in the overreached and fell 2.8 +/- 3.7% in responders (p=0.002); HRV -0.7% vs +2.1% (p=0.011); subjective readiness-to-train fell more and leg soreness rose more in the overreached. Nocturnal HR, readiness-to-train and an exercise-derived HR-running-power index each achieved >=85% positive AND negative predictive value for classifying the two groups. Supplies the actual effect sizes for the falsification thresholds below.
sources.population: 24 recreational runners undergoing an intensified block. Small n; subgroups defined post hoc by outcome (8 overreached, 12 responders), so the predictive values are optimistic.

sources.citation: Plews DJ, Laursen PB, Kilding AE, Buchheit M. Evaluating training adaptation with heart-rate measures: a methodological comparison. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2013;8(6):688-691. doi:10.1123/ijspp.8.6.688
sources.claim: In 10 runners over a 9-week intervention, correlations between performance change and single-day resting HR / Ln rMSSD were r = .35 and -.21; using the 7-DAY AVERAGE of the same measures gave r = -.62 and much stronger. Direct evidence that rocket must average HR and HRV over 7 days before comparing to baseline, and must never gate a session on one morning's number.
sources.population: 10 runners. Very small n; the effect is nevertheless the standard of practice and is consistent with the wider literature.

sources.citation: Plews DJ, Laursen PB, Stanley J, Kilding AE, Buchheit M. Training adaptation and heart rate variability in elite endurance athletes: opening the door to effective monitoring. Sports Med. 2013;43(9):773-781. doi:10.1007/s40279-013-0071-8
sources.claim: Review establishing that in elites the HRV response is EQUIVOCAL — both increases and decreases have accompanied negative adaptation, and positive fitness change has coincided with falling HRV. Source of the widely used smallest-worthwhile-change convention of 0.5 x the athlete's own baseline coefficient of variation. Important as a brake: HRV direction is not universally interpretable.
sources.population: Review; elite and well-trained endurance athletes.

sources.citation: Saw AE, Main LC, Gastin PB. Monitoring the athlete training response: subjective self-reported measures trump commonly used objective measures: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med. 2016;50(5):281-291.
sources.claim: 56 studies reporting concurrent subjective and objective measures. Subjective measures reflected acute and chronic training load with superior sensitivity and consistency to objective ones (resting and exercise HR, blood markers, oxygen consumption). Justifies giving the morning check-in real weight rather than treating it as decoration.
sources.population: Systematic review across athlete populations and sports; heterogeneous, mostly non-runners.

sources.citation: Vesterinen V, Nummela A, Heikura I, Laine T, Hynynen E, Botella J, Hakkinen K. Individual Endurance Training Prescription with Heart Rate Variability. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(7):1347-1354. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000000910
sources.claim: 40 recreational runners randomised to HRV-guided versus predefined training for 8 weeks. Quality sessions were scheduled only when morning HRV sat inside an individually determined smallest worthwhile change. Concluded nocturnal HRV can individualise endurance training. The strongest single positive RCT for HRV gating.
sources.population: 40 recreational endurance runners — a good match for this athlete.

sources.citation: Manresa-Rocamora A, Sarabia JM, Javaloyes A, Flatt AA, Moya-Ramon M. Heart Rate Variability-Guided Training for Enhancing Cardiac-Vagal Modulation, Aerobic Fitness, and Endurance Performance: A Methodological Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2021;18(19):10299. doi:10.3390/ijerph181910299
sources.claim: Pooling the trials: HRV-guided training was superior for vagal-related HRV indices (SMD 0.50, 95% CI 0.09-0.91) but NOT for resting HR (SMD 0.04, CI -0.34-0.43), and the effects on maximal aerobic and endurance performance were small and non-significant. The honest headline: HRV guidance reliably changes HRV; its effect on race performance is not established.
sources.population: Trials in healthy/trained adults; few studies, small samples.

sources.citation: Duking P, Zinner C, Trabelsi K, Reed JL, Holmberg HC, Kunz P, Sperlich B. Monitoring and adapting endurance training on the basis of heart rate variability monitored by wearable technologies: A systematic review with meta-analysis. J Sci Med Sport. 2021;24(11):1180-1192. doi:10.1016/j.jsams.2021.04.012
sources.claim: 8 studies, 198 participants. HRV-guided groups generally performed FEWER moderate/high-intensity sessions than predefined groups, yet showed a significant medium positive effect on submaximal physiological parameters (g = 0.296). Read as: the benefit of HRV guidance may be that it removes hard sessions at the wrong moment, not that it adds anything.
sources.population: 198 participants across 8 heterogeneous interventions.

sources.citation: Ranieri LE, Casado A, Martin D, Trujillo-Colmena D, Gil-Arias A, Kenneally M, Jimenez A. Performance and Physiological Effects of Race Pace-Based Versus Heart Rate Variability-Guided Training Prescription in Runners. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2025;57:1510-1522. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003671
sources.claim: 28 recreational runners randomised to heart-rate-based, race-pace-based, or HRV-guided prescription for SIX WEEKS — the same duration as this block. Main time effects for VO2max, running economy, ventilatory-threshold speeds and 7 km time trial, but NO interaction effects between groups. Over six weeks, how you choose the anchor mattered less than doing the training. Directly relevant caution against over-engineering the gating logic.
sources.population: 28 recreational distance runners, 9-10 per arm. Underpowered to detect small between-method differences.

sources.citation: Impellizzeri FM, Woodcock S, Coutts AJ, Fanchini M, McCall A, Vigotsky AD. Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio: Conceptual Issues and Fundamental Pitfalls. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2020;15(6):907-913.
sources.claim: There is no evidence supporting the use of ACWR in training-load-management systems or for injury-risk recommendations; the statistical properties of a ratio of two correlated, overlapping windows make it an inaccurate and hard-to-interpret metric. rocket should not build any gate on an acute:chronic ratio, and should be sceptical of TSB for the same mathematical reason.
sources.population: Methodological critique of the team-sport injury literature.

sources.citation: Meeusen R, Duclos M, Foster C, et al. Prevention, diagnosis and treatment of the overtraining syndrome: joint consensus statement of the ECSS and ACSM. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2013;45(1):186-205 (also Eur J Sport Sci. 2013;13(1):1-24).
sources.claim: Defines the operational distinction this block lives on: functional overreaching (short-term performance decrement that supercompensates), non-functional overreaching (decrement lasting weeks with no supercompensation), overtraining syndrome (prolonged maladaptation). PERFORMANCE DECREMENT is the definitional criterion — not HRV, not soreness. Hence the need for a scheduled performance test inside the block.
sources.population: Consensus statement; expert synthesis across athlete populations.

sources.citation: Foster C. Monitoring training in athletes with reference to overtraining syndrome. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 1998;30(7):1164-1168.
sources.claim: Origin of session-RPE load, and of training monotony (weekly mean daily load / SD of daily load) and strain (load x monotony). Illness episodes clustered after spikes in load and monotony in 25 athletes. Directly relevant to a 6-day-a-week 100 km week: sameness, not just size, is a risk factor.
sources.population: 25 experienced athletes; small, uncontrolled, illness as a proxy outcome. Treat monotony as a heuristic, not a law.

sources.citation: Nielsen RO, Parner ET, Nohr EA, Sorensen H, Lind M, Rasmussen S. Excessive progression in weekly running distance and risk of running-related injuries: an association which varies according to type of injury. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther. 2014;44(10):739-747. doi:10.2519/jospt.2014.5164
sources.claim: 874 novice runners, GPS-tracked, one year, 202 injuries. Progressing weekly distance by >30% over a two-week period was associated with 'distance-related' injuries (patellofemoral pain, ITB syndrome, medial tibial stress syndrome, patellar tendinopathy, greater trochanteric bursitis, gluteus medius/TFL) versus <10%. IMPORTANT AND USUALLY OMITTED: the overall association across all injury types was NOT statistically significant. This is the best evidence behind rocket's 15% ramp cap, and it is thinner than the cap's confidence implies.
sources.population: 874 NOVICE runners starting self-structured programmes — not an experienced marathoner. Generalisation to this athlete is an assumption, not a finding.

sources.citation: Engel FA, Masur L, Sperlich B, Duking P. Validity of VO2max estimates from the Forerunner 245 smartwatch in highly vs. moderately trained endurance athletes. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2026;126:591-603. doi:10.1007/s00421-025-05923-x
sources.claim: 35 endurance athletes, treadmill ramp with gas analysis versus two submaximal outdoor runs. The watch underestimated VO2max by 4.73 ml/kg/min on average; MAPE 2.8-4.1% in the moderately trained but 9.4-10.4% in the highly trained. The measurement error is several times larger than any plausible six-week true change, which is why Garmin VO2max is unusable as an in-block progress marker.
sources.population: 35 Tier 2-3 endurance athletes, VO2max 60.1 +/- 8.2 — fitter than this athlete, but the error structure is the point.

sources.citation: Dai J, Chen G, Gu Z, Qi Y, Xu K. Accuracy of smartwatches in predicting distance running performance. Front Sports Act Living. 2025;7:1517632. doi:10.3389/fspor.2025.1517632
sources.claim: 154 amateur runners, 288 test instances. Bias +/- limits of agreement: 5 km -20.4 +/- 44.2 s; 10 km +4.1 +/- 299.1 s; half marathon +143.8 +/- 400.4 s. Error grew sharply with distance, and the MARATHON WAS NOT TESTED AT ALL. Note this was a Huawei Watch GT Runner, not a Garmin — so it is evidence about the class of algorithm, not about Garmin specifically. I found no peer-reviewed validation of Garmin's Race Predictor at the marathon distance.
sources.population: 154 amateur runners (123 M, 31 F). Single brand, no marathon, so it cannot be transferred to this athlete's goal race.

sources.citation: Saunders PU, Pyne DB, Telford RD, Hawley JA. Reliability and variability of running economy in elite distance runners. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2004;36(11):1972-1976.
sources.claim: Establishes the typical error of laboratory running economy in trained runners, and hence the smallest worthwhile change. Cited here to make the negative point: if measuring running economy properly, with a metabolic cart, requires this much care to detect a real change, then inferring economy from a wrist device's ground-contact time and vertical oscillation is not measurement.
sources.population: 11 elite male distance runners for reliability; 70 highly trained for between-athlete variation.

sources.citation: Purdy JG. Computer-generated track-scoring tables / least-squares model for the running curve, circa 1970-1974 (Med Sci Sports; Research Quarterly). I could NOT verify the exact citation, volume or pages from a primary source, and I am not confident enough in the details to assert them.
sources.claim: Purdy points are a scoring table fitted to WORLD RECORD performances. Whatever the exact reference, that provenance is the disqualifying fact for this use: an elite-derived decay curve is optimistic at the marathon for a 24 km/week athlete for exactly the same reason Riegel's 1.06 is. Do not use for prediction here.
sources.population: World-record holders. Wrong population by construction.

sources.citation: The 'Cameron formula' (attributed to David Cameron, 1998). I could find no peer-reviewed publication, no primary source, and no reproducible derivation — only secondary descriptions on calculator websites.
sources.claim: Nothing checkable. It is described as regression on world-level times from 400 m to 50 miles, which again is an elite-anchored decay curve. Excluded on grounds of unverifiable provenance and wrong reference population.
sources.population: Unknown/unverifiable.

prescriptions.sessionName: P1 — The anchor race (Battersea Half, 2026-09-12): the single highest-value measurement in the whole block
prescriptions.structure: One-off, in three days. Race it flat out as already planned. The measurement work is entirely post hoc, from the FIT file: (a) finish time and grade-adjusted mean pace; (b) mean HR over km 3-8 versus km 16-21; (c) fastest grade-adjusted rolling pace at 400/800/1000/1500/3000/5000 m, from this race and from the previous 90 days of ordinary training files, fitted as the slope of the distance-time relation to give critical speed (the Smyth & Muniz-Pumares 2020 method — no test session required); (d) refit the personal Riegel exponent; (e) log an actual-versus-Garmin-predicted pair into the calibration table, tagged to the 10-25 km distance band.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Nothing is prescribed — this session DEFINES the anchors. Everything downstream (threshold pace, marathon pace, easy-run anchor, zone boundaries) is derived from this file. Until it exists, every pace in the block is an estimate from data that is between two and five months old.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Resets both parameters of the prediction model at once, three days before the block starts. Level comes from the finish time; decay comes from re-fitting k across this race and the 25 April 5 km. Critical speed comes from the sprint-envelope fit, which then makes the Smyth 2022 decoupling metric computable for every subsequent long run. Without this file, the block is being prescribed off a Garmin threshold pace that his own race data contradicts by ~11%.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: PRE-RACE EXPECTATION, so the result can falsify something. From the 19 July half (1:46:35 at 5:02/km, avg HR 174) plus roughly five weeks of build since, a genuine current half is 1:42-1:46. Garmin says 1:38:25. If he runs slower than 1:44, Garmin's level error is confirmed at ~8% and its 3:36:12 marathon prediction should be struck from the app immediately. WHAT TO EXTRACT: critical speed. His 19 July half at 3.306 m/s sits at ~96% of CS for a runner of that duration, giving CS ~3.44 m/s = 4:50/km — and that value independently reproduces his May marathon as 87.5% of CS, dead centre of Smyth's 82-88% band for 82,303 marathoners. Garmin's asserted LT pace of 4:20.9/km (3.833 m/s) would instead put his marathon at 78.7% CS, below even Smyth's worst-durability tertile. Two independent routes say Garmin's threshold PACE is roughly 25-30 s/km too fast while its threshold HR of 177 (88.1% of the measured HRmax 201) is credible and corroborated by his 174 bpm half average. Expect the 12 Sep file to land CS in 4:44-4:53/km.

prescriptions.sessionName: P2 — Durability probe: decoupling on every long run
prescriptions.structure: No extra session. On every run of 20 km or more, compute the Smyth 2022 metric: ratio of [%HRmax / (grade-adjusted speed / CS)] in the last 25% of the run to the same quantity over km 5-10. Also record decoupling ONSET — the first kilometre at which the running ratio exceeds 1.025. Exclude runs with a mean temperature more than 5 C from the block's median, any run with more than 100 m of cumulative ascent per 10 km, and any run with more than 3 minutes of stoppage (which rules out the 26 July stop-start shape entirely).
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Derived, not asserted: %HRmax uses the MEASURED HRmax of 201 from 2026-06-14 (not the profile's 196, not his believed 195 — those would inflate every %HRmax by 2.5-3%). Speed is normalised to critical speed computed from his own training files per Smyth & Muniz-Pumares 2020, refreshed weekly.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: This is the primary outcome of the block.
