Volume's mechanism — mitochondrial and capillary density, glycogen storage, fat oxidation at a given speed, connective-tissue and neuromuscular tolerance of repeated impact — expresses itself as the ability to hold a higher fraction of critical speed deep into a long effort. That is what decoupling measures, and it is the specific deficit his own race history shows: an exponent of 1.13-1.18 against a recreational norm of 1.07-1.09. VO2max will not move usefully in six weeks; this can.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: Baseline from the first long run of week 1 (w/c 14 Sep). Reference distribution from Smyth 2022: cohort mean 1.16 +/- 0.22, onset at 25.2 +/- 9.9 km; low group <1.10 holding 88% CS, high group >=1.20 holding 82% CS. His realised May marathon at 87.5% of CS ~4:50/km puts him near the boundary of the low/moderate groups on the fraction-of-CS axis, which makes ~1.10-1.15 the likely baseline decoupling. TARGET: baseline minus 0.05 or better by the 4 October 33 km session, with onset pushed at least 5 km later. A decoupling of 1.10 held to 42 km at CS 4:50 implies roughly 88% CS = 5:30/km = 3:52 marathon; the same durability with a 3% CS gain implies 5:20/km = 3:45.

prescriptions.sessionName: P3 — Aerobic efficiency probe: fixed-pace heart-rate check
prescriptions.structure: Embedded in two easy runs per week, no extra session. A 10-minute block at a FIXED pace on flat ground, starting at least 20 minutes into the run (past the HR-rise transient), on one of two or three repeated routes. Record mean HR over the block, plus temperature and time of day. Report the 7-day mean, never a single reading. Optionally, once per fortnight, add the Vesterinen 2017 top stage — 3 minutes at 90% HRmax — and record the SPEED achieved, which was the marker that separated high from low responders in that study.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Pace fixed at his easy anchor, derived from his own HR-pace relationship across two realised races (174 bpm at 5:02/km in the July half; 165 bpm at 5:31/km in the May marathon), giving a slope of about 18.5 bpm per minute per km. The 90% HRmax stage is 181 bpm from the measured max of 201.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Heart rate at a fixed submaximal speed is the classical index of aerobic training status (Buchheit 2014), and speed at a fixed high-submaximal HR was the marker that tracked endurance change in Vesterinen 2017. In Nuuttila 2024 the exercise-derived HR:running-speed index was one of only three markers reaching >=85% predictive value for separating overreached from responding recreational runners. It is also the cheapest possible signal: it needs no test, only a repeated route.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: EASY ANCHOR PACE 6:30/km, at which his predicted HR is about 147 bpm (73% HRmax). NOISE FLOOR: Lamberts 2004 gives a submaximal HR standard error of measurement of 1.1-1.4%, i.e. 1.6-2.1 bpm at this HR. So the smallest change worth reading on a 7-day mean is about 4 bpm (2 x SEM), and 3 bpm or less is noise. EXPECTED IF THE BLOCK WORKS: HR at 6:30/km falls 3-6 bpm across the six weeks, to roughly 141-144. Also record the Z1/Z2 boundary so he does not accidentally run his easy volume in Z2: 82.3% of CS (Muniz-Pumares 2025) with CS at 4:50/km puts the boundary at 5:53/km — everything slower than about 5:55/km is Z1. 6:30/km is comfortably inside it.

prescriptions.sessionName: P4 — Morning readiness triad (the overreaching trip-wire)
prescriptions.structure: Daily, 60 seconds. Three channels, each reduced to a 7-day rolling mean and compared to the individual baseline established over the 14 days before 14 September: (1) nocturnal/resting HR from Garmin wellness; (2) Ln rMSSD, compared against a smallest worthwhile change of 0.5 x his own baseline coefficient of variation (the Plews/Buchheit convention); (3) the existing subjective check-in, with readiness-to-train (motivation) and leg soreness given primacy over sleep and previous-day RPE, because those were the two subjective items that discriminated in Nuuttila 2024. ACTION RULE: any TWO of the three tripped for 7 consecutive days cuts the following week's volume by 25%; all THREE cuts it by 40% and removes that week's intensity entirely.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Thresholds taken from measured effect sizes, not invented. Nuuttila 2024: nocturnal HR +3.2 +/- 3.1% in the overreached versus -2.8 +/- 3.7% in responders; HRV -0.7% versus +2.1%. Plews 2013 (IJSPP): 7-day means, not single days — single-day resting HR and Ln rMSSD correlated with adaptation at r = .35 and -.21, the 7-day versions at r = -.62 and stronger.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: This is the safety layer, not the prescription layer. Its job is to catch the transition from functional to non-functional overreaching (Meeusen 2013) during a volume ramp to a level he has never reached. Requiring concordance across two of three channels is what makes it usable: each channel alone has a false-positive rate that would shred the block, and Plews 2013 (Sports Med) documents cases where HRV direction inverts its usual meaning.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: RESTING HR TRIP: +3% on the 7-day mean above his baseline of 57 smoothed = +1.8 bpm, so trip at a sustained 7-day mean of 60 bpm or higher. (His fall from 84 in March to 57 now means the baseline itself is still drifting; re-estimate it on the 14 days to 13 September rather than using March data.) HRV TRIP: 7-day mean Ln rMSSD below baseline minus 0.5 x his own baseline CV — rocket must compute that CV from his history; it cannot be assumed. SUBJECTIVE TRIP: readiness-to-train or leg soreness in his personal worst tertile on 5 of 7 days. NOTE ON SCOPE: the evidence supports using this to STOP or REDUCE, not to schedule. HRV-guided prescription raises HRV reliably (Manresa-Rocamora 2021, SMD 0.50) but its effect on endurance performance is small and non-significant, and a six-week RCT in 28 recreational runners found no advantage of HRV-guided over pace-based prescription at all (Ranieri 2025).

prescriptions.sessionName: P5 — Race rehearsal as a measurement: Lincoln Half, 2026-10-04, at marathon pace inside ~33 km
prescriptions.structure: One-off, three weeks out, already scheduled and explicitly not to be raced. Treat it as the block's dress rehearsal AND its main experiment: 6 km warm-up at easy pace, the 21.1 km race segment held at target marathon pace, then ~6 km continued. Measure (a) mean HR over the 21.1 km segment and its first-half/second-half split; (b) decoupling and decoupling onset over the whole 33 km; (c) whether target MP was actually held, or drifted; (d) fuelling executed versus planned, since this is the only chance to rehearse it.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Marathon pace derived from HIS OWN realised marathon, not from a formula: his 10 May marathon averaged 165 bpm, which is 82.1% of the measured HRmax 201, and 5:31/km, which is 87.5% of an estimated CS of 4:50/km. Ceiling for this session: the 21.1 km segment must average at or below 170 bpm (84.6% HRmax), leaving room for the final 6 km.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: This is the closest thing to a marathon-specific performance test that can be run without a marathon, and it is the sharpest available falsifier of the marathon pace target. It also supplies a long, controlled, flat, uniform-effort file — the ideal substrate for the decoupling measurement, far cleaner than a variable training long run.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: TARGET MP for the session: 5:20-5:30/km, i.e. the pace implied by holding 88-90% of a critical speed that has improved ~2-3% (giving a 3:45-3:52 marathon). PASS: he holds 5:20-5:30/km for the 21.1 km segment averaging <= 170 bpm, with decoupling over the 33 km at or below the block baseline. FAIL: he needs 175 bpm or more to hold the target pace, or decoupling exceeds baseline + 0.05, or he cannot complete the 33 km. On a fail the marathon target resets to the pace he actually held at <= 168 bpm (83.6% HRmax) — and that reset is a data-driven decision, not a loss of nerve.

prescriptions.sessionName: P6 — Final calibration and the overreaching verdict: ASICS LDNX 10K, 2026-10-11
prescriptions.structure: One-off, 13 days out, already scheduled to be run hard as the taper's only intensity. Two jobs beyond the training stimulus: (1) refit the personal Riegel exponent across the 12 September half and this 10 km, and log the actual-versus-Garmin pair into the <=10 km calibration band; (2) apply the Meeusen 2013 performance-decrement test — compare the result to the time predicted from the 12 September half via the then-current fitted exponent.
prescriptions.intensityAnchor: Run to feel and to the clock, not to a prescribed HR. The measurement is the outcome time; imposing an HR ceiling would corrupt the very variable being tested.
prescriptions.purposeMechanism: Performance decrement, not HRV and not soreness, is the DEFINITIONAL criterion separating functional from non-functional overreaching (Meeusen 2013). A block that has produced non-functional overreaching will show it here as a 10 km slower than the half predicts — and 13 days is just enough to convert the marathon into a salvage operation rather than a bad day. Also, a 10 km against a half gives the widest distance span available in-block for re-fitting the exponent.
prescriptions.derivedForThisAthlete: PREDICTION, computed the day after the half: T_10k = T_half x (10/21.0975)^k with k re-fitted at that point (his history gives k in 1.13-1.18; note the exponent is symmetric, so an unusually high k makes the BACK-predicted 10 km FASTER, not slower — rocket must apply the fit in the correct direction). Worked example: a 1:45:00 half with k = 1.15 predicts 10 km in 46:24. PASS: within 2% of prediction, or faster. WARNING: 2-4% slower AND at least one channel of P4 tripped. FAIL / non-functional overreaching: more than 4% slower, or slower AND two channels of P4 tripped for the preceding week — in which case race week becomes genuine recovery, and the marathon goal pace is reset downward by the same percentage the 10 km missed by. EXPONENT SANITY GATE: the standard error of a two-race exponent fit is roughly sigma x sqrt(2) / ln(D2/D1); with a race-to-race log-time noise of ~3%, a half-versus-10 km pair (ln ratio 0.75) gives SE(k) ~ 0.056, which propagates to about +/- 8 minutes on the marathon prediction. rocket should REFUSE to display a marathon prediction to two-minute precision it does not have.

research.intensityDistribution:
This is not my domain to prescribe, but the measurement layer needs the zone boundaries to score anything, and the boundaries must be DERIVED, so here they are with their evidence.

THE BOUNDARIES. Muniz-Pumares 2025 (119,452 marathoners, 16 weeks of training each) defines a three-zone model where critical speed is the Z2/Z3 boundary and the Z1/Z2 boundary sits at 82.3% of critical speed. For this athlete with CS estimated at 4:50/km (3.44 m/s), that gives:
- Z1 (easy): slower than 5:53/km
- Z2 (moderate/threshold-adjacent): 5:53 to 4:50/km
- Z3 (hard): faster than 4:50/km
Marathon pace of 5:20-5:30/km therefore sits in Z2, near its slow end. His easy anchor of 6:30/km sits comfortably in Z1. This matters because if he runs his 100 km week at 6:00/km "easy", most of that volume is not Z1 and the week is far harder than its distance suggests.

WHAT THE EVIDENCE SAYS ABOUT THE SHARE. The strongest applicable finding from Muniz-Pumares 2025 is that ABSOLUTE time in Z2 and Z3 was roughly CONSTANT across all performance levels; what rose with performance was Z1 volume. Marathon time correlated with volume markers and with the PROPORTION of volume in Z1 at R-squared >= 0.90, and not with the proportions in Z2 or Z3. More than 80% of the fastest group ran a pyramidal distribution — most Z1, less Z2, least Z3.

THE IMPLICATION FOR THIS BLOCK, AND IT IS THE CENTRAL ONE. The additional 40-75 km per week this athlete is adding should be almost entirely Z1. Absolute quality volume should stay roughly where it is — which is also what rocket's existing guardrail already says (maxQualitySessionsPerWeekBuild = 1). Concretely, at 100 km in week 3, something like 85-90 km in Z1 (slower than 5:53/km), 8-12 km in Z2 (which is what the 4 October marathon-pace work supplies), and 0-4 km in Z3 (the 11 October 10 km, and essentially nothing else). Vickers & Vertosick 2016 found interval and tempo volume associated with race velocity at all distances in 2,303 recreational runners, so quality is not worthless — but adding intensity on top of a volume ramp he has never survived is the one combination the evidence gives no support for.

THE HONEST CAVEAT. All of this is CORRELATIONAL. Muniz-Pumares 2025 shows that faster marathoners have run more easy volume; it does not show that adding easy volume makes a given runner faster, and the causal arrow could partly run the other way (faster runners can absorb more volume). There is no randomised trial comparing intensity distributions at a 100 km week in a runner whose history is 24 km/week, and there never will be.

MEASUREMENT CONSEQUENCE. rocket should compute and display the realised weekly Z1/Z2/Z3 split from actual files, not the planned one. A week planned as 90/10/0 that executes as 70/25/5 because the "easy" runs drifted to 5:45/km is the single most likely way this block fails, and it is invisible unless the split is measured.
research.fitForThisAthlete:
HONEST VERDICT: the measurement layer fits very well; the calibration ambition does not.

WHAT FITS. Every marker above is computable from files he already generates — no lab, no test session, no extra kit. Critical speed comes from ordinary training files (Smyth & Muniz-Pumares 2020). Decoupling comes from long runs he is running anyway. The efficiency probe is 10 minutes inside an easy run. The readiness triad is the check-in rocket already has plus two Garmin wellness fields. And by luck of scheduling, the block contains three maximal or near-maximal efforts (12 Sep half, 4 Oct marathon-pace 33 km, 11 Oct 10 km) which is an unusually rich test schedule for six weeks — most six-week blocks have none.

WHAT DOES NOT FIT — SIX WEEKS IS SHORT FOR MOST OF THIS. The submaximal-running-test evidence (Vesterinen 2017) sampled every four weeks over eighteen; it is calibrated to a longer horizon. A six-week RCT in 28 recreational runners comparing HRV-guided, HR-based and pace-based prescription found main time effects in every group and NO between-group differences (Ranieri 2025) — over this duration, elaborate gating logic did not beat doing the training. The realistic yield in six weeks is: two or three honest signals with real thresholds, not a dashboard.

WHAT DOES NOT FIT — THREE DATA POINTS IS NOT A CALIBRATION. The Garmin median factor of 1.118 is real in SIGN and roughly right in MAGNITUDE: with a race-to-race log-time noise of about 4-5%, three points give a standard error near 2.9%, so an 11.8% bias sits about four standard errors from zero. But pinning that factor to +/- 2% (which is +/- 4.5 minutes on a 3:45 marathon) would need on the order of 25 races. Worse, POOLING ACROSS DISTANCES ESTIMATES SOMETHING THAT DOES NOT EXIST: Garmin is roughly right at 5 km (it predicts 20:11 today against a 19:39 he ran in April when far less fit) and badly optimistic at the marathon. rocket should hold the calibration as three distance bands (<=10 km, 10-25 km, >25 km), require at least two efforts before applying a band at all, and shrink toward the pooled median until n >= 5 — one line: factor = (n x f_band + 2 x f_pooled) / (n + 2).

THE MORE IMPORTANT FINDING, WHICH FALLS OUT OF HIS OWN NUMBERS. His personal Riegel exponents are 1.179 (5 km to half), 1.163 (5 km to marathon) and 1.131 (half to marathon), against a canonical 1.06 and a recreational range of roughly 1.07-1.09. He is unusually bad at holding pace as distance grows — which is exactly what a 24 km/week history predicts and exactly what this block is designed to fix. Garmin's implied exponent (1.11-1.14 from its own 2026-09-07 predictions) is NOT the problem; its LEVEL is. Its 3:36:12 marathon prediction requires a critical speed 5% better than current AND holding 90% of it for 42 km — two simultaneous best cases, neither of which he has ever demonstrated. His realised May marathon held 87.5% of CS.

THE RISK THIS LAYER CREATES. Measuring things that cannot move in six weeks and then declaring success or failure on noise. VO2max estimate error is 2.8-10.4% MAPE (Engel 2026) against a plausible true six-week change of 1-3%; the estimate has already sat at 53.0 through a five-week dip, demonstrating in his own data that it does not respond. Garmin Endurance Score is a proprietary metric for which I could find no peer-reviewed validation at all — I searched and did not find one, which is not the same as proving none exists, but it is enough to disqualify it as a decision input. Wrist-derived running dynamics (ground contact time, vertical oscillation) do not measure metabolic cost; laboratory running economy needs the care documented in Saunders 2004 to detect a real change, and a watch is not doing that.

ONE MORE THING WORTH SAYING OUT LOUD. His current freshness reading of TSB +24.7 is not taper freshness — it is the arithmetic consequence of a 0 km week and a 14.8 km week. A positive TSB produced by detraining and a positive TSB produced by a taper are indistinguishable in the number and opposite in meaning. rocket should not present it as readiness three days before he races a half.
research.howToValidate:
This is the answer to his actual question. Below is the block stated as a falsifiable hypothesis, with the observations that would refute it.

THE HYPOTHESIS, IN ONE SENTENCE. Six weeks at 60/80/100/80/60 km, run almost entirely in Zone 1, will improve DURABILITY — his ability to hold a high fraction of critical speed to 42 km, currently poor (personal Riegel exponent 1.13-1.18 against a recreational 1.07-1.09) — by more than it degrades him through accumulated fatigue and injury, yielding a marathon in the 3:45-3:55 range rather than the 3:36 Garmin claims.

THE FIVE FALSIFIERS. Each names a threshold, a data source rocket already has, and a consequence. If none of them trips, the plan survived the block; that is what "the plan worked" means.

F1 — THE BLOCK WAS NOT ACTUALLY RUN. Completed km below 85% of target in two consecutive weeks. Then the 100 km hypothesis was never tested and cannot be claimed; fall back to the reversal condition already written into the block at the end of week 2. Source: rocket's own planned-versus-actual. Note the reversal condition should be judged on DELIVERED volume, not on how he says he feels.

F2 — DURABILITY DID NOT IMPROVE (the primary outcome). Decoupling at the 4 October 33 km session is at or above the week-1 baseline + 0.05, or its onset has not moved at least 5 km later. Then the block added volume without adding what the volume was for, and the marathon target resets to the pace held at <= 168 bpm in that session. Reference distribution: Smyth 2022, cohort 1.16 +/- 0.22, low group <1.10. HONEST FLAG: I know of no published typical error for field-computed decoupling, so the +/- 0.05 band is engineering judgement, not a measured noise floor. rocket should estimate its own by computing decoupling on repeated similar long runs in week 1-2 and using the spread.

F3 — AEROBIC EFFICIENCY WENT THE WRONG WAY. The 7-day mean HR at the fixed 6:30/km anchor rises more than 4 bpm above the block baseline and stays there for 10 days, on runs within +/- 5 C of baseline temperature. 4 bpm is roughly twice the Lamberts 2004 standard error of measurement (1.1-1.4%, i.e. 1.6-2.1 bpm here), so it is a real change. Consequence: cut the next week 25%. CAUTION FROM BUCHHEIT 2014: a FALLING submaximal HR is ambiguous — it can mean fitness or accumulating fatigue — so read direction only alongside F4 and the pace-at-fixed-HR reading.

F4 — AUTONOMIC AND SUBJECTIVE CONCORDANCE (the overreaching trip-wire). Two of three for seven consecutive days: 7-day mean resting HR at or above 60 (baseline 57, +3% being the effect size that separated overreached from responders in Nuuttila 2024); 7-day mean Ln rMSSD below baseline minus 0.5 x his own baseline coefficient of variation (Plews/Buchheit convention); readiness-to-train or leg soreness in his worst personal tertile on 5 of 7 days. Two of three cuts the next week 25%; all three cuts 40% and removes intensity. Rationale for requiring concordance: Saw 2016 shows subjective measures are the most sensitive single channel, Plews 2013 shows HRV direction can invert, and no single channel is specific enough to act on alone.

F5 — PERFORMANCE DECREMENT (the definitional test, Meeusen 2013). The 11 October 10 km is more than 4% slower than predicted from the 12 September half via the fitted exponent; or 2-4% slower with F4 also tripped. Then this is non-functional overreaching, race week becomes real recovery, and the marathon pace target is reduced by the percentage the 10 km missed by. This is the only falsifier that tests the definitional criterion — performance — rather than a proxy for it.

THE DECISION CALENDAR.
- 12 Sep (day 3): anchor race. Recompute CS, threshold pace, exponent, calibration. If the half is slower than 1:44, DELETE Garmin's 3:36:12 from the app. Replace the app's threshold pace of 4:20.9/km with the measured value — my two-route estimate says the true figure is near 4:50/km and that prescribing threshold reps off 4:21 would run every rep 25-30 s/km too fast.
- 28 Sep (end of week 2): the ratified reversal decision. Judge on F1 (delivered volume) and F4 (concordance), not on enthusiasm.
- 4 Oct: the 33 km marathon-pace rehearsal. Primary read on F2 and on the marathon pace target itself.
- 11 Oct: the 10 km. Final read on F5 and last exponent refit.
- 24 Oct: goal race. Post-race, log the actual-versus-predicted pair — that is the fourth calibration point, and the first ever in the >25 km band since May.

WHAT PREDICTION MODEL TO USE, AND HOW TO VALIDATE IT.
PRIMARY: Riegel with a per-athlete fitted exponent. One parameter, auditable, fits from two races, and — the reason it wins — THE PARAMETER IS ITSELF THE OUTCOME OF THE BLOCK. Blythe & Kiraly 2016 (164,746 runners) showed per-runner exponents beat any fixed exponent. Fit on the two most recent maximal efforts spanning at least a factor of three in distance; refit after every race; report SE(k) = sigma x sqrt(2) / ln(D2/D1) with sigma = 0.03, and REFUSE to show a marathon prediction when SE(k) > 0.05.
SECONDARY, AND IT SHOULD BE ALLOWED TO DISAGREE IN PUBLIC: the Vickers & Vertosick 2016 regression using sex, age, BMI, weekly mileage, interval/tempo volume and one or two prior races. It achieved MSE 208-228 min^2 against Riegel's 381 in 2,303 recreational runners, and it consumes exactly the fields rocket already holds. Caveat honestly: internally split-sample validated only, never externally replicated, self-reported data.
REJECTED: Purdy points and the Cameron formula, both anchored on world-record decay curves — wrong reference population by construction, and in Cameron's case with no verifiable primary source at all. Garmin's Race Predictor as a level: keep it only as an independent second opinion with its distance-banded correction applied, never as the displayed number.
VALIDATION PROCEDURE: rocket should keep an append-only prediction log — for every race, the prediction each model made BEFORE the race, from the data available then. After four or five races the models can be ranked on their own out-of-sample error rather than on argument. Three points is not enough to rank models; it is enough to reject one that is 12% out at the distance that matters.

WHAT THE SESSION-COMPLETION SIGNAL TELLS YOU, AND HOW IT FEEDS BACK.
The pattern of misses is more informative than the count.
- Easy midweek runs missed, long run and quality completed: logistical, not physiological. Response is to redistribute the volume, not reduce it.
- Long runs consistently cut short (actual < 90% of planned) while everything else completes: the long run is the limiter. The problem is the SHAPE of the week, not its size — split the long run, or move it to a day with more recovery in front of it.
- Sessions completed but slower than the same session two weeks earlier at equal or higher HR: physiological. This is F3 by another route and should be treated as such.
- Runs abandoned mid-session: look at the kilometre where HR crossed the Z1/Z2 boundary. If he is drifting into Z2 by km 12 of an easy run, the easy pace is set too fast and the whole 100 km week is harder than its label.
- Sameness: Foster 1998 associates high training monotony (weekly mean daily load divided by the SD of daily load) and strain with illness. With six running days a week at 100 km, monotony will be high unless one day is genuinely long and one genuinely off. Keep weekly monotony below 2.0. HONEST FLAG: this rests on a single observational study of 25 athletes with illness as the outcome — a heuristic, not a law.
THE FEEDBACK RULE, one line and it reuses config that already exists: next week's target = min(planned target, mean of the last two weeks' ACTUAL km x 1.15), using rocket's existing rampCapPct of 15. This anchors the ramp to what happened rather than to what was written, which is the single most valuable thing the completion signal can do. And compute CTL/ATL from ACTUAL sessions only — a chronic load built partly from planned-but-not-run sessions is a fiction that will read as fitness and hand him a green light he has not earned.

FINALLY, THE ONE MEASUREMENT THAT SHOULD HAPPEN BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE. Garmin asserts a lactate-threshold pair of 177 bpm at 4:20.9/km. His own 19 July half — his best genuine continuous effort — was 1:46:35 at 5:02/km averaging 174 bpm. Getting from 5:02/km to 4:21/km is a 15.8% speed increase; his own HR-pace slope across two realised races (174 bpm at 5:02, 165 bpm at 5:31) says that costs about 13 bpm, putting 4:21/km at roughly 187 bpm — well above the asserted threshold HR. Independently, an estimated critical speed of 4:50/km reproduces his May marathon at 87.5% of CS, dead centre of the 82-88% band observed across 82,303 marathoners, whereas Garmin's 4:20.9/km would put that marathon at 78.7% of CS, below even the worst-durability tertile. Two independent routes agree: the threshold HR of 177 is credible, the threshold PACE is roughly 25-30 s/km too fast. Any threshold session prescribed off it would be run at 10 km effort. That is the highest-value thing this measurement layer has to say, it is checkable in the 12 September file, and it needs to be settled before week 1 starts.
contraindications: DO NOT prescribe any pace from Garmin's stated lactate-threshold pace of 4:20.9/km. Two independent checks against his own data (his race HR-pace slope, and the fraction-of-critical-speed his May marathon represents) say it is roughly 25-30 s/km too fast. Threshold reps prescribed off it would be run at 10 km race effort, on a week where he is also adding 40-75 km of volume. The threshold HR of 177 is credible; the pace is not.

DO NOT use Garmin's VO2max estimate as an in-block progress marker. Smartwatch VO2max error is 2.8-4.1% MAPE in moderately trained and 9.4-10.4% in highly trained athletes with a mean underestimate of 4.73 ml/kg/min (Engel 2026); a plausible true six-week change is 1-3%. His own reading has already sat at 53.0 through a five-week dip, demonstrating in his own data that it does not respond. Measurement error exceeds the effect.

DO NOT use Garmin Endurance Score for any decision. It is a proprietary metric with an undisclosed algorithm, and I could find no peer-reviewed validation of it. That is not proof none exists, but it is enough to keep it out of a gate.

DO NOT infer running economy from wrist running dynamics (ground contact time, vertical oscillation, vertical ratio). These describe movement, not metabolic cost. Detecting a real change in running economy requires the laboratory care documented in Saunders 2004; there is no validated mapping from wearable running dynamics to oxygen cost that I am aware of.

DO NOT build any gate on an acute:chronic workload ratio. There is no evidence supporting ACWR in load management or injury prevention, and the statistical properties of a ratio of two overlapping correlated windows make it uninterpretable (Impellizzeri 2020). The same mathematical objection applies to reading TSB as a readiness number.

DO NOT present the current TSB of +24.7 as freshness. It is the arithmetic consequence of a 0 km week and a 14.8 km week. Detraining and tapering produce identical positive numbers and opposite meanings.

DO NOT gate individual sessions on a single morning's HRV or resting HR. Single-day correlations with adaptation are weak (r = .35 and -.21) versus strong for the 7-day mean (r = -.62 and stronger) in Plews 2013. Use 7-day rolling means, and require two of three channels to agree before acting.

DO NOT expect HRV-guided prescription to add performance. It reliably raises HRV (SMD 0.50) but its effects on aerobic fitness and endurance performance are small and non-significant (Manresa-Rocamora 2021), and a six-week RCT in 28 recreational runners found no advantage over pace-based or HR-based prescription (Ranieri 2025). Use HRV to stop, not to schedule.

DO NOT use the 26 July run (21.10 km, 17:27 stopped across 22 laps) as a performance data point, a calibration point, or a decoupling sample. Stoppages reset cardiac drift and invalidate every internal-versus-external comparison. His 19 July half is the only genuine continuous half in the record.

DO NOT compute %HRmax from the Garmin profile value of 196 or from his believed 195. Use the MEASURED 201 from 2026-06-14. The 2.5-3% error propagates into every zone boundary and every decoupling calculation.

DO NOT maintain a single scalar Garmin calibration factor. The bias is distance-dependent — roughly zero at 5 km, about 8% at the half, about 12% at the marathon. Pooling across distances estimates a quantity that does not exist. Band it (<=10 km, 10-25 km, >25 km), require two efforts per band, and shrink toward the pooled median until n >= 5.

DO NOT treat rocket's 15% weekly ramp cap as evidence-based. The nearest evidence is Nielsen 2014, in 874 NOVICE runners, where >30% over two weeks was associated with distance-related injuries — and where the overall association across all injury types was NOT statistically significant. The cap is defensible expert practice, not a trial finding, and it should be labelled as such in config/training.ts alongside the number.

DO NOT add intensity to compensate if the volume falls short. There is no evidence supporting a simultaneous volume ramp and intensity increase in a runner whose history is 24 km/week, and the whole design of the block rests on the additional volume being Zone 1. If volume is missed, the honest response is a smaller block, not a harder one.

DO NOT quote marathon predictions to two-minute precision. A well-fitted personal exponent from two races carries SE(k) of about 0.05-0.06, which propagates to roughly +/- 8-10 minutes at 42 km before any race-day variance. Display a range.

verification.tradition: Athlete monitoring and per-athlete race-model calibration — i.e. the measurement/falsification layer rather than a training tradition. Two evidence bases: (a) large-N observational running analytics (Riegel-family power laws with per-runner exponents; the Smyth/Muniz-Pumares Strava-cohort critical-speed and durability work), and (b) the sports-science monitoring literature (submaximal HR indices, 7-day-averaged vagal HRV, subjective wellness, ECSS/ACSM overreaching criteria). Verdict on the tradition itself: the citation base is real and unusually well chosen for this athlete's population. The failure is not invention — it is that the single number the whole prescription hangs on (critical speed 4:50/km) is derived by a method the research explicitly rejects, is contradicted by the athlete's own 5 km data, and is then "corroborated" by a check that is arithmetically the same calculation run twice.

checks.claim: Smyth 2022: decoupling 1.16 ± 0.22, onset 25.2 ± 9.9 km; low group (<1.1) 88 ± 6% CS, 217 ± 33 min; high group (≥1.2) 82 ± 7% CS, 239 ± 31 min; prediction error 6.45% → 5.16%; n=82,303 (13,125 female).
checks.note: Verified verbatim against the abstract (Sports Med 2022;52(9):2283-2295, doi 10.1007/s40279-022-01680-5; Smyth, Maunder, Meyler, Hunter, Muniz-Pumares). Every figure matches, including the 1.025 onset criterion. Population is genuinely this athlete's. Correctly flagged as cross-sectional — it does not show training moves decoupling.

checks.claim: Vickers & Vertosick 2016: Riegel well calibrated to the half but ≥10 min too fast at the marathon for half of runners; MSE 381 (Riegel) vs 228 (one prior race) and 208 (two); mileage and intervals predict velocity at all distances, tempo more at short.
checks.note: Verified verbatim (BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil 2016;8:26, doi 10.1186/s13102-016-0052-y). N=2,303, 2:1 train/validation split, self-reported internet survey — the research states the limitation itself. This is the single best-supported claim in the submission.

checks.claim: Muniz-Pumares 2025: 151,813 marathons, 119,452 runners, 45.1 ± 26.4 km/week; Z2 and Z3 roughly constant across performance levels, Z1 rises; >80% of the fastest are pyramidal; Z2/Z3 boundary = critical speed, Z1/Z2 = 82.3% of CS.
checks.note: All verified (Sports Med 2025;55:1023-1035, doi 10.1007/s40279-024-02137-7). One caveat the research omits: the paper states the 82.3%-of-CS Z1/Z2 transition was *assumed*, not measured — it is a modelling convention inherited into every zone boundary downstream, presented here as if it were a finding.

checks.claim: Muniz-Pumares 2025: marathon time correlated with Z1 proportion at R² ≥ 0.90 'and NOT with the proportions in Z2 or Z3'.
checks.note: The abstract says the opposite: 'the proportions of training completed in Z2 and Z3 were correlated (p<0.01, R² ≥ 0.85) with slower marathon times.' They were correlated — negatively for performance. The research repeats the false version twice (corePrinciple and intensityDistribution) and uses it to argue absolute quality volume is orthogonal to outcome. It is not what the source says.

checks.claim: Critical speed ≈ 3.44 m/s = 4:50/km, obtained by placing the 19 July half at ~96% of CS.
checks.note: Two failures. (1) Method substitution: the research cites Smyth & Muniz-Pumares 2020, whose method is the slope of the distance–time relation over 400/800/1000/1500/3000/5000 m bests — the SHORT end — and then does not use it, inverting a long-duration race through an assumed 96% instead. (2) The result is physiologically impossible against his own data: CS 3.444 m/s implies D' (anaerobic distance capacity) of 979 m for the 25 Apr 5.04 km (3:54/km) and 552 m for the 11 Apr 5.10 km (4:19/km). Typical runner D' is 150-400 m. CS ≈ 3.70 m/s (4:30/km) gives D' = 213 m from the 11 Apr run — normal. The honest CS band from his short-end data is 4:25-4:40/km, not 4:44-4:53/km.

checks.claim: 'Two independent routes' confirm CS 4:50/km — the 96% anchor, and the May marathon landing at 87.5% of CS, 'dead centre of Smyth's 82-88% band'.
checks.note: Not independent — it is one calculation counted twice. 87.5% is forced by CS = v_half/0.96 and the fixed ratio v_marathon/v_half = 0.912; it carries no information about whether 0.96 was right. Choosing 0.94 gives CS 4:44/km and 85.7% — still inside the 'band', so the check cannot fail. Two further errors: 82-88% are three GROUP MEANS (SDs 6-7%), not a band; and 87.5% is at the top of that range next to the fastest group, not 'dead centre' (which would be 85%).

checks.claim: Garmin's threshold pace of 4:20.9/km is roughly 25-30 s/km too fast; the true figure is near 4:50/km; threshold reps off it would be run at 10 km effort.
checks.note: Directionally right, magnitude roughly doubled. It inherits the broken CS above. Independent check: his own half (k = 1.179 from the 25 Apr 5 km) back-predicts a 10 km at 4:25/km — a CS/threshold of 4:50/km would mean he cannot race 10 km faster than ~4:50/km, which his April 5 km efforts refute outright. Realistic threshold ≈ 4:30-4:40/km, so Garmin is ~10-20 s/km fast, not 25-30. The contraindication survives (do not prescribe reps off 4:20.9) but the replacement number is wrong and would set threshold work ~20 s/km too slow — the opposite error, and one that wastes the block's only quality stimulus.

checks.claim: The HR-pace slope of ~18.5 bpm per min/km (174 bpm at 5:02, 165 bpm at 5:31) shows 4:21/km would cost ~187 bpm, above the asserted LTHR of 177.
checks.note: Slope arithmetic checks (18.9 bpm per min/km; 187 bpm at 4:21). The inference does not. The two anchors are races of different DURATION (107 min vs 236 min), so the 9 bpm gap conflates pace with 4 hours of cardiac drift and glycogen depletion — it is not a pace-HR relation. It is then extrapolated 16% beyond its range, and HR-vs-pace is concave near max (HR saturates), so a linear extrapolation systematically overstates HR at fast paces. Separately, LT pace is a ~30-60 min pace; a 107-minute half sits below it by definition, and sits far below it precisely in endurance-deficient runners — which is the research's own thesis about this athlete. The argument therefore contradicts its own premise.

checks.claim: Garmin's over-prediction is 'almost entirely a LEVEL error, not a decay error' (Garmin's implied half→marathon exponent 1.135 ≈ his measured 1.131).
checks.note: True only for the one pair chosen. Garmin's implied 5 km→marathon exponent is 1.112 against his measured 1.163 (5.04 km 19:39 → 42.67 km 3:55:54), and Garmin's implied 5→10 km is 1.107. The research's own banding claim — Garmin right at 5 km, ~12% optimistic at the marathon — IS a decay error by definition: a pure level error scales all distances equally. Self-contradictory within the same paragraph. (His personal exponents 1.179 / 1.163 / 1.131 all recompute exactly, so the input numbers are right; the interpretation is not. Note too that the 5 km and marathon are 5 months and one fitness state apart, so 1.163 mixes fitness into the exponent.)

checks.claim: Blythe & Kiraly 2016 (164,746 runners, 1,417,432 performances) show per-runner exponents beat any fixed exponent, ~30% RMSE improvement.
checks.note: Verified (PLOS ONE 2016;11(6):e0157257). Two qualifications the research glosses: the winning model has THREE parameters per runner, not the one-parameter Riegel it is used to justify; and Power-of-10 is British club/competitive athletes — a training age and volume this athlete does not have. The research does flag the population.

checks.claim: Nuuttila 2024: 24 recreational runners, nocturnal HR +3.2 ± 3.1% (OR) vs -2.8 ± 3.7% (RESP), HRV -0.7% vs +2.1%, ≥85% PPV and NPV for three markers; subgroups post hoc so predictive values optimistic.
checks.note: Verified verbatim (Eur J Sport Sci 2024; issue is 24(7):857-869, the research says 24(6)). Two transfer problems the research does not flag: the third marker is an 'HR-running POWER index', not the 'HR:running-speed index' the P3 prescription claims — running power is a Stryd/Polar-class metric rocket may not hold; and Nuuttila's overload was an intensity-and-load intensification in runners with an established base, not a 3-5x volume ramp from 24 km/week. The effect sizes are borrowed across a different stressor.

checks.claim: Plews 2013 (IJSPP): single-day resting HR and Ln rMSSD correlate with adaptation at r = .35 and -.21; 7-day means at r = -.62 and stronger.
checks.note: Verified but misreported. r = .35 is RHR(day) vs maximal aerobic speed; r = -.21 is RHR(day) vs 10-km performance — NOT Ln rMSSD. The single-day Ln rMSSD values are r = -.06 and -.17. The 7-day conclusion stands. Population: n = 10, and the paper studies runners 'who responded to' the intervention — pre-selected responders, measuring adaptation over 9 weeks, not detecting overreaching inside one. The 7-day-mean rule is good practice; this study is not evidence for a trip-wire threshold.

checks.claim: Lamberts 2004: submaximal HR SEM is 1.1-1.4%, so ~2 bpm at 150 bpm, so <4 bpm on a 7-day mean is noise.
checks.note: Citation verified (JSCR 2004;18(3):641-645, n=44, ICC 0.94-0.99). The number is misapplied twice, in opposite directions. (a) The 1.1-1.4% CV is from the FOURTH stage, ~90% HRmax, explicitly 'the lowest variation'; variation at low intensity was higher, so applying it to a 10-min block at 73% HRmax understates the noise. (b) The SEM of a 7-DAY MEAN is SEM/√7 ≈ 0.8 bpm, not 2 bpm, so 2×SEM on a weekly mean is ~1.6 bpm, not 4. Neither error is fatal but the '4 bpm' F3 threshold is not derived from the source it cites, and the raw stage-to-stage variation Lamberts actually reports is 5 ± 2 bpm.

checks.claim: Nielsen 2014 is the best evidence behind the 15% ramp cap and is thinner than the cap implies; >30% over two weeks associated with distance-related injuries; overall association not significant.
checks.note: Verified (JOSPT 2014;44(10):739-747, 874 novice runners, 202 injuries). The research is honest but still understates: the distance-related-injury association it relies on is ALSO non-significant — HR 1.59, 95% CI 0.96-2.66, p = 0.07. So the cap rests on an exploratory sub-analysis whose confidence interval crosses 1, in NOVICE runners on self-structured programmes. Labelling it 'expert practice, not a trial finding' in config/training.ts is the right call.

checks.claim: Engel 2026: watch VO2max unusable in-block — MAPE 2.8-4.1% moderately trained, 9.4-10.4% highly trained, mean underestimate 4.73 ml/kg/min; error exceeds a plausible 1-3% six-week change.
checks.note: Citation verified exactly (Eur J Appl Physiol 2026;126(1):591-603, Forerunner 245, n=35 Tier 2-3). The logic has a hole: this is an agreement-vs-lab study, and a systematic BIAS says nothing about sensitivity to within-athlete CHANGE — a consistently-4.7-low estimate can still track a real gain. Also this athlete (VO2max 53) sits in the moderately-trained arm the paper calls valid. The conclusion nonetheless survives on his own data — 53.0 held flat through a five-week dip — which is the stronger argument and should be the one made.

checks.claim: Dai 2025 shows smartwatch prediction error grows sharply with distance and the marathon was never tested.
checks.note: Numbers verified exactly (bias ± LoA -20.4 ± 44.2 s / +4.1 ± 299.1 s / +143.8 ± 400.4 s; Huawei GT Runner; marathon indeed untested). But the paper's own conclusion is the reverse of the use made of it: r ≥ 0.95, ICC ≥ 0.9, 'error rate less than 3%', 'accuracy exceeding 97%'. Citing a paper that concludes watch predictions are precise as evidence that they are not is selective. The 'no peer-reviewed validation of Garmin's Race Predictor at the marathon' point stands and is the honest version.

checks.claim: Vesterinen 2016 is 'the strongest single positive RCT for HRV gating' (40 recreational runners, 8 weeks).
checks.note: Verified (MSSE 2016;48(7):1347-1354). But the between-group result was 'a small between-group difference (ES = 0.42)' with no significance reported; the significant finding is within-group (3000 m improved in EXP p=0.004, not in TRAD p=0.118) — difference-in-significance, not significance-of-difference. VO2max improved MORE in the control arm (5.0% vs 3.7%). 'Strongest positive RCT' overstates a null between-group primary comparison. The research's own counterweights (Manresa-Rocamora 2021 SMD 0.50 for HRV / 0.20 n.s. for endurance; Duking 2021 g = 0.296 / 0.079 n.s.; Ranieri 2025 no interaction effects) all verified exactly and are reported fairly.

checks.claim: Foster 1998 supports keeping weekly training monotony below 2.0 on a six-day 100 km week.
checks.note: Foster 1998 verified (MSSE 1998;30(7):1164-1168, n=25, monotony = daily mean/SD, strain = load × monotony). The threshold of 2.0 appears nowhere in it — the paper reports 'individually identifiable training thresholds', mostly strain-related. 2.0 is coaching folklore presented with a citation attached. The research flags the study's weakness but not the number's absence from it.

checks.claim: Impellizzeri 2020: no evidence supports ACWR in load management; the same ratio objection applies to TSB; and the current TSB of +24.7 is detraining, not freshness.
checks.note: Paper verified (IJSPP 2020;15(6):907-913) — though the research's author list is wrong (see fabricatedCitations). The TSB point is the single best observation in the submission: +24.7 produced by a 0 km week and a 14.8 km week is arithmetically identical to, and physiologically opposite from, taper freshness. Meeusen 2013 (MSSE 45(1):186-205 and EJSS 13(1):1-24) and Saw 2016 (BJSM 50(5):281-291, 56 studies) also verified as described.

checks.claim: P2: compute decoupling as last-25%-of-run vs km 5-10 on every run ≥20 km, score against Smyth's 1.16 ± 0.22, and require baseline − 0.05 by the 4 October 33 km session.
checks.note: The primary outcome measure is confounded with distance and is rigged to fail. Smyth's reference is a FIXED 35-40 km window in a 42.2 km race; 'last 25%' of a 20 km run is km 15-20, and mean decoupling ONSET is 25.2 km — a 20 km baseline run may never reach onset at all, so baseline lands near 1.00-1.05. The 4 October comparison run is 33 km, past onset, and will read higher for reasons of duration alone. F2 will therefore trip regardless of adaptation, downgrading his marathon target on an artefact. Comparison is only valid between runs of matched distance, duration and conditions. Separately: CS and HRmax both CANCEL in the ratio (it is (HR_late/HR_early)×(v_early/v_late)), so the weekly CS refresh and the HRmax-201 contraindication are irrelevant to this metric, contrary to what P2 and the contraindications assert.

checks.claim: P3: easy anchor 6:30/km, predicted HR ~147 bpm (73% HRmax on measured max 201); expect a 3-6 bpm fall over six weeks.
checks.note: Arithmetic checks (146.7 bpm; 73.1%). Safe — comfortably under the 75% ceiling, and the fixed-pace-HR probe is well supported by Buchheit 2014 and Vesterinen 2017 (both verified). But the 147 figure rests on the same invalid cross-race HR-pace slope, and because that slope is inflated by marathon cardiac drift the true early-run HR at 6:30/km is more likely 130-140. Not dangerous, but it means the F3 baseline must be MEASURED in week 1, never seeded with 147.

checks.claim: Feedback rule: next week's target = min(planned target, mean of the last two weeks' ACTUAL km × 1.15).
checks.note: As written this destroys the ratified block on day one. His last two complete weeks are 0 and 14.8 km → mean 7.4 × 1.15 = 8.5 km, against a planned 60. Even the most generous two-week window (34.8 and 0) caps week 1 at 20 km. The rule would either be silently ignored — dead config, the exact failure mode rocket's config rules exist to prevent — or would collapse a block the athlete has ratified in writing. It needs a floor, a seeding rule for weeks containing a zero, or explicit suspension for week 1.

checks.claim: P6: refuse to display a marathon prediction when SE(k) > 0.05, with SE(k) = σ√2 / ln(D2/D1), σ = 0.03.
checks.note: The formula and the ±8-10 min propagation both check out (SE(k) = 0.0568 for a half/10 km pair; 13,800 s × ln2 × 0.0568 ≈ 9.1 min). But the rule forbids exactly the fit P6 prescribes: the 12 Sep half + 11 Oct 10 km pair gives SE(k) = 0.057 > 0.05, so the app could never show a marathon prediction from the block's own final calibration. Only a 5 km/half pair (SE 0.029) passes. Either the threshold or the prescribed pair has to change. The underlying discipline — show a range, not 3:36:12 — is right.

checks.claim: P5: hold 5:20-5:30/km for the 21.1 km race segment inside a 33 km session on 4 October, at ≤170 bpm.
checks.note: The 5:20 end is justified by 'a critical speed that has improved ~2-3%' — a gain that will not have been measured when the session is run, off a CS estimate that is itself wrong. His only marathon-pace evidence is 5:31/km at 165 bpm. Prescribing a 21.1 km continuous block faster than his realised marathon pace, 20 days before the goal race, in the middle of the largest volume he has ever run, on the strength of an assumed future adaptation, is the highest-risk single item in the submission. Anchor the session to 5:30-5:35/km and let the HR response set the marathon target, rather than the reverse.

checks.claim: P4: trip the resting-HR channel at a sustained 7-day mean of 60 bpm or higher (baseline 57, Nuuttila's +3%).
checks.note: 57 × 1.03 = 58.7, not 60. Rounding a safety trip-wire upward by 1.3 bpm on a 3-bpm effect roughly doubles the excursion required to fire it, on the one block where the athlete has ratified risk against contrary evidence. Set it at 59. Also: Nuuttila's effect is NOCTURNAL HR; Garmin's 'resting HR smoothed' is a different channel with different noise, and the research's own baseline note (57 is still drifting down from 84 in March) means a rising 7-day mean could be regression toward a stable value rather than fatigue.

checks.claim: Riegel 1981 (American Scientist 69(3):285-290), popularised in Runner's World 1977, establishes the power-law form with exponent ~1.06.
checks.note: Could not confirm from any primary index — American Scientist is not in Crossref or Europe PMC and the search budget for this session was exhausted. It is a standard, widely reproduced citation and is almost certainly genuine; the 1977 Runner's World attribution is the part I could not check at all. Flagged only because the athlete asked specifically whether the references are real: this is the one core reference I could not put my hands on. Purdy and the Cameron formula the research already declares unverifiable — that self-flagging is correct behaviour, not a fault.

fabricatedCitations: Impellizzeri 2020 — MISATTRIBUTED AUTHOR LIST. The research cites 'Impellizzeri FM, Woodcock S, Coutts AJ, Fanchini M, McCall A, Vigotsky AD' for 'Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio: Conceptual Issues and Fundamental Pitfalls', IJSPP 2020;15(6):907-913. Title, journal, volume, issue and pages are all correct, but the real authors are Impellizzeri FM, Tenan MS, Kempton T, Novak A, Coutts AJ (doi 10.1123/ijspp.2019-0864). The names given belong to a different Impellizzeri ACWR paper ('Acute to random workload ratio is as associated with injury...'). The claim itself is faithful to the real paper.
Nuuttila 2024 — WRONG ISSUE NUMBER. Cited as Eur J Sport Sci 2024;24(6):857-869; the article is 24(7):857-869 (doi 10.1002/ejsc.12115). Everything else, including all reported effect sizes, is exact.

Muniz-Pumares 2025 — CORRECT CITATION, MISREPRESENTED FINDING (the more damaging of the two). The paper is real and precisely cited, but the research asserts twice that marathon time was 'not' correlated with the proportions of training in Z2 or Z3. The abstract states those proportions WERE correlated with slower marathon times at R² ≥ 0.85. A reader checking the reference would find the source contradicting the claim it is cited for.

Dai 2025 — CORRECT CITATION, CONCLUSION INVERTED. All bias and limits-of-agreement figures are exact, but the paper concludes smartwatch predictions show 'high precision... accuracy exceeding 97%' at 5 km, 10 km and half marathon. It is cited to support the opposite proposition.

Riegel PS, American Scientist 1981;69(3):285-290 — UNVERIFIED, not disproven. Not indexed in Crossref or Europe PMC and the session's web-search budget was exhausted before I could reach a primary record. Almost certainly genuine; the accompanying 'popularised in Runner's World, 1977' attribution is entirely unchecked.

NOT fabricated, verified exactly, for the record: Vickers & Vertosick 2016 (BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil 8:26); Blythe & Kiraly 2016 (PLOS ONE 11(6):e0157257); Smyth & Muniz-Pumares 2020 (MSSE 52(12):2637-2645); Smyth et al 2022 (Sports Med 52(9):2283-2295); Muniz-Pumares et al 2025 (Sports Med 55:1023-1035); Maunder, Seiler, Mildenhall, Kilding, Plews 2021 (Sports Med 51:1619-1628 — the research's own uncertainty flag can be cleared); Lamberts et al 2004 (JSCR 18(3):641-645); Buchheit 2014 (Front Physiol 5:73); Vesterinen et al 2017 (JSCR 31(1):233-243); Vesterinen et al 2016 (MSSE 48(7):1347-1354); Plews et al 2013 (IJSPP 8(6):688-691) and 2013 (Sports Med 43(9):773-781); Saw et al 2016 (BJSM 50(5):281-291); Manresa-Rocamora et al 2021 (IJERPH 18(19):10299); Duking et al 2021 (JSAMS 24(11):1180-1192); Ranieri et al 2025 (MSSE 57(7):1510-1522); Meeusen et al 2013 (MSSE 45(1):186-205 / EJSS 13(1):1-24); Foster 1998 (MSSE 30(7):1164-1168); Nielsen et al 2014 (JOSPT 44(10):739-747); Engel et al (Eur J Appl Physiol 126(1):591-603); Saunders et al 2004 (MSSE 36(11):1972-1976). Author lists, volumes and pages all match. This is a genuinely evidence-based submission with real references — the failures are in derivation and interpretation, not invention.
arithmeticErrors: P6 WORKED EXAMPLE IS WRONG BY 1:54, AND IT INVERTS A PASS/FAIL GATE. 'A 1:45:00 half with k = 1.15 predicts 10 km in 46:24.' Correct: 6300 × (10/21.0975)^1.15 = 2669.8 s = 44:30. The stated 46:24 corresponds to k = 1.094. Since F5 declares non-functional overreaching at >4% slower than prediction and a warning at 2-4%, a 45:30 10 km reads as a comfortable PASS on their number and a WARNING on the correct one. This single slip decides whether race week becomes recovery and whether the marathon target is cut.

RESTING-HR TRIP-WIRE ROUNDED THE UNSAFE WAY. 57 × 1.03 = 58.7 bpm, stated as 'trip at a sustained 7-day mean of 60 bpm or higher'. Roughly doubles the excursion required before the safety gate fires, on the block the athlete has ratified against contrary evidence. Should be 59.

SELF-CONTRADICTORY ZONE EXAMPLE. 'If he runs his 100 km week at 6:00/km "easy", most of that volume is not Z1.' Their own Z1/Z2 boundary is 5:53/km; 6:00/km is SLOWER, hence squarely Z1. The warning is real (5:45/km would indeed be Z2) but the worked example refutes it.

'87.5% CS, dead centre of Smyth's 82-88% band.' 87.5 is at the top of that range, adjacent to the fastest group's 88%. Centre would be 85%. And 82/86/88% are three group MEANS with SDs of 6-7%, not a band — the check cannot discriminate.

SEM OF A MEAN NOT DIVIDED BY √n. Lamberts' 1.1-1.4% is a single-measurement SEM; on a 7-day mean it becomes ~0.8 bpm, so 2×SEM is ~1.6 bpm, not the 4 bpm used in F3. Compounded by taking the CV from Lamberts' ~90% HRmax stage (explicitly the lowest-variation stage) and applying it at 73% HRmax, where variation is larger. The two errors run in opposite directions; the 4 bpm figure is not derived from the cited source either way.

SE(k) RULE BLOCKS THE BLOCK'S OWN FIT. σ√2 / ln(D2/D1) with σ=0.03 gives 0.0568 for a half/10 km pair — above the stated 0.05 refusal threshold. P6 prescribes exactly that pair as the final calibration, so the app could never display a marathon prediction from it. Only a 5 km/half pair (0.0295) clears the gate. The ±8-10 min propagation itself is correct (13,800 s × ln2 × 0.057 ≈ 9.1 min).

FEEDBACK RULE COLLAPSES THE PLAN. 'Next week's target = min(planned, mean of the last two weeks' ACTUAL km × 1.15)' evaluates to 7.4 × 1.15 = 8.5 km for week 1 (his last two complete weeks are 0 and 14.8 km), against a planned 60. Needs a floor or an explicit week-1 suspension, or it becomes dead config.
'15.8% speed increase' from 5:02/km to 4:20.9/km is 15.95%. Trivial, noted only for completeness.
PLEWS CORRELATIONS MISLABELLED. r = -.21 is single-day resting HR vs 10-km performance, not single-day Ln rMSSD. The single-day Ln rMSSD values are -.06 and -.17.

RECOMPUTED AND CONFIRMED CORRECT: personal Riegel exponents 1.179 (5k→half), 1.163 (5k→mar), 1.131 (half→mar); half 3.306 m/s and 5:02.5/km; marathon 3.015 m/s and 87.5% of the assumed CS; CS 3.4434 m/s = 4:50.4/km from the 96% anchor; Garmin implied exponents 1.107 / 1.094 / 1.135; 82.3% of CS = 5:52.9/km; 88% of CS = 5:30/km → 3:52 marathon; +3% CS → 5:20/km → 3:45; HR-pace slope 18.9 bpm per min/km; 147 bpm at 6:30/km = 73.1% of 201; 177/201 = 88.1%; 181 = 90% of 201. The inputs are arithmetically clean — the errors are in the derivations built on them.
verification.riskForThisAthlete:
SUMMARY: the monitoring architecture is sound and the citation base is real. Three things would hurt him if shipped as written.

1. THE CRITICAL-SPEED NUMBER IS WRONG AND IT IS LOAD-BEARING. CS 4:50/km implies an anaerobic distance capacity (D') of 552-979 m from his two April 5 km efforts; the physiological range is 150-400 m. CS ≈ 4:30/km gives D' = 213 m — normal. Everything hangs off this: the Z1/Z2 boundary (5:53 vs 5:28/km), the verdict on Garmin's threshold pace, and the marathon target. The direction of the error is mostly conservative (easy pace set too slow is safe; a marathon target of 3:52 rather than 3:36 is defensible), but a threshold pace of 4:50 would run his one quality session ~20 s/km too slow — wasting the block's only intensity, which is the opposite failure from the one the research is guarding against. Fix by actually applying the Smyth & Muniz-Pumares method it already cites: fit CS from 400-5000 m bests in his own training files, not by inverting a 107-minute half through an assumed 96%.

2. F2, THE PRIMARY OUTCOME, IS RIGGED TO FAIL. Baseline decoupling from a 20 km run compared against a 33 km session, when mean onset is 25.2 km, guarantees the longer run reads higher for duration reasons alone. He will be told the block did not work and his marathon target will be cut on an artefact. Only compare distance-matched runs, and establish the noise floor first (the research honestly admits no published typical error exists for field decoupling).

3. THE 4 OCTOBER SESSION IS THE REAL DANGER. 21.1 km at 5:20-5:30/km inside 33 km, 20 days out, in his largest-ever volume week, at a pace whose fast end is justified by a 2-3% CS gain that will not have been measured. His only marathon-pace evidence is 5:31/km at 165 bpm. Anchor it at 5:30-5:35/km and let the HR response set the marathon target.

POPULATION VALIDITY. Better than most submissions of this kind — Smyth 2022 (82,303 recreational marathoners) and Muniz-Pumares 2025 (119,452) are genuinely his population. But every one of them averaged 45 ± 26 km/week; he averages 24. Blythe is British club runners. Nielsen is novices with a non-significant result. Nuuttila's overload was an intensity intensification in runners with an established base, not a 3-5x volume ramp. Vesterinen's monitoring cadences are calibrated to 8-18 weeks, not six. Every threshold borrowed here is borrowed across a training-age gap the research names in places and forgets in others.

THE OMISSION THAT MATTERS MOST. He is going from a 19 km four-week average to 60 km in week one — a 212% single-week jump, before the 80 and the 100. Nielsen's (non-significant) risk marker is 30% over two weeks. Yet F1-F5 contain no musculoskeletal channel at all: no pain scale, no site-specific soreness, no bone-stress or tendon trip-wire, nothing on gait or footwear. Injury is the overwhelmingly likeliest way this block ends, and the falsification apparatus cannot see it. Adding one — a daily 0-10 pain-by-site item with a hard stop on any pain that alters gait or persists at rest — would do more for him than every HRV refinement in the submission. The research also never says out loud that a 100 km week in a 24 km/week runner has no supporting evidence of any kind; it says only that adding intensity on top has none.

WHAT TO KEEP, UNCHANGED. The TSB observation (+24.7 is detraining, not freshness — identical arithmetic, opposite meaning) is the single most useful thing here. The 12 September half as the anchor measurement. Seven-day means with two-of-three concordance before acting. Distance-banded Garmin calibration with shrinkage instead of one scalar. The append-only prediction log. Refusing to display 3:36:12 to two-minute precision. Excluding the 26 July stop-start run. Labelling the 15% ramp cap as expert practice rather than a trial finding. All of that is correct, and all of it is defensible to a sceptical athlete.
